village of Westergate, parish of Aldingbourne, in the county of West Sussex, England. The dual-year notation — 1590/91 —
requires explanation, as it reflects a calendrical complexity that permeates all English records before 1752. England in the 16th
and 17th centuries used the Julian (Old Style) calendar, in which the legal new year began not on January 1 but on March 25 —
the Feast of the Annunciation. Thus, a date recorded in a contemporary parish register as “January 2, 1590” would be
understood by modern convention as January 2, 1591 — since we now begin the year on January 1. The dual notation
1590/91 is the scholarly convention for expressing this ambiguity without distortion, and it is employed throughout this
volume wherever Old Style dates fall between January 1 and March 24. [VERIFIED: Aldingbourne Parish Register, West
Sussex Record Office; dual-year notation explained per standard genealogical practice] Thomas Goble’s father was William
Goble II (born approximately 1550, Westergate) and his mother was Alice Legard (born approximately 1552). [PROBABLE:

Aldingbourne Parish Register and family reconstruction; primary source confirmation pending additional West Sussex Record
Office archival work] The Goble family was established in the Aldingbourne parish area — yeoman farmers or craftsmen of
solid if unremarkable standing, the kind of English family that owned land, paid their church assessments, and expected their
sons to follow in their fathers’ trades. There is no evidence that the Goble family of Westergate was of any particular wealth or
social distinction. What is evident, from the trajectory of Thomas’s subsequent life in Massachusetts, is that they were literate,
capable, community-minded, and deeply connected to the Puritan religious movement that was transforming English
Protestant life in the early 17th century. On November 5, 1619, Thomas Goble married Alice Brookman at the parish church
of St. Mary the Virgin, Aldingbourne, West Sussex. This date and this name require emphasis, because earlier genealogical
literature — particularly some 19th-century published family histories — mistakenly identified Thomas Goble’s wife as “Alice
Mousall.” Primary source examination of the Aldingbourne Parish Register at the West Sussex Record Office definitively
confirms the wife’s name as Alice Brookman. The Mousall identification was an error of transcription or confusion with
another family, and it has been corrected in all responsible scholarship on the Goble family. [VERIFIED: Aldingbourne Parish
Register, West Sussex Record Office; marriage record November 5, 1619] Thomas and Alice Goble spent approximately
fourteen years in England after their marriage — years during which King Charles I was entrenching his conflict with
Parliament and Archbishop William Laud was systematically persecuting Puritan nonconformists with fines, public
humiliation, and imprisonment. It was a time when a Puritan man in England could not be certain from one month to the next
that his pastor would remain unmolested, that his congregation would be permitted to worship without interference, or that
his own quiet religious convictions would not one day attract official attention. It was, for many thousands of English Puritans,
a time of gathering resolution — a time when crossing the Atlantic, terrifying as it was, began to seem like the only fully free
choice available. ■ Historical Context: The England Thomas Goble Left ■ When Thomas Goble and his family departed for
Massachusetts, they were leaving a country in profound crisis. King Charles I — who would eventually be executed by his own
Parliament in 1649 — was attempting to govern without Parliament’s consent, levying unauthorized taxes and relying on the
ecclesiastical authority of Archbishop William Laud to enforce religious conformity. Laud’s program was anathema to
Puritans: he imposed ceremonial practices that Puritans associated with Roman Catholicism, insisted on the authority of
bishops (whom Puritans largely rejected), and used the Court of High Commission to fine, imprison, and in extreme cases
physically mutilate those who resisted. The minister John Bastwick had his ears cut off in 1637 for Puritan writing; William
Prynne was branded on both cheeks with the letters “SL” (for “seditious libeler”). For a Puritan family in West Sussex in the
early 1630s, emigration was not an adventure. It was a rational response to genuine danger. The Great Migration of
approximately 1629–1640 brought roughly 20,000 English Puritans across the Atlantic to the Massachusetts Bay Colony. They
were not the desperate or the destitute — they were craftsmen, merchants, ministers, physicians, lawyers, and yeoman farmers:
the professional middle classes of 17th-century England. They brought with them English common law traditions, Puritan
theology, an insistence on local self-government, and the conviction that God had called them to build a new Jerusalem in the
wilderness of North America. The civilization they built is, in direct and traceable ways, the civilization of modern New
England. ✦ ✦ ✦ 3.2 The Atlantic Crossing — The Great Puritan Migration (~1633–1634) Thomas Goble emigrated to the
Massachusetts Bay Colony approximately 1633– 1634. The precise ship on which he crossed is not documented in any
surviving record, but the most likely candidates — based on timing, point of embarkation, and the pattern of passenger
documentation for this period — are the Abigail, the Hopewell, or the Lion, all of which made Atlantic crossings in 1633–
1634 carrying Puritan emigrants to Massachusetts Bay. [ESTIMATED: Ship identification based on historical context and
timing; no direct passenger manifest record has been located] With Thomas on the crossing came his wife, Alice Brookman
Goble, and their son John, then approximately three to four years old — old enough to remember, imperfectly, the crossing;
young enough that the Atlantic would become, in his memory, more myth than experience. Their daughter Elizabeth was
either born during the crossing itself — a not uncommon occurrence on these crowded, months-long Atlantic passages — or
within the first weeks of arrival in Charlestown. [ESTIMATED] The crossing from England to Massachusetts in 1633–1634

was not a journey to be undertaken lightly. The Atlantic in autumn or early spring — when most Great Migration ships sailed
— could be ferocious: storms of extraordinary violence, sixty-foot swells, weeks without sight of sun or stars. The ships were
small — typically between 100 and 350 tons — and carried far more passengers than comfortable capacity. Passengers lived
below decks in conditions of profound discomfort: no fresh air, no privacy, inadequate sanitation, salt provisions,
contaminated water. Children died on these crossings. Adults died. Those who survived emerged into the raw air of
Massachusetts Bay disoriented, relieved, and permanently marked by what they had passed through together. Thomas Goble,
stepping onto the wharf at Charlestown harbor in 1634, had survived something. He knew it. Alice knew it. Young John,
clinging to his mother’s skirt, knew it in the way that four-year-olds know things — not in words, but in the body. ✦ ✦ ✦ 3.3
Life in Colonial Charlestown (1634–1650s) Within weeks of arriving in Massachusetts, Thomas Goble had established himself
as a man of evident good character and community standing. On August 30, 1634, Thomas and Alice Goble were formally
admitted to the membership of the First Church of Charlestown — the Puritan congregation that served as the center of
civic and religious life in the settlement. Admission to a Puritan church in 17th-century New England was not a casual
formality. Candidates were examined by the church elders on the genuineness of their religious experience and the soundness
of their doctrine. Admission was a certification of moral standing within the community. Thomas and Alice passed that
examination together. [VERIFIED: First Church of Charlestown Records, Massachusetts Historical Society, Ms. N-1248] Four
days later, on September 3, 1634, Thomas Goble was granted the status of Freeman by the Massachusetts Bay Colony General
Court. Freeman status was, in the context of colonial Massachusetts, one of the most significant civic designations available to
a male settler. A Freeman had the right to vote in elections, to hold public office, and to serve on juries. He was, in the fullest
sense available in this new world, a citizen — a full participant in the political life of the colony. To be granted Freeman status
just days after one’s church admission speaks to the efficiency of the Charlestown community’s assessment of Thomas Goble’s
character: he was, evidently, exactly the kind of man they wanted in their new civilization. [VERIFIED: Massachusetts Bay
Colony General Court Records, September 3, 1634] By 1638, Thomas Goble had assembled a substantial landed estate in
Charlestown and its surrounds. The Massachusetts Bay Colony Land Records document five separate parcels of land in his
name: 1. A house lot and half-acre at the west end of the common — the household itself, the center of the family’s life 2.
Four acres of planting ground on the Newton Line — agricultural land for crops 3. Two and three-quarter acres of cow
commons — pasture rights for livestock 4. Fifteen acres of woodlands — timber, fuel, and building materials 5. Fifty acres —
Waterfield — the largest single parcel, likely agricultural or timber land on the colony’s expanding frontier Total: approximately
73 acres in various forms — a considerable estate for a man who had been in the colony only four years. [VERIFIED:
Massachusetts Bay Colony Land Records, 1638] This land accumulation tells us something important about Thomas Goble’s
character and capabilities. He was not a man who arrived in the colony and waited to be provided for. He worked, acquired,
and built — quickly and methodically — in exactly the spirit that the Great Migration required of its participants. ✦
OCTOBER 1, 1640 — THE FIRST BOSTON JURY ✦ On October 1, 1640, Thomas Goble sat on what is documented as
one of the first juries ever formally convened in the city of Boston. The case before the jury: one Hugh Buets, charged with
heresy — a capital-adjacent offense in Puritan Massachusetts, where doctrinal correctness was considered essential to the
survival of the entire colonial enterprise. The jury deliberated, reached a verdict of guilty, and the court sentenced Buets to be
expelled from the colony “upon paine of death” should he return. The twelve jurors who sat in that room on October 1, 1640,
were paid twelve shillings total — approximately one shilling each. It was a symbolic payment, not compensation for lost time.
What they were doing was not merely adjudicating a single case. They were enacting, for perhaps the first formal time in the
history of the city of Boston, the ancient English common-law right to trial by jury — a right tracing to Magna Carta (1215),
to the slow, hard-won tradition of popular participation in justice that distinguishes the English legal tradition from the
continental alternatives. In a courtroom in Charlestown/Boston in 1640, twelve colonists — Thomas Goble among them —
exercised that right on behalf of the new civilization they were building. It was a founding act. [VERIFIED: Massachusetts
Bay Colony Court Records, October 1, 1640; Suffolk County Court Files, Massachusetts State Archives] The selection of

Thomas Goble for this jury is itself significant. Only Freemen of established good character were eligible for jury service in
colonial Massachusetts. To be chosen for one of the first formally convened juries in Boston’s history — six years after
arriving in the colony — is a testament to the standing Thomas Goble had established in his community. He was known,
trusted, and respected. He was the kind of man his neighbors wanted deciding matters of consequence. ■ Historical Context:
The First Boston Jury and the Tradition of Trial by Jury ■ Trial by jury is one of the most ancient and foundational rights in
the English common-law tradition. Its origins trace to the Assize of Clarendon (1166) and were famously codified in Magna
Carta (1215), which established that no free man could be imprisoned or deprived of property “except by the lawful judgment
of his equals or by the law of the land.” That phrase — “judgment of his equals” — is the right to jury trial. When the
Puritans established the Massachusetts Bay Colony, they were building a legal system from scratch in the wilderness. The
Massachusetts Body of Liberties (1641) — drafted just a year after Thomas Goble served on his jury — was one of the first
codes of law in the American colonies, and it enshrined the right to trial by jury. The 1640 jury on which Thomas Goble
served was part of the colony’s effort to establish that it was a functioning legal state, not merely a religious encampment. The
American legal system, with its right to trial by jury that the Sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution later guaranteed, traces
its lineage through these early colonial courtrooms. Thomas Goble was present at the creation. Harvard College Connections
(1653–1655) One of the most remarkable documents in the Thomas Goble biographical record is a pair of entries in the
Harvard College Treasurer’s Records. In 1653 and 1655 — nearly twenty years after Thomas Goble’s arrival in Massachusetts
— the Harvard College accounts record payments of tuition fees from a family member identified as “goodman goobell”
(1653) and “old gobbell” (1655). [VERIFIED: Harvard College Treasurer’s Records, 1653–1655, Harvard University Archives]
Harvard College was founded in 1636 — just two years after Thomas Goble arrived in Massachusetts. It was established
specifically to train ministers and educated leaders for the new Puritan civilization. To have a family member attending Harvard
a generation after the patriarch arrived in the colony speaks to several things simultaneously: the family’s educational ambitions
and economic sufficiency, the respect in which they were held in the community (Harvard admissions were not entirely
egalitarian), and the remarkable speed with which a West Sussex craftsman’s family had, within one generation, positioned
itself as part of the intellectual and civic elite of colonial New England. The spelling variations — goobell, gobbell — are
characteristic of 17th-century orthographic fluidity and confirm the phonetic pronunciation of the name across spelling
variants. ✦ ✦ ✦ 3.4 Relocation and Death At some point in the late 1640s or early 1650s, Thomas Goble relocated from
Charlestown to Concord, Middlesex County, Massachusetts. Concord was at this time a relatively recently established town on
the expanding frontier of colonial settlement — a community that still felt the wilderness pressing against its edges. It was in
Concord that Thomas Goble spent his final years, and it was in Concord that he died on December 30, 1657, at approximately
sixty-six or sixtyseven years of age. His probate was recorded in Middlesex County. [VERIFIED: Middlesex County,
Massachusetts, Probate Records, December 30, 1657] The estate inventory preserved in the probate record provides a vivid,
intimate glimpse into the material world of Thomas Goble’s life: a featherbed, feather pillows, wool blankets, iron cooking
pots, and paraffin — the practical, modest furniture of a working colonial household. He was not a wealthy man at his death,
but he had built something real and lasting. His will contained the following provision for his wife Alice, preserved in the
probate record and remarkable for its combination of legal precision and evident tenderness: “I give and bequeath to Alice my
wife fair profit on all my stock so long as she liveth a widow.” The phrase “fair profit on all my stock” — meaning the income
from all his livestock and property — was a substantial bequest for the period, ensuring that Alice would be financially
independent as long as she chose not to remarry. It speaks of a man who thought about the women in his life with practical
care. ✦ ✦ ✦ 3.5 Thomas Goble’s Six Children Name Birth Year Death Year Notes and Significance John Goble ~1629,

sharp and unmistakable and which I now know I will never forget as long as I live. I think of Alice holding John with one

conducted, the tone they used, the implied threat beneath the bureaucratic language. I think of the families we knew — good

humiliated, silenced. I think of Thomas Hooker preaching that God was departing England, that England’s time was over, that
something was beginning somewhere else. I did not want to leave. I want to be honest about that, even here, even now. I did

from the register. Outside, through the small window, I can see Charlestown harbor in the September light — cold, bright,

hold. ✦ ✦ ✦ THE GOBLE–LeCOMPTE MASTER ANCESTRAL BOOK ■ VOLUME I C H A P T E R F O U R The
LeCompte Surname Norman Nobility, Huguenot Faith, and French Heritage 4.1 Etymology and Meaning The surname
LeCompte — or in its many variant forms, Le Compte, Lecomte, Le Comte, Lacount, Lecount — derives from the Old
French le comte, meaning literally “the count” or “the earl.” In the feudal social hierarchy of medieval France, a comte was a
nobleman of considerable rank, roughly equivalent to the English Earl — a territorial lord who administered a county (comté)
on behalf of the King and who held military, judicial, and economic authority over the people within his domain. The
surname LeCompte therefore signals one of two historical origins: either actual descent from a line of Frankish or Norman
counts — meaning the family itself once held comital rank — or service as a steward, administrator, or important retainer
within a count’s household, a position that would confer the name as an occupational designation of honor. The earliest
documentary record of the LeCompte name appears in an extraordinary medieval manuscript: the Cartulaire de l’abbaye de
Jumièges — a 13th-century collection of charters, deeds, and legal documents from the Benedictine abbey of Jumièges,
situated on the Seine in Normandy, one of the most important monasteries in medieval France. The entry reads: “Johannes le
Comte” — John the Count — appearing in the context of a land transaction or legal witness record. [VERIFIED: Cartulaire
de l’abbaye de Jumièges, 13th century, published edition] Jumièges Abbey was one of the great Norman ecclesiastical
institutions, deeply embedded in the political and social fabric of Normandy. The appearance of the LeCompte name in its
records places the family squarely in the Norman aristocratic and administrative world. The surname is particularly prevalent in
Normandy and Picardy — the two northern French provinces that had the most intimate historical connection with the
English crown through the Norman Conquest of 1066 and its centuries of political aftermath. Antoine LeCompte, born in

Calais approximately 1620, would have been born into a family with deep Norman roots in precisely this region — a region
that was simultaneously the most French and the most Anglo-Norman in all of France, given Calais’s 211-year history of
English occupation (1347–1558). The name LeCompte, in this context, carried the weight of centuries of Norman aristocratic
identity: it was a family name that remembered when its bearers had been men of consequence in a world defined by feudal
rank and military service. The LeCompte name carries a documented heraldic tradition — a formal family coat of arms —
registered in the United States National Huguenot Society’s register. The existence of a recognized coat of arms is consistent
with the family’s claim to French noble or near-noble ancestry and is further evidence that the LeCompte family, whatever its
precise position in the French social hierarchy, understood itself as a family of distinction with a heraldic identity that
preceded and survived its Protestant faith and its eventual diaspora. Huguenot families who registered arms with the National
Huguenot Society were required to document their descent from a Huguenot refugee ancestor — confirming that the
LeCompte arms tradition was carried into America by a documented Huguenot emigrant. French Huguenot refugees landing
at Dover, England, in 1685, following Louis XIV’s revocation of the Edict of Nantes. Antoine LeCompte had already fled
France for Maryland approximately thirty years earlier, anticipating the catastrophe that would eventually expel between
200,000 and 400,000 of his fellow Huguenots. Source: Universal History Archive / Getty Images [IMAGE PLACEHOLDER:
Heraldic coat of arms associated with the LeCompte family; map of Normandy and Picardy, France, showing geographic
heartland of the LeCompte name] ✦ ✦ ✦ 4.2 The Huguenot Heritage — Faith, Persecution, and Refuge The Huguenots
were French Protestants — followers of the Reformed (Calvinist) branch of the Protestant Reformation — who flourished in
France from the mid16th century onward, reaching perhaps 1.8 million people at their peak, approximately 10% of the French
population. They were concentrated particularly in the southern and western regions of France, in cities with strong merchant
and artisan economies, and in the northern provinces of Normandy and Picardy where proximity to Protestant England and
the Netherlands made Reformed theology both accessible and politically protected. The LeCompte family of Calais and
Normandy was part of this northern Huguenot community. The history of the Huguenots in France is, above all, a history of
persecution. The French Wars of Religion — eight separate civil conflicts between 1562 and 1598 — killed an estimated 3
million people and devastated the country. The individual events of this period are almost impossible to comprehend in their
violence. The Massacre of Vassy (March 1, 1562) — in which approximately 60 Huguenot men, women, and children were
killed by soldiers of Francis, Duke of Guise, while worshipping in a barn — triggered the First War of Religion and
established the pattern of anti-Huguenot mob violence that would characterize the next four decades. The St. Bartholomew’s
Day Massacre (August 23–24, 1572) — in which thousands of Huguenot nobles and their followers who had gathered in Paris
for the wedding of Henry of Navarre were systematically butchered, with the violence spreading from Paris to the provinces
over the following weeks — remains one of the most horrifying events in the history of Western Christianity. Contemporary
estimates of the total dead range from 5,000 to 30,000. The Huguenot nobility of France was decimated in a single night. The
Edict of Nantes (1598), issued by Henry IV — himself a former Huguenot who converted to Catholicism to secure the
French throne, famously remarking that “Paris is well worth a Mass” — granted the Huguenots a fragile religious and political
autonomy. They were permitted to worship in designated locations, to maintain a number of fortified towns as places of
refuge (most notably La Rochelle), and to hold public offices. It was an imperfect peace, but it was peace, and for
approximately thirty years the Huguenot community lived within its protections. The fall of La Rochelle in 1628 — when
Cardinal Richelieu’s forces besieged the great Huguenot stronghold for fifteen months, ultimately starving the garrison and
civilian population into surrender — ended the Huguenots’ political and military autonomy definitively. They were no longer a
state-within-a-state with defensible territory. They were a tolerated religious minority, dependent entirely on royal goodwill —
and royal goodwill, in 17th-century France, was an increasingly unreliable commodity. Antoine LeCompte’s decision to leave
France for England and then for Maryland was made in this context: after La Rochelle but before the final catastrophe, by a
man who could read the direction of events. He was not wrong. The final catastrophe arrived in 1685, when Louis XIV issued
the Edict of Fontainebleau, revoking the Edict of Nantes, declaring Protestantism illegal in France, and ordering all Protestant

pastors to leave the country. Between 200,000 and 400,000 Huguenots fled France in the subsequent years — to the
Netherlands, to England, to Prussia, to South Africa, and to the American colonies. They took with them their skills, their
capital, their networks, and their extraordinary resilience. France, by expelling them, impoverished itself economically and
culturally for generations. Antoine LeCompte had already been gone for thirty years. He had seen it coming. ■ Historical
Sidebar: The Huguenot Exodus — A Refugee Crisis of the First Order ■ The Huguenots who fled France between 1628 and
1700 were not, by and large, the poor or the desperate. They were skilled artisans, master craftsmen, merchants, physicians,
lawyers, military officers, engineers, and intellectuals — the productive middle and upper-middle classes of French society.
Huguenot silk weavers transformed the English textile industry. Huguenot watchmakers established the Swiss and English
clock-making traditions. Huguenot silversmiths, glassblowers, papermakers, and financiers reshaped the economies of every
country that received them. In Prussia, Frederick William I welcomed 20,000 Huguenot refugees and credited them with
jumpstarting the Prussian economy. In England, the Huguenot contribution to commerce, science, and the arts was enormous:
the Bank of England itself was co-founded by Huguenot capital. In Maryland — where Antoine LeCompte arrived
approximately 1655 — they joined a colony that was, by the terms of the Maryland Toleration Act of 1649, committed to
religious freedom for all Trinitarian Christians. It was the natural destination for a Huguenot Protestant in the 1650s: a place
that had, by law, made religious persecution illegal. The irony is striking: Antoine LeCompte had to cross two oceans and a
continent to find the religious freedom that France had promised him and then withdrawn. ✦ ✦ ✦ 4.3 LeCompte Name

5.1 Origins in Calais, Picardie (~1620) Antoine LeCompte was born approximately 1620 in the city of Calais, in the province
of Picardy (Picardie), in the north of France. To understand Antoine, one must understand Calais — for no other city in
France had quite its particular character, its particular mixture of French and English identity, its particular position on the
knife-edge of two civilizations. [PROBABLE: birth in Calais based on family records and genealogical documentation] Calais
sits at the narrowest point of the English Channel — the Strait of Dover — where on a clear day the white cliffs of England
are plainly visible from the French shore. The crossing is approximately 21 miles. For the medieval and early modern world,
this made Calais the gateway between England and France: a city defined entirely by its position between two nations,
perpetually contested, perpetually cosmopolitan, perpetually aware of its own strategic significance. Edward III of England
captured Calais in 1347 after an eleven-month siege — the story of the six Burghers of Calais, who offered their lives to
Edward in exchange for the city’s survival, is one of the most celebrated acts of self-sacrifice in medieval history. Calais
remained under English control for 211 years — until January 8, 1558, when the Duke of Guise captured it for France. It was

only 62 years before Antoine’s birth that Calais became definitively French — and in 1620, the city still carried within it the
living memory, the English-influenced architecture, the mixed-language street culture, of its long English occupation. Antoine
LeCompte was born into a Huguenot family in this city — Protestant in a violently Catholic France, Anglo-Norman in a city
that had only recently reasserted its Frenchness, educated in a family tradition that the 1819 LeCompte Manuscript suggests
was connected to French noble or near-noble circles. His subsequent military career in the English army speaks to connections
across the Channel that were, in Calais, natural: a city at the crossroads of two nations produces men who can move between
them. Antoine was such a man. The English Channel that most 17th-century Frenchmen regarded as an uncrossable cultural
barrier was, for a Calais-born Huguenot with English connections, simply the view from the harbor. As a Huguenot from a
noble or near-noble family in violently Catholic France, Calais represented both danger — increasingly so as the post-La
Rochelle crackdown on Huguenot autonomy intensified — and a gateway to safety. His family’s probable connections to both
French Protestant nobility and the English merchant and military world explain his subsequent path: military service in
England, marriage in London, emigration to Maryland. Each step was rational, purposeful, and ultimately successful. Antoine
LeCompte was not a man who was swept along by events. He was a man who read events accurately and acted on what he
read. A 1671 map of Maryland showing the Chesapeake Bay and Potomac River — created during the very years Antoine
LeCompte was establishing his plantation “St. Antoine” on the Choptank River in Dorchester County. Taylor’s Island lies in
the Choptank/Chesapeake region visible on this map. Source: Corbis/Getty Images [IMAGE PLACEHOLDER: Map of
Calais circa 1620 showing the Anglo-French border region; historical illustration of a 17th-century Chesapeake Bay plantation]
✦ ✦ ✦ 5.2 Military Service in King Charles I’s English Army According to the 1819 LeCompte Manuscript — the remarkable
oral history dictated by Thomas and Daniel LeCompte and recorded by Benjamin Woodward LeCompte — Antoine
LeCompte served approximately eleven years in King Charles I’s English Army. [VERIFIED: 1819 LeCompte Manuscript]
This service, beginning most likely in the late 1630s or early 1640s, places Antoine at the center of one of the most convulsive
periods in English history: the English Civil War (1642–1651), which pitted the Royalist forces of King Charles I against the
Parliamentarian forces eventually led by Oliver Cromwell, ending in Charles’s defeat, trial, and execution on January 30, 1649.
For a Huguenot Protestant, the choice of sides in the English Civil War was not straightforward. Puritans and other Reformed
Protestants were predominantly on the Parliamentary side — they were the people who believed in the sovereignty of
conscience and scripture over royal and episcopal authority, and they regarded Charles I’s perceived Catholic sympathies
(reinforced by his Catholic wife, Henrietta Maria of France) with profound suspicion. But a Huguenot from a noble Norman
family, accustomed to serving kings, connected to the English Royalist aristocracy through the Anglo-Norman network of
Calais, might reasonably have found himself on the Royalist side — serving a king who was, whatever his religious failings, the
legitimate monarch of England. The 1819 Manuscript’s account of Antoine’s military honors is worth quoting in full, as it has
been preserved in the family tradition: “joined the British army and fought eleven years for the King of Great Britain and
when the wars were over his name was so great, and for his valor, had him knighted and the title of ‘Monsieur’ given to him,
and his coat of arms.” — Thomas LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte, as dictated to Benjamin Woodward LeCompte, 1819 The
claim of English knighthood warrants careful evaluation. In 2004, a search by William Hunt, Windsor Herald at the College of
Arms in London, found no record of an English knighthood conferred upon Antoine LeCompte — the College of Arms
maintains comprehensive records of all English knighthoods and would be the definitive authority on this question. The most
likely explanation is that the family tradition of knighthood reflects the conferral of French noble arms — a recognition of
Antoine’s LeCompte family heraldic tradition from the continent — rather than a formal English knighthood, possibly
combined with some form of royal Royalist recognition of his service that did not rise to the level of a recorded English
knighthood. The tradition of “valor” and distinguished service is entirely historically plausible; the specific title of English
knight remains unverified. The coat of arms, however, is documented — registered with the National Huguenot Society —
and is genuine. When Charles I was executed on January 30, 1649, Antoine LeCompte — a royalist, a Protestant, a man who
had given eleven years of his military life to a king who no longer existed — was without a political homeland. England under

Cromwell was not a hospitable place for a Huguenot soldier who had fought for the king. France under Louis XIII and the
increasingly powerful Cardinal Mazarin was not a hospitable place for a Huguenot of any kind. The American colonies
represented the only available horizon. Antoine set his face toward it. ✦ ✦ ✦ 5.3 Maryland — Arrival and Early Settlement
(~1655– 1659) Antoine LeCompte arrived in Maryland approximately 1655 — making him among the earliest European
settlers of that colony, in the generation immediately following Maryland’s founding in 1634. Maryland had been established as
a proprietary colony by Cecil Calvert, 2nd Baron Baltimore, as a haven for English Catholics — but in a remarkable act of
pragmatic tolerance, the Maryland Toleration Act of 1649 had extended religious freedom to all Trinitarian Christians,
Protestant and Catholic alike. For a Huguenot Protestant arriving from a France where his faith was increasingly illegal,
Maryland was the only logical destination in the American colonies: a colony that had written religious toleration into its legal
code. [VERIFIED: Antoine LeCompte arrival in Maryland corroborated by land and court records beginning 1655] Antoine’s
early Maryland records reveal a man already engaged with the colony’s economy and legal systems within months of arrival.
On February 7, 1655, Antoine assigned his right to two hundred acres to one Ishmael Wright — a transaction that indicates he
had already qualified for a headright land claim and was using that claim as currency in a business arrangement, whether for
supplies, services, or commercial partnership. This early land transaction is the first documentary evidence of Antoine
LeCompte in Maryland, and it establishes immediately that he was not a passive settler waiting to be directed — he was an
active agent in the colony’s economic life. [VERIFIED: Maryland State Archives, Land Office Records] In 1657, the Calvert
County records note that Antoine was charged three hundred pounds of tobacco for killing three wolves — the colonial
bounty system paid settlers for eliminating predators that threatened livestock. Three wolves in a single year speaks to a man
who ranged widely through the Maryland wilderness, who was comfortable in frontier environments, and who kept livestock
worth protecting. It also suggests that Antoine had moved from his initial Calvert County location into the broader wilderness
of the Maryland tidewater — ranging through forests and wetlands where wolves still roamed in numbers. This was not a man
who settled comfortably into a safe corner of the colony and waited for civilization to arrive. He was operating at the edge of
it. ✦ ✦ ✦ 5.4 The “St. Antoine” Land Grant — January 17, 1659 [VERIFIED] On January 17, 1659, Antoine LeCompte
earned one of the most significant land grants in the early history of Dorchester County, Maryland: eight hundred acres — a
parcel of exceptional size for the period — obtained through the headright system. Under the Maryland headright system, a
settler earned fifty acres of land for each person whose passage to Maryland he paid. To qualify for 800 acres, Antoine paid the
passage of Thomas Raymond, Barbara Crouch, and Thomas Jones — sixteen people in total at fifty acres per head. This was a
substantial capital expenditure, indicating that Antoine had accumulated significant resources during his first four years in
Maryland. [VERIFIED: Maryland State Archives, Land Office Records, MSA S 11] The parcel was surveyed on August 13,
1659, and Antoine named it “St. Antoine” — also rendered in records as “Antonine” and “St. Anthonia.” The naming is
significant. To name 800 acres of Maryland wilderness after oneself — to place your own name on the landscape, in the
cartographic and legal record of the colony — is an act of extraordinary self-assertion. This is not the behavior of a man who
considered himself a temporary resident or a cautious minor investor. This is the behavior of a man who intended to be
permanent, who understood that the land would outlast him, and who chose to ensure that when posterity looked at the map,
it would see his name. The plantation “St. Antoine” was located in Dorchester County, Maryland, on the Choptank River —
the broad, beautiful tidal river that flows westward across the Delmarva Peninsula into the Chesapeake Bay — in the area of
what is now known as Taylor’s Island. Eight hundred acres. Named for himself. On the edge of the known world. This is who
Antoine LeCompte was. ✦ ✦ ✦ 5.5 Marriage to Hester Dottando — London, July 11, 1661 [VERIFIED] Following the
survey of his Maryland land grant in August 1659, Antoine returned to Europe — a transatlantic journey that speaks to his
continued connections with the English and continental world, and to sufficient economic success in Maryland to finance such
a voyage. It was on this European visit that he met and married Hester (Esther) Dottando, a woman born in Dieppe,
Normandy, France. The choice of Hester Dottando is revealing on multiple levels. She was a Norman woman — from the
same great province of northern France that had given the LeCompte name its heraldic history — and she was, almost

certainly, a Huguenot Protestant. Dieppe was a major Huguenot center in Normandy, a port city with strong Protestant
traditions and extensive commercial connections to England. Two Norman Huguenots — one from Calais, one from Dieppe
— met in London and married in a London chapel. They spoke the same language, carried the same faith, had survived the
same persecution, and now chose together to return to the Maryland wilderness and make it home. They married on July 11,
1661, in London. [VERIFIED: London Parish Records, London Metropolitan Archives] Then they sailed for Maryland,
carrying with them everything that a family needs to begin: each other, and the will to persist. ✦ ✦ ✦ 5.6 Life on Taylor’s
Island — Planter, Merchant, and Justice The LeCompte household established itself on Taylor’s Island in Dorchester County,
Maryland, on the shores of the Choptank River — a landscape of extraordinary beauty and genuine frontier danger. The
Choptank is a broad, tidal river flowing through marshland, cypress swamp, and mixed forest, rich in fish, waterfowl, and
game. In the 1660s, it was also the edge of European settlement — beyond the plantation clearings, the forest was the domain
of Native American peoples who had seen European settlement encroach for decades with understandable alarm. Antoine
operated as both a planter — growing tobacco and corn, the economic staples of the Chesapeake region — and a merchant,
trading goods along the river network. The History of Dorchester County by Elias Jones (1902), based on local documentary
records, preserves an account of Antoine’s frontier defense operations that is one of the most vivid passages in the LeCompte
family history: when hostile Native American bands approached the plantation, Antoine “would disperse them by firing his
large guns, and it is said, killed some of them.” The image is almost cinematic: the French Huguenot veteran of the English
Civil War, on his self-named 800-acre Maryland plantation, loading and firing a cannon into the tree line to hold his ground.
The eleven years of military service had not left him. He knew exactly what to do. Antoine LeCompte served as Justice of
Dorchester County from 1669 to 1671 — the highest civic office available at the county level in colonial Maryland. To be
appointed Justice was to be recognized as one of the most responsible, capable, and respected men in the county — an
appointment that required the approval of the Maryland Provincial Government and reflected genuine standing in the
community. A French-born Huguenot, appointed to the Maryland bench less than fifteen years after his arrival in the colony: it
is a remarkable trajectory, and it speaks to the qualities that Antoine LeCompte carried with him from Calais across the
Atlantic. ✦ ✦ ✦ 5.7 Death and Legacy The last documentary record of Antoine LeCompte alive is dated September 9, 1673.
He died thereafter in Dorchester County, Maryland, at approximately age 53 — not an old man by modern standards, but a
man who had lived with extraordinary fullness. He had been a soldier, a transatlantic emigrant, a colonial planter, a frontier
justice, a husband, and a father. He had named 800 acres of Maryland wilderness after himself. He had fired cannon balls into
the Maryland forest and held his ground. He had done it all in a language not entirely his own, in a country not his birth
nation, in a civilization that was still being invented as he participated in inventing it. On July 17, 1680, the Maryland Chancery
Records note that “Mark Cordea and Esther, his wife, executrix of Anthony LeCompte, deceased” — indicating that Hester
(Esther) LeCompte had remarried (to Mark Cordea) and was executing the estate of her first husband. [VERIFIED: Maryland
Chancery Records, July 17, 1680] The estate administration speaks to a man who had left real property to be administered —
the 800-acre “St. Antoine” plantation, livestock, goods, and the commercial interests of a successful Chesapeake planter.
Antoine’s legacy was not merely genealogical. It was economic, civic, and geographic — his name on the Maryland land map,
his descendants spreading through Maryland and eventually across the American continent, his cannon still echoing,
metaphorically, in every subsequent chapter of LeCompte family history. ✦ ✦ ✦ 5.8 The Naturalization of Hester and
Children — June 6, 1674 [VERIFIED] Following Antoine’s death, Hester LeCompte faced the legal situation common to
widows of foreign-born settlers: as a French-born alien, she and her children had not automatically acquired English subject
status simply by residing in Maryland. On June 6, 1674, Hester LeCompte and all of her children were formally naturalized as
British subjects. [VERIFIED: Maryland Archives, Naturalization Records, v. ii, pp. 400–402] This naturalization — a single
legal act that transformed a French Huguenot widow and her children into English colonial subjects — is one of the most
consequential documents in LeCompte family history. It secured the family’s property rights, their legal standing in Maryland
courts, and their social position in the colony. Without it, Hester and the children would have been legally vulnerable as alien

residents. With it, they were full members of the colonial society that Antoine had worked to build. It was Hester’s act of
completion — finalizing what Antoine had begun. Children of Antoine and Hester LeCompte Name Birth Death Marriage /
Notes John LeCompte ~1662, Maryland ~1705 Eldest son; born in Maryland after Antoine and Hester’s return from London.
Carried the family name forward. [VERIFIED] Moses LeCompte Maryland, ~1663 1720 The Blind Patriarch. Went blind at
approximately age 22 in Dorchester County, Maryland. Despite this, fathered eleven children. Died 1720, Dorchester County.
His extraordinary character is detailed in Chapter 6. [VERIFIED] Philip LeCompte Maryland, ~1665 Before 1705 Died before
1705; unmarried in surviving records. [PROBABLE] Anthony LeCompte Jr. Maryland, ~1667 Unknown Carried the father’s
name. Subsequent records uncertain. [ESTIMATED] Hester LeCompte Maryland, ~1669 Unknown Married Skinner. Further
records to be detailed in Name Birth Death Marriage / Notes Volume II. [PROBABLE] Katherine LeCompte Maryland,
~1671 Unknown Further records uncertain. [ESTIMATED] ✦ ✦ ✦ 5.9 Imagined Voice — Antoine LeCompte Taylor’s
Island, Dorchester County, Maryland ■ ~1662 ■ Imagined Voice — Creative Reconstruction Based on Documented
Historical Facts ■ The events described — land grant January 17, 1659; naming of “St. Antoine”; marriage to Hester
Dottando in London July 11, 1661; frontier defense accounts (Jones, History of Dorchester County, 1902); cannon use
documented — are all [VERIFIED] by primary source documentation. The interior experience is historical fiction. The river
goes pink at this hour, and then the color deepens to something I have no name for in either French or English — a color that
belongs to this river specifically, to the marsh grass and the cypress and the particular way the light comes off the water just
before dark. I stood here last Tuesday evening when I heard them moving through the trees on the east side, and I went to the
cannon without thinking about it, the way you go to a thing you have done for eleven years, the way the body knows before
the mind decides, and I touched the match to the charge and the sound went out through the forest like a word, and the forest
went quiet. I stood here afterward in the smoke and thought: I am still doing this. Forty-two years old and still doing this. I
think of Calais. I think of the harbor at Calais on a clear morning with England visible across the water, those white cliffs that
the English love so extravagantly, and I think of my father pointing at them when I was perhaps seven years old, telling me
that the English had stood on our ground for two hundred years and had only just been persuaded to leave. He was proud that
they were gone. I was not sure, even then, that I felt the same way. The English were practical. The English understood that a
man could be Protestant and still be a man of consequence. The French — my France, the France of Richelieu and the
Bourbon kings — had not yet learned this. I think of London. I think of the chapel where Hester and I were married — a
small room, not grand, not the kind of church you see in the history paintings, but full of the particular quality of English
light through old glass, and Hester’s voice in Norman French repeating the vows, and my own voice answering her, and the
minister’s English completing the three-language ceremony like a contract written in three scripts. I brought her here. To this.
Eight hundred acres of Maryland wilderness and a cannon near the treeline and the most beautiful river I have ever seen going
pink in the evening. I owe her a debt I cannot calculate. She has never asked me to. The plantation is still rough. The main
house is solid but the outbuildings want work and the south field was not fully cleared before the rains. There is always more
to do than the day contains. But I look at the land — my land, St. Antoine, named for me, on the maps of this colony in my
name — and I feel what I imagine a count might have felt standing on his comté in the old France, the France before the wars,
the France where a man of my family could look at the landscape and say: this is mine, and I will hold it. The France of that
feeling is gone. But the feeling itself came with me across the water. It is standing here beside me right now, at the edge of the
Choptank River, watching the color go out of the sky. I am making sure this lasts. I am making very sure of it. ✦ ✦ ✦ THE
GOBLE–LeCOMPTE MASTER ANCESTRAL BOOK ■ VOLUME I C H A P T E R S I X The First American
Generation Children of Thomas Goble and Children of Antoine LeCompte (1640s–1700) 6.1 Daniel Goble (~1640/41 –
1676) — Ancestor of the Ohio Line Daniel Goble, the youngest son of Thomas and Alice Brookman Goble, was born
approximately 1640–1641 in Charlestown, Massachusetts — making him almost certainly the child born in the same year that
his father sat on the first Boston jury. October 1, 1640: Thomas Goble in a Charlestown courtroom, one of twelve men
exercising the foundational right of English common law. Sometime that same year or early the next: a new Goble child

arriving in the world, breathing the air of colonial Massachusetts, knowing nothing yet of juries or rights or the civilization
being built around him. The coincidence is not merely poetic. It anchors Daniel’s birth in one of the most documented years
of his father’s American life. [VERIFIED: Daniel Goble identified in Massachusetts Bay Colony records; birth year derived
from family genealogical documentation] Daniel Goble grew up in a Charlestown that was transforming rapidly from a raw
frontier settlement into a functioning colonial town. In the sixteen years between Thomas Goble’s arrival (1634) and Daniel’s
young adulthood (approximately 1655–1660), Massachusetts had established its legal code (the Body of Liberties, 1641),
founded Harvard College, expanded its territorial claims, and begun the slow, difficult process of building the legal and civic
institutions of a new civilization. Daniel Goble did not know a frontier Charlestown. He knew a colonial New England town
with schools, churches, courts, and markets — a world his father had helped to build. Daniel Goble died in 1676, at the height
of King Philip’s War — the devastating conflict between the colonial New England settlements and the Wampanoag
confederacy under Metacom (King Philip), which killed approximately 600 English colonists and thousands of Native
Americans and destroyed twelve colonial towns before Metacom was killed in August 1676. Whether Daniel Goble’s death in
1676 was connected to this conflict — combat death, disease, displacement, or simply coincident timing — is not documented
in any surviving record. The timing is haunting. Thousands of New England colonists died in King Philip’s War; Daniel Goble
was thirty-five or thirty-six years old when it happened, the right age and demographic profile to have been among those
casualties. We cannot say definitively that he fell in that war. We can say that he died in its year, in its place, in the right
demographic, and that the silence of the record is itself a kind of testimony. Despite his early death, Daniel Goble’s son —
Daniel Goble Jr. (born 1669) — carried the family line forward. It is through Daniel Jr.’s subsequent migration south and west,
over the following century, that the Goble line would eventually arrive in Ohio and produce Shane Goble of Jefferson,
Ashtabula County. Daniel Goble Sr. is thus the critical link in the chain — the man through whom the founding generation’s
legacy was transmitted to the American interior. [PROBABLE: Daniel Goble identified as Ohio line ancestor through
genealogical documentation; detailed in Volume II] ✦ ✦ ✦ 6.2 Moses LeCompte (Maryland – 1720) — The Blind Patriarch
Of all the remarkable figures in the first American generation of the Goble and LeCompte families, Moses LeCompte stands
apart for reasons that have nothing to do with military valor or civic achievement, though his descendants would demonstrate
both. Moses LeCompte, the second son of Antoine and Hester (Dottando) LeCompte, was born in Maryland — naturalized
as a British subject on June 6, 1674, alongside his mother and siblings. [VERIFIED: Maryland Archives, Naturalization
Records, v. ii, pp. 400–402] At approximately age twenty-two — in the early 1680s — Moses LeCompte went blind. Consider
what this meant in Dorchester County, Maryland, in the 1680s. There was no medical treatment for whatever condition caused
his blindness — no ophthalmology, no surgery, no corrective devices of any meaningful kind. Blindness in the 17th-century
colonial world was a devastating disability, in an environment that was defined by the absolute necessity of physical capability.
Farming, hunting, navigation, construction, trade — every activity on which survival in a tidewater Maryland plantation
depended required vision. A blind man in 1680s Maryland was, by the logic of his world, dependent: on family, on neighbors,
on whatever charity an impoverished and frontier-pressed community could offer. Moses LeCompte defied this logic
completely. Despite going blind at twenty-two, Moses went on to father eleven children. He died in 1720 in Dorchester
County, Maryland — approximately forty years after losing his sight, four decades during which he managed a household,
maintained family relationships, participated in the economic and social life of his community, and produced a posterity large
enough to spread across two more centuries of American history. [VERIFIED: Moses LeCompte documented in Maryland
records; eleven children documented in 1819 LeCompte Manuscript] The 1819 LeCompte Manuscript — dictated by two of
Moses’s own blind grandsons or great-grandsons, Thomas and Daniel LeCompte — records Moses’s family with the
specificity of an oral tradition that had been carefully maintained across generations. The fact that blindness appeared again in
subsequent generations — Thomas and Daniel LeCompte were themselves blind when they dictated the 1819 Manuscript —
suggests the possibility of a hereditary visual condition in the LeCompte line, though the medical documentation to confirm
this does not survive. What does survive is the evidence of character: blind men who refused to be defined by their blindness,

who carried their family’s history in their heads and took steps to ensure it was recorded, who built marriages and families and
civic lives in circumstances that most people would regard as prohibitive. This is not a footnote in the LeCompte story. This is
the LeCompte story — a demonstration of the particular quality of resilience that appears, over and over, in the people who
carry this name. To encounter Moses LeCompte in the genealogical record is to encounter something almost impossible to
look at directly: a man who was robbed of his sight at twenty-two, in a world with no support systems and no
accommodations for disability, and who responded by fathering eleven children over the following four decades. It asks a
question that genealogy does not usually ask: what was Moses LeCompte like? What kind of man, what quality of character,
what depth of will, produced that response to that loss? We cannot answer with documents. We can answer only with silence
and respect. ✦ ✦ ✦ 6.3 Other Children of Thomas Goble and Antoine LeCompte John Goble (~1629–1676): The eldest
child of Thomas and Alice, born in England and approximately four years old at the Atlantic crossing. John is thus, among the
Goble children, the only one who could have carried a genuine memory of England — the smell of West Sussex, the texture
of the Aldingbourne church, the sound of his parents’ voices in a country that no longer existed for any of his younger
siblings. He died in 1676, the same year as his younger brother Daniel, in the dark year of King Philip’s War. Thomas Goble Jr.
(~1631/1635–1690): The second son, who carried his father’s name and lived to see the beginning of the new century’s final
decade. His line branches off in directions that will be traced more fully in Volume II, as the family spreads through the
expanding New England frontier. Elizabeth Goble (1633/1634–1689): The child who may have been born on the Atlantic —
or in the first weeks of life in Massachusetts — Elizabeth lived to 1689, more than fifty years after the crossing that may have
coincided with her birth. If she was indeed born on the ship, she was in the most literal possible sense a daughter of the
Atlantic: a new world child who began in the in-between place, at sea. Mary Goble (February 27, 1636–1725): The longest-
lived of Thomas Goble’s children, Mary lived to approximately eighty-nine years — a remarkable lifespan for any era,
extraordinary for 17th–18th century colonial New England. She was born in Charlestown two years after her parents arrived,
lived through King Philip’s War, through the witchcraft panic of 1692, through three colonial wars and the slow
transformation of Massachusetts from Puritan theocracy to something resembling a secular political community. Mary Goble,
born 1636, died 1725: she was a bridge across almost a century of American colonial history. Sarah Goble (May 1638–1717):
Born four years after the family’s arrival, Sarah lived to approximately seventy-nine years. Her life spans the entire formative
period of colonial New England, from the earliest decades of settlement through the early 18th century. John LeCompte
(~1662–~1705): The eldest child of Antoine and Hester, John was born in Maryland after his parents’ return from their
London wedding. He was a Maryland-born LeCompte — the first generation of the family to have known nothing but the
American world. His descendants will be traced in Volume II. Philip LeCompte (~1665–before 1705): The short-lived Philip
left no surviving documented descendants in the Maryland records, dying before 1705 and apparently without issue. His life is
a reminder that not every branch survives — that family history is also a history of lines extinguished, of stories that ended
too soon. Anthony LeCompte Jr. (~1667–unknown): Carrying his father’s name into the second Maryland generation. His
subsequent history is to be detailed in Volume II as the family spreads through the Chesapeake tidewater in the early 18th
century. Katherine LeCompte (~1671–unknown): The youngest documented LeCompte child, Katherine’s subsequent history
is uncertain in surviving records. Volume II will trace what can be recovered of her line and those of her sisters. ✦ ✦ ✦ THE
GOBLE–LeCOMPTE MASTER ANCESTRAL BOOK ■ VOLUME I C H A P T E R S E V E N The 1819 LeCompte
Manuscript A Rare Genealogical Treasure In the year 1819, in Dorchester County, Maryland, two elderly men sat together in a
room and began to speak. Their names were Thomas LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte, and they were fourth-generation
descendants of Antoine and Hester LeCompte — great-grandsons of the French Huguenot soldier who had fired cannon into
the Maryland tree line and named 800 acres of wilderness after himself. Thomas and Daniel were blind. They had been blind
for years. And what they were doing, on that particular day in 1819, was dictating from memory a comprehensive genealogical
history of every known descendant of Antoine and Hester LeCompte — two centuries of family, held entirely in the minds of
two men who could not see the paper on which their words were being recorded. The man who wrote down what they said

was Benjamin Woodward LeCompte, a younger relative who understood what Thomas and Daniel possessed and had the
wisdom to sit down and listen. The document that resulted — known as the LeCompte Family Manuscript of 1819 — is one
of the most extraordinary genealogical documents in American history. [VERIFIED: LeCompte Family Manuscript, 1819,
referenced in multiple independent genealogical studies] Consider what Thomas and Daniel had accomplished. They could not
read. They had never read a genealogical record, never consulted a parish register, never cross-referenced a land grant with a
probate record. What they had, instead, was memory — a specific, carefully maintained, deliberately preserved oral tradition of
family knowledge, passed down through four generations of LeCompte family life in Dorchester County. They knew the
names, birth years, death years, marriages, children, and family branches of the entire LeCompte posterity from Antoine and
Hester onward — not because they had looked it up, but because they had been told, and had remembered, and had told
others, in the ancient tradition of human memory as living archive. The genealogical content they dictated covers two centuries
of LeCompte family history: Antoine and Hester’s children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and great-great-grandchildren,
with their marriages, their migrations, their civic and military records, and the various branches of the family as it spread
through Maryland, Virginia, and beyond. The document is not perfect — memory, even trained oral memory, distorts and
omits — but it is remarkably accurate where it can be cross-referenced against surviving documentary records. The account of
Antoine’s military service, his knighthood claim, his coat of arms, and his arrival in Maryland — all preserved in the 1819
Manuscript — have been substantially corroborated by independent documentary research, even where specific details remain
uncertain. One must sit with the scene itself for a moment. Two old blind men, in a room in Maryland, in 1819. They cannot
see the light coming through the windows. They cannot see Benjamin Woodward LeCompte’s hand moving across the paper.
They cannot see each other’s faces. But they can speak. And what comes out of their mouths is the entire genealogy of a
family that began in Calais, in the reign of Louis XIII, in the shadow of Cardinal Richelieu’s anti-Protestant campaign — a
family that crossed oceans and survived wars and fired cannons and went blind and fathered eleven children while blind, and

/ Riffe The surname that Penny Sue Riffe-Goble carries through her father Rinfrod L. Riffe has traveled far from its German
origins — both geographically and orthographically. Understanding the spelling variants of the name illuminates the family's
migration path as precisely as any map. REIFF (Germany, Rhineland-Palatinate, c. 1500s–1700s) — The original German
spelling. From Middle High German reif, meaning a hoop or ring, particularly the iron or wooden hoop used in barrel-making.
Pronounced approximately "RIFE" in German. The doubled final consonant is standard German orthographic practice. RIFE
/ RYFE (Pennsylvania, c. 1710s–1770s) — The first American adaptation, reflecting the Anglicization of the German sound.
Pennsylvania court and church records from the early 18th century show this spelling commonly used by the family's first
American generations. RIFFE (Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Ohio, c. 1770s–present) — The settled American spelling,
adding the terminal "e" in the French-influenced Anglophone orthographic tradition of the Southern states. This is the
spelling the family carried through the Great Wagon Road migration and that it carries today. RIFF (occasional variant) — A
further simplification found occasionally in census records and legal documents, particularly in the mid-19th century, where
census enumerators wrote what they heard. Each spelling shift marks a cultural threshold. Reiff is a German craftsman in the
Rhineland. Rife is a Pennsylvania farmer learning to navigate English-language courts. Riffe is an American frontier family
staking its claim in the Virginia highlands. They are all the same family. The name changed; the blood did not. Table of

— The Reiff Family Origins (1649–1728) The Name and Its Meaning Before we follow Penny's ancestors across an ocean and
down the spine of the Appalachian Mountains, we must begin with a word. Specifically, a German word: Reif. In Middle High
German — the language spoken throughout the Germanic lands during the medieval period — reif meant a hoop or ring.
Not the decorative kind: the functional kind. The iron hoop that held a barrel together. The wooden hoop that kept a bucket

from falling apart. The precise, load-bearing circle of metal that was the signature product of one of the most essential crafts
of the medieval economy: cooperage. A cooper made barrels, casks, tubs, vats, buckets, and churns. In the world before
plastics, before industrial manufacturing, before refrigeration, the barrel was the universal storage and transportation container.
Wine traveled in barrels. Beer was fermented in barrels. Grain was stored in barrels. Salted fish and meat were preserved in
barrels. Gunpowder was packed in barrels. The prosperity of almost every other trade depended on the quality of the cooper's
craft. A poorly made barrel — staves that didn't fit precisely, hoops that weren't driven tight enough — could cost a merchant
his entire shipment of wine, or rot a winter's worth of preserved meat. Cooperage was not a minor craft. It was foundational.
The earliest Reiff ancestors were almost certainly coopers. Their name, derived from the iron and wooden hoops they made,
was the medieval equivalent of a professional title — a craftsman's badge of identity worn in the surname. Imagine the
workshop: the smell of green oak being split into staves, the sharp mineral tang of iron heating in the forge, the rhythmic
percussion of the hoop driver striking the driving ring around a half-finished barrel, the staves compressing and locking under
the pressure into a vessel so tight it would hold wine without a single drop of seepage. This was the craft of the Reiff family.
This was the skill that gave them their name. The Etymology of Reiff — Two Possible Roots Root One — The Cooper's
Hoop: Middle High German reif = a hoop, ring, or band. Specifically the iron or wooden hoop used in barrel-making
(cooperage). The family's professional identity as craftsmen embedded in the surname itself. This is the most widely accepted
etymology. Root Two — The Germanic Personal Name Rīchfrit: Some linguists trace certain Reiff variants to the ancient
compound Germanic personal name composed of rīch (powerful, mighty, rich) + frit (peace) — meaning "powerful peace" or
"peace through strength." This suggests an alternate lineage from a distinguished personal name becoming a family surname.
These dual roots are not mutually exclusive — both speak to the family's essential character: the careful craftsman and the
warrior-peacemaker simultaneously. The Rhineland-Palatinate — Where It All Began The region the family came from is one
of the most beautiful and most foughtover pieces of landscape in European history. The Rhineland-Palatinate — Rheinland-
Pfalz in modern German — occupies the southwestern corner of what is now Germany, centered on the great curve of the
Rhine River as it flows northward from Switzerland toward the North Sea. In Penny's ancestors' time, this was not Germany
(which did not exist as a unified nation until 1871) but a collection of small German principalities of which the Electoral
Palatinate — the Kurpfalz — was among the most important. Picture it: the Rhine moving broad and powerful through a
landscape of terraced vineyards climbing impossibly steep slopes, the vines heavy with grapes in September, the whole valley
wreathed in morning mist that burns off by mid- morning to reveal hills crowned with medieval fortresses — Marksburg,
Rheinfels, Gutenfels. The market towns of the valley were built in the halftimbered Fachwerk style: exposed oak beams filled
with whitewashed plaster, the whole structure leaning slightly forward over narrow cobblestone streets, upper stories
overhanging the lower. Cathedral spires rose above the rooflines. Mill wheels turned in the millraces of tributary streams. On
Sundays, the church bells of a dozen villages rang simultaneously across the valley in an uncoordinated but somehow beautiful
discord. The Rhine Valley in the Rhineland-Palatinate — the ancestral homeland of the Reiff/Riffe family. The vine-terraced
hills, the great river, the medieval fortresses overlooking the water: this was the world Penny's ancestors left behind. (Getty
Images) This was a world of deep roots. The Reiff family had been part of this landscape for generations — their cooper's
workshop probably in one of the market towns, serving the wine merchants and river traders who made the Rhine valley
prosper. They would have spoken the Palatine German dialect, attended a Reformed Protestant church (the dominant
confession in the Palatinate after the Reformation), participated in the guild system that regulated their trade, and measured
their lives by the rhythms of the Rhine — its floods in spring, its low water in summer, its freezing in the deepest winters. And
then everything fell apart. Repeatedly. Catastrophically. Over the course of seventy years. Seventy Years of Catastrophe The
Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) was the defining catastrophe of the seventeenth-century German world. What began as a
religious conflict between Protestant and Catholic princes became a general European war that ravaged the German lands for
three decades. The Rhineland-Palatinate was among the most heavily damaged regions in Europe. Armies — Swedish, French,
Imperial, Spanish — marched back and forth across the valley, consuming everything in their path: crops, livestock, stored

grain, timber, the accumulated wealth of generations. Historians estimate that the war reduced the Rhineland's population by
approximately one-third through a combination of violence, famine, and disease. Entire villages were burned. The
sophisticated agricultural economy of the Rhine valley was reduced to subsistence-level survival. The peace of 1648 brought
nominal relief, but the Palatinate's troubles were far from over. Marshal Turenne's French armies devastated the region in 1674
during the Franco-Dutch War. Then, in 1688–1689, Louis XIV ordered the deliberate, systematic destruction of the Palatinate
as a military strategy — burning Heidelberg, Mannheim, Speyer, Worms, Oppenheim, and dozens of smaller towns in a
campaign of calculated destruction that left the region in ruins. The burning of Heidelberg — one of the great Renaissance
cities of Europe — shocked the civilized world. The old castle above the city, already damaged, was shattered by French
engineers. The city itself was reduced to smoking rubble. For the Reiff family, watching this destruction from wherever in the
Palatinate they lived, the calculation must have become increasingly clear: there was no future here. The land they had worked
for generations had been fought over too many times. The armies would come again. There was a better world somewhere, if
you were willing to cross the ocean to find it. The Winter of 1708–1709 — The Final Push If the wars had weakened the
Palatine families' attachment to their homeland, the winter of 1708–1709 severed it entirely. Historical records from across
Europe document this as one of the coldest winters in recorded history. The Rhine River froze solid — not merely iced over
but frozen to depth, bearing the weight of men and wagons. Temperatures dropped far below anything the 18th-century
thermometer had previously recorded. Livestock perished in their stalls. Fruit trees were killed to the root, eliminating decades
of orchard investment overnight. And, in a detail that seems almost symbolic: the wine froze in the casks. The barrels that the
Reiff cooperage tradition existed to produce — the barrels that held the Rhine valley's most valuable product — could not
protect the wine against cold so extreme that the liquid itself solidified. That winter sent tens of thousands of Palatine families
toward the ports. They had endured the Thirty Years' War. They had endured Turenne and Louis XIV's burning campaigns.
They had endured poverty and political instability. But when the wine froze in the barrels, something broke. Approximately
13,000 Palatine refugees reached England in the summer of 1709; many thousands more streamed toward the Dutch ports for
passage to America. The Great Palatine Migration had begun in earnest. Pennsylvania Dutch — A New World Identity
William Penn had been traveling through the Rhineland since the 1670s, preaching religious tolerance and the practical virtues
of his new colony. His message resonated deeply with Reformed Protestant families who had spent decades as targets of
Catholic armies and French ambition. Pennsylvania offered something that seemed almost mythological after the previous
century: religious freedom, cheap land, and peace. The letters that came back from early settlers confirmed it. Men who had
been marginal farmers in an overcrowded, wardamaged European landscape found themselves prosperous Pennsylvania
landowners within a generation. The Palatine German community that established itself in southeastern Pennsylvania — in the
counties of Montgomery, Bucks, Lancaster, Berks, and York — became one of the most successful immigrant communities in
colonial American history. They spoke German (not Dutch — "Dutch" was the English corruption of "Deutsch"), attended
Reformed and Lutheran churches, built their farmhouses in the Fachwerk style adapted to Pennsylvania timber, decorated their
household goods with the distinctive painted folk art tradition (painted furniture, pottery, fraktur documents), and sang in the
shape-note tradition that would survive on the American frontier long after its European origins were forgotten. They were,
collectively, the backbone of Pennsylvania's colonial agricultural economy — the German farmer was proverbially the most
productive of all colonial farmers. A Pennsylvania colonial farmhouse — representative of the architectural tradition brought
by the German Palatine families from the Rhineland. The Reiff family settled in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, in the
early 18th century, likely building in this tradition. (Getty Images) Peter Reiff Sr. — The Immigrant Patriarch The earliest
documented American ancestor of the Riffe family is Peter Reiff Sr. The precise date of his arrival in Pennsylvania is not
currently established in the documentary record, but the birth of his son Peter Reiff Jr. approximately 1725– 1728 in
Montgomery County, Colony of Pennsylvania, places the family's American arrival in the early 1710s to mid-1720s. They were
among the great wave of Palatine German immigrants who flooded into Philadelphia between 1710 and 1730, following the
1709 catastrophe and attracted by Penn's promises. Montgomery County, where the family settled, lies immediately northwest

of Philadelphia — close enough to the city's markets to sell agricultural surplus, far enough into the country to find affordable
land. The landscape is rolling limestone country, well-watered, with rich bottomland along the numerous creeks that feed into
the Schuylkill River. For a family accustomed to the Rhine valley's wine-country landscape, the gentle hills and clear-running
creeks of Montgomery County would have felt, if not exactly familiar, at least hospitable. Their congregation was Christ
Evangelical Church at Bieber Creek — a German Reformed church that served as the spiritual and social anchor of the Reiff
family's New World life. In the 18th century, the church was not merely a Sunday obligation. It was the primary institution of
community life: the place where children were baptized (and the record made that would survive into the genealogical
databases of the 21st century), where marriages were contracted and witnessed, where deaths were mourned and bodies
committed to the churchyard ground, where disputes were arbitrated, where neighbors became family and family became
neighbors. The congregation at Bieber Creek was the Reiff family's world within the world. Documented Genealogical Facts
