✦ ✦ C H A P T E R T H R E E The Great Wagon Road — Peter Riffe Heads South (1771) America's First Highway By
1771, Peter Reiff Jr. was approximately forty-three to forty-six years old. He had lived his entire life in Montgomery County,
Pennsylvania, in the tight German-speaking community his father had helped establish. He knew his neighbors, his
congregation, the layout of the county's roads, the price of grain at the Philadelphia market. He was, in every external sense,
settled. But Pennsylvania was changing. Land prices in the settled counties were rising as the colonial population expanded.
The good bottomland that had been cheap when Peter Reiff Sr. arrived was now expensive and increasingly scarce. Younger
sons — and Pennsylvania German families tended to have many children — could not expect to inherit enough acreage to
support a family in the manner they had grown up with. Meanwhile, word was traveling up and down the Pennsylvania
German communities of a road to the south — a great road that ran all the way through Virginia and into the Carolinas,
passing through valleys of remarkable agricultural promise where land was cheap and plentiful. In 1771, Peter Riffe made his
decision. Pennsylvania's road network, including the Great Wagon Road corridor — the route by which Peter Riffe Jr. carried
his family south from Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, to the Virginia highlands in 1771. (Buyenlarge/Getty Images) The
Road Itself The Great Wagon Road was not what the name suggests to modern ears. It was not a highway. It was a dirt track,
in many places little more than a rutted path worn into the earth by decades of wagon wheels, horse hooves, and human feet.
From Philadelphia it ran through Lancaster and York in Pennsylvania, then crossed the Potomac River into Maryland at the
crossing near Hagerstown, then turned south through the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia — that long, gorgeous valley
between the Blue Ridge Mountains to the east and the Allegheny ridges to the west — and continued all the way to the Yadkin
River country of North Carolina and beyond. In spring, the road was a river of mud. In summer, a river of dust. In winter, the
river crossings could be treacherous and the mountain gaps snow-choked. But the road was always busy — a continuous
human river flowing southward and westward, carrying the overflow of the established colonies toward the open frontier.
Pennsylvania Germans in their heavy Conestoga wagons, loaded with household goods, farm tools, seed grain, and the pieces
of furniture that were too precious to leave behind. Scots-Irish families from Ulster, more likely to travel light and move fast.
Black walnut and cherry desks and spinning wheels and iron cooking pots making the journey from established farmstead to
new wilderness in the back of a canvas-covered wagon. Children walking beside the wheels to spare the horses. Dogs trotting
alongside. Livestock driven ahead in a loose herd, the cattle occasionally breaking for the roadside forest and requiring
retrieval. Peter Riffe, a man in his mid-forties, made this journey deliberately. He was not fleeing — he was choosing. The
distinction matters. The man who walks away from everything he has built in order to build something larger elsewhere is
making a statement about his fundamental orientation toward life: forward, always forward, whatever the cost. This is the first
great Riffe migration — the template for all that would follow. What He Left Behind In leaving Montgomery County, Peter
Riffe left behind everything the previous generation had built: the farm, the congregation at Bieber Creek, the community of

German speakers who shared his language and his faith and his understanding of the world. He left behind the graves of his
parents. He left behind neighbors who had known him since childhood, who called him by his German name, who shared the
particular jokes and complaints and seasonal customs of the Pennsylvania Dutch community. We should not romanticize this.
It was not easy. The Pennsylvania German community was tight-knit precisely because the world outside it was so foreign. To
leave was to step outside the protective membrane of the familiar and into a world where your language was not spoken, your
customs were not shared, your church might be miles away if it existed at all. Peter Riffe was a brave man — not in the
dramatic sense, but in the quiet, determined sense that asks the most of ordinary human courage. Wythe County, Virginia
(1771) The road brought him south and west to Wythe County, Virginia — a land that must have seemed almost impossibly
beautiful to a man accustomed to the gentler Pennsylvania landscape. Wythe County occupies a high valley in the southwestern
Virginia highlands, where the Ridge and Valley geology of the Appalachians produces a series of parallel ridges and valleys
oriented northeast to southwest. From a hilltop in Wythe County you could see ridge after blue ridge fading into the distance
— the blue haze that gives the Blue Ridge its name caused by the terpene compounds released by the surrounding forests of
oak, hickory, and pine. The New River — one of the oldest rivers in North America, flowing paradoxically northward through
the mountains — cut through the landscape in graceful meanders. The valley bottoms held rich black limestonederived soil
that rewarded the farmer who was willing to clear the timber and work the ground. Peter Riffe was willing. Records document
his acquisition of land in Wythe County in 1771. The first years of settlement were the hardest: the first cabin, built quickly
against the approaching winter, half-finished and cold; the first winter spent in a structure that leaked wind and weather; the
first spring planting on ground hastily cleared of tree stumps, the corn going in between the stumps because there was no time
to remove them before the planting season. But the soil rewarded the effort. A man who could survive the first two or three
years on a new Appalachian farmstead — who could feed his family through those first brutal winters, who could get enough
acres cleared and productive before his capital and his reserves ran out — was on solid ground thereafter. The land, once
tamed, was generous. Peter Riffe and the American Revolution Peter Riffe did not merely farm in Virginia. He fought for it.
Records document his service in the Virginia Militia under Captain Howe — the local militia units that were the backbone of
the Revolutionary War effort in the frontier counties, where the Continental Army had little presence and the defense of the
community fell to the men who lived there. For a man whose family had fled European tyranny — who had grown up on
stories of what Louis XIV's armies had done to the Palatinate, of religious persecution and political oppression — the choice
to fight for American independence carried a resonance that went beyond ordinary patriotism. It was personal. The freedom
that Pennsylvania and Virginia offered — the freedom to own land, to worship without state coercion, to govern oneself —
was precisely what the family had crossed an ocean to find. When the British threatened it, Peter Riffe took up arms. Frontier
militia service in southwestern Virginia was not the romantic kind of warfare that appears in popular history. It was ugly and
close and constant. The British strategy on the southern and western frontier encouraged Cherokee raids against American
settlements, creating a situation where families in southwestern Virginia faced the threat of attack from multiple directions
simultaneously. The militia's job was less about set-piece battles and more about patrol, counter-raid, and the constant vigilance
that comes from knowing that the edge of safety is also the edge of violence. Peter Riffe lived in that world and served in it.
At his death around 1799, Peter Riffe left a substantial family — eight or more known children — who would carry the name
and the character into every creek hollow and ridge community of the Southern Appalachians. The cooperage family from the
Rhineland had become, in the space of a single generation on American soil, a frontier family whose sons would push further
west and south with each new generation, always moving toward the next open ridge, the next unclaimed hollow, the next
promise of land and freedom. Peter Riffe Jr. — Documented Facts Item Record Birth c. 1725–1728, Montgomery County,

Generations (1763–1850) Gabriel Conrad Riffe — Deeper Into the Mountain Gabriel Conrad Riffe was born in 1763 in
Rockland Township, Berks County, Pennsylvania — probably among the older children in Peter Riffe Sr.'s family, born before
the 1771 move to Virginia. He grew up, therefore, at the intersection of two worlds: the Pennsylvania German world of his
birth, still close enough to touch; and the Appalachian frontier world that his father was building in Wythe County. When
Gabriel reached adulthood, he chose the frontier — and went further into it than his father had. Gabriel pushed west and
north from Wythe County into the territory that is now Logan County, West Virginia. In Gabriel's lifetime, this was still
Virginia — West Virginia would not exist until the Civil War split the state in 1863 — but it was the far western edge of it:
deep mountain country, far from the settled Tidewater culture of eastern Virginia, a world unto itself. Logan County occupies
the drainage basin of the Guyandotte River and its tributaries — steep ridges of highgrade bituminous coal and magnificent
timber, the creek valleys narrow and the ridge crests sharp, the whole landscape compressed and folded in the way that only
Appalachian geology produces. In Gabriel's time, none of this was coal country yet. The mines would come later — much
later — with the arrival of the railroad in the 1880s and 1890s. In Gabriel's time, Logan County was subsistence farming
country, pure and simple. You grew what you ate. You raised what you wore. You built what you lived in. The forest and the
creek and the kitchen garden and the hog lot were the entire economy. Subsistence Life in the Appalachian Mountain World
Picture a Logan County farmstead in the early 19th century. The cabin was built of logs, chinked with clay and moss, with a
single large fireplace serving as both heat source and cooking range. The fireplace was enormous — it had to be, because it
was also a forge, a smokehouse entrance, and the warmth against which the family slept on the coldest nights of a West
Virginia winter. The windows were greased paper or, for more prosperous families, salvaged glass. The floor might be
puncheon — split logs laid flat — or packed dirt, or, for the ambitious, rough-sawn planks. The work never stopped. Spring
meant planting — corn was the staple, interplanted with beans and squash in the traditional Three Sisters system that the
Appalachian farmers had learned, directly or indirectly, from the Native American agricultural tradition. Summer meant
cultivation, weeding, tending, and the endless processing of what the garden produced — beans strung and dried to make
leather britches, fruit dried on boards in the sun, cucumbers put into brine. Fall meant harvest, butchering (the hogs killed
when the first hard frost came and the temperature would hold the meat without spoilage), and the curing, smoking, salting,
and storing of everything that had to carry the family through the winter. Winter meant firewood — always more firewood —
and the making and mending of clothing and tools, and the long evenings by the fire when stories were told and songs were
sung and the oral tradition carried forward everything that had no other way of being remembered. "The Appalachian
farmstead was not a simple life. It was a complete civilization in miniature — every skill, every craft, every form of knowledge
had to be present in a single family or they did not survive. What looks like poverty to the outside eye was, from the inside, a
comprehensive self-sufficiency that the industrial world has never matched." — On the Appalachian subsistence tradition
What the Mountains Made of People The Appalachian environment did something specific to the human character of the
families who lived in it for generations. Outsiders have been describing — and misunderstanding — this for two centuries.
The qualities that the mountains produced in Appalachian people are not defects. They are sophisticated adaptations to a
demanding ecological and social environment. Self-reliance. In a hollow where the nearest neighbor might be half a day's walk
away and the nearest doctor a full day's ride, you learned to solve your own problems. You set your own broken bones, pulled
your own teeth, birthed your own children, built your own structures, fixed your own machinery. Not because you didn't want
help — but because help was simply not available most of the time. Self-reliance was not a philosophy; it was a survival
strategy that became, over generations, a character trait so deeply embedded it was indistinguishable from instinct. Fierce
attachment to specific place. The particular hollow. The particular ridge. The particular creek where you caught catfish as a
child and buried your grandmother and learned to walk. Appalachian place attachment is not mere sentiment — it is identity.
Who you are is inseparable from where you are from. The Riffe family cemeteries in Greenup County, Kentucky, and
Wyoming County, West Virginia, are not merely burial grounds. They are identity claims — proof that this ground belongs to
this family in the most permanent sense available: the sense of the dead who will not leave. Oral tradition. When books are

scarce and literacy is uneven — as it was in the Appalachian mountain communities through most of the 19th century — the
oral tradition becomes the primary vehicle for everything that matters: family history, medical knowledge, legal tradition,
religious teaching, entertainment, and the transmission of skills from generation to generation. The Appalachian ballad
tradition, the storytelling tradition, the shape-note singing tradition — these are not folk arts. They are information
technologies. They are how knowledge survived without paper. Community solidarity within the in-group, wariness toward
outsiders. Appalachian community life was intensely cooperative within the extended family and immediate neighborhood —
the barn-raising, the quilting bee, the harvest gathering, the mutual aid in sickness and bereavement. But toward strangers,
toward institutions, toward outsiders who had not yet proven themselves — the Appalachian response was watchful reserve.
This, too, is a sophisticated adaptation. In a community where law enforcement was distant and the state's protective capacity
was minimal, you could not afford to trust everyone. Trust was earned, slowly, and once earned, it was absolute. The Potter
Line — The Scots-Irish Thread Woven into the Riffe heritage alongside the German Palatine craftsman tradition is a second
ancestral thread of equal historical significance: the Scots-Irish tradition embodied in the Potter family. The details of the
specific genealogical connection between the Potter and Riffe families require further primary source documentation — but
the cultural and geographic overlap is complete and unmistakable. The Riffe-Potter intermarriage, whenever and however it
occurred, brought together the two dominant cultural streams of the Appalachian frontier in a single family. The Scots-Irish
— a term that requires unpacking — were not simply Irish people with Scottish surnames. They were a distinct historical
community: Scottish Presbyterians who were transplanted to northern Ireland (Ulster) in the 17th century as part of the
English "Plantation" policy, where they lived for two or three generations before the combination of religious discrimination,
rackrenting landlords, and the promise of American land sent them across the Atlantic. They came in enormous numbers —
particularly to Pennsylvania and then down the Great Wagon Road into the Appalachian frontier — bringing with them a
culture forged in two different kinds of exile: the Scottish border country and the Irish plantation. The result was a people
who were fiercely independent, clan-loyal, deeply suspicious of central authority, religiously intense (Presbyterian by tradition,
though they converted to Baptist on the American frontier), and culturally extraordinary. The music the Scots-Irish brought to
the Appalachian frontier — the Child ballads of the Scottish-English border country, the fiddle tunes that accompanied them,
the dance traditions, the keen sense of musical narrative — became the foundation on which American country music,
bluegrass, and old-time music were eventually built. When the Potter family intermarried with the Riffe family, they brought
this musical heritage into the bloodline. The German Palatine craftsman tradition — systematic, community-minded,
industrious, shape-note- singing — merged with the Scots-Irish warrior-folk tradition — individualist, fierce, musically
brilliant, politically passionate. This synthesis is, in the most literal sense, the bloodline that produced Penny Sue Riffe-Goble. ▸

William Riffe, 93 Years on the Mountain (1803–1897) A Life That Spanned an Era William Riffe was born July 18, 1803, in
Tazewell County, Virginia. He died April 22, 1897, in Wyoming County, West Virginia — age 93 years, 9 months, and 4 days.
He was buried in the Riffe Cemetery in Wyoming County. Sit with those dates for a moment, because they are extraordinary.
In 1803, Thomas Jefferson was in the first year of his second presidential term. The Lewis and Clark Expedition had not yet
departed. Napoleon was First Consul of France, not yet Emperor. The United States was twenty-seven years old. There were
fifteen states in the Union. In 1897, when William Riffe died, William McKinley was about to become the twenty-fifth
president. The transcontinental railroad had been complete for twenty-eight years. The Appalachian coalfields that surrounded
him had been transformed beyond recognition by industrial extraction. The Supreme Court had just ruled in Plessy v.
Ferguson, entrenching segregation. The world that William Riffe was born into and the world he died in were separated not
merely by ninety-three years but by what might as well have been centuries of human change. What William "Fighting Bill"
Riffe Witnessed — 1803 to 1897 Born while Jefferson still lived · War of 1812 · Indian Removal Act and Trail of Tears ·
Mexican-American War · California Gold Rush · The coming of the railroad · The Civil War and West Virginia statehood

(1863) · Reconstruction and its failure · The Gilded Age and the rise of industrial capitalism · The transformation of the
Appalachian coalfields · The beginning of the great labor wars The "Fighting Bill" Character His nickname was not unusual in
the Appalachian naming tradition, but it was specific. "Fighting Bill" indicated something about his character that his
neighbors found worth recording — the quality of not backing down, of maintaining himself in the face of pressure. In
Appalachian culture, "fighting" carried a meaning broader than its literal sense. It was existential as much as physical: fighting
to remain who you are, on land that is yours, by rules you have set. The Appalachian man who was called a fighter was not
necessarily a brawler — though he might have been that too — but someone who refused to be diminished, who met the
forces that would reduce him with a stubborn insistence on his own full personhood. Fighting Bill lived through everything
the 19th century threw at the Appalachian mountain communities, and he outlasted essentially all of it. Ninety-three years is
not merely longevity — it is a statement about constitutional robustness and psychological endurance. You do not survive nine
decades in Appalachian West Virginia by accident. You survive it by being built, from the bones out, for endurance. The Civil
War in the Appalachian Counties When the Civil War came to West Virginia — and it came with particular violence, because
West Virginia was the Civil War's most literal border territory, the state born of the conflict itself — Fighting Bill was fifty-
eight years old. He would have been a living memory of everything that came before, and an observer of the war's reshaping
of everything around him. The war in the Appalachian counties was not the war of set-piece battles and grand strategy that
the eastern theater produced. It was guerrilla warfare: neighbor against neighbor, burned barns and stolen livestock, ambushes
on creek-bottom roads, the casual violence of men who knew each other's families and chose to harm them anyway. West
Virginia's 1863 creation as a separate Union state split communities and families that had been unified for generations. The
German-descended families of the region broadly tended toward Union sentiment — they had no investment in the Tidewater
planter aristocracy's slavebased economy, and many of their families carried, at some level of cultural memory, the awareness
that they had come to America to escape aristocratic tyranny, not to preserve it. But individual choices in the Appalachian
counties were shaped by local circumstances, family alliances, and the immediate selfinterest of specific communities. Fighting
Bill survived the Civil War. He was in Wyoming County, West Virginia, when the war ended. He continued to live there for
another thirty-two years — long enough to see the industrial transformation that the railroads and the coal companies brought
to the mountains he had known as untouched wilderness. The Coal Economy and the Mountain's Transformation The
coalfields of southern West Virginia — Logan, Wyoming, Mingo, McDowell counties — were among the richest deposits of
bituminous coal in the world. As long as there was no reliable way to get the coal out of the mountains, they were, from the
industrial capitalist's perspective, merely beautiful. The railroad changed everything. When the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway
pushed into the coalfields in the 1870s, and when the Norfolk and Western followed into the southern fields in the 1880s, the
transformation of the Appalachian mountains from subsistence farming country into industrial extraction zones began with
the speed and thoroughness of a force of nature. The coal companies bought or leased mineral rights from families who often
didn't fully understand what they were signing. Company towns appeared where farmsteads had stood. The company store
replaced the family's self-sufficient economy with a cash-wage and scrip economy that kept miners permanently indebted. The
forests that had sustained subsistence families for generations were clear-cut to provide mine timbers and railroad ties and
charcoal for iron furnaces. The creeks that had been clean and full of fish were choked with coal slack and mine drainage. The
mountains that Fighting Bill had known as a young man — when you could look from a ridge top and see nothing but forest
to the horizon — were being remade as an industrial colony of northeastern capital. Fighting Bill lived to see the beginning of
this. He died in 1897, before the great mine labor wars that would follow in the first decades of the 20th century — before
Blair Mountain (1921), before the Baldwin-Felts detective agency's most notorious violence, before the full catastrophe of the
industrial extraction economy played out. But he saw enough to know that the world was changing in ways that the mountain
communities had not chosen and could not control. He was buried in the Riffe Cemetery, Wyoming County, West Virginia —
the family's signature on that specific corner of the mountain landscape. The cemetery says: we were here. We mattered. We
are not going away. Nineteenth-century West Virginia — the architectural and landscape world in which William "Fighting

Bill" Riffe lived his remarkable 93-year life. He was born into a frontier subsistence community and died watching the
industrial transformation of the mountains he had known. (Getty Images) ✦ ✦ ✦ P a r t F o u r Greenup County, Kentucky
Chapters 6–7 C H A P T E R S I X Kentucky — The Family's American Heart (Greenup County) The Place Itself If the
Riffe family has a spiritual home in America — the place that, more than any other, holds the family's deepest roots in
American soil — it is Greenup County, Kentucky. Established in 1803 (the year Fighting Bill Riffe was born, as if by historical
coincidence), Greenup County occupies the northeastern corner of Kentucky where the state meets the Ohio River across
from Lawrence and Scioto counties of Ohio. It is a world that straddles the border between river-bottom life and mountain
life, between the broad flat commerce of the Ohio River and the tight, folded geology of the Appalachian foothills pressing in
from every direction. Picture it in the 19th century, before the roads were paved and the strip mines altered the ridgelines:
forested ridges dropping steeply to narrow creek hollows, the hollows widening as they descended toward the river, the creek
bottoms opening into small flats of rich bottomland where gardens and tobacco patches occupied every acre of level ground.
In autumn, the hills turned every shade of red, orange, gold, and brown — the maples going crimson, the hickories gold, the
oaks maintaining their russet brown well into November. In spring, the creek bottoms flooded — the creeks rising out of their
banks, spreading brown water across the bottomland, depositing the rich silt that would feed another season's garden. In
summer, the hollows were green tunnels of humidity, the lightning bugs rising out of the grass at dusk in a silent fireworks
show. In winter, snow sealed the ridge roads and the community contracted to the creek-bottom world, neighbors closer by
necessity. The great Ohio River — boundary between Kentucky and Ohio, artery of 19thcentury American commerce — was
visible from the northern ridges. Flatboats, keelboats, and later steamboats moved up and down its broad brown current. The
river was both boundary and connection: it separated Kentucky from Ohio but also linked them, carrying commerce and
people and, eventually, the Riffe family across its width as the 20th century's economic pressures drove them northward. The
Iron Economy Greenup County's 19th-century economy was shaped by iron. The region's hillsides contained outcroppings of
iron ore, and the surrounding forests provided charcoal for the furnaces. A string of iron furnaces operated in the county
through the first half of the 19th century — using the county's ore, its timber, its water power, and its labor — and the rivers
carried the finished iron northward to the markets of Cincinnati and Pittsburgh. The ironworker's life was brutal and
communal: the roar and heat of the blast furnace, the physical danger of the molten metal, the round-the-clock operation that
a furnace's economics demanded, the camaraderie of men who worked together in extreme conditions. As Pittsburgh's
Bessemer steel furnaces came online in the second half of the 19th century and made charcoal-iron production economically
obsolete, the Greenup County iron industry collapsed. The furnaces went cold. The men who had worked them shifted to
whatever the economy offered next: coal mining in the hills behind the county, timber harvesting, river commerce, and —
increasingly — the factory towns of the Ohio River north bank, where Portsmouth and its neighboring industrial cities offered
wages that Kentucky's subsistence economy could not match. The Riffe Family Cemeteries — York, Greenup County The
most eloquent documents the Riffe family left in Greenup County are not census records or court filings. They are the two
family cemeteries at York: the Riffe Family Cemetery and the Riffe Zion Ridge Cemetery. These burial grounds, carved into
the ridgetop landscape of the York community, are the family's most permanent statement of presence and identity. The Zion
Ridge Cemetery's name is itself a theological claim. "Zion" in the Hebrew scriptures is the holy mountain — the high place
where God dwells, the promised homeland, the destination of the long journey. When the Appalachian Baptist community
named their ridge cemetery "Zion Ridge," they were asserting that this specific piece of Kentucky ground was their holy
mountain — their promised place, the destination of everything that had come before. The German Palatine and Scots-Irish
streams that had traveled for a century and across an ocean to find this ridge had, in naming their cemetery Zion, declared that
the journey was over. This was the place. This was home. The Ohio River, c. 1840 — the great waterway that defined the
world of Greenup County, Kentucky, where the Riffe family established their American home. The river was boundary,
highway, and economic artery. W.S. Riffe worked in Ohio; his body came home to Kentucky ground for burial. (Heritage
Images/Getty Images) The Annual Cemetery Cleaning In the Appalachian community tradition, the cemetery cleaning — held

once a year, typically in late summer — was among the most important communal gatherings of the year. The entire extended
family came: those who still lived nearby and those who had moved away to Ohio or Indiana or beyond, all returning to the
home ground for the annual ritual of memory and maintenance. The grass around the graves was cut and cleared. Fresh
flowers were planted. Headstones that had settled or toppled were straightened. The names carved in stone — names that
might be known only from family stories to the youngest generation — were read aloud, and the stories attached to those
names circulated once more through the assembled family. After the work was done, there was food. The cemetery cleaning
was also a reunion feast: spread on wagon tailgates and blankets near the graves, the food of the community — deviled eggs,
fried chicken, corn bread, stack cake, pinto beans, pickled beets, apple butter — the specific foods of the Appalachian
foodways tradition. The cemetery cleaning was where the living came to remember the dead and, in doing so, to remind
themselves who they were. For the Riffe family, gathering at York, Greenup County, the cemetery cleaning was an affirmation:
we are Riffes, we are from here, and we belong to each other. Willard Shields "W.S." Riffe and Maime "Minnie" Fritz Riffe
Willard Shields Riffe — known as W.S. — was Penny Sue Riffe-Goble's greatgrandfather. He was born in the 19th century in
the Greenup County community, part of the established Riffe presence in that corner of Kentucky. He married Maime
"Minnie" Fritz Riffe — whose Fritz surname may represent another Pennsylvania German thread in the family's heritage, the
Fritz name being common in the German Palatine communities of Pennsylvania and Virginia. W.S. and Minnie had at least
three known children: Arnold Cloyd (born 1906, the subject of the next chapter), Willard Jr., and others whose documentation
requires further Ancestry.com research. The family followed the pattern of the Appalachian border community: living in
Kentucky, working in Ohio. W.S. Riffe died in Portsmouth, Ohio, in 1941 — Portsmouth being the large industrial city on the
Ohio side of the river, directly across from the Kentucky hills where the family had its roots. But he was buried in the Riffe
Zion Ridge Cemetery at York, Greenup County, Kentucky. The pattern is instructive: a man crosses the Ohio River to find
work in the industrial economy. He lives and works and eventually dies in Ohio. But his family brings his body home across the
river to Kentucky for burial. Ohio was where you worked. Kentucky was where you belonged. The cemetery was the final
proof of that distinction — the place where the body returned to the ground it had always intended to return to. The Fritz
Family — A Possible German Palatine Connection Maime "Minnie" Fritz Riffe carried the Fritz surname — a name with deep
German Palatine roots. Fritz is a common German surname derived from the given name Friedrich (Frederick), meaning
"peaceful ruler." The Fritz name appears frequently in the Pennsylvania German communities of the 18th century and in the
Appalachian communities that descended from them. If Minnie Fritz's family was of German Palatine origin — which her
surname strongly suggests — then the union of W.S. Riffe and Minnie Fritz brought together two Palatine German
Appalachian families, reinforcing rather than diluting the German heritage already present in the Riffe line. Further research
into the Fritz family is a high priority; see Appendix E. ✦ ✦ ✦ C H A P T E R S E V E N Arnold Cloyd Riffe — A Life Cut
Short (1906–1935) This chapter carries the weight of loss that runs through every family's history. It is written with the full
human gravity that Arnold Cloyd Riffe's brief life deserves — not melodrama, but honest acknowledgment of what it means
when a man dies at twenty-nine and leaves three children in the worst economic crisis in American history. Birth — Lewis
County, Kentucky (March 31, 1906) Arnold Cloyd Riffe was born on March 31, 1906, in Lewis County, Kentucky — a county
that lies just west of Greenup County along the Ohio River, a continuation of the same river-and-ridge landscape that the
Riffe family had inhabited for decades. Lewis County in 1906 was quiet, rural, agricultural — tobacco and corn country, the
Ohio River visible from the northern hills, the county seat of Vanceburg a small market town where farmers brought their
produce and their legal business on Saturday mornings. Arnold was born into a world that still retained much of the 19th
century's character: one-room schoolhouses, church communities as the primary social institution, the rhythms of planting and
harvest governing the year. He was the son of W.S. Riffe and Minnie Fritz Riffe — a child of the established Riffe presence in
northeastern Kentucky, growing up with a sense of who he was and where he came from. The Riffe name meant something in
Lewis and Greenup counties. It meant presence, continuity, identity. His childhood was shaped by the particular pleasures and
privations of rural Appalachian Kentucky in the early 20th century: swimming in the creek hollows in summer, gathering

chestnuts in the fall before the blight destroyed the great chestnut forests of the eastern United States in the 1910s (a loss so
total that an entire generation experienced it as the disappearance of a familiar and beloved presence from the landscape),
learning to farm alongside his father, attending the community church, navigating the complex social world of a small rural
county where everyone was related to everyone else by blood or marriage or both. Growing Up Riffe To grow up a Riffe in
Greenup and Lewis counties in the early 20th century was to grow up embedded in a specific identity. The family cemeteries
on the ridge were not merely graveyards — they were documents, genealogies in stone, proof that the family had been here for
as long as anyone could remember and intended to remain. Arnold grew up knowing the family stories: where the name came
from, who had come before, what the family had survived. He grew up knowing that he was part of something that extended
in both directions from his own brief moment in the world — backward into the mountains and the Pennsylvania Dutch
country and the Rhineland beyond, and forward into the children he would one day have. As he entered adulthood, the
automobile was transforming American life even in the rural counties of Kentucky. The first cars appeared on county roads.
The oneroom schoolhouse was giving way to consolidated schools. Radio was beginning to connect the isolated rural
communities to the broader national culture. Arnold Cloyd Riffe came of age in the transitional world between the old
Appalachian rural life and the emerging 20th-century industrial world — a world that required a man to move, to cross the
river, to follow the wages wherever they led. Marriage to Lu Bertie Logan Cole He married Lu Bertie Logan Cole — born
1910, Lewis County, Kentucky. Two Appalachian families joining in the pattern that had repeated for generations: families who
had known each other through the church community, through shared neighbors, through the overlapping social world of the
creek-hollow county, coming together in the marriage of their children. Lu Bertie Logan Cole carried two family names —
Logan and Cole — that represent their own Appalachian heritage threads, the Logan name carrying Scots-Irish resonance and
the Cole name widespread through Appalachian Kentucky and Virginia. Arnold and Lu Bertie followed the border
community's established pattern: across the Ohio River to Scioto County, Ohio, where the industrial towns of the north bank
— Portsmouth, New Boston, Lucasville — offered wages that Lewis County's agricultural economy could not match. They
settled in Porter Township, Scioto County, Ohio, in the early 1930s — a couple in their twenties with young children, trying to
make a life in a world that was systematically coming apart around them. The Great Depression in the Ohio Valley — May
1935 To understand what Arnold Cloyd Riffe's death meant, you must understand what the Ohio Valley in 1935 actually was: a
landscape of compressed catastrophe. The Great Depression had been grinding for six years. The shoe factories of
Portsmouth — once among the most productive in the world — had cut their workforces to a fraction of previous capacity.
The steel foundries were operating at half-speed or less. Men lined up in the mornings outside factory gates hoping for day
labor. Gardens in every backyard and vacant lot had been expanded beyond anything peacetime prosperity would have
required, because the garden was often the difference between eating and not eating. The extended family networks that had
always been the Appalachian community's social safety net were stretched to their limits — every aunt with a spare room had
someone sleeping in it, every cousin with a garden row had someone helping tend it in exchange for a share of the produce.
For Arnold Cloyd Riffe, a man in his late twenties with three children — Edna Mae, Estil Elwood, and baby Faye Ellen, barely
a year old — the Depression was not an abstract economic concept. It was a daily reality of compressed choices and
compressed options. The specific nature of Arnold's work in Porter Township is not documented, but the context tells us
what his world looked like: a man trying to provide for a young family in a county where work was scarce, wages were falling,
and the constant low-grade anxiety of economic insecurity was as much a feature of daily life as the weather. "He died at
twenty-nine. His youngest child was barely one year old. The Depression was in its sixth year. The Ohio River was a quarter-
mile away. And the woman he left behind had twenty-five years of life ahead of her, and three children, and no safety net
except her own character." — Arnold Cloyd Riffe (1906–1935) and Lu Bertie Logan Cole Riffe (1910–1984) Death at Twenty-
Nine — May 12, 1935 Arnold Cloyd Riffe died on May 12, 1935, in Porter Township, Scioto County, Ohio. He was twenty-
nine years old — twenty-nine years, one month, and twelve days, to be precise. The specific cause of his death is not currently
documented in the available records, but the period provides grim context: tuberculosis was still claiming young adults in the

Ohio Valley with brutal regularity in the 1930s; pneumonia could kill a healthy man in a week in an era before antibiotics;
industrial accidents and work injuries — the daily hazards of the physical labor that formed the economic backbone of the
river towns — were endemic. Whatever took Arnold Cloyd Riffe from this world, it took him young, and the loss reverberated
through the lives of everyone who came after him. Consider what his death meant in practical terms. Lu Bertie was twenty-five
years old. Edna Mae was a young child. Estil Elwood was a young child. Faye Ellen was barely one year old — young enough
that she would have no memory of her father at all. There was no Social Security in May 1935 — the Social Security Act was
not signed until August 1935. There was no state welfare system of meaningful scale. There was no life insurance for a
working-class man in Porter Township, Ohio. There was the church, the family network, the extended community of
Appalachian migrants in Scioto County, and Lu Bertie's own character. That was the entire safety net. The Return to Kentucky
Ground Arnold Cloyd Riffe was carried back across the Ohio River and buried in the Riffe Family Cemetery at York, Greenup
County, Kentucky — the same ground where his ancestors lay. This final journey across the river is one of the most eloquent
statements in the entire Riffe family history. He had crossed the river alive, following the wages northward as his family had
done for decades. He came home to Kentucky in death. Whatever Ohio had offered him — employment, wages, a life in the
industrial world — it had not made him an Ohioan. He was a Kentucky Riffe. The cemetery at York was his home ground,
and it received him at the end. Arnold Cloyd Riffe — Documented Facts Item Record Birth March 31, 1906 · Lewis County,
Kentucky Parents Willard Shields "W.S." Riffe and Maime "Minnie" Fritz Riffe Wife Lu Bertie Logan Cole (b. 1910, Lewis
County, Kentucky) Children Edna Mae Riffe · Estil Elwood Riffe · Faye Ellen Riffe (b. c. 1934) Residence at death Porter
Township, Scioto County, Ohio Death May 12, 1935 · Age 29 · Cause: not yet documented Burial Riffe Family Cemetery ·
York, Greenup County, Kentucky Relationship to Penny Paternal grandfather of Penny Sue Riffe-Goble Lu Bertie — The
Hidden Hero Lu Bertie Logan Cole Riffe is the hidden hero of this chapter and one of the hidden heroes of the entire Riffe
family history. She lived from 1910 to 1984 — nearly fifty years after Arnold's death. She was widowed at twenty-five. She
raised three children through the remainder of the Great Depression, through World War II, through the postwar boom, and
into the mid-1980s. She did it alone, and she did it in the tradition of Appalachian women going back to the mountain
communities of the 18th century — without complaint, without the luxury of surrender, with the fierce pragmatic love that
says: I cannot fix what has happened, but I can make sure these children eat and are loved and become people who can stand
on their own ground. The daily choices that constitute survival over fifty years of widowhood are invisible in the documentary
record — they don't appear in census columns or court filings. But they were real, and they mattered. Every morning Lu
Bertie rose and got her children fed and sent them toward their futures, and she did it without a husband and without a safety
net and without anyone telling her she was remarkable. She was. She is. And her son Rinfrod L. Riffe — the grandfather of
Shane and Zac — was shaped by watching her do it. ▸ Lu Bertie Logan Cole Riffe's survival story parallels that of Carman E.

P T E R E I G H T Rinfrod L. Riffe — Shane and Zac's Maternal Grandfather A Name Unlike Any Other Rinfrod. Let the
name sit for a moment. It is not a common name. It is not found in the standard books of American given names. It does not
appear in the Biblical tradition. It is not a president's name or a saint's name or a celebrity's name. It is, in the truest possible
sense, a Riffe name — a name that exists in this family and possibly in this family alone, invented or adapted by parents who
wanted to give their child something that was unmistakably, irreducibly his own. This is quintessentially Appalachian creative
naming practice. In the mountain communities of the 19th and early 20th centuries, where the same dozen surnames — Riffe,
Potter, Cole, Logan, Blair, Webb, Justice — repeated across generation after generation of intermarried families, and where the
same first names (William, John, James, Mary, Elizabeth, Sarah) similarly recurred, the desire to give a child a distinctive name
was understandable and common. The solution: invent one. Draw on family surnames used as given names. Compress two
admired names together. Adapt a sound or syllable from a grandmother's maiden name. Create something that will be entirely
your child's own in a world where everything else — surname, county, church, occupation — was shared with cousins and

neighbors and second cousins twice removed. "Rinfrod" sounds, to modern ears, like a compressed compound: "Rin-" from
some family name, "-frod" perhaps related to the Germanic "fred" (peace) — as in Alfred, Manfred, Wilfred. Or perhaps it is a
purely invented construct, assembled for the sound of it, the way that Appalachian parents occasionally named their children
for the sheer music of the syllables. Whatever its origin, it is a name that says: this child is one of a kind. This is Rinfrod L.
Riffe, and there is no one else by that name in the world. Growing Up in the Shadow of Loss Rinfrod L. Riffe grew up in the
aftermath of his father Arnold's 1935 death. Given Arnold's death date and Rinfrod's relationship to Penny (born 1961),
Rinfrod was likely born in the late 1920s or early 1930s — which means he was very young when Arnold died, possibly a
toddler, possibly not yet born (depending on his exact birth year, which requires primary source confirmation). He may be one
of Arnold's three documented children — Edna Mae, Estil Elwood, Faye Ellen — or a child not yet documented in the
available records. This is a research gap that Ancestry.com work should resolve. What is certain is the world he grew up in:
raised by Lu Bertie Logan Cole Riffe, in the Porter Township area of Scioto County, Ohio, in the depths of the Great
Depression and through the difficult years that followed. Growing up fatherless in 1930s Appalachian Ohio meant growing up
quickly. It meant understanding early that the world did not automatically provide for you, that the people who loved you were
doing everything they could, and that your job was to be worthy of that effort. It also meant growing up shaped by a mother
whose character — Lu Bertie's forty-nine years of quiet heroism — was the primary model of adult behavior available to him.
The World He Came Of Age In Rinfrod's formative years coincided with the most dramatic sequence of events in 20th-
century American history: the end of the Depression, followed immediately by World War II, followed by the postwar boom
that transformed American working-class life with unprecedented speed. The Ohio Valley in the 1940s — flush with wartime
production and then with peacetime prosperity — was a very different world from the Depression-era poverty of the 1930s.
The shoe factories of Portsmouth ran full shifts. The steel foundries produced. Wages rose. The GI Bill opened higher
education and homeownership to men who would never have imagined either before the war. The Riffe family, like hundreds
of thousands of Appalachian Ohio families, participated in this transformation. They moved northward — from the Scioto
County river towns toward Columbus — following the labor market and the social mobility that the postwar economy briefly
made available to working-class families who had the energy and the will to pursue it. Penny's Father Rinfrod L. Riffe fathered
Penny Sue Riffe — born November 22, 1961, at Grant Hospital in Columbus, Ohio. By 1961, the family had made the journey
that hundreds of thousands of Appalachian families made in the postwar decades: northward from the Scioto County river
communities to Columbus, the state capital and Ohio's largest city, following the jobs and the opportunities that the city
offered. Columbus in 1961 was a growing, prosperous, postwar industrial city — automobile manufacturing, steel, rubber,
food processing — and it offered wages and stability that the depopulating river counties of southern Ohio no longer could.
The Logan and Cole family threads that Lu Bertie brought into the Riffe line through her own heritage — the Logan name
carrying probable Scots-Irish origin, the Cole name widespread through Appalachian Kentucky and Virginia — await their
own chapter of research. They are documented in Appendix C as a priority for future investigation. Research Priorities —

Appalachia Grant Hospital, November 22, 1961 She arrived on a Thursday morning — November 22, 1961 — at Grant
Hospital on the east side of Columbus, Ohio. The year: John F. Kennedy's first year in the White House. America was at the
height of its postwar confidence. The space race was accelerating toward its lunar destination. The Civil Rights Movement was
gathering the momentum that would reshape the nation. And in a maternity ward in Columbus, Ohio, a girl came into the
world whose surname was Riffe and whose astrological natal chart placed her Sun, Moon, and Mercury simultaneously in the

sign of Scorpio — a configuration that would take three hundred years of family history to fully explain. There is a somber
historical resonance to her birthday. November 22, 1963 — two years later, on her second birthday — President Kennedy was
assassinated in Dallas, Texas. For the rest of her life, the anniversary of her birth would share its date with one of the defining
tragedies of 20th-century American history. For a triple Scorpio — whose sign governs death and transformation, the hidden
costs of power, the weight of what cannot be changed — this coincidence of dates carries a particular weight. Not as
superstition, but as a marker of the world she was born into: a world of great promise and great shadow simultaneously. The
Great Appalachian Migration Penny's birth in Columbus was not a coincidence of geography. It was the destination of a
journey that had been building for decades. The postwar internal migration of Appalachian families to Ohio's cities was one of
the largest and least-documented population movements in 20th-century American history. Beginning in the late 1930s and
accelerating through the 1940s and 1950s, hundreds of thousands of families from eastern Kentucky, West Virginia,
southwestern Virginia, and the Appalachian counties of Ohio moved northward — to Columbus, to Cleveland, to Dayton, to
Akron, to Cincinnati — following the industrial jobs that the cities offered and fleeing the poverty and lack of opportunity
that the coal economy's decline had inflicted on the mountain communities. These families — called Appalachian migrants,
often called much less respectful things by the urban residents who received them — were not rootless or desperate. They
were a specific cultural community with a specific heritage, making a rational economic decision within the context of an
economy that had systematically stripped their home communities of their economic base. They brought their culture with
them: their music, their food, their church communities, their family networks, their particular understanding of what loyalty
and community meant. The Appalachian community in Columbus in the 1950s and 1960s was large, tight-knit, and largely
invisible to the broader city — occupying specific neighborhoods on the south and east sides, maintaining their traditions,
staying connected to the family networks that extended southward to Kentucky and West Virginia. Penny Sue Riffe grew up in
this world. She was nominally a Columbus girl — born at Grant Hospital, resident of the city from birth. But she was formed
in the Appalachian tradition: the food, the church, the music, the particular quality of family loyalty and community solidarity
that the mountain culture had been producing for generations. Appalachian Identity in Columbus The Appalachian
community in Columbus maintained its cultural identity with a stubbornness that was itself a cultural inheritance. They cooked
the specific foods of the Appalachian tradition — cornbread baked in cast iron (never sweet, never with sugar — that was a
northern aberration), pinto beans cooked long with fatback, fried potatoes, creasy greens gathered in spring, stack cake built in
the mountains-of-Kentucky tradition. They listened to country music and bluegrass when the city's cultural establishment had
not yet decided those were respectable forms. They attended small Baptist and Pentecostal churches where the emotional
directness of the worship tradition was undiluted by urban sophistication. They visited relatives in Kentucky and West Virginia
on weekends and holidays, maintaining the family networks that were the community's social infrastructure. Penny absorbed all
of this. She grew up knowing who she was — a Riffe, from the Appalachian tradition — even if the mountains themselves
were far away. The mountains were present in the kitchen, in the church, in the music, in the quality of stubbornness and
loyalty and emotional depth that her family carried forward from the Kentucky ridge into the Columbus neighborhood.
Meeting Kevin Goble At some point — the specific circumstances await the family's own confirming memory — Penny Sue
Riffe met Robert Kevin Goble, born July 20, 1962, at Grant Hospital, Columbus, Ohio. Their union brought together two of
the most historically complex family lines in the American ancestral record: the Riffe Appalachian heritage on Penny's side,

carrying the English colonial line documented in Volume I and the Acadian French LeCompte heritage documented in
Volume II. Together they made a family that is, in the most literal genetic and cultural sense, a summary of America's most
significant ancestral streams: English colonial, Acadian French, and Appalachian German-Scots-Irish. Shane and Zac Goble
carry all of it. Mother of Two — The Next Generation Zachary "Zac" Goble was born in July 1987 at Grant Hospital,

S i x The Revolutionary War Connection Chapter 10 C H A P T E R T E N The Fighting Captain — Henry Connelly (Conley)
and the Appalachian Warrior Tradition Source Note — Captain Henry Connelly The information in this chapter derives from
a document prepared by Cheryl Conley Bolden, sourced from WikiTree, dated April 1, 2023. The specific genealogical
connection between Captain Connelly and the Goble family's Riffe/Logan/Cole network requires further primary source
documentation via Ancestry.com. This chapter presents the documented history of Captain Connelly while flagging that the
specific genealogical link to the Goble family is under active research. See Appendix D for full research priorities. Captain of a
Hundred Men In 1777 — the second year of the American Revolution, when the outcome was still deeply uncertain and the
British military machine still seemed overwhelmingly powerful — Captain Henry Connelly was given command of a cavalry
unit of one hundred men. His primary mission was suppressing Tory activity in the Carolina highlands: specifically targeting a
man named Fanning, born Johnston County, North Carolina in 1754, who had made himself infamous by murdering patriots,
burning their houses, and — most spectacularly — capturing the Governor of North Carolina and turning him over to the
British. This was not a gentleman's war of formal exchanges and rules of engagement. It was close, personal, and brutal —
neighbor against neighbor in the Carolina and Virginia highlands, where Tory and Patriot families lived in the same
communities, knew each other's names and children, and chose to kill each other anyway. Captain Connelly commanded his
cavalry in this world, tracking Tory guerrillas through the same mountain landscape that the Riffe and Potter families were
simultaneously farming and fighting to defend. The Battle of Cowpens — January 17, 1781 Captain Henry Connelly's most
famous engagement was one of the most brilliantly executed battles in the entire American Revolution: the Battle of
Cowpens, fought on January 17, 1781, outside what is now Spartanburg, South Carolina. The document describing Connelly's
service calls Cowpens "the beginning of the end of British rule" in America — and historians have largely agreed with this
assessment. The battle was General Daniel Morgan's masterpiece. Morgan faced a force of British regulars and Loyalist cavalry
under the formidable Lieutenant Colonel Banastre Tarleton — "Bloody Tarleton," whose reputation for ruthlessness had
made him the most feared British officer in the southern campaign. Morgan had a mixed force: Continental Army regulars,
Virginia and Carolina militia (notoriously unreliable in open battle), and cavalry. The conventional wisdom said that militia
would not stand against trained British regulars — and Tarleton planned his attack on exactly that assumption. Morgan turned
the militia's characteristic behavior into a weapon. He placed them in front, told them to fire two volleys and then — crucially
— to retreat in an organized manner behind the Continentals. Tarleton, seeing the militia appear to retreat, assumed the
Americans were breaking and pressed his attack — exactly as Morgan had planned. The militia retreated in order, the
Continentals held their ground, and then the American cavalry — including Captain Connelly's unit — swung around both
British flanks in a double envelopment. The British force was trapped between the rallied militia coming from one direction
and the Continental regulars from another, with the cavalry sealing their escape. In less than an hour, the battl

e was over: Tarleton's force was effectively destroyed, with over 800 men killed or captured against American losses of around
75. Tarleton himself barely escaped with his life. The Battle of Cowpens, January 17, 1781 — Captain Henry Connelly's finest

hour. General Daniel Morgan's tactical masterpiece destroyed Tarleton's force in under an hour, turning the tide of the
southern campaign. (Buyenlarge/Getty Images) Captain Connelly was at Cowpens. His cavalry was part of the envelopment
that made Morgan's plan work. He was there, in the frozen January fields outside Spartanburg, on the day that changed the
trajectory of American independence. "The Old Man Is a Dutchman" In 1833, Captain Henry Connelly — now an old man
— applied for and was awarded a Revolutionary War veteran's pension. The attorney who prepared his pension papers, Henry
C. Harris, added a note that has survived in the historical record and that is, for the purposes of this volume, one of the most
illuminating documents we have: "The old man is a Dutchman, and when I made out his statement, I could scarcely
understand everything he said." This is extraordinary. A man who fought for American independence in 1777 — who
commanded cavalry at Cowpens in 1781 — still spoke in 1833 with such a heavy German accent that his own attorney could
barely understand him. "Dutchman" here means "Deutsch" — German. Captain Connelly was of German heritage, a
Pennsylvania German or Rhineland-Palatinate German immigrant or the son of one, who went to war for an America he
believed in so deeply that he risked his life for it — and who, fifty-six years later, still carried Germany in his voice. This
connects Captain Connelly directly to the same cultural world as the Riffe family. The Pennsylvania German / Rhineland
Palatinate community was large and geographically widespread in the late 18th century, and the number of German-
background individuals who served in the Revolutionary War — in both the Continental Army and the militia — was
significant. The cultural overlap between the Connelly community and the Riffe community, in the same Appalachian
Kentucky geography, is complete. Hager Hill, Kentucky — The Appalachian Settlement After the Revolution, Captain
Connelly moved his family from North Carolina to Hager Hill, Johnson County, Kentucky — on the Big Sandy River, which
forms the border between eastern Kentucky and West Virginia. Johnson County lies in the heart of the Appalachian Kentucky
coalfield country — adjacent to Lawrence County and not far from Greenup County, where the Riffe family had its deepest
American roots. Captain Connelly was settling into the same cultural and geographic world as the Riffe family — the
northeastern Kentucky river country where German Palatine and Scots-Irish families had been building their communities for
decades. After his first wife Ann died, Captain Connelly married Temperance Blair Hitchcock — the Blair name carrying its
own Appalachian Scots-Irish resonance. The Blair family is documented throughout the Appalachian Kentucky and Virginia
communities, often associated with the Scots-Irish Presbyterian tradition. Sidebar: Loretta Lynn, Crystal Gayle, and the
Connelly-Appalachian Musical Heritage Captain Henry Connelly is documented as the maternal fourth great-grandfather of
two of American country music's most iconic artists: Loretta Lynn (born Loretta Webb, 1932, Butcher Hollow, Johnson
County, Kentucky) and her younger sister Crystal Gayle (born Brenda Gail Webb, 1951, Paintsville, Johnson County,
Kentucky). Both were born in the same Johnson County where Captain Connelly settled after the Revolution — less than a
century and a half after his arrival in the Big Sandy River country. This connection is significant for the Goble family for a
reason that goes beyond celebrity. It confirms that the Connelly-Appalachian Kentucky cultural world — the same world the
Riffe family inhabited — is the world that produced American country music. The ballad tradition, the fiddle tradition, the
musical narrative intelligence of the Appalachian communities that the Riffe and Potter and Logan and Cole families were part
of: this is where country music came from. When Penny Sue Riffe-Goble hears a country song — really hears it, in the way
that something resonates in the bones before the mind processes it — she is hearing her own heritage. The mountains are
speaking. They always were. Note: The genealogical documentation of the Loretta Lynn / Crystal Gayle Connelly connection
comes from the same WikiTree-sourced document (Cheryl Conley Bolden, 4/1/2023) that provides the Captain Connelly
information. It is offered here as documented family history of the Connelly line, pending confirmation of the specific
genealogical link to the GobleRiffe family. The Presbyterian-to-Baptist Shift Captain Connelly's religious trajectory is perfectly
representative of the Appalachian frontier experience. He was Presbyterian in North Carolina — the natural religious home of
a Scots-Irish or German Reformed man in the colonial South. When he moved to Kentucky, he became Baptist. This was not
apostasy or casual religious drift. It was a response to the structural realities of the frontier. The Presbyterian church required
an educated, ordained clergy — ministers trained at established seminaries. On the Kentucky frontier, there were no

seminaries. The supply of ordained Presbyterian ministers was entirely inadequate to the demand of the frontier population.
The Baptist church, by contrast, operated on a model of lay preaching: any man whom the congregation recognized as called
by God could preach, baptize, and administer the Lord's Supper. The Baptist emphasis on personal conversion experience, on
the direct encounter with the divine that needed no priestly intermediary, was perfectly suited to the frontier community's
individualist character and its geographic isolation from established ecclesiastical structures. The frontier stripped away the
formal Presbyterian structure; the Baptist tradition replaced it with something more immediate, more emotionally direct, and
more suited to the mountain life. The Riffe family made this same transition — from the German Reformed tradition of the
Pennsylvania Palatine community to the Baptist tradition of the Appalachian frontier. The church changed; the faith deepened.
The mountain communities found in Baptist worship an emotional intensity that matched the intensity of the lives they lived.

What the Mountains Made — Appalachian Culture as Family Inheritance The Riffe family's Appalachian heritage is not merely
a geographical fact — a matter of where the family happened to live across several generations. It is a living cultural
inheritance: a specific set of practices, values, aesthetic traditions, and ways of understanding the world that were formed in
the mountain communities of Virginia, West Virginia, and Kentucky and that have persisted in the family's character long after
the mountains themselves were left behind. This chapter is a portrait of that inheritance — of what the mountains made, and
what they gave to Penny Sue Riffe-Goble and through her to Shane and Zac Goble. The Ballad Tradition The most important
cultural gift that the Scots-Irish community brought to the Appalachian frontier was its music — specifically, the ballad
tradition of the Scottish-English borderlands. The ancient ballads — Child ballads, in the classification of 19th-century scholar
Francis James Child — are narrative songs of remarkable power and antiquity: Barbara Allen, with its tale of love refused and
its twin deaths; Lord Thomas and Fair Eleanor, with its triangle of desire and violence; The House Carpenter, with its
supernatural seduction and tragedy at sea; scores of others, each carrying a complete world of human experience compressed
into rhyming stanzas. These songs, maintained in the British Isles by a literate tradition of printed broadsides and manuscript
collections, were preserved on the Appalachian frontier by something more powerful than paper: the human voice, passing
from mother to daughter, from father to son, generation after generation in the mountain hollows where the songs were the
primary entertainment, the primary emotional education, and the primary vehicle for thinking about the big questions — love,
death, betrayal, loyalty, revenge, grace. The Appalachian ballad singers preserved songs that had been largely forgotten in their
country of origin, maintaining a living musical tradition that scholars in the early 20th century would travel to the mountains
specifically to document before it disappeared. It did not disappear. It transformed. The ballad tradition — maintained by
families exactly like the Riffes and Potters and Logans and Coles of northeastern Kentucky — became the foundation on
which American country music was built in the 20th century. When the Carter Family recorded their first sides for Victor
Records in Bristol, Tennessee, in 1927, they were drawing on exactly this tradition. When Bill Monroe developed bluegrass in
the 1940s, he was systematizing what the mountain music tradition had been doing informally for two centuries. When Loretta
Lynn sang about coal miners' daughters, she was singing from within the same cultural world that Captain Henry Connelly had
settled into at Hager Hill, Johnson County, Kentucky, two centuries earlier. Shape-Note Singing From the German Palatine
thread of the family — the Reiff/Riffe line and quite possibly the Fritz line as well — came a different musical tradition:
shape-note hymn singing. Shape-note notation is a musical literacy system that uses differently shaped note heads (triangle,
square, diamond, circle) to represent the four syllables of the musical scale (fa, sol, la, mi), allowing singers who cannot read
conventional musical notation to participate in harmonized four-part vocal music. The system was developed in New England
in the late 18th century, spread through the German Reformed and Lutheran communities of Pennsylvania, and then carried
southward down the Great Wagon Road into the Appalachian communities where it took deep root. Sacred Harp singing —
the most prominent surviving shape-note tradition — is still practiced throughout the American South today, particularly in
Alabama, Georgia, and Tennessee. Its sound is unlike any other choral tradition: roughedged, modal, ancient-sounding, with all
four voice parts singing simultaneously in an unaccompanied texture that fills a room with harmonic overtones and demands

the full physical commitment of every singer. It is, at its heart, a community practice — a way of making music together that
requires no professional musicians, no instruments, no trained choir director. Anyone who can read the shapes can sing.
Everyone sings. The singing is the point. Foodways — The Appalachian Table You can tell the history of the Riffe family
from what they cooked. The specific foods of the Appalachian tradition are not merely culinary preferences — they are a
direct inheritance from the frontier subsistence economy and from the specific agricultural conditions of the mountain
communities. Cornbread. Baked in cast iron. Never sweet — that sweetness is a northern innovation that Appalachian cooks
still regard with suspicion. Made from stoneground yellow or white cornmeal, mixed with buttermilk and eggs, baked in a
skillet that has been preheated in the oven until the batter sizzles when it hits the iron. The crust that forms on the bottom and
sides is the point — crackling, darkbrown, carrying the flavor of iron and heat. Corn was the staple grain of the Appalachian
frontier, and cornbread was its primary expression. Pinto beans with fatback. The mountain food that has sustained more
Appalachian families through more hard times than any other single dish. The beans cooked long — four, five, six hours —
with a piece of salt pork for flavor, until the broth thickens and the beans surrender completely into a smoky, creamy, almost
meaty pot. Served with cornbread for the soaking. This is the meal that carried the Riffe family through the Depression,
through the coalfield poverty, through the hard winters on the Kentucky ridge. Creasy greens. Watercress and other cresses
gathered wild from the creek banks in early spring — the first fresh green of the year after a winter of preserved and dried
food. The gathering of creasy greens was a seasonal event, a communal ritual, the first sign that winter was releasing its grip.
The taste: sharp, slightly bitter, unmistakably alive. Leather britches. Green beans threaded on string and hung to dry — a
preservation method that predates canning, that requires nothing but string and a dry, airy space. The dried beans,
reconstituted by long cooking in the winter months, have a concentrated, smoky flavor entirely unlike their fresh counterpart.
They are the taste of the Appalachian frontier's resourcefulness: nothing wasted, everything saved, summer extended into
winter through the simplest possible means. Stack cake. The Appalachian wedding cake — a towering structure of thin, dry
gingerbread layers separated by cooked dried-apple filling, each guest at the wedding bringing one layer as a contribution to the
bride's cake, the height of the cake indicating the number of friends and family who had contributed. Stack cake is not elegant.
It is not beautiful in the conventional sense. But it is a document of community — a literal accumulation of everyone who
showed up and brought something. Quilting The Appalachian quilt tradition is not decorative in its origins — it is functional,
social, and documentary. Quilts were necessary: warm bed coverings for mountain winters that could be brutally cold in the
drafty log cabins of the early 19th century. They were made from worn-out clothing — the good fabric cut out of a husband's
Sunday suit when the suit itself was past saving, a daughter's dress when it was too worn to mend, a grandmother's apron
when it was beyond use. Nothing was wasted. The quilt was the final transformation of every piece of fabric that had ever
passed through the family. Quilting bees were among the primary social events of the mountain community — gatherings of
women around a quilting frame in someone's parlor or on a summer porch, the conversation flowing across the frame while
fingers worked, the community's knowledge and gossip and care and counsel circulating through the assembled women. The
quilt that emerged was not merely a blanket. It was the community's collective work, and it carried in its fabric fragments the
physical memory of the family's life: the dress from the wedding, the shirt from the funeral, the apron from ten thousand
mornings at the kitchen fire. The names of Appalachian quilt patterns tell the family story: Double Wedding Ring (the
interlocking circles of marriage), Bear's Paw (the mountain wildlife that surrounded the homestead), Log Cabin (the
fundamental domestic structure of the frontier), Jacob's Ladder (the Biblical ladder from earth to heaven, the aspiration
embedded in the design). Every pattern is a piece of Appalachian cultural memory. The Church — More Than Religion In the
mountain communities, the Baptist or Methodist church was not merely a place of worship. It was the community's primary
social institution — the organization that provided everything the state did not: welfare for the poor, education for the
children, mutual aid in sickness and bereavement, the public witnessing of the events that constituted a life's legal and social
existence. You were baptized in the church. You were married in the church. Your marriage was recorded in the church
register. Your death was mourned in the church. Your body was carried from the church to the churchyard. The church was

not a Sunday obligation; it was the spine around which the community's entire life organized itself. The revival meeting — the
great outdoor or brush-arbor gathering where an itinerant preacher would spend days working through a community,
preaching morning and evening, calling sinners to conversion — was the emotional climax of the mountain church calendar.
Revival was not entertainment, though it provided the kind of intense communal emotional experience that was rare in the
isolated mountain life. Revival was the community's annual renewal — the occasion for confessions, for reconciliations, for the
public declaration of faith that sealed a person's membership in the community of the saved and the community of their
neighbors simultaneously. In the mountain Baptist and Methodist traditions, these were the same community. Oral Tradition
— The Memory of the Family In the mountain communities where books were scarce and literacy was uneven through most
of the 19th century, the oral tradition was the primary technology of memory. Family history was not written down — it was
told. On the porch in the summer evenings. Around the kitchen fire in winter. At the cemetery cleaning, where the family
gathered and the stories of the dead circulated among the living. At the quilting bee, where the community's accumulated
knowledge moved across the frame with the needle and thread. The capacity to hold and transmit a family's entire history
through spoken narrative — to know who came before, where they came from, what they did and suffered and survived —
was not a parlor accomplishment. It was a community necessity. Without the oral tradition, the family had no past. Without
the past, the family had no identity. Without identity, the family had no future worth making. The oral tradition was the chain
that connected the generations — the thing that made a community more than a random collection of individuals. "In the
Appalachian tradition, the storyteller is not an entertainer. The storyteller is the keeper of the community's memory — the
person who holds the past for everyone else, who makes sure that the dead are not forgotten and that the living know what
they are inheriting." — On the Appalachian oral tradition The "Home Place" — Identity in Landscape No concept in
Appalachian culture carries more weight than the "home place." Not "home" in the general sense — the house you live in, the
address you give people — but the home place: the specific piece of earth that defines a family's identity, the ground that the
family has worked and inhabited and loved across so many generations that the family and the land have become inseparable.
You do not merely live on the home place. You are from the home place. The distinction is everything. For the Riffe family,
the home place is the York community of Greenup County, Kentucky, and specifically the two family cemeteries on the ridge
— the Riffe Family Cemetery and the Riffe Zion Ridge Cemetery. These burial grounds are the family's home place in its most
concentrated and permanent form: the ground to which the living have returned in death, generation after generation,
asserting through the act of burial that this specific ridge is where the family belongs. W.S. Riffe died in Ohio and came home
to Kentucky for burial. Arnold Cloyd Riffe died in Ohio and came home to Kentucky for burial. The Ohio River could be
crossed for work. It could not be crossed for belonging. Belonging was in Kentucky. ▸ For the metaphysical analysis of the
