terms used throughout Volume V in language accessible to family members who are not practitioners of astrology,
numerology, or related traditions. Term Definition Anaretic (Critical) Degree The 29th degree of any zodiac sign — the final
degree before the sign changes. A planet at the anaretic degree is considered to be at its most concentrated, urgent, and intense

expression. In Shane's chart, Jupiter at 29°32' Pisces is at the anaretic degree — the maximum concentration of Piscean
wisdom at the zodiac's final Term Definition threshold. Ascendant (Rising Sign) The zodiac sign that was rising on the eastern
horizon at the exact moment of birth. The Ascendant describes the outer personality, the first impression one makes, and the
lens through which the personality expresses itself in the world. Shane's Ascendant is Leo at 16°30' — the solar, generous,
creatively authoritative outer expression. Ayanamsa The angular difference between the tropical zodiac (which begins at 0°
Aries on the spring equinox) and the sidereal zodiac (which uses the actual constellations). The Lahiri ayanamsa, used in this
volume, is currently approximately 23°51' — meaning every planet's tropical position is shifted back that amount to obtain the
Vedic sidereal position. Celtic Tree Calendar (Ogham) The ancient Irish and Celtic system of assigning trees to periods of the
year and to the people born during those periods. Each tree carries specific symbolic qualities, mythological associations, and
descriptions of personality and destiny. The system is based on the Ogham alphabet, each letter of which corresponds to a
tree. Chinese Zodiac The twelve-year cycle of Chinese cosmological tradition, each year associated with a specific animal sign
(Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Goat, Monkey, Rooster, Dog, Pig) and one of five elements (Wood, Fire,
Earth, Metal, Water). The combination of animal sign and element produces a 60-year cycle, after which the cycle repeats.
Term Definition Detriment When a planet is in the sign opposite its home sign (domicile), it is in detriment — the sign least
compatible with its natural expression. Shane's Saturn in Cancer is in detriment: Saturn (structure, discipline, boundaries) is in
the sign of emotional nurturing, where its structural qualities are most challenged. Planets in detriment must work harder to
express their gifts. Domicile When a planet is in the sign it naturally rules, it is in its domicile — its home. A planet in domicile
operates freely and fully, without the contradictions that arise from inhabiting a less compatible sign. Shane's Mercury in Virgo
is in domicile (Mercury rules Virgo); Shane's Jupiter in Pisces is in domicile (Jupiter traditionally rules Pisces). Exaltation Each
planet has one sign in which it expresses its highest quality — its exaltation. A planet in exaltation performs at maximum
quality, though not necessarily at maximum comfort (exaltation is different from domicile). Shane's Moon in Taurus is exalted
(Moon's exaltation is Taurus); Shane's Venus in Pisces is exalted (Venus's exaltation is Pisces); Shane's Mercury in Virgo is both
in domicile AND exalted — the doubly dignified Mercury. Fall When a planet is in the sign opposite its exaltation, it is in its
fall — the sign in which it is most challenged to express its highest qualities. A planet in fall is not disabled, but it requires
conscious cultivation to express well. Term Definition Haplogroup A genetic population group sharing a common ancestor,
identified through Y-chromosome DNA (paternal line) or mitochondrial DNA (maternal line) testing. Haplogroups are used in
genealogical research to identify broad ethnic and geographic origins across deep time — often tens of thousands of years.
Not yet tested for the Goble family; recommended as a future research step. Hellenistic Sect In ancient Greek and Hellenistic
astrology, every chart is classified as either diurnal (born while the Sun is above the horizon — daytime birth) or nocturnal
(born while the Sun is below the horizon — nighttime birth). This classification determines which planets are most actively
helpful (benefics) and most challenging (malefics) in the chart. Life Path In numerology, the Life Path number is calculated by
adding all digits of the birth date until a single digit (or Master Number) is reached. It is considered the most fundamental
number in a person's numerological profile — the essential assignment of the incarnation, the primary frequency of the life's
trajectory. Lot of Fortune In Hellenistic astrology, the Lot (or Part) of Fortune is a calculated point in the natal chart that
indicates where fortune and material prosperity are most naturally available to the individual. It is calculated from the
relationship between the Sun, Moon, and Ascendant. In Shane's chart, the Lot of Fortune falls in Virgo — confirming that
fortune Term Definition flows through Mercury's analytical and communicative function. Master Number In numerology, the
numbers 11, 22, and 33 are Master Numbers — they are not reduced to single digits because they carry a higher frequency
than their reduced equivalents. Master Number holders are considered to carry amplified gifts and amplified challenges. Zac's
Life Path 33 is the Master Teacher — the rarest of the three Master Numbers. Moon Sign The zodiac sign the Moon occupied
at the moment of birth. The Moon sign describes the emotional nature, inner life, instinctive responses, and the quality of
feeling that most characterizes the individual's private experience. Shane's Moon in Taurus (exalted) gives his inner emotional
life a quality of groundedness, sensory richness, and reliable stability. Nakshatra In Vedic astrology, the 360° zodiac is divided

into 27 equal segments called nakshatras, each spanning 13°20'. Each nakshatra has a ruling deity, a ruling planet, specific
symbols, and characteristic qualities. The nakshatra in which a planet falls provides a finer-grained description of that planet's
expression than the sign alone. Shane's Mercury in Magha nakshatra (the nakshatra of the ancestral spirits) is the most
significant nakshatra placement in the family constellation. Natal Chart The map of the sky at the exact moment and location
of a person's birth. The natal chart shows the positions of all planets, the Sun, the Term Definition Moon, and significant
calculated points (like the Ascendant and North Node) in the zodiac. It is the foundational document of astrological analysis.
North Node The North Node of the Moon (also called the True Node or Dragon's Head) indicates the soul's evolutionary
direction in this lifetime — the quality and experiences the individual is developing toward. The South Node (opposite the
North) indicates the qualities the individual brings from previous experience and may overrely on. Shane's North Node at
15°59' Sagittarius indicates his soul's direction toward philosophical expansion, higher learning, and cross-cultural encounter.
Planetary Dignity The condition of a planet based on its relationship to the sign it occupies. The essential dignities are:
domicile (+5 in Bonatti's system), exaltation (+4), triplicity (+3), term (+2), face (+1). Planets with no dignity score are called
"peregrine." Planets in detriment or fall score negatively. Shane's chart contains four planets with essential dignity
simultaneously — Moon exalted, Mercury doubly dignified, Venus exalted, Jupiter in domicile. Sabian Symbol A system of 360
symbolic images — one for each degree of the zodiac — channeled by clairvoyant Elsie Wheeler and organized by astrologer
Marc Edmund Jones in 1925. The Sabian Symbol for a planet's degree provides an intuitive, imagistic description of the
quality of that degree. Shane's 5° Aries Sabian Symbol is "A Term Definition Triangle with Wings" — synthesis given the
capacity for flight. Sun Sign The zodiac sign the Sun occupied at the moment of birth — the most widely known element of
Western astrology. The Sun sign describes the core identity, the essential self, and the quality of the individual's fundamental
life force. It is the sign most people refer to when they say "I am a Scorpio" or "I am a Cancer." Tzolkin The 260-day sacred
calendar of the ancient Mayan civilization, consisting of 20 day signs combined with 13 galactic tones, producing 260 unique
day-sign/tone combinations before the cycle repeats. The Tzolkin was used for divination, ceremonial timing, and the
characterization of individuals born on specific calendar days. Appendix E Consolidated Bibliography — All Five Volumes

and English Roots 2.1 Meaning and Etymology The surname Goble is classified by etymologists primarily as a metonymic
occupational surname — that is, a family name derived from an object associated with a person's trade or profession, rather
than from a personal characteristic or place of origin. The name derives from the Old French word gobel, meaning a "drinking
vessel" or "cup," and was applied to craftsmen who made, sold, or were otherwise associated with goblets and drinking cups

during the medieval period. This class of craft was economically significant in medieval English market towns, and the name
would have been a recognizable professional identifier in its time. A secondary, equally documented origin traces the name to
the Germanized form Göbel, itself a short form or diminutive of the Old High German personal name Godebert — a
compound of the elements god ("good" or "God") and beraht ("bright" or "famous"). In this derivation, Goble functions as a
patronymic surname — one derived from an ancestor's personal name — and would have been carried into England by
Germanic settlers, particularly in the periods following the Norman Conquest (1066) and subsequent waves of continental
European immigration. This German origin explains the surname's presence in Pennsylvania Dutch country and the American
Midwest, where German immigrant communities anglicized names like Göbel to Goble, Gobble, or Gabel. In English records,
the name appears most consistently in southern England, particularly in the counties of West Sussex, Surrey, and Kent —
areas with a long history of French and Flemish cultural influence due to their proximity to the English Channel. The Goble
family of Westergate, near Aldingbourne in West Sussex, represents the most thoroughly documented English origin of the
American Goble line. 2.2 Geographic Distribution In England, the Goble name was concentrated in the Aldingbourne parish
area of West Sussex through the 16th and 17th centuries. Following the emigration of Thomas Goble to Massachusetts in the
1630s, the American line proliferated through New England, then spread south and west through New Jersey, Pennsylvania,
Maryland, and ultimately into the Ohio Valley by the early 19th century. In the United States today, the Goble surname is most
common in Ohio, Indiana, and other Great Lakes states — a direct legacy of the westward migration described in Section 4 of
this report. 2.3 Name Variants and Related Surnames Variant Language / Origin Geographic Association Notes Goble Old

Westergate, near Aldingbourne, West Sussex, England — a small rural parish in the coastal lowlands of southern England,
within sight of the English Channel. [VERIFIED] His father was William Goble II (born approximately 1550, Westergate),
and his mother was Alice Legard (born approximately 1552). The Goble family had been established in the Westergate-

America at approximately the peak of the Puritan Great Migration — the period between 1629 and 1640 during which
approximately 20,000 English Puritans crossed the Atlantic to escape religious persecution under Charles I and establish godly

Etymology, Noble Origins, and Huguenot Heritage 6.1 Meaning and Etymology The surname LeCompte carries one of the
most aristocratically significant etymologies in the catalog of French surnames. Deriving from the Old French le comte,
meaning "the count" or "the earl," the name was originally either a title borne by a member of the medieval French nobility, or
an occupational designation for someone who served as a steward or manager of a count's household — a position of
considerable trust and status in feudal society. In either case, the name signals proximity to power and the upper levels of
medieval social organization. The earliest documentary records of the name date to the 12th and 13th centuries. A reference to
"Johannes le Comte" appears in the Cartulaire de l'abbaye de Jumièges — a 13th-century manuscript from the famous
Benedictine abbey of Jumièges in Normandy, France — confirming the name's deep Norman roots. The name was
particularly prevalent in Normandy and Picardy, the two northern French provinces most closely associated with the history of
England following the Norman Conquest of 1066. [VERIFIED based on manuscript records] The LeCompte name carries a
documented heraldic tradition — that is, a family coat of arms — consistent with its noble or near-noble origins. Family
tradition among documented American descendants of the LeCompte line holds that the arms reflect their connection to the
French comital class, and the name is registered in the U.S. National Huguenot Society's register of qualified Huguenot
ancestors as well as the Huguenot Society of America. 6.2 Huguenot Religious Significance The Huguenot Heritage — Faith,
Persecution, and Refuge The Huguenots were French Protestants, followers of the Reformed (Calvinist) tradition of
Christianity, who faced intense and often violent persecution in Catholic France from the mid-16th century onward. The Edict
of Nantes (1598) granted them a degree of religious tolerance, but its revocation by Louis XIV in 1685 — the Edict of
Fontainebleau — triggered the mass exodus of an estimated 200,000 to 400,000 Huguenots from France, scattering them
across England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia, South Africa, and the American colonies. Many Huguenot families, like the
LeComptes, had already begun emigrating decades before the formal revocation, driven by escalating persecution during the
mid-17th century Wars of Religion. Their contribution to American colonial life was enormous: Huguenot immigrants
brought advanced craft skills, mercantile expertise, and a tradition of civic and religious independence that profoundly shaped
early American culture. Descendants of documented Huguenot immigrants may apply for membership in the Huguenot
Society of America (founded 1883) and the National Huguenot Society. 6.3 LeCompte Name Variants Variant Language /

earned an 800-acre land grant, returned to Europe to marry his wife Hester in London, and ultimately established a
prosperous planter and merchant household on the shores of the Chesapeake Bay. Through his descendants, Shane Goble
carries a direct heritage of Huguenot faith, French nobility, and pioneering American settlement. 7.1 Origins in Picardie,
France Antoine LeCompte was born approximately 1620 in the city of Calais, Picardie (Picardy), France. Calais was — and
remains — one of the most strategically significant cities in France, situated at the narrowest point of the English Channel and
serving as the primary crossing point between England and continental Europe. In the early 17th century, it was a city of

intense cultural mixing, home to French, Flemish, English, and Spanish communities, and deeply caught up in the religious
conflicts of the time. [PROBABLE based on family records and genealogical documentation] Calais had been under English
control from 1347 until its fall to France in 1558 — within living memory of Antoine's birth — giving the city a uniquely
Anglo-French character and making English a language with some currency there. For a young Huguenot man of likely noble
background, this border city represented both a place of religious danger (Catholic France was openly hostile to Protestants)
and a gateway to Protestant England. It is probable that Antoine's family had connections to both the French Protestant
nobility and the English merchant or military world, explaining his subsequent service in the English royal army. 7.2 Military
Service and Emigration Antoine LeCompte served for approximately eleven years in King Charles I's English Army — a
remarkable detail that speaks to both his ambition and his calculated navigation of a dangerous political landscape. He would
have entered English service during the tumultuous 1640s, when Charles I was engaged in the English Civil War against
Parliamentary forces. When Charles I was defeated and executed in 1649, Antoine — loyal to the royalist cause — found
himself in a precarious position under Cromwell's Commonwealth government. Rather than adapt to the new order, he chose
emigration. [VERIFIED] Antoine arrived in Maryland approximately 1655 — just over two decades after the colony's
founding — making him among the earliest European settlers of that colony and among the very first LeCompte immigrants
to arrive in America. Maryland in 1655 was still a raw frontier colony, but it had the significant advantage of religious
tolerance: the Maryland Toleration Act of 1649, passed under Lord Baltimore's Catholic proprietorship, extended religious
freedom to all Trinitarian Christians — making it the natural destination for a Huguenot Protestant seeking a new home.
[VERIFIED] 7.3 Settlement in Maryland On January 17, 1659, Antoine LeCompte earned an 800-acre land parcel in
Maryland's Chesapeake Bay through the headright system — the colonial mechanism by which land was granted to settlers
who paid the passage of other immigrants to the colony. His 800-acre tract was called "St. Antoine" (also recorded as
"Antonine"), reflecting his own name and suggesting a degree of personal pride and perhaps devotion. The headrights he
claimed were for transporting Thomas Raymond, Barbara Crouch, and Thomas Jones to the colony. [VERIFIED] Following
this land grant, Antoine returned to Europe — perhaps to France, or to England — where he met Hester (Esther) Dottando,
born in Dieppe, Normandy, France. Their marriage took place on July 11, 1661, in London, England, after which they
returned together to Maryland to establish their permanent home. [VERIFIED] The LeCompte household was established in
Dorchester County, Maryland, specifically on Taylor's Island, on the shores of the Choptank River flowing into the
Chesapeake Bay. Antoine worked as both a planter and merchant — a dual role characteristic of successful Chesapeake
settlers, who combined agricultural production (tobacco was the primary cash crop) with trade and commerce. [VERIFIED]
Antoine LeCompte died after September 9, 1673 — the date of the last document in which he appears as a living person — at
approximately age 53, in Dorchester County, Maryland. [VERIFIED] 7.4 Children and Naturalization Following Antoine's

Testing Is Recommended for This Family Shane Goble's ancestral lines present several specific opportunities where DNA
testing can resolve or confirm genealogical uncertainties that documentary research alone cannot easily address. The gaps in
the direct Goble line between the 18th-century New Jersey generations and the 20th-century Ohio Kevin Goble, and the
challenge of connecting Rae LeCompte to the Maryland LeCompte dynasty, are precisely the types of problems that genetic
genealogy is designed to solve. Multiple testing strategies are recommended below, each targeting a different aspect of Shane's
ancestry. Y-DNA Testing — The Goble Paternal Line Y-DNA testing analyzes the Y chromosome, which is passed virtually
unchanged from father to son across generations. Because only men carry the Y chromosome, only male descendants of the
direct Goble paternal line can take this test. For Shane Goble, Y-DNA testing would directly test his Goble paternal line —
linking him genetically to other male Goble descendants across all generations from Thomas Goble (1590) to the present. ●
Recommended Test Level: Y-111 or Big Y-700 (available through FamilyTreeDNA) — the higher marker counts provide
significantly more matching power and haplogroup precision ● What to Expect: Matches with other Goble-surname males
who have tested; identification of Shane's Y-DNA haplogroup (likely R1b, common in Western European male lines);
potential discovery of a genetic cousin who has already resolved the documentary gap between New Jersey and Ohio Goble
generations ● Recommended Project: The Goble Family Association DNA Project on FamilyTreeDNA welcomes all male
Goble descendants and aggregates Y-DNA results specifically to resolve questions like the ones Shane faces. Joining this
project and contributing results would both advance Shane's personal research and contribute to the broader Goble
genealogical community Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) Testing — The Maternal Line Mitochondrial DNA testing analyzes

the mitochondrial genome, passed from a mother to all of her children. Shane can take this test to trace his direct maternal
line — his mother, his mother's mother, and so on back through all-female descent. While this does not directly address the
Goble or LeCompte lines researched in this report, it would reveal Shane's complete ancestral profile by adding the maternal
dimension. For the LeCompte line specifically, any female descendants of Rae LeCompte through female-line descent could
contribute mtDNA that might connect to LeCompte female ancestors in Maryland. ● Recommended Test: Full Mitochondrial
Sequence (FMS) test through FamilyTreeDNA ● What to Expect: Haplogroup identification; matches with distant maternal-
line cousins; potential connection to French or Norman female ancestors consistent with Huguenot heritage Autosomal DNA
Testing — AncestryDNA and 23andMe Autosomal DNA testing tests all 22 pairs of autosomes and is the broadest
genealogical DNA test available. Unlike Y-DNA and mtDNA, it captures ancestry from all family lines — both paternal and
maternal — but is most useful within the past five to seven generations (roughly to the mid-1800s). For Shane, autosomal
testing would: ● Identify genetic cousins across all family lines, including Goble, LeCompte, and Shane's maternal family ●
Provide ethnicity estimates consistent with a mixed English-Puritan and French-Huguenot heritage (expect elevated Western
European, specifically English and French/Norman percentages) ● Allow chromosome mapping — identifying which

in Fire, Forged by Faith (Continued) 28.2 The French Wars of Religion — A Century of Bloodshed The French Wars of
Religion were eight civil wars fought intermittently between French Catholics and Huguenots (French Calvinist Protestants)
from 1562 to 1598 — thirty-six years of massacre, siege, assassination, and atrocity that killed an estimated three million
people and tore France apart. To understand why the LeCompte family fled, one must understand what it meant to be a
Protestant in 16th-century France. The violence was not abstract or distant. It arrived in homes, markets, and churches without
warning, and no corner of the kingdom — not even the bilingual borderlands of Calais and Picardy where the LeCompte
family lived — was safe from it. The Massacre of Vassy (March 1, 1562): The Duke of Guise and his armed retinue attacked a
congregation of Huguenots worshipping in a barn in the town of Vassy, Champagne. Sixty were killed and more than two
hundred wounded. Women and children were among the dead. This single atrocity triggered the First War of Religion and
began three decades of escalating violence. The Huguenots were not rebels or traitors — they were farmers, tradespeople,
soldiers, and minor nobility who held a different theological conviction about salvation, and they were slaughtered for it. The
St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (August 23–24, 1572): The most horrific single event in the Wars of Religion. On the eve of
the feast of St. Bartholomew, on orders from King Charles IX and his mother Catherine de Medici, Catholic mobs in Paris
butchered Huguenot nobles who had gathered for a royal wedding. The killing spread to the provinces. In total, historians
estimate 5,000–30,000 Protestants were murdered across France in the weeks following the massacre. The Pope ordered the
bells of Rome rung in celebration. In England, Queen Elizabeth I went into mourning. In Picardy and Calais, Huguenot
communities barricaded their doors and prayed. This was the world into which Antoine LeCompte's parents were born — and
the shadow under which he himself came of age. By the time Antoine LeCompte was born in approximately 1620 in Calais,
the Edict of Nantes (1598) had technically brought peace. Henri IV, a former Protestant who converted to Catholicism to take
the French throne — reportedly saying "Paris is worth a Mass" — had granted Protestants substantial rights including freedom
of worship in designated places, the right to hold public office, and the maintenance of garrisoned towns. But the peace was
fragile, and every generation of Huguenots grew up knowing it could be revoked at any moment. Antoine grew up watching it
shatter. Between 1620 and 1629, Huguenot rebellions led to the Peace of Alès (1629), which stripped Protestants of their
military and political privileges while nominally preserving their religious rights. Then came Cardinal Richelieu's consolidation
of royal power under Louis XIII, and the stage was set for catastrophe. Fifty years after Antoine left for England came the
catastrophic Edict of Fontainebleau (1685), by which King Louis XIV revoked all Protestant rights, banned Protestant
worship, ord

ered the destruction of Protestant churches, and required the baptism of all Protestant children as Catholics. An estimated
200,000–400,000 Huguenots fled France in the years surrounding this decree — one of the largest refugee crises in European
history to that point. Those who stayed faced the Dragonnades — the quartering of brutal cavalry soldiers in Protestant
homes to terrorize families into converting. Antoine LeCompte did not wait for that. He left decades earlier, sometime before

1655 when records place him in Maryland, likely departing Calais in the late 1640s or early 1650s after the English Civil War
ended and new opportunities opened in the English colonies across the Atlantic. ✓ Verification Note — Section 28.2: French

Section 29: Caleb Goble — Revolutionary War Frontiersman and Spy (1760–1838) 29.1 The Road from New Jersey to
Revolution Caleb Goble was born on March 1, 1760, in Morristown, Morris County, New Jersey — the son of Daniel W.
Goble and Rhoda Doud. He entered the world in one of the most consequential places in colonial America. Morristown was
not merely a town; it would become the crucible of American independence. General George Washington chose Morristown
as his winter headquarters twice — first in 1777 after crossing the Delaware and routing the British at Trenton and Princeton,
and again in the catastrophic winter of 1779–1780, the coldest winter of the 18th century, during which 28 successive
blizzards struck the encampment at Jockey Hollow. It was there that Washington's ragged Continentals suffered conditions
worse than Valley Forge, surviving on bark and shoe leather while the British wintered comfortably in New York City. Caleb
grew up watching history arrive on horseback. By the time he was fifteen, the rhetoric of revolution had turned to musket fire.
His community — Scotch-Irish, Dutch, and English settlers intermarried across generations — was profoundly invested in the
patriot cause. New Jersey's position between New York (British-controlled) and Philadelphia made it a war zone from the first
shots fired at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. For a young man of Caleb's generation in Morristown, military service
was not a choice to be weighed — it was a community expectation, a family duty, and often a matter of survival. 29.2 Service
Record: Militia, Rangers, and the Secret War Caleb Goble's military record spans the full arc of the Revolutionary War, from its
uncertain early days through its grinding frontier conclusion. His documented service includes at least four distinct
assignments across multiple commands: Year(s) Unit / Commander Notes 1776 Capt. Benjamin Rice's Militia Company
Caleb's first recorded service, at age 16. The year of the Declaration of Independence — Year(s) Unit / Commander Notes
and the year Washington's army nearly collapsed after the fall of Fort Washington and the retreat across New Jersey. Rice's
company operated in the Morris County theater. 1777 Capt. James Brinton's Company The year of Morristown's first winter
encampment. Caleb, now 17, served under Brinton during a year that included Brandywine, Germantown, and Saratoga — the
turning point that brought France into the war on the American side. 1778–1779 Capt. Charles Crawford's Company, Jackson's
Fort; and brothers Ebenezer & Daniel in Capt. John Miller's Company, First Battalion, Washington County Caleb was posted
to Jackson's Fort under Capt. Crawford, a frontier fortification defending settlers against British-allied Loyalist and Indigenous
raids. Simultaneously, his brothers Ebenezer and Daniel served in Capt. John Miller's Company, First Battalion, Washington
County — suggesting the entire Goble family of military age was mobilized. The New Jersey frontier was not a distant theater;
Loyalist raiders operated within miles of Morristown, burning Year(s) Unit / Commander Notes farms and terrorizing families
in what amounted to a brutal internal civil war. 1778–1783 Rangers of the Frontier — acting one year as a Spy The most
remarkable entry in Caleb's record. He served with the Rangers of the Frontier for the final years of the war, and his pension
application explicitly states he served "acting one year as a spy." Frontier Rangers operated in small, highly mobile units along
the contested border zones, gathering intelligence on British and Loyalist movements, guiding Continental forces, and
disrupting enemy supply lines. A spy in this era operated without uniform, without the protections of the laws of war, at
constant risk of summary execution if captured. This was among the most dangerous duties the Continental cause assigned.
The New Jersey theater of the Revolutionary War is often overshadowed by the great set-piece battles in Pennsylvania and
New York, but historians increasingly recognize it as a savage internal conflict. New Jersey was divided almost equally between
patriots and Loyalists. Neighbors denounced neighbors; farms were burned; families were split. The war Caleb Goble fought
was not a uniform drama of heroic charges — it was a grinding, intimate, often lawless struggle for survival and political
control of communities he had grown up in. His role as a spy for one full year places him among the most covert and
personally exposed actors in that conflict. 29.3 After the War: The Long Journey to Ohio After the Treaty of Paris (1783),
Caleb Goble — like thousands of veterans — had to rebuild a life from the wreckage of eight years of war. He remained in
New Jersey through his twenties, but the pull of western land was irresistible for a man of his generation and temperament.

Building a New Home (1798–1993) 30.1 Why Ohio: Land, Freedom, and Community Ohio was not merely a destination for
the Goble family — it was a promise. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 had created the legal and moral framework that
made Ohio irresistible to families like the Gobles. Three forces drove the migration. Land. The Ordinance opened the
Northwest Territory to systematic settlement, dividing it into townships of 36 square-mile sections available at approximately
$1 per acre (reduced from $2 by the Land Act of 1800). Revolutionary War veterans received bounty-land warrants — paper
grants exchangeable for specific parcels — making Ohio especially attractive to men like Caleb Goble who had earned their
land with eight years of service. The Miami, Muskingum, and Scioto river valleys offered some of the most fertile agricultural
soil on the continent, glacially deposited over millennia and ready for the plow. Freedom. The Northwest Ordinance contained
a clause with enormous moral weight: "There shall be neither slavery nor involuntary servitude in the said territory." Ohio
entered the Union in 1803 as a free state — the first state carved from the Northwest Territory. For families of Scots-Irish,
English, and Huguenot Protestant stock who had fought for selfdetermination, a free state was not an abstraction; it was a
foundational value. Community. Migration in this era was rarely individual. Families moved in clusters — brothers, cousins,
and neighbors relocating in waves to the same counties. The Ohio county records document multiple Goble family members
arriving in Butler, Champaign, and surrounding counties within a decade of each other. Shane's direct line follows this chain
from New Jersey through Kentucky into Ohio's southwestern counties, and ultimately northward to Ashtabula County and
Jefferson, Ohio. 30.2 Ohio County Records — The Goble and LeCompte Paper Trail The following table summarizes
