Primary Sources and Records Closing Essay Foreword: Setting the Stage An invitation to inhabit the past — and to meet an
ordinary man whose family lived an extraordinary story. Imagine standing in the village of Westergate, West Sussex, England,
on the second day of January in the year 1591. The rolling chalk downs rise and fall in every direction, their bare winter flanks
pale against a grey English sky. The smell of hay, of woodsmoke from cottage fires, of cold mud on the lane — these are the
scents of every January this village has ever known. The Church of St. Mary the Virgin at nearby Aldingbourne stands as it has
stood for four centuries, its Norman stonework cold and patient, its bell rope trembling as the parish bell rings in the new year.
In a thatched farmhouse within earshot of that bell, a widow named Alice Goble brings a son into the world. She has been
without her husband William for not quite two years. She has other children to keep. There is work to do, and not enough coin
to do it with. She names the boy Thomas. That child — Thomas Goble — will live to see the reign of four English monarchs.
He will cross three thousand miles of ocean in the hold of a wooden ship barely larger than a modern house. He will clear
forest and break ground on the edge of a wilderness that has no name in English. He will stand in the first jury room in
Boston and help decide a man's fate. He will pay the tuition of Harvard College in sacks of corn and bushels of wheat. He
will move his aging bones to the frontier town of Concord, draft his will with careful hands, and die there in the December
cold of 1657, his estate spread across several parcels of land he had accumulated acre by careful acre over two decades of
labor. But Thomas's story does not end with his death. It continues, with compounding drama, through his children —
through a son who fought in the most devastating war colonial New England would ever know, through a daughter who
outlived all her siblings, through a youngest son whose life would end on a public gallows recorded in the diaries of two of the
most famous Puritan figures of the age. The Goble family's drama is written into official court records, into the private pages
of Samuel Sewall's diary, into the registers of Harvard College, into the parish books of a Sussex church, and into the dark,
contested, morally complex pages of King Philip's War. This is their story. This is the story of Thomas Goble of Colonial
Massachusetts. P A R T O N E The Goble Family Roots in England c. 1540 – 1619 1.1 — The Village of Westergate and the
Goble Ancestors Before there was a Goble in America, there was a Goble in Sussex — a farming family rooted in the chalk
soil of one of England's most ancient landscapes. The village of Westergate lies in the coastal plain of West Sussex, England,
sheltered to the north by the long green ridge of the South Downs and open to the south toward the Channel coast not five
miles distant. It is a hamlet of the most modest kind — a cluster of farmsteads and cottages gathered loosely around lanes
that have been rutted by cart wheels since before memory. The fields surrounding Westergate in the sixteenth century were still
organized in the ancient medieval strip pattern: long narrow plots divided among the village families, worked communally in a
rhythm of plowing, sowing, fallow, and harvest that had not changed in essence since the Conquest. The hedgerows were thick
with hawthorn and elder. Sheep grazed the Downs above, and cattle pastured in the low meadows below. It was a world of
mud and labor, of seasons and church bells, of the smell of turned earth in spring and the sweet rot of fallen apples in
autumn. It was here, in this landscape, that the Goble family put down its roots. William Goble, recorded in documents as

William Goble "de Westergate," was born somewhere between 1540 and 1550 in Westergate, in the parish of Aldingbourne,
West Sussex. The designation "de Westergate" — of Westergate — was the era's common way of anchoring a man to his
home place, distinguishing him from others of the same name in the county. He was a man of the land, a husbandman or
small farmer, a figure of exactly the kind who formed the backbone of rural England in the reign of Queen Elizabeth I. He
would have known the rhythms of the liturgical year as intimately as he knew the agricultural one: Plough Sunday at
Candlemas, Easter, Lammas harvest thanksgiving, Michaelmas. The Church of England under Elizabeth, still finding its
footing between the old Catholic forms and the new Protestant theology, was the organizing institution of every English
village, and the church at Aldingbourne — St. Mary the Virgin, a Norman-era building of flint and stone — was the Goble
family's spiritual and civic home. It was there that all significant moments in family life were recorded: births, marriages,
deaths, written in the careful hand of successive parish clergymen into registers that have, remarkably, survived to the present
day. Around 1573, William Goble married Alice Legard (also recorded simply as Alice in some documents) in Middleton,
Sussex, a neighboring parish just a short walk from Westergate. The marriage would produce at least six children over the
following two decades, all baptized at St. Mary's Aldingbourne: ● William Goble Jr. — born 1582 ● Joanna Goble — born
1585 ● Nycho Goble — born 1586, died in infancy the same year ● Elizabeth Goble — born 1588 ● John Goble — born
approximately 1588 ● Thomas Goble — born January 2, 1591 — the youngest, and the subject of this biography William
Goble "de Westergate" did not live to see his youngest child grow beyond infancy. He died on May 1, 1593, and was buried at
Aldingbourne Parish Church. Thomas was approximately two years and four months old when his father was laid in the
churchyard. The widow Alice was left with the farm, with several children ranging in age from perhaps eleven years old down
to an infant who had not yet seen his third birthday. How she managed is not recorded; how she survived must have required
the help of neighbors, the charity of the parish, and the labor of her older children. The Goble household in those years after
William's death would have been a place of careful economy, of making do, of early mornings and long evenings and never
quite enough of anything. Thomas Goble grew up knowing poverty — and knowing work. St. Mary the Virgin, Aldingbourne,
West Sussex — the Norman-era parish church where Thomas Goble was baptized on January 2, 1591, where his parents
William and Alice were married, and where his father William was buried on May 1, 1593. All Goble family records from this
period are preserved in the Aldingbourne Parish Register. 1.2 — The Roanoke Era: England's First American Dream and the
Goble World The years of Thomas Goble's birth and his father's life coincided precisely with England's first, failed, haunting
attempt to establish a colony in the New World. The following section examines that extraordinary coincidence honestly, and
evaluates the evidence — and the absence of evidence — for any Goble connection to the Roanoke voyages. In the years
between 1584 and 1590, while William and Alice Goble were farming their Sussex fields, baptizing their children at
Aldingbourne, and struggling through the ordinary difficulties of Elizabethan rural life, England was embarking on its first
sustained attempt to plant a permanent colony on the coast of North America. The story of Roanoke Island — the so-called
"Lost Colony" — is one of the most haunting mysteries in all of American history, and it unfolded in precise temporal and
geographic parallel with the Goble family's life in Sussex. The chronology of the Roanoke expeditions was as follows: ● 1584
Reconnaissance: Sir Walter Raleigh, having received a royal charter from Queen Elizabeth I to establish an English colony in
Virginia, dispatched captains Philip Amadas and Arthur Barlowe to explore the Carolina coast. They reconnoitered Roanoke
Island and returned with two Native men, Manteo and Wanchese, and enthusiastic reports. The English public was captivated.
● 1585–1586 Military Colony: A force of approximately 108 men under the command of Governor Ralph Lane established a
military outpost on Roanoke Island. They quarreled with the local Secotan people, murdered their chief Wingina, and were
ultimately evacuated by Sir Francis Drake after a terrible winter. ● 1587 — The Lost Colony: A new and more ambitious
expedition under Governor John White departed with 117 settlers — men, women, and children — with the intention of
establishing a permanent civilian colony. Among those who landed on Roanoke Island in July 1587 was John White's daughter
Eleanor, wife of Ananias Dare, who gave birth on August 18, 1587 to Virginia Dare — the first English child born in the
Americas. John White was persuaded to return to England for additional supplies. He would not see his daughter or

granddaughter again. ● 1588: The crisis of the Spanish Armada consumed all available English shipping. The relief ships
White had arranged were commandeered by the Crown. He could not return. ● 1590: Finally, after an agonizing three-year
absence, John White managed to secure passage on privateering ships owned by London merchant John Watts: the Hopewell
under Captain Abraham Cocke and the Moonlight. They were not naval vessels; they were privately financed merchant-
privateer ships whose ordinary crew manifests were not formally preserved for the historical record. White's ships arrived at
Roanoke Island on August 18, 1590 — the third birthday of Virginia Dare, had she lived. They found the settlement
completely abandoned. The houses had been taken down. The palisade remained, but carved into its post was a single word:
CROATOAN. No survivors were ever found. The mystery endures to this day. Map of the Roanoke area, 1590 — engraved by
Theodor de Bry after a watercolour by English colonist John White, Governor of the Lost Colony. This map was published in
Thomas Harriot's A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia (1590) and represents the most detailed
cartographic record of the Roanoke expeditions. The Goble family of Sussex was living through all of these events in parallel.
A Note on the Historical Record — The Question of Goble and Roanoke: The known official passenger and colonist lists for
all Roanoke expeditions between 1584 and 1590 — preserved in Richard Hakluyt's The Principal Navigations, Voyages,
Traffiques, and Discoveries of the English Nation, in John White's own accounts, and maintained by the National Park Service
and the Lost Colony Research Group's Alphabetized List — do not include any person with the surname Goble. However, an
important distinction must be made. The crew lists of the 1590 Hopewell and Moonlight — the privateer vessels that
discovered the abandoned colony — are largely incomplete. These were privately financed merchant vessels, not Royal Navy
ships, and their ordinary working crew manifests (as opposed to their officers and notable passengers) were not formally
preserved in the way that naval records were. Consider the circumstances: William Goble was alive in Sussex during every one
of these voyages. He died May 1, 1593 — three years after the Hopewell returned from Roanoke. Sussex men were among the
most frequently recruited sailors and laborers for Atlantic voyages from English south coast ports. Thomas Goble himself was
born on January 2, 1591 — months after White's final Roanoke voyage in August 1590. While no documentary confirmation
exists that any Goble served on these ships, the familial, geographic, and temporal proximity makes any oral tradition of a
Goble family connection to this era worth recording as historical context. This document presents the facts without
embellishment: the connection remains unconfirmed by surviving records, but is equally undisproven by them. The honest
historian can say no more and no less than that. What can be said with certainty is this: the world into which Thomas Goble
was born in 1591 was a world newly electrified by the idea of America. The Roanoke expeditions had been public knowledge,
discussed in taverns and in marketplaces, described in the popular pamphlets of the era. By the time Thomas was old enough
to hear stories at his mother's knee, the Lost Colony was already a mystery, a cautionary tale, a tantalizing ghost. The dream of
the New World was in the English air. It would take Thomas Goble another four decades to act on it — but it was a dream he
had been breathing since birth. 1.3 — Thomas Goble's Childhood and Youth (1591– 1619) Thomas Goble grew up in the
years of the late Elizabethan and early Jacobean era — a time of extraordinary cultural ferment in England and extraordinary
hardship for ordinary rural families like the Gobles. Shakespeare was writing his greatest plays. The King James Bible was
being compiled. The enclosure of common fields was displacing farming families across southern England, driving the rural
poor from land their families had worked for generations. In the towns, unemployment and vagrancy were rising. In the
parishes, the tension between the established Church of England and the growing movement of godly Protestant reformers
— the Puritans — was becoming impossible to ignore. Thomas, growing up fatherless after 1593, would have been put to
work from an early age. In the agricultural economy of rural Sussex, children were a labor resource: they tended livestock,
carried water, pulled weeds, gleaned fields after harvest. By his early teens, Thomas would have been doing the work of a man.
He learned to plow, to reap, to manage the rhythms of a farming year — skills that would serve him directly when he broke
ground in colonial Charlestown forty years later. The religious climate of Thomas's youth was charged and increasingly
anxious. James I, who came to the throne in 1603 when Thomas was twelve, had initially raised Puritan hopes at the Hampton
Court Conference, but quickly dashed them. "No bishop, no king," James declared, making clear that he would tolerate no

challenge to the episcopal structure of the Church of England. The Puritans — those who wished to "purify" the church of
what they saw as its residual Catholic corruptions — were increasingly marginalized, increasingly watched, increasingly
pressured. In Sussex, as across England, the godly and the conformists eyed each other across the parish church aisle. The
tensions of Thomas Goble's world were not just economic. They were spiritual, existential, defining. At some point in his late
twenties or early thirties, Thomas Goble encountered Alice Brookman, daughter of a Sussex family. The courtship, conducted
in the manner of the era — with the knowledge and approval of family and parish — culminated in a formal betrothal and
then a wedding. 1.4 — The Marriage of Thomas Goble and Alice Brookman (November 5, 1619) On November 5, 1619 —
the very anniversary of the Gunpowder Plot, a date already charged with Protestant significance in the English calendar —
Thomas Goble and Alice Brookman were married at Aldingbourne Parish Church, West Sussex. The record of this marriage
survives in the Aldingbourne Parish Register, one of the primary documentary anchors of Thomas Goble's biography. It is
worth pausing to reconstruct the scene. St. Mary the Virgin at Aldingbourne is a building of Norman origin — its oldest
sections dating to the twelfth century — built of local flint and stone, with a squat tower, a nave of considerable antiquity, and
a churchyard full of the accumulated dead of the parish. On a November morning in 1619, the church would have been cold,
lit by candles and whatever pale light filtered through the windows. The congregation would have been the neighbors and
families of both parties — farmers in their plain woolen coats, women in their bonnets, the children fidgeting in the pews. The
ceremony followed the Book of Common Prayer, the same words that had united English couples since the reign of Edward
VI. Thomas Goble was twenty-eight years old. Alice Brookman was approximately nineteen. ◆ A Note on the Historical
Record Earlier genealogical research sometimes identified Thomas Goble's wife as Alice Mousall. Newly examined marriage
records confirm her correct maiden name as Alice Brookman. The surname Mousall (or Mousal) appears in a different context
in the family — it is associated with a later generation, not with Alice herself. This correction is documented in the records
examined for this biography. Alice Brookman was born around 1600 in Sussex. Of her parentage and family background, the
records are sparse — she exists in the documentary record primarily through her marriage, her children, and her widowhood.
But she was clearly a woman of extraordinary resilience: she would cross an ocean in her thirties, raise six children on the
colonial frontier, survive the death of her husband, manage an estate as executor of his will, and — if the records are to be
trusted — outlive him by at least several years. In an era when women left almost no independent documentary trace, Alice
Brookman Goble's quiet persistence across the documentary record is itself a kind of testimony. Their first documented child,
John Goble, was born approximately June 30, 1629 in Sussex — a full decade after the marriage. The gap between the 1619
wedding and the 1629 birth of John has provoked genealogical speculation: it is possible that children were born and died in
the intervening years leaving no surviving record, or that the couple's fertility was delayed. Thomas Goble Jr. followed around
1631, and Elizabeth around 1633 — the precise timing complicated by the family's impending emigration. It was in this period,
with three young children and a turbulent England all around them, that Thomas and Alice Goble made the most
consequential decision of their lives. P A R T T W O The Great Migration — Crossing the Atlantic 1633 – 1634 2.1 — Why
They Left England In the early 1630s, tens of thousands of English Puritans reached the same conclusion: England was lost.
The New World was the only hope. The year 1633 was, for English Puritans, a year of culminating crisis. William Laud was
appointed Archbishop of Canterbury by King Charles I — and with that appointment, the persecution of those who
dissented from the Church of England's established forms acquired a new, systematic ferocity. Laud was a high churchman
who loved ceremony, hierarchy, and order. To him, the Puritan emphasis on plain worship, personal Biblical study, and the
sovereignty of individual conscience was not merely theologically wrong — it was politically seditious. He used his authority to
silence, fine, imprison, and physically mutilate Puritan ministers who defied his directives. Men had their ears cut off. Others
were pilloried. The most prominent Puritan intellectuals faced ruin. This came against a broader political backdrop of Charles
I's "Personal Rule" — the eleven years from 1629 to 1640 during which the King governed without Parliament, having
dissolved that body after it attempted to limit his power. Without Parliament, there was no political avenue for reform.
Without reform, there was no future for the godly in England. The conclusion was inescapable: leave. The Great Puritan

Migration of 1630 to 1640 would ultimately bring approximately 20,000 people across the Atlantic to Massachusetts Bay
Colony. It began in earnest in 1630 with John Winthrop's fleet of eleven ships carrying roughly 700 settlers. By 1634, when the
Gobles arrived, Charlestown and Boston were functioning towns with established churches, courts, and growing populations.
The migration was at its height. Thomas Goble was forty-two or forty-three years old when he made this decision. He had
spent his entire life in Sussex. He had a wife of approximately thirtythree, three children under five years old, and whatever
land or goods he had accumulated in two decades of farming. He was not a young adventurer. He was a middle-aged farming
man choosing to uproot everything he had ever known because — based on every piece of evidence his biography offers —
he was a committed Puritan who believed that the godly community he sought could only be built in the New World. 2.2 —
The Voyage (1633–1634) The ships of the Great Migration crossed the Atlantic between April and September each year, when
the weather of the North Atlantic was at its most survivable. The Gobles departed England sometime in 1633 or early 1634
— the exact ship of their passage is not confirmed in surviving records. Vessels commonly used for the migration in this
period included the Abigail, the Hopewell, and the Lion; the Gobles may have traveled on one of these or on another vessel of
the same class. What is certain is the reality of the crossing. To understand what Thomas and Alice Goble endured, one must
understand what an Atlantic voyage in 1634 actually meant. The vessels of the migration era were typically between 100 and
200 tons burden — wooden ships of the smallest oceanic class, barely sixty to ninety feet long. The passengers were crammed
below decks in the 'tween deck space, a low ceiling cavity between the cargo hold and the main deck, where headroom was
barely four feet and the berths — rough wooden shelves — were packed as tightly as the ship's owners could manage.
Ventilation was minimal. Light was scarce. The smells of salt water, bilge, livestock (carried for food), unwashed bodies, and
occasionally death were inescapable. The crossing took between six and twelve weeks, depending on winds and weather. The
North Atlantic in the shoulder seasons was treacherous: sudden gales could drive a ship hundreds of miles off course, shred
its sails, or — in the worst case — roll it over. Passengers spent days at a time unable to leave their berths as the ship pitched
and rolled in Atlantic swells. Children cried. The sick vomited. The Puritan faithful prayed, held Bible readings, and sang
psalms with a fervor born partly of genuine faith and partly of the very human need to impose meaning on chaos. ◆ At Sea:
A Puritan Crossing "The winds were contrary and the sea very rough, so that our ship made little way... the people were
generally very sick, especially the women and children." — Typical account of a Great Migration crossing, from the journals of
the era. The Gobles' experience, with at least two young children aboard, would have been identical. Thomas and Alice crossed
with young children — John was approximately four or five, Thomas Jr. was two or three, and Elizabeth's birth date of 1634
places her either at the very end of the pregnancy during the voyage or born immediately upon arrival. The possibility exists
that Elizabeth was born at sea, a not uncommon occurrence on these crossings. The ship that brought the Gobles to
Massachusetts Bay also brought them to the threshold of their new lives — battered, exhausted, possibly grieving (if any child
had died en route), and arriving on a shore that smelled of pine forest and possibility. On August 30, 1634, "Thomas Goble
and Alice his wife" were formally admitted to the First Church of Charlestown, Massachusetts. This date is the fixed
documentary anchor of their arrival — the moment the Goble family entered the colonial record of the New World. The
admission to a Puritan church required examination by the elders, a public confession of faith, and the approval of the existing
congregation. It was not a casual formality. It was the central act of Puritan community: to stand before your neighbors and
declare yourself one of the elect. Three days later, on September 3, 1634, Thomas Goble received his papers as a Freeman at
the General Court of Massachusetts Bay Colony. This was an achievement of the first order. Freeman status — full citizenship
in the colony — was restricted to property-owning members of a recognized Puritan church. It conferred the right to vote, to
hold office, to sit on juries, and to participate in the governance of the colony. Thomas Goble, arriving as a stranger barely
three days in his new home, had moved immediately to establish himself as a full and equal citizen of the community. In a
colony where status was everything and new arrivals were watched carefully, this was the move of a man who understood how
power worked and intended to claim his proper place within it. 2.3 — Charlestown, Massachusetts: Their New Home Colonial
Charlestown in 1634 was a settlement of approximately three hundred to four hundred souls, clustered on a triangular

peninsula that jutted northward into the confluence of the Charles River and Boston Harbor. Across the water, visible from
Charlestown's shore, lay the newer settlement of Boston, established in 1630 on the Shawmut Peninsula. The two
communities were already rivals in commerce and allies in faith, connected by boat and — when the harbor froze in winter —
by foot across the ice. Charlestown occupied the Mishawum Peninsula, a piece of land defined by three modest hills: Bunker's
Hill to the north, Breed's Hill in the center, and Moulton's Hill to the south. The settlement clung to the waterfront and
climbed the lower slopes of these hills in a scatter of wooden houses, their frames of rough-hewn timber, their walls of
clapboard or wattle-and-daub, their roofs of thatch or board. The paths between them were dirt — dust in summer, mud in
spring and autumn, ice in winter. The church — the First Church of Charlestown — was the physical and spiritual center of
the community, its meetinghouse simple and plain, its congregation the governing body of the town in everything but name.
The air of Charlestown smelled of wood smoke from a hundred fires, of the salt harbor, of pine resin from freshly cut timber,
of cattle and pigs kept in yards close to the houses. The sounds were the sounds of axes on wood, of hammers on nails, of
livestock, of children, of the harbor wind, and — always — of the church bell marking the hours of a Puritan day that began
at dawn and ended at dark. Beyond the settled area, barely a quarter mile from the outermost houses, the forest began: old-
growth New England woodland, dense and dark, full of the sounds of unknown birds and the distant crash of falling timber.
The wilderness pressed in on every side. This was the edge of the known world. Into this world, Thomas Goble brought his
family and began to build. His first recorded land grant came immediately: 4 acres of "planting ground on Newton Line" —
granted in 1634 as part of the colony's systematic distribution of land to newly arrived freemen. The family's first home was
almost certainly a timber-framed structure of one or two rooms, with a massive central chimney serving both heating and
cooking, a packed earth or rough-plank floor, small windows shuttered against the cold, and walls chinked with clay and moss
against the New England wind. It would have been cold in winter, smoky, crowded. It would have been home. P A R T T H R
E E Building a Life in the Colony 1634 – 1657 3.1 — Establishing the Goble Estate (1634–1651) Over the course of two
decades, Thomas Goble transformed himself from a newly arrived immigrant into one of the established landholders of
colonial Charlestown — an achievement that speaks to extraordinary industry, thrift, and social acumen. Land was everything
in colonial Massachusetts. It was wealth, it was security, it was status, it was the tangible evidence of God's favor — for the
Puritans believed, with a directness that would seem startling today, that worldly prosperity was a sign of divine election. A
man who accumulated land was a man whom God was blessing. Thomas Goble accumulated land. By 1638 — just four years
after his arrival — Thomas owned at least five distinct parcels in or near Charlestown: Table 1: Thomas Goble's Land
Holdings, c.1638 Parcel Description Notes 1 House and ½ acre at west end of common Primary family residence 2 4 acres
Linefield, southwest Cambridge line Farming/planting land 3 2¾ acres cow commons ¾ acre sold to W. Baker, 1654 4 15
acres woods Timber resource 5 50 acres Waterfield Largest holding; likely grazing/hay land By 1651, Thomas was also
recorded as owning land at Cambridge — evidence of continued accumulation even as he entered his sixties. The total
landholding represents a substantial agricultural enterprise for a colonial farmer of his era: approximately 73 acres of mixed
farmland, woodland, and commons rights, plus his house lot. What managing this land meant in practice was a daily reality of
physical labor that is difficult to fully imagine from the distance of modern life. The fifteen acres of woodland required
selective cutting for building timber and firewood, with the cleared areas gradually converted to fields. The fifty acres of
Waterfield required fencing, draining if it was low-lying ground, and seasonal management of the cattle that would have grazed
it. The arable parcels needed annual plowing — done with oxen, the iron-shod plow cutting through soil that still contained
the roots of the great trees that had been cleared and burned only years before. Corn was the primary crop: Indian corn
(maize), adopted from the Native peoples whose knowledge had saved the first English settlers from starvation. Wheat and rye
completed the mix. The cattle, sheep, and pigs required daily tending, fencing, feeding through the long winter months when
the snow lay deep and the temperature dropped below zero for weeks at a time. Thomas Goble managed all of this. He
managed it with Alice, with his growing children as they came of age, and almost certainly with occasional hired or indentured
labor. He was, by any measure, a man of substance in his community. 3.2 — Growing Family in the New World The Goble

household in Charlestown grew steadily through the late 1630s and into the early 1640s. Thomas and Alice's children, those
born in England and those born in the colony, filled the house with the noise and work and worry of a large family on the
colonial frontier. The children of Thomas Goble Sr. and Alice Brookman, in order: ● John Goble — born approximately June
30, 1629 in Sussex. The eldest child, he made the crossing with his parents as a small boy. He would later return to England
and die there by 1676, never coming back to Massachusetts. ● Thomas Goble Jr. — born approximately 1631 in England or
Charlestown; married Mary (Mousall or Gove); lived to November 22, 1690. ● Elizabeth Goble — born 1634, in Charlestown
(possibly en route during the crossing); married first John White of Sudbury, then Thomas Carter; died after 1682. ● Mary
Goble — baptized February 27, 1636 in Charlestown; married Daniel Dean (Deane); died 1705. ● Sarah Goble — baptized
May 27, 1638 in Charlestown; married John Shepard; died November 30, 1717 — the last surviving child of Thomas Sr. ●
Daniel Goble — baptized July 18, 1641 in Charlestown; the youngest child; married Hannah Brewer; whose dramatic fate is
the subject of Part V of this biography. The rhythm of Puritan family life in this household was structured and unrelenting.
The day began before dawn, with the lighting of the fire — a critical task, since losing the fire in a New England winter could
threaten life. Morning prayers were said as a family before the first meal. The children's labor was assigned by age and sex: the
boys working alongside their father in the fields and woodlot, the girls alongside Alice in the house — spinning wool into
thread, knitting stockings and caps, cooking over the open fire, preserving food in salt and vinegar and smoke for the long
winter months, carrying water from the well, making soap and candles, tending the kitchen garden of herbs and vegetables. On
Sundays the entire family walked to the meetinghouse for the morning service, returned home for a cold dinner (no cooking
on the Sabbath), and returned for the afternoon service. The minister's sermons could last two hours. There was no talking
during the sermon. Children who fidgeted were corrected. It was an austere life by modern standards, but it was also a life of
community, of purpose, of the profound Puritan conviction that every act of daily labor — every loaf of bread baked, every
furrow plowed, every psalm sung — was an act of worship to an attentive God. The Gobles were not suffering. They were
living, in every sense they understood, the life they had crossed an ocean to build. 3.3 — Thomas Goble as a Respected
Citizen The documentary record of Thomas Goble's public life in Charlestown contains two entries that, taken together,
reveal a man of genuine standing in his community: his service on what was likely the first jury in Boston, and his payment of
Harvard College tuition in agricultural commodities. Each deserves careful examination. The First Jury in Boston — October
1, 1640 On October 1, 1640, Thomas Goble took his seat as one of twelve jurors in the General Court of Massachusetts Bay
Colony — what is believed to have been the first jury ever to convene in Boston. The case before them was that of Hugh
Buets, a man accused of heresy against the established Puritan orthodoxy of the colony. To sit on this jury was to exercise the
highest civic responsibility in the colony. Thomas Goble — a man who had arrived in America barely six years earlier, who had
been born in a small Sussex village to a widowed mother — was now one of twelve citizens charged with determining the
religious soundness of a man's soul. ◆ Primary Record: The First Boston Jury, 1640 "Hugh Buets was tried for heresy. The
jury found him guilty — his 'person and errors are dangerous for infection of others.' Buets was ordered out of the
jurisdiction by October 24, 'upon paine of death and not to returne, upon paine of being hanged.'" Massachusetts Bay Colony
Court Records, Vol. 1, 1628–1641. Thomas Goble served on this jury. Each juror was paid twelve shillings — one shilling
each. The General Court room in Boston in 1640 was a spare, plain space — a room in a timber-framed building, lit by candles
and the grey October light through small windows. The judges sat at a raised table in their plain black coats and stiff collars,
their faces serious with the weight of God's business. Thomas Goble sat among eleven of his neighbors and peers, listening to
the accusations against Hugh Buets, weighing the testimony, and ultimately rendering the verdict that sent a man out of the
jurisdiction under sentence of death if he returned. The jury was paid twelve shillings in total — one shilling each. It is one of
the first identifiable moments in the history of the American jury system, and Thomas Goble was there. Harvard College
Tuition — 1653–1655 Harvard College was founded in 1636 — just two years after Thomas Goble arrived in Charlestown. It
was an institution born of the same Puritan impulse that had driven the Great Migration: the conviction that the godly
community required educated ministers, and that America must not be left without the resources to educate them. By the

1650s, Harvard was a functioning if modest institution, located in Cambridge just across the Charles River from Charlestown.
Its students paid their tuition not always in coin — hard currency was perpetually scarce in the colony — but in agricultural
goods, which the college then sold or consumed. In three successive entries in the Harvard College tuition records, a man
identified as "goodman goobell" and "old gobbell" made payments for a student: ◆ Harvard College Tuition Records —
Thomas Goble December 13, 1653: "goodman goobell" paid 1 pound, 16 shillings "in Indian" (cornmeal/corn) January 15,
1654: "goodman goobell" paid 1 pound "in wheatt and Indian" December 8, 1655: "old gobbell" paid 1 pound, 14 shillings, 6
pence — specifically: 17 shillings "in wheatt" and 7 shillings, 6 pence "by Indian" The student being supported was almost
certainly one of Thomas's sons — the most likely candidate being Thomas Jr., though the exact identification cannot be
confirmed from surviving records. What can be said with absolute certainty is this: Thomas Goble, born fatherless in a small
Sussex farming village in 1591, was in the 1650s paying Harvard College tuition in corn and wheat on behalf of his child. The
arc of that life — from the widow Alice's cottage at Westergate, through the Atlantic crossing, through two decades of
clearing forest and plowing fields in colonial Massachusetts — culminating in sacks of grain delivered to the gates of what
would become one of the world's great universities — is one of the most eloquent statements about the ambition and
achievement of the Great Puritan Migration that the documentary record contains. Thomas Goble did not arrive in America
with wealth or connections or a great name. He arrived with labor, with faith, with determination. The Harvard tuition
payments are the measure of what that determination could achieve. 3.4 — The Move to Concord and Later Life By the early
1650s, Thomas Goble and at least some of his family appear in the records of Concord, Massachusetts — a town
approximately twenty miles due west of Charlestown, founded in 1635 as one of the first inland settlements in the colony. The
move from the relative security of the established coastal town to the frontier meant something specific in the 1650s: it meant
forest on three sides, it meant greater distance from the courts and the markets, it meant a smaller and more exposed
community, and it meant proximity to the complex and increasingly fraught relationships between English settlers and the
Native peoples of the interior. Concord in the 1650s was a town of perhaps forty or fifty households arranged around a
common, a meetinghouse, and the confluence of the Concord and Assabet Rivers — the Musketaquid, as the Native
Pennacook people called it. The meadows along the river were rich with hay grass that flooded and fertilized annually. The
upland fields were stony but workable. The forest was everywhere, pressing to the edge of the common and beginning again
on the far side of every field. In these same woods, decades later, Henry David Thoreau would build his cabin at Walden Pond
and write his account of solitary life in the New England wilderness. Thomas Goble and his son Daniel walked through those
same woods in the 1650s and 1660s, cutting timber, hunting, and farming the same land. The relationship between Concord's
English settlers and the local Native communities — primarily Nipmuc and Pennacook peoples — was still, in the 1650s,
primarily one of wary coexistence. Trade occurred. Land transfers occurred, though often on terms that benefited the English.
Some Native people had converted to Christianity and lived in designated "praying towns" — communities of Christian
Indians who had adopted English dress, worship, and settlement patterns. The peace that Massasoit had maintained with
Plymouth Colony since 1621 extended, in various forms, to the interior settlements. Thomas Goble lived out his last years in
this borderland world, in the contested and beautiful landscape between the English coastal towns and the Native homeland of
the deep interior. Walden Pond, Concord, Massachusetts. The Goble family — including Daniel Goble and his wife Hannah
Brewer — lived south of Walden Woods in the 1660s and 1670s, in the same general landscape that Henry David Thoreau
would later immortalize in Walden (1854). Thomas Goble Sr. spent his final years in this same frontier community before his
death in December 1657. 3.5 — Thomas Goble's Last Will and Testament (November 30, 1657) Thomas Goble wrote his will
on November 30, 1657 in Concord, Massachusetts. He was approximately sixty-six or sixty-seven years old. The will was
proved at court on December 29, 1657, and the estate was inventoried on December 11, 1657, indicating that Thomas died in
the first two weeks of December 1657. The estate inventory, conducted before the will was formally proved, was the standard
colonial procedure for ensuring that the deceased's assets were accurately assessed before distribution. The will opens with
Thomas Goble of Concord — his adopted town, the frontier community where he had spent the final chapter of his long life.

He names his wife Alice as executor, entrusting to her the management and distribution of his estate. The bequests reflect the
family he had built: "Thomas Goble of Concord..." — To Alis [Alice] my wife... His three sons — "the eldest of which being
now in England" — if John does not come for his portion it is to be divided equally among the other two sons. His son
Thomas's two children Thomas (the third) and Stephen are mentioned. His three daughters — one [Sarah] was not yet married
at time of writing. — Last Will and Testament of Thomas Goble, Concord, November 30, 1657; Middlesex County Probate
Records The will reveals several important facts. First, Thomas knew in November 1657 that his eldest son John was in
England — confirming that John had at some point returned across the Atlantic. Second, Thomas was already a grandfather:
his son Thomas Jr. had children named Thomas (the third) and Stephen by this date. Third, his daughter Sarah was still
unmarried — a detail that locates her precisely in the timeline of the family. Fourth, Alice was trusted entirely with the
execution of the estate — a clear statement of the partnership at the heart of this marriage. ◆ The 1675 Land Sale: A
Primary Source Confirmation On March 26, 1675 — nearly eighteen years after Thomas Sr.'s death — his surviving adult
children conducted a formal sale of land formerly belonging to their father. The document names: Thomas Goble [Jr.], Daniel
Goble, Daniel Deane (husband of Mary Goble), and John Shepard (husband of Sarah Goble), and John White of Sudbury —
"as well as our wives respectively in acknowledgement of their full and free consent." This land sale document is one of the
most valuable primary sources in the Goble family record, simultaneously confirming the family relationships, the survival of
Thomas's children into the 1670s, and the existence of the Concord land holdings. Alice Goble survived her husband,
continuing to manage the Concord property as its executor. She died sometime after December 1657, her exact death date not
recorded in surviving documents. She had outlived her homeland, her husband, her eldest son's American residence, and — if
she lived long enough — perhaps the early childhoods of her grandchildren. She had crossed an ocean and built a family that
would last. It was enough. P A R T F O U R The Second Generation Children of Thomas Goble Sr. — 1630s to 1680s 4.1 —
John Goble (born approximately June 30, 1629, Sussex) John Goble was the eldest child of Thomas and Alice — born in
England, brought to Massachusetts as a small boy, and eventually returning to the country of his birth. He appears in a 1654
deposition when he was described as being "about 25" — placing his birth convincingly in the 1629 range. By 1657, when his
father composed his will, John was firmly enough established in England that Thomas specifically noted "the eldest of which
being now in England," conditionally assigning John's share to his brothers if he did not return to claim it. He did not return.
John Goble died by 1676 — the land sale of March 1675 was conducted without him, his portion having evidently been
forfeited or already distributed. He left no recorded American descendants, the only child of Thomas Goble Sr. whose line did
not continue in the New World. 4.2 — Thomas Goble Jr. (born approximately 1631– 1635, England/Charlestown) Thomas Jr.
grew up on the family farm in Charlestown, the second son and — after John's permanent removal to England — effectively
the eldest son present in Massachusetts. He married Mary (variously listed in genealogical records as Mary Mousall or Mary
Gove — a confusion that may reflect either a remarriage or a clerical inconsistency in the records). Together they raised a
substantial family in Charlestown: ● Thomas Goble III — born 1656, died 1724 — the continuation of the main Goble line ●
Stephen Goble — born 1659, executed September 1676 (see Part V) ● Mary Goble — born 1661, died 1714 ● Kevin Goble
— born 1663, died 1670 — died in childhood ● Ruth Goble — born 1663, died 1726 ● John Goble — born 1668 ● Abigail
Goble — born 1669, died 1705 Thomas Jr. served in Captain Prentice's Company during King Philip's War (1675–1676) —
one of three Goble men who fought in that conflict, and the only one whose service would not end in catastrophe. He lived to
see the war's end, the execution of his youngest brother Daniel and his own son Stephen, the gradual restoration of peace, and
the slow rebuilding of the colonial communities that the war had devastated. Thomas Goble Jr. died November 22, 1690 in
Charlestown, at approximately sixty years of age — having survived everything that the seventeenth century had thrown at
him. 4.3 — Elizabeth Goble (born 1634, Charlestown) Elizabeth, the eldest child born in the New World (or possibly at sea en
route), married first John White of Sudbury — a match documented by 1654. She later married Thomas Carter. She died after
1682 in the Charlestown and Middlesex area, leaving descendants through both marriages. Her appearance in the 1675 land
sale document (through her husband John White of Sudbury) confirms her survival into that period. 4.4 — Mary Goble

(baptized February 27, 1636, Charlestown) Mary Goble was baptized in Charlestown in February 1636, one of the first
children of the family to be born in the New World. She married Daniel Dean (also written Deane) and appears alongside her
husband in the 1675 land sale document as one of the executing parties of her father's estate lands. She lived until 1705 —
long enough to see the Goble family's dramatic story fully play out, including the executions of her youngest brother and her
nephew, the end of King Philip's War, and the gradual recovery of colonial Massachusetts in the decades that followed. 4.5 —
Sarah Goble (baptized May 27, 1638, Charlestown) Sarah Goble was baptized in Charlestown in the spring of 1638, the fifth
child of Thomas and Alice. Her father's will of November 1657 noted specifically that she was "not yet married" at the time
of his writing — placing her marriage after late 1657. She subsequently married John Shepard, with whom she appears in the
1675 land sale document. Sarah Goble Shepard died on November 30, 1717 — the last surviving child of Thomas Goble Sr.,
outliving her father by sixty years and outliving all of her siblings. She had witnessed, from her long life's vantage point, the
entire arc of her family's story in the New World: the arrival, the building, the war, the tragedy, and the survival. She was
seventy-nine years old when she died — an extraordinary age for the colonial era — and with her death the last living memory
of Thomas Goble Sr. passed from the world. 4.6 — Daniel Goble (baptized July 18, 1641, Charlestown) — The Most
Dramatic Story Daniel Goble was the youngest child of Thomas and Alice — baptized in Charlestown in July 1641, just three
and a half years before the death of his father would deprive him of a paternal figure. He grew up in the

Charlestown household, working the family land, and eventually settled in Concord — the same frontier town where his father
had spent his final years. On February 25, 1663/64, Daniel married Hannah (Anna) Brewer in Sudbury, Massachusetts.
Hannah was born in Cambridge on January 18, 1644/45, the daughter of John Brewer and his wife Anne — a colonial family
of standing in the Cambridge community. Daniel and Hannah settled south of Walden Woods in Concord, in the shadow of
the same great forest that stretched westward into the Native homeland. Their four children were: ● Hannah Goble — born
1666 ● Daniel David Goble Jr. — born 1669, died 1733 ● John Goble — born 1671, died 1723 ● Alice "Ellis" Goble — born
1673, died 1718 — she became the first wife of Nathaniel Woods of Groton, Massachusetts, documented in the New England
Historical & Genealogical Register, Spring 2018, Vol. 172, p. 103, by Allan Gilbertson When King Philip's War erupted in the
summer of 1675, Daniel Goble's children were between two and nine years old. He enlisted in Captain Manning's Company
— the unit that would participate in the most massive single military action of the entire war. The story of what happened
next is told in Part V. P A R T F I V E King Philip's War (1675–1676) The Goble Family at the Center of History 5.1 — The
Road to War The war that came to New England in 1675 had been building for a generation. It was the result of fifty years of
English expansion into Native lands, of broken promises and legal manipulation, of the slow strangulation of the
Wampanoag, Nipmuc, and Narragansett peoples by the settler colonial project that Thomas Goble had been a part of since
1634. Understanding the war requires understanding the decades that preceded it. When the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth in
1620, the sachem (chief) of the Wampanoag Confederacy was Massasoit, a figure of enormous political skill and pragmatic
wisdom. Massasoit had just watched his people devastated by an epidemic (probably smallpox or leptospirosis) that had killed
up to ninety percent of the coastal Native population between 1616 and 1619. Weakened and surrounded by rival Native
nations, Massasoit made a strategic alliance with the English newcomers — an alliance that provided mutual protection and
trade, and that endured for the rest of his life. This was the peace that allowed the Plymouth Colony and, later, Massachusetts
Bay Colony to establish themselves without a general war during their most vulnerable years. Massasoit died around 1661. His
elder son, Wamsutta — whom the English called "Alexander" — inherited the Wampanoag leadership. Within a year, he was
summoned to Plymouth Colony by colonial authorities who suspected him of plotting against the English. On his journey
home from this confrontation, Wamsutta fell suddenly ill and died. His Wampanoag people believed he had been poisoned.
They were almost certainly right to be suspicious. Wamsutta's younger brother, Metacom — "King Philip" to the English —
became sachem. He had watched the English encroach upon Wampanoag lands for decades, using legal instruments the Native
people did not fully understand, debt obligations they could not escape, and the sheer weight of an ever-growing colonial
population that needed ever more land. By the early 1670s, Metacom was secretly building a military alliance among the

Wampanoag, Nipmuc, and other peoples. The English learned of it, tried and executed three Wampanoag men accused of
betraying the plot, and in June 1675, the war began. A contemporary illustration depicting Native forces attacking English
colonial settlements during King Philip's War (1675–1676). The war devastated both communities across Massachusetts,
Connecticut, and Rhode Island. Three members of the Goble family — Thomas Jr., Daniel, and Stephen — served in the
colonial military forces. The Goble family's involvement in the war's most controversial episode became one of colonial New
England's most dramatic criminal cases. The terror that swept through colonial Massachusetts in the summer and autumn of
1675 was unlike anything the colonists had experienced. Towns on the frontier — exactly the frontier where the Goble family
lived — were raided and burned. Families were killed in their fields and at their doorsteps. The ordered, enclosed world of the
Puritan settlement dissolved into chaos at its edges. Concord, home of the Goble family, was directly in the path of the war's
violence. 5.2 — The Goble Men Go to War Three members of the Goble family served in the colonial military forces of King
Philip's War: ● Thomas Goble Jr. — son of Thomas Sr. — served in Captain Prentice's Company ● Daniel Goble —
youngest son of Thomas Sr. — served in Captain Manning's Company ● Stephen Goble — son of Thomas Jr., grandson of
the patriarch — served in Captain Wheeler's Company Of these three, Daniel Goble's service was the most historically
significant — and ultimately the most devastating. Captain Manning's Company participated in what remains the largest single
military action of King Philip's War: the Battle of the Great Swamp Fort, December 19, 1675. The Narragansett people — the
most powerful Native nation in southern New England — had largely stayed out of the war in its early months, attempting to
maintain neutrality. The English colonial governments decided, with a ruthlessness that still shocks the historical conscience,
not to wait for the Narragansett to join Metacom's forces. In December 1675, a combined colonial force of approximately one
thousand men, drawn from Massachusetts, Plymouth, and Connecticut colonies, marched into the swamps of Rhode Island in
bitter winter conditions. They located the Narragansett's winter fortress — a large fortified village on an island in the Great
Swamp, its palisade walls and barkcovered longhouses sheltering perhaps three thousand people, the majority of whom were
women, children, and elderly noncombatants who had gathered for the winter. On December 19, 1675, the colonial forces
attacked. They found a breach in the palisade wall and poured through it, setting fire to the longhouses. Men, women, and
children were killed by the hundreds — some by musket fire, many by the fire itself as the longhouses burned. The colonial
loss was also severe: seventy men killed, one hundred and fifty wounded. But the Narragansett nation was, in a single
afternoon, effectively destroyed as a military force. Those who escaped fled into the winter wilderness without food or shelter.
Hundreds more died in the weeks that followed. Daniel Goble was there. He had spent December 19, 1675 fighting in that
swamp, watching those fires, and carrying home whatever he witnessed. It is impossible to know precisely what he saw or what
he thought. But the Great Swamp battle was one of the defining experiences of King Philip's War — an act of colonial
violence that radicalized both sides and made the conflict more savage in its final months. When Daniel Goble returned from
that campaign, he was a different man than the one who had left Concord in the summer. The Concord Council had already
issued, on August 30, 1675, an order that "any Indians found more than a mile from the center of their villages, except in the
company of English or on service, the English are at liberty to shoot them down or arrest them." This order — a shoot-on-
sight directive — gave legal cover to the worst impulses of men who had spent months at war and who had returned home to
find their frontier communities still frightened, still angry, and still capable of the most extreme violence. 5.3 — The
Hurtleberry Hill Massacre (August 7, 1676) By August 1676, King Philip's War was effectively over. Metacom had only a
handful of followers remaining. The killing that occurred on Hurtleberry Hill on August 7, 1676 — eight months after the
Great Swamp — was not an act of war. It was murder. The colonial court system would say so explicitly. The events of
August 7, 1676 can be reconstructed from the court records of the subsequent trial. A large group of English soldiers
encountered, in the woods of Hurtleberry Hill near Concord, Massachusetts, a Native guide named John Stoolemester and his
charges: three Christian Indian women and three young children. These were "Praying Indians" — Native people who had
converted to Christianity, adopted English customs, and lived in the designated praying towns established by the Puritan
missionary John Eliot. They were not enemy combatants. They were explicitly exempt from the wartime kill orders.

Stoolemester explained their purpose: they were picking berries. The soldiers, initially, accepted this explanation. According to
witness testimony later given at trial, the soldiers "called to them, exchanged bread and cheese for fruit, then moved off." But
four men stayed behind, or returned: ● Daniel Goble of Concord, age approximately 35 ● Stephen Goble, nephew of Daniel
and son of Thomas Jr., age approximately 17 ● Daniel Hoar of Concord ● Nathaniel Wilder of Lancaster ◆ August 7, 1676
— Hurtleberry Hill, Concord, Massachusetts Six Christian Indian women and children — people who had converted to
Christianity, who lived in designated praying towns, who were explicitly exempted from the wartime kill order — were
murdered on a summer hillside. Their coats were stolen. Their bodies were left where they fell. What followed was a massacre.
The six Christian Indian women and children — people whose faith in English protection and English law was ultimately and
catastrophically misplaced — were killed. Their bodies were left in the woods. Their coats were taken by the killers before they
rode away. When John Stoolemester returned and could not find his charges, he searched for two days. The six bodies were
eventually found in the woods of Hurtleberry Hill. Andrew Pittimee and Thomas Speen — husbands of two of the murdered
women — immediately brought charges. The four English soldiers were identified and arrested. The site of these events —
Hurtleberry Hill — is located in present-day Concord and Lincoln, Massachusetts, in the same landscape where Henry David
Thoreau would later gather huckleberries and write about the beauty of the New England countryside. 5.4 — The Trial (1676)
The trial of Daniel Goble, Stephen Goble, Daniel Hoar, and Nathaniel Wilder took place in the colonial courts in 1676. It was,
by the standards of the era and by the treatment of Native Americans in colonial law, a remarkable proceeding: Native men's
testimony was taken seriously, weighed against the testimony of English men, and ultimately found more credible. The defense
arguments put forward for the four accused men were: 1. The Concord Council's August 30, 1675 order had authorized
shooting any Indian found more than a mile from their village. 2. The General Court had previously supported aggressive
action against Native people. 3. Witnesses were produced who claimed — apparently falsely — that the victims had not had
permission to be at Hurtleberry Hill. The prosecution countered with evidence that dismantled each defense point: ● The
victims were Christian Praying Indians, explicitly and specifically protected under colonial law even during the war. ● The
soldiers had demonstrably acknowledged the Indians' peaceful purpose — they had exchanged bread and cheese for berries.
They then returned specifically to kill them. This was premeditated murder, not a mistake in the heat of battle. ● The
testimony of Andrew Pittimee and Thomas Speen, corroborated by physical evidence and multiple witnesses, established the
facts of the crime beyond the court's reasonable doubt. The verdict was unanimous: all four men were found guilty and
sentenced to hang. The Puritan court — a court that had conducted and sanctioned the Great Swamp massacre, a court
operating in a society that was actively enslaving and selling captured Native people at thirty shillings each — nevertheless
drew a line at the murder of Christian converts who had placed themselves under English protection. Daniel Hoar and
Nathaniel Wilder subsequently pleaded for mercy and were pardoned by the court. Daniel Goble and Stephen Goble were not.
5.5 — The Executions (September 1676) Daniel Goble was identified by the court as "the ringleader" of the Hurtleberry Hill
murders. He and his seventeen-year-old nephew Stephen — the grandson of Thomas Goble Sr. — were condemned to die.
Stephen Goble was executed the week before Daniel — sometime in mid-to-late September 1676. He was approximately
seventeen years old. The grandson of a man who had paid Harvard tuition in corn, the son of a man who had fought with the
colonial army through King Philip's War, Stephen Goble went to the gallows on the Boston and Roxbury Neck at an age when
the full moral weight of what he had done may not yet have been comprehensible to him. September 26, 1676 Daniel Goble
— Executed by Hanging Boston and Roxbury Neck, Massachusetts Bay Colony Convicted of the murder of six Christian
Indian women and children at Hurtleberry Hill, August 7, 1676 Recorded in the diaries of Samuel Sewall and Increase Mather
Daniel Goble's execution was delayed because he was ill — the court waited until he had recovered sufficiently to be hanged.
On September 26, 1676, Daniel Goble was hanged on the Boston and Roxbury Neck — the narrow strip of land connecting
the Boston peninsula to the mainland, where the colonial gallows stood. His execution was a public event, witnessed by a
gathered crowd and recorded in the private diaries of two of the most significant figures in Puritan New England: ◆
Historical Record: Two Diaries, One Execution Samuel Sewall — Boston magistrate, later one of the judges in the 1692 Salem

Witch Trials, and later still the only Salem judge to publicly repent his role in those proceedings — recorded the execution of
Daniel Goble in his famous diary. Increase Mather — Boston's most prominent Puritan minister, father of Cotton Mather,
author of numerous treatises on divine providence and the war — also recorded the execution in his diary. That two such
prominent men both felt compelled to record this event is itself a measure of how extraordinary it was — an English colonial
soldier executed for the murder of Native people was not a common occurrence in seventeenthcentury Massachusetts.
Hannah Brewer Goble was left a widow with four children ranging in age from approximately three to ten years old. Daniel
left a will naming Hannah and children Daniel, John, Hannah, and "Ellis" (Alice). The youngest, Alice "Ellis" Goble, was
approximately three years old when her father was hanged. She would live until 1718, becoming the first wife of Nathaniel
Woods of Groton, Massachusetts — documented in the New England Historical & Genealogical Register of Spring 2018.
Hannah Brewer Goble's subsequent life — how she managed to raise four small children alone on a Concord farm after her
husband's execution, in a community that had just lived through the most devastating war in its history — is not documented
in surviving records. But she managed. The children survived. The line continued. 5.6 — Context and Legacy of the Trial The
trial and execution of Daniel and Stephen Goble stands as one of the most historically remarkable episodes in the entire
colonial New England record. Several aspects of the case deserve particular attention: First: It was one of the very few
instances in colonial New England — perhaps the most thoroughly documented — in which English colonists were tried,
convicted, and executed specifically for the murder of Native American people. The colonial legal system routinely failed to
protect Native life; this case is a documented, if imperfect and partial, exception. Second: The testimony of Andrew Pittimee
and Thomas Speen — Native men whose wives had been murdered — was accepted and credited by an English colonial court
over the counter-testimony of English witnesses who were apparently lying. This is a significant, if easily overlooked, moment
in the history of colonial justice. Third: The case demonstrates the profound moral contradiction at the heart of Puritan
colonial society. This was a society that could wage what we would now call genocidal warfare against Native peoples —
burning their winter camps, enslaving survivors, displaying the head of Metacom on a pole for twenty years — and
simultaneously execute its own soldiers for murdering Christian converts who had placed themselves under English protection.
This is not hypocrisy in the simple sense. It is the full, complicated, contradictory truth of what that society actually was:
capable of terrible violence and capable, in specific cases, of something that resembled justice across racial lines. Fourth: The
location — Hurtleberry Hill in present-day Concord/Lincoln, Massachusetts — places this event in a landscape that
Americans associate primarily with the American Revolution (the "shot heard round the world" was fired in Concord in April
1775) and with Thoreau's transcendentalist vision of nature. The Hurtleberry Hill murders are part of that landscape's deeper,
darker, more complicated history. P A R T S I X The Third Generation and Legacy 1676 and Beyond 6.1 — Thomas Goble
III (born 1656, died 1724) The grandson of the patriarch — son of Thomas Jr. and Mary — was born in 1656, just a few
years before his grandfather Thomas Sr. died in Concord. He was approximately twenty years old when his uncle Daniel and
his brother Stephen were executed in 1676. He survived the war, survived the executions, and continued the Goble name in
Massachusetts. He died in 1724, at approximately sixty-eight years of age — having carried the Goble lineage through one of
the most turbulent periods in colonial history into the relative stability of the early eighteenth century. Through Thomas III,
the Goble name continued in Massachusetts and spread to other states in the generations that followed. 6.2 — The Remaining
Goble Family After the War After the executions of Daniel and Stephen Goble in September 1676, the family was shattered
— but not destroyed. Thomas Goble Jr. lived until 1690, a man who had outlived the war, outlived two of his closest family
members on the gallows, and endured the knowledge that his own son Stephen had participated in an act for which the
colonial court hanged him. What Thomas Jr. thought of all this — of the war, of Stephen, of Daniel, of the trial — is not
recorded. He left no diary. He left only the documented fact of his survival. Sarah Goble Shepard, the last surviving child of
Thomas Sr., lived until 1717 — forty-one years after the executions. She was thirty-eight years old in September 1676. She had
known Daniel and Stephen Goble as her baby brother and her nephew. She lived with the memory of what happened for four
more decades, into a Massachusetts that was already beginning to look back on the seventeenth century as a different and

terrible age. Alice "Ellis" Goble — Daniel's youngest child, named in his will as "Ellis" — became, as documented by Allan
Gilbertson in the New England Historical & Genealogical Register (Spring 2018, Vol. 172, p. 103), the first wife of Nathaniel
Woods of Groton, Massachusetts. She died in 1718 at approximately forty-five years of age. Her mother Hannah Brewer
Goble had raised her in the aftermath of execution and war. She married, she built a life, and she died leaving her own
descendants in the Massachusetts that her grandfather Thomas Goble Sr. had helped to build. 6.3 — The Legacy of Thomas
Goble Sr. Thomas Goble Sr. arrived in America in August 1634 with his wife, his children, his faith, and his two hands. He had
no connections, no prior wealth in the colony, no great name. He was a middle-aged farming man from a small Sussex village,
and he built from that foundation one of the most fully documented lives of the ordinary colonial Massachusetts settler.
Within twenty-three years of his arrival, he had: ● Achieved Freeman status — full colonial citizenship — within days of his
arrival ● Accumulated five distinct land parcels totaling approximately 73 acres ● Served on what was likely the first jury ever
to convene in Boston ● Paid Harvard College tuition in corn and wheat on behalf of his child ● Raised six children to
adulthood on the colonial frontier ● Moved his family to the frontier community of Concord ● Died leaving a will that was
executed by his capable and trusted wife His family's story encompasses, in microcosm, the full narrative of
seventeenthcentury New England: the Great Puritan Migration, the building of colonial institutions, the first Boston jury,
Harvard College's earliest years, King Philip's War in all its moral complexity, and one of colonial New England's most
dramatic and historically significant criminal trials. The Goble family is not famous. Thomas Goble Sr. is not remembered in
the history books that most Americans learn from. But he is remembered in the parish registers of Aldingbourne, in the court
records of Massachusetts Bay, in the tuition ledgers of Harvard, and in the diaries of Samuel Sewall. He is remembered
because he lived fully, worked hard, raised his family, and because history — in all its drama — found his children even when
he was gone. P A R T S E V E N Comprehensive Timeline c. 1540 – 1717 Date Event c. 1540 William Goble "de Westergate"

CLOSING ESSAYThe Measure of an Ordinary Man Thomas Goble's life spans nearly seven decades — from the last years
of Elizabeth I's England, through the tumultuous reigns of James I and Charles I, across three thousand miles of ocean, and

into the raw, dangerous, astonishing world of colonial New England. He lived through the crisis of the Roanoke mystery, the
persecution of Archbishop Laud, the Great Puritan Migration, the founding of Harvard College, the first Boston jury, the
tentative and finally shattered peace between English settlers and the peoples of the interior, and the devastating cataclysm of
King Philip's War — though mercifully he died before the last of these. He was not a general, a governor, or a famous
minister. He held no position of great power. He wrote no published works. He left no letters that have survived. He was a
farmer, a father, a juror, a property owner, a taxpayer. He paid Harvard tuition in corn. He moved his family to the frontier. He
died quietly in Concord with a modest will and an estate that reflected two decades of steady, patient, determined labor. But
what his life built — and what his children's lives revealed — is the full complexity of seventeenth-century New England in
miniature. His son Thomas Jr. fought in a colonial army that committed what we would now recognize as war crimes at the
Great Swamp. His youngest son Daniel fought in the same war, witnessed the same violence, and then participated in a murder
that the colonial court found — to its credit — could not be excused or overlooked. His grandson Stephen went to the
gallows at seventeen. His daughter Sarah lived to seventy-nine, carrying all of it in memory. His granddaughter Alice, named
"Ellis" in her father's last will, built a new life and family in Groton, Massachusetts — her father hanged, her grandfather dead
before she was born, her inheritance one of the most turbulent family histories in the colonial record. The Hurtleberry Hill
case — the murder of six Christian Indian women and children and the subsequent trial and execution of Daniel and Stephen
Goble — stands as one of the most historically significant episodes in colonial Massachusetts justice. In a society that
routinely denied Native Americans legal standing, the court in 1676 accepted the testimony of Andrew Pittimee and Thomas
Speen, weighed it against the testimony of Englishmen who were apparently lying, and executed two of its own for murder
across racial lines. This was not justice in the full sense — the Narragansett winter camp was still burning, Metacom's head was
still on its pole in Plymouth, and hundreds of surviving Natives were being sold into slavery at thirty shillings each. But it was
a moment when the Puritan legal system did something it rarely did: it acknowledged, in the most definitive way available to it,
that the lives of six Christian Indian women and children had mattered. Thomas Goble Sr. could not have imagined any of
this when he stood in the church at Aldingbourne on November 5, 1619, and married Alice Brookman in the grey November
light. He was twenty-eight years old. The ocean was three thousand miles away. America was a rumor, a dream, a place where a
man who had been born fatherless in a small village might — with God's favor and his own labor — build something that
would last. He built it. It lasted. And the full human cost and human achievement of what he built — in faith and in tragedy, in
ambition and in violence, in the corn he carried to Harvard and the land he cleared with his own hands — is the story of
colonial New England itself. This is the story of Thomas Goble of Colonial Massachusetts. It is over. It continues. This
biography was compiled from primary colonial records, genealogical research, and historical scholarship. All dates and facts
have been sourced from the primary documents listed in Part IX. Where uncertainty exists in the historical record, it has been
explicitly acknowledged in the text. Compiled July 2026 • Sources: Aldingbourne Parish Register • Massachusetts Bay Colony
