F O R E W O R D A Letter to Shane Goble Jefferson, Ashtabula County, Ohio | July 2026 Dear Shane, The document you
hold in your hands — or perhaps on your screen, in the ordinary miracle of this age — is a companion to something that
came before it: the Goble & LeCompte Family Ancestral Research Report, completed in July 2026, which laid out in
methodical, documentary form the names, dates, vital records, and verified genealogical findings of your family lines. That
report was a map. This one is the territory. A map is indispensable. But a map does not tell you what the air smelled like when
a young Englishman walked off a ship into the harbor at Charlestown in 1634, squinting into a New World he had crossed
three thousand miles of open ocean to reach. It does not tell you what a man felt when he hid for months in a Pennsylvania
forest, listening for the footfall of raiders who would not hesitate to kill him. It does not tell you what it cost a Frenchman to
leave behind everything he had ever known — his language, his land, his country — because the faith he held in his heart had
been declared a crime against the kingdom. This companion volume exists to tell you those things. Or rather, to reconstruct
them as faithfully and honestly as the historical record permits, drawing on parish registers, colonial court documents, military
pension records, probate inventories, Maryland land grants, and one of the most remarkable oral-history manuscripts in
American genealogical literature. Where the record is silent — as it inevitably is, across the gulf of centuries — this document
will say so plainly. The "Imagined Voice" passages scattered through these chapters are creative reconstructions, clearly labeled
as such, grounded in what we know but not to be mistaken for direct quotation or documented fact. What the record is not
silent about is this: you carry in your DNA the double inheritance of two extraordinary men from the seventeenth century.
One is Thomas Goble, born January 2, 1590, in the small Sussex parish of Westergate on the English coastal plain — an
English Puritan who crossed the Atlantic in the great migration of 1634 and became, among other things, a member of what
is believed to be the first jury ever convened in Boston. The other is Antoine LeCompte, born approximately 1620 in Calais,
on the Franco-Flemish border — a French Huguenot, a Calvinist Protestant in a violently Catholic France, who served in the
English army, sailed to the Chesapeake Bay, and carved a fortified plantation out of the Maryland wilderness on an island in
the Choptank River. Thomas Goble left England because of religious persecution. Antoine LeCompte left France for the
same reason. The two men never met. They lived three thousand miles apart and belonged to entirely different worlds. Yet
here, in Jefferson, Ohio, in 2026, their lines have long since merged — woven together by generations of migration, marriage,
and the long westward drift of American family life. The story of how that happened is one of the most improbable and
moving journeys in American family history. It is your journey, Shane. These are your people. Read their stories. — The
Compiler, Jefferson, Ohio, July 1, 2026 C H A P T E R O N E "The Man from Westergate" Thomas Goble (January 2,
1590/91 – December 1657) Born in the shadow of the English Channel, he would cross three thousand miles of ocean to
help build a civilization. He was a juryman, a landowner, a father of six, and a church elder — and he arrived in Boston in a
year when Boston had barely decided it was a city. The village of Westergate lies in the coastal lowlands of West Sussex,
England, a few miles inland from the English Channel, tucked into the flat agricultural plain that stretches east toward
Aldingbourne and west toward Chichester. In January 1590 — in the old Julian calendar reckoning that split the new year
across two numbers, so that the date reads "1590/91" — a boy named Thomas Goble was born there into a Sussex family of
modest yeoman stock. His father was William Goble II, born approximately 1550, himself the product of generations of
Sussex soil. The name "Goble" is older than England as we know it. Etymologists trace it to the Old French word gobel,
meaning a drinking vessel — a goblet — suggesting that somewhere in the medieval past, an ancestor of this family was a
craftsman or merchant who worked with cups, a trade common enough in a world where taverns and feast halls required their
wares by the hundreds. A secondary etymology reaches further back, to Old High German Godebert, meaning "God-bright"
— a name that carries within it both piety and luminance, qualities that would characterize the Goble line through the
centuries to come. By whatever path the name arrived in Sussex, it was Thomas's name, and he carried it to the New World.
On November 5, 1619, Thomas Goble stood before the altar of Aldingbourne Parish Church and married a woman named
Alice Brookman. The marriage is confirmed in the West Sussex parish records — a plain documentary entry that nonetheless
represents the beginning of a family line that would not stop moving for the next four hundred years. Earlier genealogical

literature sometimes identified Thomas's wife as "Alice Mousall," but careful examination of the primary source establishes
Alice Brookman as the correct name. She was the woman who would cross an ocean with him, who would give birth to their
daughter Elizabeth somewhere in the mid-Atlantic or on the Massachusetts shore, and who would outlive him in the
wilderness of the New World. England in the 1620s and early 1630s was a kingdom in spiritual ferment. The Puritan
movement — a reform effort within the Church of England demanding a more rigorous, Scripture-centered Protestantism —
had been gathering force for decades, and under King Charles I, those who dissented from the established church's
ceremonies and hierarchy faced fines, harassment, and imprisonment. The years between 1629 and 1640 became known as the
Great Migration: approximately twenty thousand English men, women, and children crossed the Atlantic to the Massachusetts
Bay Colony in search of the freedom to worship as their consciences demanded. Thomas Goble was among them. He
emigrated approximately 1633 to 1634, most likely aboard one of the ships actively serving the Charlestown trade routes —
the Abigail, the Hopewell, or the Lion are the most probable candidates. With him came his wife Alice and their son John,
who was then three or four years old. Sometime during the crossing or shortly after arrival, Alice gave birth to their daughter
Elizabeth — a child who entered the world, quite literally, between two continents, in the churning and uncertain space of the
Atlantic crossing. The documentary evidence of Thomas's arrival in the New World is precise and unambiguous. On August
30, 1634, Thomas and Alice were formally admitted to the First Church of Charlestown — an ecclesiastical record that fixes
them in Massachusetts and establishes their standing as committed members of the Puritan community. Three days later, on
September 3, 1634, Thomas Goble was granted freeman status by the Massachusetts Bay Colony General Court. This was not
a trivial honor. Freeman status conferred the full rights of colonial citizenship: the right to vote in colony elections, to hold
public office, to serve on juries. It required that the applicant be an adult male in good standing in a recognized church
congregation. Thomas had been in Massachusetts less than two weeks, and already he was a recognized citizen of the new
republic in the wilderness. Within four years of arrival, he had assembled an estate of remarkable scope for a new immigrant.
By 1638, Thomas held five separate land parcels in and around Charlestown: a house and half-acre lot at the west end of the
common; four acres of planting ground on the Newton Line; two and threequarter acres of cow commons; fifteen acres of
woodlands; and fifty acres of a parcel called Waterfield. These were not the holdings of a man clinging to survival. These were
the holdings of a man building a life, with intention and confidence, in the New England soil. And then came October 1, 1640
— the day that fixed Thomas Goble permanently in the legal history of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and, arguably, in the
civic history of America itself. On that date, Thomas Goble served on what is believed to be the first jury ever formally
convened in Boston. The case before them concerned one Hugh Buets, charged with heresy. The jury found Buets guilty, and
the court ordered him expelled from the jurisdiction "upon paine of death" if he ever returned. The twelve men who sat in
judgment — Thomas Goble among them — were paid a total of twelve shillings for their service, roughly one shilling apiece.
It was not a princely sum for a moment of historical consequence. Historical Context THE FIRST BOSTON JURY —
October 1, 1640 The institution of trial by jury is one of the foundational pillars of the Anglo-American legal tradition, traced
to Magna Carta (1215) and enshrined in the English common law that the Puritan settlers brought with them across the
Atlantic. But in 1634, when Thomas Goble arrived in Charlestown, the Massachusetts Bay Colony was still developing its
formal legal infrastructure. Courts were assembled, judges appointed, and the machinery of colonial governance slowly
erected. The first formally convened jury in Boston — October 1, 1640 — represents the colony's maturation into a
functioning legal state. That Thomas Goble was among its members speaks to his standing in the community: only freemen of
established good character would have been selected. The case — heresy — may seem remote to modern sensibilities, but in a
Puritan colony founded explicitly on religious conformity, doctrinal deviance was not a private matter. It was a civic one. The
verdict against Hugh Buets was, in its own way, the colony defining its boundaries. And Thomas Goble helped draw that line.
The years between 1640 and 1655 find Thomas aging into the role of established patriarch and community elder. Between
1653 and 1655, the Harvard College Treasurer's accounts record payments under the names "goodman goobell" and "old
gobbell" — almost certainly Thomas, paying tuition fees for a son or ward enrolled at the college. Harvard had been founded

in 1636, just two years after Thomas set foot in Charlestown; to have a child within its walls a generation later was no small
testament to the family's standing and ambitions in the new world. By the 1650s, Thomas had relocated from Charlestown to
Concord, in Middlesex County — following the pattern of so many Massachusetts settlers who moved progressively inland as
the frontier expanded. It was there that he died, sometime before December 30, 1657, the date on which his will was probated
in Middlesex County. The inventory of his estate is a quiet, tender catalogue of a life: one featherbed, two feather pillows and
wool blankets, one small featherbed, two bolsters, two blankets, and one trundle bed. Forty pounds of paraffin. Two iron pots.
A man who had crossed an ocean with nothing now left behind the comforts of a modest but respectable household. His will
contained a line that still rings with the plainspoken affection of the age: "I give and bequeath to Alice my wife fair profit on
all my stock so long as she liveth a widow." Thomas Goble, jury member and freeman and Puritan pilgrim, made sure Alice
was provided for. He left behind six children: John (born approximately 1629), Thomas Jr. (approximately 1631–35), Elizabeth
(approximately 1634, the Atlantic child), Mary (born February 27, 1636), Sarah (born May 1638), and Daniel (born
approximately 1640–41). It is Daniel — the youngest, perhaps born the very year his father sat on the first Boston jury —
through whom the Ohio Goble line descends. Imagined Voice Thomas Goble — Charlestown, Massachusetts, August 1634 I
have seen the harbor now. It is nothing like what I expected and everything I hoped. The water here is cold even in August,
and the settlement — what they call the town — clings to the hills as though it is still deciding whether to stay. We were
admitted to the church three days ago, Alice and I both, and it was the first moment since Westergate that I felt the ground
solid beneath me. Not the ground of the ship, which moves always, nor the ground of England, which I will never touch
again. This ground. They have given me rights here. Citizen, they call it — Freeman of the Colony. I signed my name in the
General Court record this morning, September the third, 1634. There is land to be had. There is work to be done. There is, for
the first time in years, no man with authority over my conscience but God. Clearly labeled as historically informed creative
reconstruction based on documented records. The facts of admission to First Church (August 30, 1634) and freeman status
(September 3, 1634) are documented. The interior experience is the author's informed interpretation. Not a direct quotation.
✦ ✦ ✦ C H A P T E R T W O "The Long March West" Daniel Goble, Daniel Jr., Kevin, and the New Jersey Generations
(1640–1800) A family's history is not only the story of its most prominent members but of the quiet generational motion —
the slow drift southward and westward, decade by decade — that moves a line from one coast to another over the span of two
centuries. Daniel Goble was born approximately 1640 or 1641, the youngest of Thomas and Alice's six children, into a
Charlestown that was already transforming from a frontier outpost into a functioning colonial town. He grew up in the years
when Massachusetts was becoming something — a society with courts and churches, with land surveys and market days, with
a Harvard College and a General Court and the beginning of a civic life. His father had helped build it. Daniel was born into
it. He died in 1676, relatively young, in what was one of the most catastrophic years in New England history — the year of
King Philip's War, the devastating conflict between colonial settlers and an alliance of Wampanoag and allied tribes that nearly
destroyed the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Whether Daniel's death was connected to that conflict is not documented; but the
timing is haunting. He left behind a son who would carry the family name south and west. That son was Daniel Goble Jr.,
born May 21, 1669, in Concord, Massachusetts. He married Sarah Houghton, born July 30, 1672, in Lancaster, Worcester
County, Massachusetts — a woman from the Worcester County frontier, a region that had suffered grievously in King Philip's
War. Together, Daniel Jr. and Sarah made the move that would define the family's trajectory for the next century: they migrated
to New Jersey, joining the broad southward movement of Massachusetts families into the mid-Atlantic colonies that
characterized the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. New Jersey in 1700 was a colony in formation — a
patchwork of Quaker settlements, Scottish proprietorships, and newly arrived families from New England and the Dutch-
influenced Hudson Valley. Daniel Jr. lived there until after 1724, the last date at which he appears in the record. His son Kevin
would be born on New Jersey soil, and it was Kevin who would root the Goble name so firmly in Morris County that it would
not move again for a generation. Kevin Goble was born July 12, 1700, in New Jersey — the first Goble in the direct line who
was not born in Massachusetts. He married a woman named Mary, born approximately 1701, on December 26, 1724, in

Morristown, New Jersey, in what was surely a Christmas-season wedding in the Presbyterian church that anchored the town's
community life. Kevin and Mary had seventeen or more children — a number that strains modern comprehension but was not
unusual in a colonial household where children were both a blessing and a labor force, where infant mortality made large
families a hedge against loss. Among those children were Jonas Goble and Daniel W. Goble, each of whom would found his
own branch of the sprawling Goble family tree. Kevin Goble died March 29, 1783, in Morristown — the very year the Treaty
of Paris officially ended the Revolutionary War and established the United States of America as a sovereign nation. He had
lived through the entirety of colonial America: born before the century turned, dying in the moment of national
independence. He was, in the truest sense, a man of the old world becoming the new one. Morris County, New Jersey, in the
eighteenth century was no quiet rural backwater. It was one of the most industrially and politically active regions in colonial
America. The county's iron forges — fed by the ore-rich Highlands and the fast-running streams of the Raritan watershed —
produced the cannon, shot, and hardware that would supply the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War. The
Presbyterian churches of Morristown were centers not only of worship but of Whig political sentiment, hotbeds of the
patriot cause. George Washington wintered his army in Morristown in 1776–77 and again in the brutal winter of 1779–80, the
coldest winter of the eighteenth century, when soldiers froze in their huts on the hills above a town where Kevin Goble was
then a middle-aged man with grown sons. Jonas Goble, born approximately 1707, was one of those sons. He married Melatiah
Town (1702–1768, Morristown) and fathered Henry Goble, born approximately 1748, who would marry Lydia Conger on
December 11, 1765, in Morris County. Henry's sons would be among the first Gobles to push into Ohio and Indiana — the
far edge of the American frontier in the early nineteenth century, a land that had been wilderness within living memory. But it
was Jonas's brother Daniel W. Goble — born approximately 1735, son of Kevin and Mary — who executed the most dramatic
and consequential migration of his generation. In 1773, Daniel W. Goble organized and led a migration of twenty to twenty-
five families from Morris County, New Jersey, westward into Washington County, Pennsylvania, along a waterway called
Tenmile Creek. This was no individual journey. This was a community in motion — the Axtell and Lindley families among the
travelers — a whole social world transplanting itself from the settled East to the raw western frontier of Pennsylvania, three
years before the Revolution would make that frontier a theater of war. Daniel had married Rhoda Doud on February 17, 1751,
in Morristown, and the children born of that marriage would grow up not in New Jersey but in the Pennsylvania wilderness.
One of those children was a boy named Caleb, born in 1760, who would become the most vividly documented member of the
Goble family in the era of the founding of the nation. ✦ ✦ ✦ C H A P T E R T H R E E "Spy in the Wilderness" Caleb
Goble, Revolutionary Patriot (March 1, 1760 – March 22/23, 1838) He was sixteen years old when he picked up a musket and
walked into the Revolution. He spent the next six years in the forests of the Pennsylvania frontier, doing work so dangerous
that the word for it was borrowed from a profession of intrigue: spy. Caleb Goble was born March 1, 1760, in Morristown,
Morris County, New Jersey, the son of Daniel W. Goble and Rhoda Doud. He was thirteen years old when his father led the
great migration of Morris County families westward to Washington County, Pennsylvania, along Tenmile Creek — and so the
first years of his adolescence were spent not in the settled comfort of New Jersey but in the still-raw borderland of western
Pennsylvania, where the forest came to the edge of every clearing and where the frontier had not yet decided whose it was. In
1776, the year the Declaration of Independence was signed in Philadelphia, Caleb Goble was sixteen years old. He enlisted in
Captain Benjamin Rice's Company of the Washington County, Pennsylvania Militia and served one month at Jackson's Fort
under Captain Charles Crawford. It was his first experience of military service, and it would not be his last. In 1777, Caleb
served a six-month tour as a substitute for his brother Daniel Goble in Captain James Brinton's Company, Colonel Crawford's
Regiment. During this service, he helped construct two of the most significant fortifications on the western Pennsylvania
frontier: Fort McIntosh and Fort Laurens. These were not ornamental installations. They were the outermost edge of
American military presence in a region where British-allied Native American forces conducted regular raids on settlements —
burning farmhouses, destroying crops, and killing or capturing the families that had come west to homestead. Building these
forts was dangerous, exhausting, and strategically vital. And then came the work that would define Caleb Goble's military

career: from approximately 1778 to 1783 — a span of roughly five to six years — he served in the Rangers of the Frontier at
Lindley's Fort, Washington County, Pennsylvania. For one full year within that service, he acted as an Indian Spy: a scout who
moved alone or in small teams through the forests gathering intelligence on the movements of British-allied Native American
forces on the western Pennsylvania frontier. Historical Context THE FRONTIER SPY — What It Meant in 1779 The term
"Indian Spy" in the Revolutionary-era militia records does not carry the moral ambiguity of later usage. It referred to a specific
military function: a scout who operated in advance of settlements and fort garrisons, moving through the forest to observe,
track, and report on the movements of British-allied forces and their Native American partners. The western Pennsylvania
frontier in 1778–1783 was a genuine war zone. British commanders at Detroit and Niagara coordinated with Shawnee,
Delaware, Wyandot, and Mingo warriors to conduct raids into Kentucky and Pennsylvania settlements. The goal was to
prevent American expansion westward — to terrorize settlers into abandoning the frontier. A frontier spy operated with
minimal support, often traveling days or weeks at a time in forested terrain, sleeping rough, reading the landscape for signs of
war parties — disturbed leaves, recently abandoned campsites, the direction of smoke. A mistake meant death or capture. The
men who did this work were extraordinarily skilled woodsmen, and they were extraordinarily brave. Caleb Goble did it for a
year. He came home. Caleb's brothers served alongside him. Ebenezer Goble, born 1757 in Morristown, who would die March
28, 1813, in Washington County, Pennsylvania, and Daniel Goble both appear in the records of Captain John Miller's
Company, First Battalion, Washington County, serving together in 1782. The Goble brothers had come west together as boys.
They fought the Revolution together as men. The war ended in 1783. Caleb Goble came out of the forest alive. In 1786, in
Washington County, Pennsylvania, he married Sarah Leasure and began the family that would define the rest of his long life —
a life that unfolded across the next half-century in a series of moves that traced the opening American frontier westward, step
by careful step. By 1794, Caleb appears in the tax records of Maysville, in Mason County, Kentucky — the Ohio River gateway
town that served as a staging post for families moving north and west. By approximately 1798, he had crossed the river into
Ohio, settling in Clermont County in the southwestern corner of the new state. Around 1802, he moved to Warren County,
near the town of Lebanon. Around 1811, he was near Troy, in Miami County. Finally, he settled in Shelby County, Ohio, where
he would spend the last decades of his life and where he would be buried at Medaris Cemetery. He and Sarah had fifteen
children — a family so large it strains the imagination, born across the decades of Caleb's westward migration, children born
in Pennsylvania and Kentucky and Ohio, a mobile, multiplying family that spread itself across the new American states like
seed on the wind. One of those children, a son named John, would later be the subject of a published account in The Sidney
(Ohio) Journal on April 7, 1871, under the title "Early Life of a Pioneer" — the next generation's testimony to what it had
meant to grow up on Caleb Goble's frontier. In 1832, at the age of seventy-two, Caleb Goble sat down and applied for a
Revolutionary War pension. He was an old man by then, remembering a young man's war from fifty years past. The
application, dated October 31, 1832, was initially unresolved — the machinery of pension bureaucracy moved slowly, and the
records of frontier militia service were scattered and incomplete. The Pennsylvania pension was not finally approved until
1855 — seventeen years after Caleb Goble died. He never received the pension he had earned. He had, however, lived a life
that the pension could not have adequately compensated anyway. Caleb Goble died March 22 or 23, 1838, in Shelby County,
Ohio, at the age of seventy-eight. He had been alive before the United States existed. He had helped make it possible.
Imagined Voice Caleb Goble — Lindley's Fort, Washington County, Pennsylvania, 1779 The forest is not silent. That is the
first thing a man learns, if he lives long enough to learn anything out here. The forest talks constantly — it rustles and creaks
and drips and cracks — and what a spy must learn is not to hear the forest, but to hear the thing that is wrong in it. A branch
that bends the wrong way. A bird that stops. A silence that lasts a half-breath too long. I have been out here three days this
time. I sleep with my back to a tree and my rifle across my knees. I know where the war party came through two days ago — I
found the fire ring, still warm, and the moccasin prints in the mud by the creek. I sent word back to the fort. That is all I can
do. That, and keep moving, and stay alive, and come home to tell what I have seen. Clearly labeled as historically informed
creative reconstruction based on documented records. Caleb Goble's service as an Indian Spy at Lindley's Fort, Washington

County, Pennsylvania (1778–1783) is documented in Revolutionary War military records and his 1832 pension application. The
interior experience is the author's informed interpretation. Not a direct quotation. ✦ ✦ ✦ C H A P T E R F O U R "Born in
Fire, Forged by Faith" Antoine (Anthony) LeCompte Sr., Huguenot Patriarch (~1620 – after September 9, 1673) He was born
in one of the most contested cities in Europe, in one of the most persecuted religious minorities in the history of
Christendom. He would become a soldier, a landowner, a justice of the peace, and the patriarch of a dynasty that would
stretch, unbroken, to the present day. Calais, in the early seventeenth century, was a city of layered identities and long
memories. It had been under English control for two centuries — from 1347 to 1558 — within living memory of Antoine
LeCompte's birth around 1620. Even after its return to French sovereignty, it remained a bilingual, Anglo-French borderland
at the narrowest point of the English Channel, where the white cliffs of Dover were visible on clear days across twenty-one
miles of cold gray water. A child born in Calais around 1620 grew up hearing English in the markets, French at the hearth, and
Flemish from the traders who crossed from the Low Countries. The city was a crossroads and a fault line both. The name
"LeCompte" carried its own layered history. It derives from the Old French le comte — "the count" or "the earl" — signifying
either actual descent from nobility or long service as the steward or administrator of a count's household. The name's deep
Norman roots are confirmed by the thirteenth-century manuscript Cartulaire de l'abbaye de Jumièges, which contains the
reference "Johannes le Comte" — an ancestor perhaps of this very line, already bearing the name in the age of the Crusades.
Whether Antoine's family had genuine noble blood or bore a name that gestured toward a noble connection it could no longer
prove, the name itself was a statement: this family had once stood near the centers of power. But in seventeenth-century
France, Antoine LeCompte was not a man of power. He was a Huguenot — a French Calvinist Protestant — in a kingdom
that had been trying, with increasing violence, to resolve the question of religious diversity for over a century. The French
Wars of Religion (1562– 1598) had killed an estimated three million people. The Massacre of Vassy on March 1, 1562 — sixty
Huguenots slaughtered while worshipping in a barn — had ignited the wars. The St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of August
23–24, 1572, had seen thousands of Huguenot nobles and their households butchered in Paris and across France in a
coordinated orgy of violence that shocked Protestant Europe. The Edict of Nantes (1598) had offered a fragile peace. But
when Cardinal Richelieu's forces besieged and took La Rochelle in 1628 — the great Huguenot stronghold on the Atlantic
coast — the last military protection of the Huguenot community collapsed. Historical Context THE HUGUENOT
EXODUS — Europe's Greatest Refugee Crisis of the 17th Century The Huguenots — French Calvinist Protestants —
constituted roughly ten percent of France's population at their peak in the 1560s, perhaps a million people. Over the following
century, religious war, massacre, forced conversion, and legal persecution reduced their numbers dramatically. The fall of La
Rochelle in 1628 ended their political autonomy. The revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 would ultimately drive an
estimated two hundred thousand Huguenots into permanent exile — to England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia, South Africa,
and the American colonies. Those who fled were not the poor or the desperate. They were skilled artisans, merchants,
physicians, lawyers, military officers, and intellectuals — the productive middle and upper-middle class of French society. Their
departure impoverished France and enriched everywhere they went. In South Carolina, Huguenot families established the rice
plantations. In New York, they built the textile trade. In Maryland — where Antoine LeCompte arrived around 1655 — they
joined a colony already defined by its experiment in religious tolerance. The Huguenot diaspora was, in modern terms, a
refugee crisis of the first order. Antoine LeCompte was one of its earliest representatives in the Chesapeake. After La Rochelle
fell, Antoine fled Catholic France for England. There he served approximately eleven years in the army of King Charles I — a
period of military service that embedded him in the turbulent politics of the English Civil War era. Family tradition, preserved
in the 1819 LeCompte Manuscript dictated by his blind descendants, holds that Antoine's valor was so great that "his name
was so great, and for his valor, had him knighted and the title of 'Monsieur' given to him, and his coat of arms." A 2004 search
by William Hunt, Windsor Herald at the College of Arms in London, found no record of English knighthood for Antoine
LeCompte — suggesting that the Arms the family carried into the New World may have been French noble arms brought
from the continent rather than an English royal grant. The tradition of valor, at least, rings plausible for a man who spent his

entire subsequent life on frontiers. When Charles I was executed on January 30, 1649, and the English monarchy fell to the
Puritan Commonwealth, Antoine LeCompte — a royalist, a Protestant, and a man without a political homeland — turned his
eyes westward. He emigrated to the English colony of Maryland, arriving approximately 1655. Maryland's Toleration Act of
1649, passed just as Antoine was watching the English political order collapse, had granted religious freedom to all Trinitarian
Christians — making it the only English colony where a Huguenot Protestant could legally worship and live without fear of
persecution. It was the natural destination. The land records tell his story with the laconic precision of colonial bureaucracy.
On February 7, 1655, Antoine assigned his right to two hundred acres to Ishmael Wright. In 1657, Calvert County charged
him three hundred pounds of tobacco for killing three wolves — the standard colonial bounty, evidence that he was already
ranging widely through the Maryland wilderness, doing the practical work of frontier settlement. Then came the great claim.
On January 17, 1659, Anthony LeCompte earned an eight-hundred-acre land parcel through the headright system — paying
the passage of three individuals (Thomas Raymond, Barbara Crouch, and Thomas Jones) to Maryland, each headright worth a
specified acreage under colonial law. The grant was surveyed on August 13, 1659, and named, with unmistakable personal
pride, "St. Antoine" — also recorded in variants as "Antonine" and "St. Anthonia." Eight hundred acres in what would
become Dorchester County, Maryland, on the Choptank River, stretching to the edge of the Chesapeake Bay. It was his land.
His name on it. In the midst of this colonial enterprise, Antoine returned to Europe. He met Hester Dottando, born in
Dieppe, Normandy, France — another Norman, another French Protestant, another refugee from the wars of religion that
had rearranged their world. They married in London on July 11, 1661, in a ceremony recorded in the London parish registers.
Then they sailed together for Maryland and the plantation he had named for himself. The LeCompte plantation on Taylor's
Island, Dorchester County, was genuine wilderness in 1659. Very few Europeans had settled in the region. Antoine brought
armed servants and fortified the settlement against attack. The historical record, preserved in the LeCompte family accounts
and the History of Dorchester County, states plainly that when hostile Native American bands approached, he "would disperse
them by firing his large guns, and it is said, killed some of them." This was the reality of frontier plantation life in the mid-
seventeenth-century Chesapeake: a Frenchman, recently arrived, defending a name he had placed on a map with the tools of
violence and determination. Antoine served as a Justice of Dorchester County from 1669 to 1671 — the same administrative
role that Thomas Goble had filled in Massachusetts a generation earlier, the civic duty of the established man, the colony
requiring its most capable members to govern as well as to settle. He appears in the Maryland Archives in this capacity, his
name now Anglicized to "Anthony" in the colonial record. His last documented appearance alive is September 9, 1673. He
died sometime thereafter, in Dorchester County, Maryland. On July 17, 1680, the Chancery Records note "Mark Cordea and
Esther, his wife, executrix of Anthony LeCompte, deceased" — Hester had remarried, but she had administered her first
husband's estate, and it is through her that the line continued. Imagined Voice Antoine LeCompte — Taylor's Island,
Dorchester County, Maryland, ~1662 Hester has been here three months now. She does not say that she is afraid, but I know
her face. I built this place before she came — I had to build it before she came, because I would not bring her here to nothing.
The land is extraordinary. The Choptank River in the morning light is something I could not have imagined in Calais or in
London. We have planted tobacco. We have planted corn. The servants are reliable and the guns are maintained. When the
men came to the edge of the clearing two weeks past — I could see them in the tree line, watching — I ordered the large gun
discharged. They did not come again. Hester heard the shot from the house. She came to the door and looked at me with
those eyes. I told her we were safe. We are. I named this place for myself, for Antoine, for St. Antoine — because I wanted
something in this world to carry my name forward. I think it will. Clearly labeled as historically informed creative
reconstruction based on documented records. The land grant "St. Antoine" (January 17, 1659), marriage of Antoine and
Hester in London (July 11, 1661), and frontier defense accounts are documented in Maryland State Archives and Elias Jones's
History of Dorchester County, Maryland (1902). The interior experience is the author's informed interpretation. Not a direct
quotation. On June 6, 1674, Hester and all her children by Antoine were naturalized as British subjects. The petition recorded
in the Maryland Archives names them fully: Hester herself, born in Dieppe, Normandy; John (born approximately 1662 in

Maryland); Moses (born in Maryland; reportedly blind at age twenty-two, yet reportedly the father of eleven children); Philip
(Maryland; died before 1705, unmarried); Anthony Jr. (Maryland); Hester (Maryland; married Skinner); and Katherine
(Maryland). Six children. An entire line, certified as belonging to the new world, on a summer day in 1674. ✦ ✦ ✦ C H A P T
E R F I V E "The Blind Brothers Remember" Moses LeCompte and the 1819 Manuscript Memory is its own kind of
inheritance. In 1819, two men who could not see sat down in a Maryland county and dictated, from pure memory, the history
of a family that stretched back two hundred years to a refugee from a French religious massacre. What they produced is one of
the most extraordinary genealogical documents in American history. Moses LeCompte was the second son of Antoine and
Hester. He was born in Maryland, naturalized a British subject alongside his mother and siblings in June 1674, and he carries in
the genealogical record one of the most striking biographical details in the entire Goble-LeCompte family history: at the age
of twenty-two, Moses LeCompte went blind. The cause is not documented. Disease — smallpox, perhaps, or some other
colonial scourge — is the most likely explanation, though accident cannot be ruled out. What the record does document is the
apparent fact that Moses, blind at twenty-two, went on to father eleven children and continued the family line with a
determination that borders on the extraordinary. The blindness did not stop him. The family he created did not diminish. He
died in 1720, in Dorchester County, Maryland, and left behind a progeny that would multiply and migrate across two more
centuries. The generations after Moses trace a slow accumulation and movement. William LeCompte, born approximately
1685, lived and died in Maryland. Moses LeCompte II, born approximately 1710 in Dorchester County, married Elizabeth
Wheeler and continued the line. Hugh LeCompte, born approximately 1740 in Maryland, served as the custodian of the
LeCompte Family Bible — a volume published in Philadelphia by the firm of Kimber and Sharpless sometime between
approximately 1784 and 1800, passed from eldest son to eldest son for three generations, and now displayed in Richmond,
Virginia. These are the quiet documentary details of a family in motion: a Bible passed hand to hand, a name carried forward,
a bloodline threading itself through the decades. But it is the year 1819 that gives this chapter its title and its heart. In that year,
in Dorchester County, Maryland, two brothers sat down with a younger kinsman named Benjamin Woodward LeCompte and
began to talk. Their names were Thomas LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte. They were fourth-generation descendants of
Antoine and Hester. And they were both blind. What they dictated to Benjamin Woodward LeCompte over the course of that
session — or those sessions; we do not know how long it took — was a comprehensive oral history of all known descendants
of Antoine and Hester LeCompte: names, dates, relationships, family branches, the trajectory of a family across nearly two
centuries. These two men, who could not read a single word, had carried the entire genealogy of the LeCompte family in their
minds, memorized and maintained and passed down through the oral tradition of a family that had learned, perhaps from its
patriarch's own example, that what you hold in your memory cannot be burned or confiscated or legislated away. The
manuscript they produced through Benjamin Woodward's pen is now held by the Maryland Historical Society in Baltimore. It
is one of the most remarkable genealogical documents in the American record — not for its scholarly apparatus or its
documentary rigor, but for what it represents: the human capacity to carry a story, intact and alive, across generations that have
no written access to it, and to set it down before it is lost forever. The manuscript preserves family tradition about Antoine —
including the account of his military service and the claim of knighthood — that n

o official record confirms or denies. It preserves the names of branches long since obscured by time. It preserves the family as
a living thing, not a set of dates in a ledger. Thomas and Daniel LeCompte dictated that manuscript in the year 1819. Moses
LeCompte, their great-great-grandfather, had gone blind in approximately 1684 — a hundred and thirty-five years earlier.
Whether the blindness that afflicted Moses and his fourth-generation descendants was genetic, environmental, or simply a dark
biographical coincidence, we cannot say. What we can say is that the two men who preserved the LeCompte family history did
so without the use of their eyes. They saw their family in their minds, and they spoke it into the future. "...joined the British
army and fought eleven years for the King of Great Britain and when the wars were over his name was so great, and for his
valor, had him knighted..." — Thomas LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte, as dictated to Benjamin Woodward LeCompte,
Dorchester County, Maryland, 1819; held by the Maryland Historical Society, Baltimore Consider the scene with the weight it

deserves: two elderly men, blind, seated perhaps by a window through which they cannot see the Maryland light, their voices
low and steady as they unspool a genealogy that begins in Calais, in the age of Richelieu and the English Channel and the wars
of religion, and arrives here, in this room, in this moment, in the mouths of two men who cannot see the paper on which their
words are being written. It is an act of extraordinary fidelity — to family, to memory, to the dead who must be kept alive in
speech because they cannot be kept alive any other way. ✦ ✦ ✦ C H A P T E R S I X "Ohio Convergence" The LeCompte
Line Comes West; Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte Two rivers, running separately for two centuries, eventually find the same
valley. The Goble line came out of New England, through New Jersey, through Pennsylvania, through the Kentucky and Ohio
frontiers. The LeCompte line came out of Normandy, through Maryland, through the generations of the Chesapeake. They
met in Ohio. The westward migration of the LeCompte family did not happen all at once. It happened the way all such
migrations happened in the early American republic: gradually, generationally, one family at a time following the roads and
rivers and rumors of good land that pointed toward the interior of the continent. The first clear signal of the family's evolving
trajectory appears in the name of Francis Asbury LeCompte, born approximately 1770–1800 in Maryland. He was named,
family tradition suggests, after Francis Asbury — the English-born Methodist bishop who became one of the most
consequential religious figures in early American history, riding an estimated three hundred thousand miles on horseback
across the new republic, preaching and organizing Methodist congregations in frontier settlements from Georgia to Maine. To
name a child after Francis Asbury was to announce a religious identity: this was a family that had moved, across the
generations, from the French Calvinist Protestantism of Antoine LeCompte the Huguenot refugee toward the frontier
Methodist Christianity that was reshaping American religious life in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Antoine
had fled Catholic France for the right to worship as a Calvinist. His descendants had become Methodists on the American
frontier. The arc of faith across two centuries and an ocean is one of the most quietly remarkable transformations in the
family's story. Francis Layton Foxwell LeCompte, born approximately 1800–1830, represents the transitional generation — the
one whose life spans Maryland origins and Ohio or Midwest arrival. Benjamin Berry LeCompte Sr., born approximately 1830–
1870 and dying in 1989 at an advanced age, is among the most remarkable links in the entire generational chain: a man whose
birth connected him to the antebellum era and whose death fell in the final decade of the twentieth century, bridging the world
of the Huguenot plantation on the Choptank River and the world of satellite television and interstate highways in a single
human lifetime. Howard Raymond LeCompte, born November 14, 1947, in Dayton, Ohio, and dying February 4, 2009, in
Celina, Mercer County, Ohio, represents the documented twentieth-century Ohio branch. Son of Jacque Howard Le Compte
(1924–2010) and Myrtle L. Dryden (1923–2010), married to Katherine Louise Hogan (1947–1972), Howard's life and death
are documented in the Ohio Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Center Obituary Index and the U.S. Obituary Collection. He is
the Ohio LeCompte line made visible in the record of a particular, individual human life. And then come the names that close
the circle: Rae LeCompte and Kevin Goble. Rae LeCompte — Shane's paternal grandmother — appears in the 1940 and 1950
United States Federal Census records, a presence confirmed by the U.S. Cemetery and Funeral Home Collection and the
Global Find a Grave Index. She was an Ohio woman, documented and real, carrying in her surname the four-hundred-year
journey from Calais, through London, through the Maryland Chesapeake, through the generations of westward migration, to
the Ohio she called home. Kevin Goble — Shane's paternal grandfather — was born approximately 1920 to 1935 in Ohio. He
appears in the U.S. Public Records Index (1950–1993), in U.S. City Directories, in Ohio Divorce Abstracts, and in the U.S. Find
a Grave Index. He was an Ohio man, like his wife — carrying in his name the equally long journey from Westergate, West
Sussex, through Charlestown and Concord and Morris County and Washington County and Clermont County and Warren
County and Miami County and Shelby County, to the Ohio both lines had been moving toward for two centuries without
knowing it. When Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte married, the two journeys became one. The man whose distant forebear
was the English Puritan jury foreman of the first Boston trial — and the woman whose distant forebear was the Huguenot
soldier who fired his cannon at the edge of a Maryland marsh to protect his plantation — were joined together in the ordinary,
extraordinary way that American families have always been joined: by proximity, by affection, by the slow convergence of lives

that had been moving toward each other for four hundred years without anyone planning it. Notable Collateral LeCompte
Descendants The LeCompte line produced, in its collateral branches, a number of figures of national significance: ●
Congressman Joseph LeCompte — U.S. Representative from the Maryland LeCompte line in the nineteenth century, carrying
the family's civic tradition into the halls of the national legislature. ● Congressman Karl M. LeCompte — U.S. Representative
in the twentieth century, continuing the family's remarkable thread of public service. ● Rowan LeCompte — American stained
glass artist of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, whose work appears in major American cathedrals including the
National Cathedral in Washington, D.C. In his art, the Huguenot family's ancient relationship with light — literal and spiritual
— finds its most luminous expression. ✦ ✦ ✦ C H A P T E R S E V E N "What the DNA Tells Us" Genetic Genealogy and
the Goble-LeCompte Lines The documentary record is not the only record. In the twenty-first century, the story of a family is
also written in molecules — in the Ychromosome passed from father to son, in the mitochondrial DNA passed from mother
to child, in the autosomal inheritance that shuffles and recombines across every generation. What does the genetic evidence
add to this story? The Goble Family Association DNA Project on FamilyTreeDNA is one of the older and more active
surname DNA projects in American genealogy, founded in November 2003 and maintained ever since by descendants of the
various Goble lines across America and internationally — including English, German, Australian, Irish, and South African
branches of the name. The project's goals are practical and direct: to confirm documented relationships between Goble
families in different states, to determine whether specific lines are genetically connected, to clarify whether the name "Goble"
in any given line traces to English, German, or French origins, and — in some branches — to detect potential Native
American admixture from the frontier generations. The paternal haplogroup of the Thomas Goble line has not been
definitively published in the public record available to this document. But the genetic context is clear. Y-DNA haplogroup R1b
is the dominant haplogroup among men of Western European descent, carried by approximately seventy percent of English
men. Given Thomas Goble's documented West Sussex English origins, R1b — or a sub-branch of it specifically associated
with the English coastal counties — is the most likely result for the Goble paternal line. A Y-DNA test taken by a proven
male-line descendant of Thomas Goble through his son Daniel and the Ohio branch could confirm this haplogroup and
potentially connect Shane to male-line Goble cousins across America and England, resolving documentary gaps that paper
records cannot bridge. The Goble DNA Project itself has identified the precise nature of those gaps: as the project's own
documentation acknowledges, "most brick walls seem to occur in the 1700s or 1600s when censuses and tax lists were scarce."
This is exactly the gap Shane's family faces — the period between the New Jersey Gobles of Morris County and the Ohio
emergence of Kevin Goble. A Y-DNA test comparing Shane's result against other project participants could provide genetic
evidence of connection where paper trails have grown thin. The WikiTree profiles for the Goble family document, in the
DNA connections sections, what autosomal evidence already exists for this line. The profile for Ebenezer Goble (Caleb's
brother, 1757–1813) shows documented public matches with AncestryDNA and 23andMe testers carrying estimated shared
DNA values of approximately 0.78% and 0.39% — consistent with fifth-through-seventh cousin relationships, the expected
range for descendants of a common ancestor living four to six generations back. These matches are registered on GEDmatch
under kit numbers including M891174, MY2532114, A655359, T595034, and FTDNA kits #879557 and #391992. The
network of genetic connection is already partially mapped. It awaits a Goble descendant willing to add their DNA to the map.
On the LeCompte side, the picture is complementary and equally promising. The website lecompte.net, maintained by
Kirkwood A. LeCompte, hosts an active DNA Comparison section where LeCompte descendants are systematically
documenting shared DNA results in an effort to confirm common descent from Antoine and Hester — to find, in the
molecular record, the echo of a marriage that took place in London in 1661. For the maternal line — specifically, the
mitochondrial DNA of female-line descendants of Hester Dottando LeCompte — testing would likely reveal a haplogroup in
the H or HV range, the dominant Western European maternal haplogroups, with possible French or Norman-specific sub-
branches that could be traced to the Normandy coast where Hester was born. For Shane personally, the genetic picture of his
ancestry is rich with possibility. His autosomal DNA carries markers from both the English Puritan West Sussex Goble line

and the French Huguenot Picardy/Normandy LeCompte line — and the ethnic percentages such a test would return are likely
to show elevated Northwestern European and French/Norman genetic signatures, precisely what one would expect from the
double inheritance of a Sussex yeoman farmer and a Calvinist refugee from the border of France and Flanders.
Recommended Actions for Shane ● Y-DNA test (37 or 67 markers minimum) through FamilyTreeDNA — then join the
Goble DNA Project to compare against other Goble-surname male participants. ● Autosomal DNA test through
AncestryDNA, 23andMe, or MyHeritage — then upload raw DNA data to GEDmatch for cross-platform matching. ● Check
the LeCompte DNA Comparison page at lecompte.net and submit results to Kirkwood LeCompte's project if a match to the
LeCompte line is confirmed. ● Review WikiTree profiles for Ebenezer Goble (1757–1813) and Antoine LeCompte Sr. for
existing match lists that may include distant cousins already in the databases. Lineage Societies Shane May Qualify For ●
Huguenot Society of America (founded 1883) — Qualification requires documented descent from a Huguenot who arrived in
the American colonies before 1685. Antoine LeCompte arrived approximately 1655. Shane qualifies. ● National Huguenot
Society — Same qualifying criterion. Shane qualifies through the Antoine LeCompte line. ● Daughters of the American
Revolution / Sons of the American Revolution — Qualification requires descent from a documented Revolutionary War
patriot. Caleb Goble's service is verified through military records and his 1832 pension application. Shane qualifies. ● Goble
Family Association — The active organization maintaining the Goble DNA Project and broader Goble genealogical research.
Membership connects Shane to a community of thousands of Goble descendants worldwide. ✦ ✦ ✦ C H A P T E R E I G
H T "Jefferson, Ohio — Where the Lines Rest" A Meditation on Arrival Every migration has an endpoint — or rather, a
resting place, because the lines of a family never truly stop moving. But for now, the lines rest here: in Jefferson, Ashtabula
County, Ohio, in the twenty-first century, in the person of Shane Goble. Consider the geography of what has brought you
here, Shane. Consider the arc of it, the improbable and irreversible westward tilt of it, the way two streams — neither knowing
the other existed — moved toward the same valley over the course of four centuries. One stream began in Westergate, West
Sussex, on a January morning in 1590, when a boy named Thomas Goble entered the world in the coastal lowlands of
southern England. It moved to Charlestown, Massachusetts, in 1634 — crossing three thousand miles of open ocean in a
wooden ship barely larger than a modern suburban house. It moved to Concord, Massachusetts, then south and west to Morris
County, New Jersey, where Kevin Goble married Mary in a Christmas-season ceremony in 1724 and had seventeen children
who filled the county with Goble descendants. It moved west again to Washington County, Pennsylvania, in 1773, when Daniel
W. Goble led twenty-five families over the mountains. It moved through the Revolution — through Caleb Goble's years in the
forest, listening for the footstep that would mean death, carrying intelligence back to forts built from raw timber on the
Pennsylvania frontier. It crossed the Ohio River. It moved through Clermont County and Warren County and Miami County
and Shelby County. And eventually, by the paths that brought Kevin Goble to Ohio, it arrived. The other stream began in
Calais, France, sometime around 1620, when a child named Antoine was born in a bilingual border city where the English
coast was visible on clear days. It moved to England, to the army of Charles I, to a military career in someone else's civil war.
It crossed the English Channel again in the opposite direction, to Maryland, to the Chesapeake Bay, to eight hundred acres
named "St. Antoine" on the edge of a tidal river where a Frenchman with a cannon and a French wife from Normandy built a
fortified plantation and became a colonial justice of the peace. It moved through the generations of the Chesapeake —
through Moses and William and Moses II and Hugh and the custodians of the family Bible — and then, when America called
families westward, it too began to move. Through Maryland to Ohio, through the generations of Francis Asbury LeCompte
and Benjamin Berry LeCompte, through Rae LeCompte's documented presence in the census records of a twentieth-century
Ohio. And then the streams met. Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte, in Ohio, in the ordinary way that people meet and marry
and make families, not knowing — how could they have known? — that they were the living confluence of a four-hundred-
year double journey. Not knowing that their union joined the line of the first Boston juror to the line of the Huguenot soldier
on the Choptank River. Not knowing that their grandchildren would one day be able to read about it in a document like this
one. What does it mean to be the living endpoint of four centuries of migration, faith, war, land-claiming, and survival? It

means, at minimum, this: that you are not accidental. That every decision made by every ancestor in this book — Thomas's
decision to board the ship, Daniel W.'s decision to lead the families west, Caleb's decision to walk into the Pennsylvania forest
in 1778, Antoine's decision to flee Calais for England, to marry Hester in London, to sail back to Maryland and fire his cannon
at the edge of the wilderness — all of those decisions made you possible. The survival of each of these people, in
circumstances that killed others, made you possible. There is a word for what Thomas Goble and Antoine LeCompte shared,
separated by three thousand miles of geography and a lifetime of different experience: dissent. Both men left their homelands
not for fortune but for the freedom to believe what they believed. Thomas Goble was an English Puritan who would not
submit to Charles I's religious conformity. Antoine LeCompte was a French Huguenot who would not submit to Cardinal
Richelieu's Catholicism. The faith that drove them both out of the old world and into the new was not the same faith — the
Puritan and the Calvinist Reformed traditions, while related, were distinct — but the underlying act was the same: a man
saying, at the cost of everything he knew, I will not pretend to believe what I do not believe. That refusal is in your DNA,
Shane, more literally than we can fully account for. You were born in 1993, in Williamsville, New York. Your brother Zachary
Goble was born July 10, 1987. You both live now in the orbit of Jefferson, Ashtabula County, Ohio — a town in the
northeastern corner of the state, not far from the Pennsylvania border that Caleb Goble's generation crossed when it was
wilderness, not far from the Lake Erie shore that the great migration routes ran along as families poured westward into the
new American interior. Jefferson is the endpoint for now. It is the place where the lines rest. Thomas Goble's jury foreman's
hand, signing a verdict in Boston in 1640. Antoine LeCompte's large gun booming across the Choptank marshes in 1662.
Caleb Goble's cold feet on a Pennsylvania forest floor in 1779. Moses LeCompte's unseeing eyes, turned toward some inner
landscape where the family history lived in its fullness. Two blind brothers in 1819, speaking a family into the future. And here,
in Jefferson, Ohio, in 2026 — the future they were speaking to. The line continues. ✦ ✦ ✦ A Note on Sources and Method

clearly before consulting the endnotes. Verified Historical Fact: All biographical claims, dates, place names, land records, court

survives in the parish register. THE TRAGEDY William Goble died May 1, 1593 and was buried at Aldingbourne. Thomas
was just TWO YEARS OLD. He grew up fatherless in a small Sussex hamlet — yet would one day become one of colonial
Massachusetts's most respected landowners. THE CHILDREN William Jr. (b.1582), Joanna (b.1585), Nycho (b.1586 — died
same year), Elizabeth (b.1588), John (b.~1588), and THOMAS (b. Jan 2, 1591) — the youngest and the one who would cross

AUGUST 7, 1676 Hurtleberry Hill Near Concord, Mass. THE FOREST CRIME A summer clearing — peaceful until it
wasn't HURTLEBERRY HILL — August 7, 1676 Near Concord, Massachusetts · The event that ended the Goble men's
story MORNING — THE BERRYPICKERS John Stoolemester, an armed Nipmuc guide allied with the English, watched
over his charges: three Christian Indian ("Praying Indian") women and three young children, peacefully picking berries on

Hurtleberry Hill in the woods near Concord. MIDDAY — THE SOLDIERS ARRIVE A company of English soldiers
encountered the group. Stoolemester explained their peaceful purpose. The soldiers acknowledged this — and shared bread
and cheese with the berry-pickers in exchange for fruit. Then the company rode on. THE RETURN — FOUR MEN
LINGER Four men separated from the company and doubled back: DANIEL GOBLE (age 35), STEPHEN GOBLE (age
~17), Daniel Hoar of Concord, and Nathaniel Wilder of Lancaster. Veterans of a brutal war — men who had watched friends
die — living under a shoot-on-sight order. THE MURDERS Six Christian Indian women and children — explicitly exempted
from the wartime kill order, living in designated praying towns — were murdered. Their bodies were left where they fell. The
killers stole their coats before riding away. JUSTICE DEMANDED — TWO DAYS LATER Stoolemester returned to find
his charges missing. Two days of searching. Six bodies found in the woods. Andrew Pittimee and Thomas Speen — Native
husbands of two of the murdered women — immediately pressed charges in the English colonial court. Sources:
Massachusetts Colonial Court Records (1676) · Diary of Samuel Sewall (Sept. 26, 1676) · Diary of Increase Mather (1676) ·
NEHGR Vol. 172, p. 103 (2018) 1 2 3 4 5 THE TRIAL OF DANIEL & STEPHEN GOBLE — 1676 Colonial justice at a
crossroads — one of the most significant trials in early American legal history THE DEFENSE ARGUMENT 1: The
Concord Council's order of August 30, 1675 permitted killing any Indian found more than one mile from their village without
English escort. ARGUMENT 2: The General Court had previously condoned such actions against Native people throughout
the course of the war. ARGUMENT 3: Defense witnesses were produced — falsely claiming the victims had not had
permission to be at Hurtleberry Hill. ⚖ CONCLUSION: These arguments did not persuade the judge or the jury. THE
PROSECUTION FACT 1: The victims were CHRISTIAN PRAYING INDIANS — explicitly protected under colonial law,
living in designated praying towns. FACT 2: The soldiers had ALREADY acknowledged the group's peaceful purpose and
departed — then deliberately returned to kill. FACT 3: Native testimony from Andrew Pittimee and Thomas Speen was
accepted as valid by the court — a remarkable act of colonial jurisprudence. FACT 4: The murders were premeditated. The
stolen coats proved pillaging intent. ⚖ VERDICT — C OURT OF MA SS A CH U SET TS BAY C O LO NY, 1676 ALL
FOUR DEFENDANTS FOUND GUILTY — SENTENCED TO HANG. · Daniel Hoar & Nathaniel Wilder later received
pardons. · DANIEL GOBLE and STEPHThis case is historically recognized as one of the only instances in colonial New

LEGACY OF THOMAS GOBLE — WHY THIS STORY MATTERS ✦ Seven reasons this one colonial family illuminates
the entire American colonial experience TA KE AWAY I THE IMMIGRANT'S JOURNEY Thomas arrived at age 42 with
nothing but faith and labor. Within 6 years he owned five parcels of land and served on the first jury in Boston. The colonial
dream — earned, not given. TA KE AWAY I I THE ROANOKE MYSTERY The Goble family lived in Sussex throughout all
Roanoke voyages 1584–1590. The crew lists of the 1590 privateer fleet were never preserved. The oral tradition cannot be
confirmed — but cannot be disproven. TA KE AWAY I I I THE FIRST JURY On October 1, 1640, Thomas Goble sat on

DNA Matters for Genealogy The science of genetic genealogy has fundamentally transformed what it means to research
family history. Before the Human Genome Project — the landmark international scientific collaboration completed in April
2003 that produced the first full sequence of the human genome — a genealogist's only tools were paper: birth records,
church registers, census pages, court documents, and land deeds. These documentary records are invaluable, but they have

hard limits. They begin wherever literacy and record-keeping began for a given family and extend no further back. For the
Goble and LeCompte families, extraordinary documentary evidence reaches to approximately 1590 in West Sussex, England,
and to 1655 in Calais, France. Beyond those horizons, the paper trail goes dark. DNA does not. [Verification: Human Genome
Project completion date and scope — National Human Genome Research Institute, NIH, 2003. Genetic genealogy
methodology — International Society of Genetic Genealogy (ISOGG) standards.] Documentary genealogy and genetic
genealogy are fundamentally different disciplines that answer different questions. Documentary genealogy asks: Who were
your ancestors by name, and what did they do? It works forward and backward through time using the written evidence human
civilization has left behind. Genetic genealogy asks a different question entirely: What populations do you descend from, and
how long ago? It works by reading the actual chemical record inscribed in every cell of your body — a record that has been
faithfully copied and passed down since life itself began. When a paper record is lost, burned, or was never created, the DNA
record remains unchanged. Your genome does not care whether a courthouse burned in the Civil War or whether a French
Huguenot ancestor fled persecution in such haste that no document survived the crossing. The genetic evidence endures
regardless. Shane Goble's 23andMe Personal Genome Service results accomplish something remarkable: they serve
simultaneously as independent confirmation of the documentary genealogical record compiled in Part I of this series, and as a
window into ancestral time that no paper record could ever open — reaching not centuries but hundreds of thousands of
years into the human story. Every major finding from the documentary research is cross-validated by the genetic evidence. The
dominant English ancestry, the French Huguenot signal of Antoine LeCompte, the deep British Isles roots — all confirmed.
But the DNA also reveals new information that no archive on earth could provide: the specific Bronze Age population that
carried Shane's paternal line into Britain 4,500 years ago, the Mesolithic hunter-gatherers who were Shane's maternal ancestors
long before farming reached Britain, and four specific genetic fragments inherited from an encounter with Neanderthals
50,000 years before the first human being ever picked up a pen. In this way, documentary evidence and DNA evidence work
precisely as two independent witnesses to the same story — each confirming the other, each adding what the other cannot see.

Section 16: Haplogroups — Your Ancient Ancestral Highways While ancestry composition analysis measures the
contributions of many different ancestors across many different family lines, haplogroup analysis is something entirely
different and, in its own way, more profound. Haplogroups are specific branches on the human family tree, defined by
particular genetic mutations — called Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms, or SNPs — that arose once in a single individual at a
specific point in history and were then passed unchanged from that individual to all of their descendants in a single line of
descent. Crucially, haplogroups are not averages or composites. They trace two very specific ancestral lines with complete
fidelity across thousands of generations. The paternal haplogroup, carried on the Y-chromosome, is passed exclusively from
father to son to son across every generation — tracing the direct paternal line: Shane's father's father's father's father, back in
an unbroken chain to a specific ancestral population tens of thousands of years ago. Only males carry a Y-chromosome;
paternal haplogroups are male-line only. The maternal haplogroup, carried in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), is passed from
mother to all children — but only daughters pass it further. This traces the direct maternal line: Shane's mother's mother's
mothe

r's mother, back through time with equal fidelity. Together, these two haplogroups provide a precise, high-resolution genetic
signature for two specific lines out of the thousands of ancestral lines that converge to produce any living person.

BCE) The formation date of R-Z198 — approximately 2,550 BCE — places the origin of Shane's direct paternal line squarely
in one of the most dramatic and consequential periods in British prehistoric history: the arrival and expansion of the Bell
Beaker people. The Bell Beakers were a Bronze Age culture named for their distinctive inverted-bell-shaped pottery,
identifiable at archaeological sites across a vast arc of Europe from the Iberian Peninsula to the British Isles. They originated
ultimately from the Pontic-Caspian Steppe — the vast grasslands of modern Ukraine and Russia — and their westward
migration across Europe in the third millennium BCE was not a gentle cultural exchange. It was, in the most precise genetic
terms available, a population replacement of extraordinary scale. A landmark 2018 study published in Nature by Olalde and
colleagues, analyzing ancient DNA from 400 individuals across prehistoric Europe, found that the arrival of Bell Beaker
migrants corresponded to the replacement of approximately 90% of the existing genetic ancestry of Britain within just a few
centuries. The pre-existing Neolithic farming population — who had built megalithic monuments including Stonehenge —
was largely displaced by these newcomers. The Bell Beaker migrants carried R1b haplogroups overwhelmingly, and R-Z198 is a
direct descendent branch of that Bell Beaker genetic signature. [Verification: Bell Beaker genomic transformation of Britain —

genetic record paints a vivid picture. They were horsemen — among the first cultures to use horses not merely for food but
for transport and warfare, giving them a dramatic mobility advantage over settled populations. They were skilled metalworkers
who worked copper and early bronze into weapons and tools. They buried their dead individually rather than in communal
megalithic tombs, typically in round barrows (earthen burial mounds) that survive by the hundreds across the English
landscape, including in Sussex. Bell Beaker graves are often accompanied by weapons — daggers, arrowheads — and by their
signature pottery. These were not peaceful traders who happened to share their pottery styles; they were an expanding, mobile,
militarily capable population whose genetic signal, carried in Shane Goble's Y-chromosome today, testifies to their
overwhelming success as colonizers of a new land. Shane carries Bronze Age Steppe warrior DNA, preserved and transmitted
faithfully from that era to the present day in an unbroken male-line chain. [Verification: Bell Beaker culture archaeology —

One of the most scientifically remarkable findings of the genomics era — and one that would have seemed like science fiction
just two decades ago — is the discovery that modern humans of non-African ancestry carry, in their living cells, actual DNA
inherited from Neanderthals. Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) were a separate human species who evolved in Europe
and Western Asia over hundreds of thousands of years before anatomically modern humans arrived from Africa. For a long
time, scientists debated whether these two species had ever interbred. The answer, definitively established by the complete
sequencing of the Neanderthal genome from specimens found at Vindija Cave, Croatia, published in Nature in 2014 by Prüfer
and colleagues, is unambiguous: they did. Approximately 50,000 to 60,000 years ago, as modern humans migrated through the
Levant and into Western Asia, they encountered and interbred with Neanderthal populations. The result is that all people of
nonAfrican ancestry today carry between approximately 1% and 4% Neanderthal DNA — actual genetic sequences that have
been passed down, copied faithfully in every cell division, for fifty millennia. [Verification: Neanderthal genome sequencing
and interbreeding discovery — Prüfer et al., "The complete genome sequence of a Neanderthal from the Altai Mountains,"
Nature 505, 43–49, 2014. Neanderthal DNA in nonAfrican populations — Green et al., Science, 2010.] 23andMe identifies
specific Neanderthal-derived variants (SNPs) in each customer's genome by comparing against the confirmed Neanderthal
genome sequences. These are not estimates or statistical averages — they are specific, identified locations in the genome where
the DNA sequence matches the Neanderthal form rather than the form typical of fully modern humans. Each such variant is
a molecular fossil: a tiny piece of Neanderthal biology that was preserved when a modern human and a Neanderthal had
children together 50,000 years ago, and that has been carried forward every generation since in an unbroken chain of human
reproduction. Shane Goble has been identified as carrying more Neanderthal DNA than 74% of 23andMe customers — a
modest but meaningful distinction that places him in the upper quarter of Neanderthal genetic inheritance. [Verification:

Shane's health predisposition results is a slightly increased genetic risk for celiac disease — a chronic autoimmune condition in
which the body's immune system reacts to gluten (a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye) by attacking the lining of the small
intestine. The genetic risk factors for celiac disease are primarily the HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 variants in the human
leukocyte antigen system, which regulates immune response. Importantly, these variants are remarkably common —
approximately 30% of the general population carries one or both — but only about 1% of the total population ever develops
clinical celiac disease. Carrying these HLA variants is a necessary but not sufficient condition for celiac; environmental triggers,
gut microbiome, and other factors all play roles in whether the condition actually develops. Having an increased genetic risk
means that heightened awareness and monitoring is prudent, not that celiac disease is inevitable or even likely. Celiac disease
frequently goes undiagnosed for years because its symptoms — digestive discomfort, fatigue, nutrient malabsorption, brain
fog, skin rashes — are common and nonspecific. If any family member experiences chronic unexplained digestive issues,
fatigue disproportionate to lifestyle, or iron/B12 deficiency resistant to supplementation, discussion with a gastroenterologist
and a celiac antibody blood test (specifically the anti-tTG IgA test) would be clinically reasonable given this genetic context.
The most important immediate action: share this finding with all first-degree biological relatives, as HLA-DQ variants are
inherited and may be present in siblings, parents, and children. [Verification: HLA-DQ variant frequency in general population

understood — the replacement of the earlier Neolithic farming populations who had built Stonehenge and the megalithic
