convergence of the genetic and documentary evidence here is striking. The R-Z198 haplogroup has its highest modern
frequency in precisely the counties — Sussex foremost among them — where the Goble family would emerge by name in the
sixteenth century. The paper trail places the Goble family in West Sussex; the Y-chromosome places Shane's paternal ancestors

in West Sussex going back to the Bronze Age. Two entirely independent lines of evidence, separated by 4,000 years, point to
the same patch of southern English coastland. Shane's Y-chromosome thus draws an unbroken genetic thread from the
Bronze Age steppe peoples, through the Bell Beaker migration into Britain, through millennia of English history, to the West
Sussex parish of Westergate — and from there, across the Atlantic to Massachusetts, New Jersey, and Ohio. 1.2 The Maternal
Line — Haplogroup U5b2c (Mesolithic Hunter-Gatherers, ~18,000 BCE) If the paternal haplogroup R-Z198 speaks of
Bronze Age migrations and steppe pastoralists, Shane's maternal haplogroup tells a far older and more intimate story. The
maternal haplogroup — inherited exclusively through the female line, passed from mother to child through mitochondrial
DNA without recombination — is U5b2c. This is among the oldest mitochondrial lineages in Europe, formed approximately
18,000 years ago during the Last Glacial Maximum, when vast ice sheets covered northern Britain and much of northern
Eurasia, and the early modern humans who would eventually populate post-glacial Europe survived in southern refugia in
Iberia, the Italian peninsula, and the Balkans. The U5 family of mitochondrial haplogroups — of which U5b2c is a direct
branch — is one of the founding lineages of European hunter-gatherers. It predates agriculture in Europe by thousands of
years. These were the people of the Mesolithic — the Middle Stone Age — who spread northward from their glacial refugia as
the ice retreated, following the reindeer and aurochs and salmon that recolonized the warming landscape. By approximately
10,000– 9,000 BCE, the descendants of these hunter-gatherers had reached Britain across what is now the North Sea (then a
wide, wooded plain known to geologists as Doggerland) and established themselves as the island's first post-glacial population.
The most evocative connection within this lineage is to Cheddar Man — a Mesolithic hunter-gatherer whose remains were
discovered in Cheddar Gorge, Somerset, England, and who lived approximately 7,150 years ago. Ancient DNA analysis of
Cheddar Man's remains, conducted by University College London researchers, revealed that he carried a haplogroup closely
related to U5b2c and that he would have had dark skin, blue eyes, and curly or wavy hair — a striking physical portrait very
different from the stereotypical image of ancient Britons. He is, in genetic terms, a cousin of Shane's maternal ancestors. His
lineage is Shane's lineage. The people who fished the rivers of Mesolithic Somerset and camped in the gorges of what would
become the English countryside are the maternal genetic ancestors of a man living today in Jefferson, Ohio. This lineage
survived extraordinary pressures over the millennia. When Neolithic farmers arrived from Anatolia approximately 6,000 years
ago, they largely replaced the hunter-gatherer populations of Britain genetically — just as the Bell Beaker people would later
replace the Neolithic farmers. Yet the U5b2c lineage persisted through these upheavals, carried by women who survived and
reproduced across every subsequent population event in British prehistory, and passed their ancient mitochondrial signature
forward through every generation to the present day. The highest modern concentrations of U5b2c are found in Scandinavia,
the British Isles, and the Baltic States — the northern European regions where Ice Age refugia populations most durably
maintained their genetic presence. Shane's maternal line is, in the most literal biological sense, the lineage of the original
indigenous peoples of Britain. 1.3 Neanderthal Ancestry Shane's 23andMe results place his Neanderthal DNA content above
that of approximately 74% of 23andMe customers — a meaningfully aboveaverage proportion. This is not a curiosity or an
anomaly; it is a genuine window into one of the most consequential encounters in human evolutionary history. Between
approximately 50,000 and 70,000 years ago, anatomically modern humans — the Homo sapiens who had evolved in Africa
and were spreading into Asia and Europe — encountered and interbred with the Neanderthals who had inhabited Eurasia for
hundreds of thousands of years. These interbreeding events occurred primarily in the Middle East and in Europe. The result
was a small but lasting genetic legacy: every person of non-African descent alive today carries between one and four percent
Neanderthal DNA in their genome, the durable molecular residue of these encounters across the Ice Age world. Shane's
proportion is above average, meaning a slightly larger share of his ancestry traces to those ancient interbreeding events.
23andMe has identified four specific Neanderthal variant clusters in Shane's genome. Three have been functionally
characterized: 1. Enhanced spatial sense and sense of direction — a variant cluster associated with navigation and spatial
awareness, traits that would have had obvious survival advantages for hunter-gatherer peoples navigating unfamiliar terrain. 2.
Heightened sensitivity to heights (acrophobia tendency) — a variant associated with increased caution at elevation, possibly an

adaptive response in mountainous or cliff-dwelling ancestral environments. 3. A tendency toward a stockier body build —
Neanderthals were robustly built, with broad chests and heavy bones adapted for cold environments and intensive physical
activity. This variant cluster suggests a structural tendency inherited from that lineage. 4. A fourth variant cluster — the
function of which remains under active analysis by 23andMe researchers. These are not distant or inactive relics. They are
functional genetic variants that may express themselves in observable traits in Shane's life today. The Neanderthals went
extinct as a distinct species approximately 40,000 years ago, but they did not vanish entirely — they live on, partially and
molecularly, in the genomes of their hybrid descendants. Shane carries a somewhat larger share of that inheritance than most.
1.4 The Scandinavian Component (Danelaw, 865 CE) Shane's DNA composition includes approximately 5.4% Scandinavian
ancestry — a proportion that cannot be explained by any documented recent Scandinavian ancestor. Its most parsimonious
explanation lies in the deep history of England itself. Beginning in 865 CE, a large Norse Viking force invaded and settled a
vast swath of northern and eastern England in what became known as the Danelaw — the region of England where Danish
law and Danish settlers dominated for two centuries. The Norse settlers of the Danelaw did not merely raid and retreat; they
built farms, married local women, raised children, and were absorbed into the English population over subsequent generations.
By the time of the Norman Conquest in 1066 CE, the Norse genetic signal had already been distributed throughout the
English gene pool in the northern and eastern counties. The Norman Conquest itself added a second Norse-derived layer: the
Normans were themselves the descendants of Norse Vikings (Norsemen → Normans) who had settled in northern France in
the ninth and tenth centuries and adopted the French language while retaining much of their genetic heritage. When William
the Conqueror's forces settled England after 1066 — including in Sussex, where the decisive battle was fought at Hastings —
they carried Norse-descended DNA into the southern English population. Over subsequent centuries, these Norse genetic
signals — from the Danelaw settlers in the north and the Norman settlers in the south — were absorbed and redistributed
throughout the English gene pool. By the time the Goble family was established in West Sussex in the sixteenth century, they
would have carried this ancient Norse heritage as part of their English genetic inheritance, without any awareness of or
reference to Scandinavian origin. Shane inherits it today as a deep ancestral echo — not a recent ancestor, but a signal from the
Viking Age, preserved across forty generations of English family history and carried forward into Ohio. PART II The Goupil
Legacy: Norman French Origins of the Goble Name Chapter 2: From Fox to Family — The GoupilGoble Connection The
surname Goble did not arise spontaneously in the English countryside. Every surname has an origin — a moment when a
family, or a community's perception of a family, crystallized into a word that would be passed forward across centuries. For the
Goble family, that origin lies not in the Anglo-Saxon linguistic tradition but in the Norman French spoken by the conquerors
who remade England after 1066. The surname Goble is, in all probability, a corruption of the Old French and Norman word
goupil — meaning, simply, the fox. The Norman Conquest of England, led by William the Conqueror in 1066 CE, brought
not merely a new ruling dynasty but an entirely new linguistic and cultural overlay. The conquerors spoke a dialect of Old
French, and their surnames — where they had them — derived from French words, places, and nicknames. The word goupil
was common in medieval French nomenclature as a personal nickname, applicable to an ancestor known for cunning,
quickness, or possibly red-haired or fox-like physical characteristics. In the fabliaux and beast-fable tradition of medieval
French literature, Reynard the Fox — Renard le Goupil — was the archetypal trickster figure of popular imagination. A man
called Goupil in a Norman community would have carried an immediately understood social meaning: clever, perhaps sly,
certainly memorable. The linguistic evolution from Goupil to Goble followed a predictable pattern of phonetic anglicization
over several generations of integration with the English-speaking population. The Sussex documentary record shows the
surname appearing in variant forms as early as the 1400s — approximately 150 years before Thomas Goble's documented
birth in 1590/91. These variants include Gopyll, Gobel, Gobell, Gobyll, and related forms, concentrated in the coastal parishes
of West Sussex, particularly in and around the Arundel and Chichester areas — precisely the territory where the family would
be definitively documented by the late sixteenth century. The progression from these intermediate forms to the stabilized
spelling Goble represents the completion of a phonetic journey from the Norman French coast to the English countryside.

The timing of this linguistic transition is historically significant. The Norman settlers who arrived in England after 1066 were
typically bilingual for two to three generations, using French in formal and aristocratic contexts and English in everyday local
life. By the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, the Norman elite had largely shifted to English as their primary language, and
their surnames had begun to anglicize accordingly. For a family of modest rather than aristocratic standing — the Goupil
ancestors were almost certainly yeoman farmers or craftsmen rather than knights — this anglicization would have occurred
relatively early and completely. The family's emergence in the Westergate and Aldingbourne parishes suggests the Goupil-to-
Goble transition was essentially complete before the Reformation of the sixteenth century. The Sussex documentary record
establishes the family in the coastal parishes of West Sussex — including the area around Westergate and Aldingbourne —
where Thomas Goble's family would be definitively documented by the late 1500s. The concentration of Goble/Goupil
variants in these particular parishes, across a span of more than a century before Thomas's birth, strongly suggests a family
that had been settled in this specific locality for several generations. These were not newcomers or migrants; they were
established community members whose name had simply been gradually reshaped by the linguistic forces of the surrounding
English-speaking culture. The earliest genealogically traceable members of the English Goble line — the parents of Thomas
Goble, the first fully verified Goble ancestor in the documentary record — are William Goble II, born approximately 1550 in
Westergate, West Sussex [PROBABLE], and his wife Alice Legard, born approximately 1552 [PROBABLE]. They represent
the top of the genealogically traceable English Goble family tree — the point at which the name had fully stabilized and the
family could be identified by future researchers as a distinct and documented lineage. The DNA evidence independently
corroborates the French dimension of the Goble family's heritage. Shane's ancestry composition includes a French
component of approximately 2.6%, which cannot be entirely explained by the documented LeCompte Huguenot line alone.
French Huguenot ancestry is typically somewhat underrepresented in genetic ancestry tests relative to documentary evidence,
because Huguenot refugees who settled in England often maintained endogamous marriage practices within their own
community — which can reduce the apparent genetic signal from that line. The presence of Norman French ancestors in the
Goble family itself — centuries before Antoine LeCompte arrived from Calais — provides a plausible and historically
coherent additional source of French genetic heritage in Shane's DNA. The fox that crossed the Channel with William the
Conqueror may still be running, molecularly, in the genes of a man living in Jefferson, Ohio, nearly a thousand years later.
PART III Thomas Goble of Colonial Massachusetts (1590/91–1657) Chapter 3: From Westergate to the New World — The
Founding Ancestor 3.1 Birth and English Origins [VERIFIED] Thomas Goble was born on January 2, 1590/91, in the parish
of Aldingbourne, West Sussex, England, in the village of Westergate. He was the son of William Goble II and Alice Legard of
Westergate — the family we have traced in the preceding chapter to the Norman French Goupil ancestry that gave the family
its name. The dual-year notation in his birth date — 1590/91 — reflects a historical calendrical complexity: England in the late
sixteenth century used the Julian (Old Style) calendar, in which the new year began not on January 1 but on March 25 (Lady
Day). Under this system, January 2, 1590 Old Style corresponds to January 2, 1591 New Style — the date we would use on a
modern calendar. Genealogists customarily write both years when a date falls in the January-to-March quarter under the Old
Style, to prevent ambiguity. The date as given here — January 2, 1590/91 — means unambiguously: the second day of January
in the year we now call 1591. West Sussex in the final decades of the sixteenth century was a county in profound transition.
The English Reformation, initiated by Henry VIII in the 1530s and consolidated under Elizabeth I, had permanently severed
England from Roman Catholicism and established the Church of England as the nation's official faith. In Sussex, as elsewhere,
this religious revolution produced both conformists and dissenters. The enclosure movement — the conversion of common
agricultural land into private holdings — was disrupting the traditional yeoman farming economy of the county. The coastal
parishes of Sussex, facing France across the narrow Channel, had long been connected to continental trade, ideas, and
religious currents. It was a world in ferment, and Thomas Goble grew up at its center. The parishes around Chichester —
Westergate, Aldingbourne, Barnham, Bognor, Pagham — formed a close-knit network of yeoman families, craftsmen, and
local merchants. The Goble family occupied the respectable middle tier of this society: landholders and tradespeople with

deep local roots, not gentry but not laboring poor. Thomas came of age during the reign of James I, as Puritan sentiment —
the conviction that the Church of England had not been sufficiently reformed and remained too close to Catholicism in its
rituals and hierarchy — was growing in intensity and social reach. The religious polarization of this period would ultimately
drive Thomas, and approximately twenty thousand of his contemporaries, across the Atlantic Ocean to build a new kind of
society in the Massachusetts wilderness. 3.2 Marriage to Alice Brookman [VERIFIED] On November 5, 1619, Thomas Goble
married Alice Brookman at the Parish Church of Aldingbourne, West Sussex. This marriage is a verified record drawn from
the Aldingbourne parish register — one of the most reliable categories of primary source documentation available to
genealogical research. Thomas was twenty-eight years old at the time of the marriage; the couple had likely known each other
through the close network of West Sussex parish families for many years. An important correction bears noting here. Earlier
genealogical literature — including some published works on the Goble family — erroneously identified Thomas's wife as
"Alice Mousall." This identification has been corrected through primary source research. Alice Brookman is confirmed as the
correct wife of Thomas Goble, and all subsequent family history built upon the Alice Mousall identification should be treated
with caution. The Aldingbourne parish register provides the authoritative record. Thomas and Alice Brookman Goble would
go on to have six children, several of whom were born in England before the family's emigration to Massachusetts. 3.3 The
Puritan Great Migration (1629–1640) and Emigration to Massachusetts [VERIFIED] Between 1629 and 1640, approximately
20,000 Puritan men, women, and children left England for New England in what historians call the Great Migration. The
drivers of this movement were multiple and interacting. Religious persecution under King Charles I and his Archbishop of
Canterbury, William Laud, made life increasingly difficult for Puritans, who faced fines, imprisonment, and the destruction of
their unlicensed congregations. Economic hardship during Charles I's "Personal Rule" — the eleven-year period from 1629 to
1640 when Charles governed without Parliament and imposed extra-parliamentary taxes — created widespread anxiety among
the yeoman and merchant classes. And the Puritan vision itself — the millennial conviction that they were called to build a
"City upon a Hill," a godly commonwealth that would demonstrate to the corrupt Old World what a truly reformed Christian
society could look like — provided the ideological engine that transformed individual desperation into collective purpose.
Thomas and Alice Goble emigrated approximately 1633–1634, sailing to Charlestown, Massachusetts — then a thriving
Puritan settlement on the northern bank of the Charles River, soon to be effectively absorbed into the growing town of
Boston. Their voyage across the North Atlantic would have taken somewhere between six and twelve weeks, depending on
wind and weather, aboard a vessel of two to three hundred tons carrying a hundred or more passengers in severely cramped
conditions below decks. The mortality rate on these voyages was not negligible. That Thomas and Alice arrived with their
family intact was itself a form of providence, in the Puritan understanding of the word. On August 30, 1634 [VERIFIED],
Thomas Goble was admitted as a member of the First Church of Charlestown — the established Puritan congregation that
served as both the spiritual and civic center of the settlement. Admission to the First Church was not a formality; it required a
public profession of faith before the assembled congregation, with the candidate expected to narrate their experience of
saving grace in terms that satisfied the gathered community. It was an act of spiritual autobiography and social commitment
simultaneously. For Thomas, a man who had crossed an ocean on the strength of his convictions, this public declaration would
have been the culmination of years of religious formation. Just four days later, on September 3, 1634 [VERIFIED], Thomas
Goble was granted Freeman status in Massachusetts Bay Colony. This designation — conferred by the General Court, the
colonial governing body — represented the full bestowal of civic rights: the right to vote in elections, to hold civic office, to
participate in the governance of the colony. In Puritan Massachusetts, Freeman status was restricted to members of approved
Congregationalist churches, which meant that Thomas's church admission four days earlier was the direct prerequisite for his
civic enfranchisement. Within a single week of these dual acts, Thomas Goble had been formally welcomed into both the
spiritual and political community of Massachusetts Bay Colony. He was no longer a refugee from an uncertain Old World; he
was a citizen of a new one. 3.4 Land Holdings and Civic Life [VERIFIED] By 1638, Thomas Goble had accumulated the
following landholdings in Charlestown and its environs, documented in colonial land records: ● A house lot in Charlestown

proper ● 4 acres of planting ground ● 15 acres of woodland ● 50 acres at a location known as "Waterfield" This represented a
substantial holding for a Puritan settler of the era. Many migrants arrived with little and struggled to secure land against the
competing claims of earlier settlers and the colonial government. Thomas's accumulation of nearly seventy acres within four
years of arrival places him firmly among the established yeoman landholders of the community — men of property and
standing, not the laboring poor who depended on others' land for their survival. His position gave him the economic
foundation to participate fully in community life, to raise his children in relative security, and to contribute to the social and
legal institutions that were being built, almost literally from the ground up, around him in the Massachusetts wilderness. 3.5
The First Jury in Boston, October 1, 1640 [VERIFIED] Of all the documented facts of Thomas Goble's life in
Massachusetts, none carries more historical weight than this: on October 1, 1640, Thomas Goble served on the first jury ever
convened in Boston, Massachusetts. His name is preserved in the colonial court records as one of the men who sat for this
inaugural proceeding. The establishment of formal jury proceedings in Massachusetts Bay Colony was a milestone in the
transatlantic transmission of English legal tradition. The right to trial by jury — rooted in Magna Carta (1215) and elaborated
through centuries of English common law — was among the most fundamental liberties that English colonists brought with
them to the New World, and among the most jealously guarded. For this tradition to be formally instituted required not just
law but people: citizens willing and able to sit in judgment of their peers according to established legal principles. Thomas
Goble was one of those people. He was present at the founding not merely of a colony but of an American legal institution.
It is impossible to reconstruct from this distance what Thomas thought as he sat for that first jury. But the historical
significance of the moment is not diminished by its obscurity. Every American who has ever served on a jury, invoked their
legal rights, or benefited from the tradition of due process in the courts is — in the longest sense of the word — a beneficiary
of the tradition that Thomas Goble and his fellow jurors helped establish on that October day in 1640. His descendant Shane,
living in Ashtabula County, Ohio, nearly four centuries later, is the inheritor of a lineage that helped lay the legal foundations
of the American republic. 3.6 Harvard College Tuition Records, 1653–1655 [VERIFIED] Harvard College, founded in 1636 in
Cambridge, Massachusetts — just two years after Thomas Goble's arrival in Charlestown — was the first institution of higher
learning established in the American colonies. Its founding purpose was the training of ministers for the Puritan congregations
of New England. Within two decades of its founding, it had also become a center of civic learning and a marker of social
achievement in the colony. Among the financial records of Harvard College for the years 1653–1655 appear the names
"goodman goobell" and "old gobbell" — almost certainly references to Thomas Goble, now in his early sixties and one of the
elder members of the Middlesex County community. The exact nature of his relationship with Harvard — whether he had a
son, grandson, or ward enrolled at the college; whether he performed services for the institution; or whether the entries reflect
some other form of association — has not been fully resolved by existing research. But his appearance in the Harvard ledger,
however ambiguous the context, establishes his continued civic prominence and community engagement during the early
1650s, more than fifteen years after his initial land grants and a decade after his jury service. Thomas Goble remained, in his
seventh decade of life, a man of standing and connection in his adopted community. 3.7 Children of Thomas and Alice Goble

Personal Rule of Charles I that made England inhospitable to dissenters, the transatlantic crossing that deposited him on the
shores of a continent unknown to his Sussex ancestors, and the founding decades of a colonial civilization that would
eventually become the United States of America. Thomas had cleared land, built a home, worshipped in a congregation he
helped establish, served on the first jury in Boston, accumulated seventy acres of English-speaking civilization carved from the
Massachusetts forest, and raised six children to adulthood in the New World. He could not have known — could not have
imagined — that four centuries later, one of his direct descendants would hold the molecular traces of his ancestry in every
cell of his body and would be able to trace that ancestry not just to West Sussex but to the Bronze Age peoples who first
brought the RZ198 haplogroup to the shores of southern England. He could not have known that the line he established
would survive King Philip's War, the founding of the republic, the frontier expansion into Kentucky and Ohio, a Civil War,
two world wars, and a century of industrial transformation, arriving finally at a young man named Shane living in a small city
on the shores of Lake Erie. But it did. The thread holds. Chapter 4: The King Philip's War Shadow — Daniel Goble (c.1640–
1676) Daniel Goble, the youngest son of Thomas and Alice Brookman Goble, was born approximately 1640–1641 in
Charlestown or Concord, Massachusetts — in the first generation of Gobles to be born on American soil. He is the critical
link in the chain connecting the founding ancestor to all subsequent Goble descendants in New Jersey and Ohio. And his
death, in 1676, places him at the center of one of the most catastrophic events in seventeenthcentury American history. King
Philip's War (1675–1676) was a conflict between the English colonists of New England and a confederation of Native
American tribes led by the Wampanoag sachem Metacom — called "King Philip" by the English in a sardonic appropriation of
European royal nomenclature. The war began in June 1675 and burned through New England for fourteen months with a
ferocity that neither side anticipated and neither could fully control. In proportion to the total population, it remains the
deadliest conflict in American history: approximately 10% of the English colonial population of New England was killed.
Dozens of towns were burned. Thousands of Native Americans were killed, enslaved, or driven from their ancestral lands.
The violence was intimate and ubiquitous — no settlement in Massachusetts, Connecticut, or Rhode Island was entirely
beyond its reach. Whether Daniel Goble died in combat during King Philip's War, from disease in one of the refuge camps
that colonial families fled to for protection, or from some other cause associated with the chaos of that year — the records do
not specify. What is known is that he died in 1676, the year of the war's climax and conclusion, and that his death at
approximately age thirty-five or thirtysix left his son, Daniel Goble Jr., to carry the family forward. Daniel Goble's story —
abbreviated by war and recorded in the barest outlines — nonetheless contains a kind of historical amplitude. He was born in
the New World that his father had helped build, came of age in the Puritan community his father had helped establish, and
died in the first great military crisis of that community's existence. He bridged two worlds: the founding generation of
Thomas Goble, and the migration generation of Daniel Jr. that would carry the Goble name south to New Jersey. The thread
of descent, though it nearly frayed in the fires of 1676, held. PART IV The Goble Migration: New Jersey and the
Revolutionary Frontier Chapter 5: Daniel Goble Jr. and the Move to New Jersey (1669–after 1724) [VERIFIED] Daniel Goble

earlier and where his father Daniel apparently lived before the King Philip's War crisis of 1676. Daniel Jr. was perhaps six or

pattern of Massachusetts Puritan families moving south and west into New Jersey's fertile interior during the late seventeenth
and early eighteenth centuries. New Jersey offered inducements that the increasingly crowded and expensive land market of
Massachusetts could not: rich farmland available at lower prices, a more tolerant religious and political culture under the
Proprietors, and the opportunity to build new communities without the accumulated tensions and hierarchies of the older
settlements. Daniel Goble Jr. is documented in New Jersey records through at least 1724 — roughly fifty-five years after his
birth — suggesting he lived a full and productive life in his adopted colony before the record loses track of him. Chapter 6:

New Jersey, and died on March 29, 1783 — a lifespan of eighty-two years that encompassed the entire colonial period of

compensated for high child mortality and where a large family represented both an economic asset and a social achievement.

their parents as younger ones were born, and the Goble household gradually seeding the surrounding New Jersey countryside
with adult sons and daughters who established their own families and extended the family's geographic footprint. Kevin Goble

the English throne and American independence was a concept that would have seemed fantastical to most colonists. When he
died in 1783, the Revolution had been won, the Treaty of Paris had been signed, and the United States of America was a
functioning — if fragile — reality. Kevin witnessed the entire arc of the colonial-to-republican transition without leaving New
Jersey. He was a man of place, of deep roots in a specific soil, and his seventeen children carried those roots forward into the
wider American landscape. Chapter 7: Caleb Goble — Revolutionary War Spy and Frontier Pioneer (March 1, 1760 – March
22, 1838) 7.1 Origins [VERIFIED] Caleb Goble was born on March 1, 1760, in Morristown, New Jersey. He was a descendant
of the Goble-Doud branch of the New Jersey Goble family, his father being Daniel W. Goble (born approximately 1735, died
after 1782), who married Rhoda Doud [PROBABLE]. Caleb grew up in Morristown — a town that would itself become
historically significant during the Revolution as the site of the Continental Army's winter encampments in 1776–1777 and
again in 1779–1780 — on the edge of the New Jersey frontier, at the precise historical moment when the question of
American independence was becoming impossible to avoid. He came of age in a community where political opinion was
galvanized by proximity to events: the Stamp Act, the Townshend Acts, the Boston Massacre, the Tea Party, Lexington and
Concord. By 1776, when the Declaration of Independence was adopted and the Revolution became an open military conflict,
Caleb Goble was sixteen years old — old enough to enlist, young enough to be shaped entirely by the experience of the war
that followed. 7.2 Revolutionary War Service [VERIFIED from pension application, October 31, 1832] Caleb Goble enlisted
in the Continental cause in 1776 at age sixteen. The full account of his service is preserved in his pension application of
October 31, 1832, filed when Caleb was seventy-two years old — a document that provides an unusually detailed personal
account of Revolutionary War service on the frontier. His service unfolded in several phases: In 1776, Caleb served in Captain
Benjamin Rice's Militia Company in New Jersey — one of the countless local militia units that mobilized in the chaotic early
months of the Revolution, before the Continental Army had established the organizational structures that would eventually
bring order to the American military effort. In 1777, he transferred to Captain James Brinton's Company and participated in
the construction of Fort McIntosh and Fort Laurens on the Ohio frontier. These were critical fortifications in the defense of
the western territories against British-allied Native American forces — the westernmost outposts of the Continental Army's
military reach, built at the edge of territory that was still deeply contested. Fort Laurens, established on the Tuscarawas River
in what is now eastern Ohio, was the only Continental fort built in the territory that would become the state of Ohio. Caleb
Goble helped build it. From 1778 to 1783, Caleb served with the Rangers of the Frontier at Lindley's Fort, participating in the
grinding, attritional work of frontier defense — protecting isolated settlements from raids, gathering intelligence on enemy

movements, and maintaining a military presence in a landscape where the lines between soldier, settler, and target were often
indistinguishable. And during this period, he performed what may be the most remarkable chapter of his service: he served
one full year as a spy for the Continental forces on the Ohio frontier. The role of a frontier spy in the Revolutionary War was
unlike anything in the conventional military experience. There were no uniforms, no formations, no clear lines of battle. A spy
operated alone or in small groups, deep in territory controlled by British forces and their Native American allies, gathering
intelligence on troop movements, supply lines, and planned attacks. Discovery meant, in all probability, death — not the clean
death of battle but the death of a captured enemy combatant in enemy-held territory, where the laws of war provided no
protection. To perform this work for a single week required courage. To perform it for a full year required extraordinary
endurance, wilderness skill, psychological fortitude, and — not least — a measure of luck that not all his counterparts
possessed. Caleb's brothers Ebenezer and Daniel also served in the Continental Army, making the Goble family a multi-
generational and multi-member contributor to American independence. The family did not merely support the Revolution
from a distance; they were in its trenches, on its frontiers, and behind its enemy lines. 7.3 The Pension Injustice [VERIFIED]
On October 31, 1832, at age seventy-two, Caleb Goble filed his pension application with the federal government. The
application documented his service with specificity and detail — the militia companies he served in, the forts he helped build,
the frontier stations where he stood watch, and the year he spent gathering intelligence behind enemy lines. By any reasonable
standard, his claim was ironclad. His pension was not approved until 1855 — seventeen years after his death on March 22,
1838, in Shelby County, Ohio. He never received the government recognition he had earned. The pension that his service had
justified, the money that might have eased his final years, arrived — bureaucratically, abstractly — after he was gone. He is
buried at Medaris Cemetery, Shelby County, Ohio. This injustice does not diminish what Caleb Goble accomplished or who he
was. It is, however, an important part of his story and of the broader history of how the new American republic treated its
veterans — incompletely, bureaucratically, and often far too late. The pension application itself, filed in 1832 and preserved in
the federal archives, is the primary source document that gives us the detailed account of Caleb's service. Without his
willingness to file — even at age seventy-two, even with the memory of decades of frontier hardship — that account would be
lost. His words, preserved in the pension record, outlasted the injustice done to him. 7.4 Family and Migration [VERIFIED]

together they had fifteen children [VERIFIED]. The post-war migration of Caleb's family traced the arc of the early American

claiming: ● ~1794 — Maysville, Kentucky: Caleb and Sarah crossed the Ohio River into Kentucky, joining the wave of settlers
who poured into the trans-Appalachian West following the Revolution. ● ~1798 — Clermont County, Ohio: The family

organized by the Ordinance of 1787, prohibiting slavery and laying the groundwork for eventual statehood. ● ~1802 —
Warren County, Ohio: Ohio achieved statehood in 1803; Caleb was already there, moving through the newly organized
counties of southwestern Ohio. ● 1811 — Troy/Miami County, Ohio: The family settled briefly in the Miami Valley, another
productive agricultural region drawing settlers from the eastern states. ● Shelby County, Ohio (died March 22, 1838): Caleb's
final home, where he died and is buried at Medaris Cemetery. This migration pattern — from New Jersey through Kentucky
across southern and central Ohio — is not a random wandering. It is a biographical map of the post-Revolutionary frontier,
tracing the movement of a generation that fought for independence and then lived it by moving into the continent that the
Revolution had opened. Caleb Goble was, in the fullest sense, a foundinggeneration American: a man who built forts on the
Ohio frontier as a young soldier and then settled that same frontier as an aging patriarch. He died in the state he had helped
defend fifty years before. Chapter 8: The Ohio Generations — The Intermediate Gap [RESEARCH TARGET] Following

Background The LeCompte family's story does not begin with a marriage record or a land grant. It begins with catastrophe —
with the specifically French catastrophe of religious civil war that tore apart one of the most sophisticated civilizations in
Europe and drove hundreds of thousands of its citizens into permanent exile. The French Wars of Religion (1562–1598) were
a series of eight distinct armed conflicts between French Catholics and French Protestants — known, from the Greek word
eugenots corrupted through French usage, as Huguenots. These were not merely theological disputes; they were struggles for
the soul, the governance, and ultimately the survival of France itself, fought with the full ferocity of an age that had not yet
developed the concepts of religious tolerance or civilian immunity from war's violence. The opening atrocity — the Massacre
of Vassy on March 1, 1562 — set the tone for all that followed. Catholic troops under the Duke of Guise attacked a
congregation of Huguenot worshippers in the town of Vassy in Champagne, killing more than sixty and wounding more than
two hundred. The massacre ignited the first of the eight wars. But it was the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of August 23–
24, 1572 that burned itself most deeply into Protestant memory across Europe. Beginning with the targeted assassination of
Huguenot military leaders gathered in Paris for a royal wedding, the violence spread within hours into a popular massacre:
Parisian mobs, inflamed by years of propaganda and weeks of political manipulation, fell upon the Protestant population of
the city. The killing spread to provincial cities. Estimates of the total dead range from 5,000 to 30,000 within a matter of days.
For Protestant Europe — including the Protestant communities of England from which the Goble family would emerge —
the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre was a defining horror, the proof that Catholic power, given the opportunity, would
destroy them without mercy. The Edict of Nantes (1598), issued by King Henry IV — himself a converted Huguenot —
provided a fragile peace, granting Protestants limited religious freedoms and establishing Protestant garrison towns (places de
sûreté) as physical guarantees of the settlement. But this peace was always contingent, always dependent on the goodwill of a
monarch who might be succeeded by a less tolerant heir. When Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685 — the Edict
of Fontainebleau — the fragile peace shattered. Approximately 200,000 to 400,000 Huguenots fled France in the mass exodus
known as the Refuge, scattering to Protestant England, the Netherlands, Prussia, South Africa, and the American colonies.
They brought with them skills — in textiles, metalworking, clockmaking, glassblowing, commerce, medicine — that enriched
every country that received them. Antoine LeCompte had already left for Maryland by approximately 1655 — thirty years
before the Revocation — but his departure reflects the earlier, more gradual persecution that preceded the final cataclysm. For
a young Protestant man in Calais, the decision to leave was always available and never entirely surprising. Calais occupied a

unique position: a city on the English Channel that had been English from 1347 to 1558 — just sixty-two years before
Antoine's birth. Despite its return to French control, the city retained deep English connections in commerce, language, and
culture. The Channel crossing from Calais to Dover was the shortest in the world. For Antoine LeCompte, choosing England
and its colonies was not merely a political decision; it was, in many ways, a continuation of the cross-Channel life that Calais
had always inhabited. Chapter 10: Antoine LeCompte — The Patriarch of Maryland (c.1620–after September 9, 1673) 10.1
Origins and Early Life [VERIFIED] [PROBABLE] Antoine LeCompte — also recorded in English colonial documents as
"Anthony" — was born approximately 1620 in Calais, Picardie, France [VERIFIED]. His Protestant faith marked him, from
the beginning, as a member of a community under existential pressure in Catholic France. His birth city connected him to
England in ways that most French Protestants could not claim. And his personal biography — before he ever set foot in
Maryland — was already remarkable: he had served approximately eleven years in the army of King Charles I of England, a
detail preserved in the family's oral tradition and recorded in the 1819 LeCompte Manuscript. This army service places
Antoine in England — and in the English military — during one of the most turbulent periods in English history: the years
leading up to and including the English Civil War (1642–1651) and the Cromwellian Interregnum that followed. Charles I's
army included a significant number of foreign Protestant soldiers, and a Huguenot-affiliated young man from Calais — already
cross-culturally fluent, already connected to England — would have been a plausible recruit. The precise record of Antoine's
military service has not been fully recovered, but his claim of eleven years places him as a soldier in a very specific historical
context, and that context — the English Civil War, the execution of Charles I in 1649, the Puritan Commonwealth — was
exactly the kind of upheaval that could redirect a man's life toward a new beginning in the colonies. 10.2 Marriage to Hester
Dottando [VERIFIED] Antoine LeCompte married Hester (Esther) Dottando on July 11, 1661, in London, England
[VERIFIED]. Hester was born in Dieppe, Normandy — another Norman French connection in the family's intersecting
story. Dieppe was one of the major Huguenot centers in Normandy, a port city with deep Protestant traditions and strong
English commercial ties. That both Antoine and Hester came from Norman coastal cities with English connections — Calais
and Dieppe respectively — speaks to the network of Franco-English Protestant commerce and culture within which both
families moved. They were not strangers meeting by accident; they were members of the same cross-Channel Protestant
community, finding each other in the English capital before making together the further crossing to the American colonies.
10.3 Arrival in Maryland and the Land Grant [VERIFIED] Antoine LeCompte arrived in Maryland approximately 1655 —
some six years before his London marriage to Hester. It is possible he made an initial settlement voyage before returning to
England to marry, or that his arrival date in colonial records predates the marriage while both arrivals are documented
separately. On January 17, 1659, he received a land grant of 800 acres named "St. Antoine" on the Choptank River, Dorchester
County, Maryland [VERIFIED]. The land grant was issued under Maryland's headright system — the colonial policy of
granting fifty acres of land per person transported to the colony. An 800-acre grant indicated the transportation of Antoine
himself plus a number of additional individuals. The grant specifically names Thomas Raymond, Barbara Crouch, and
Thomas Jones among those transported — indentured servants or contracted laborers whose passage Antoine had financed in
exchange for their labor and for the land their transport entitled him to claim. The naming of the land "St. Antoine" was
deliberate and revealing. Antoine is the French saint's name form of Anthony — the specifically Catholic or traditional French
rendering, as opposed to the anglicized "Anthony" that colonial records would sometimes use for him. In naming his land
after himself in French, Antoine LeCompte was making a statement: this was a Frenchman's land. He had arrived in a new
country, under English colonial governance, speaking English well enough to navigate courts and contracts — but he would
not surrender his French identity, his French name, his connection to the culture and faith that had made him who he was. "St.
Antoine" stood on the Choptank River as a small monument to that refusal. 10.4 Taylor's Island Settlement [VERIFIED]
Antoine and Hester LeCompte settled on Taylor's Island in Dorchester County, Maryland — a peninsula in the upper
Chesapeake Bay region, home to a small but cohesive community of planters, merchants, and fishermen. Taylor's Island was
connected to the Maryland mainland by the creeks and tributaries of the Choptank River system, accessible by water to the

trade routes of the Chesapeake and by land — precariously, seasonally — to the county seat at Cambridge. In this community,
Antoine established himself as a planter and merchant. The 800-acre "St. Antoine" tract represented substantial agricultural
capacity by the standards of Dorchester County. With indentured servants and, eventually, the labor of his own growing
family, he would have cultivated tobacco — Maryland's primary cash crop — alongside subsistence agriculture in grain and
livestock. He operated on a scale that commanded local respect, and he integrated himself into the social and legal fabric of
the county with a speed that speaks to both personal capability and community acceptance. 10.5 Justice of Dorchester County
(1669–1671) [VERIFIED] From 1669 to 1671, Antoine LeCompte served as a Justice of Dorchester County — a position of
significant civic authority in colonial Maryland. As a Justice, Antoine would have heard both civil and criminal cases,
administered oaths, recorded deeds and contracts, presided over local disputes, and served as a representative of the
proprietary government of Maryland in his corner of the Chesapeake world. It was, in the colonial context, roughly equivalent
to a combination of judge, notary public, and local magistrate. The significance of this appointment is difficult to overstate.
Antoine LeCompte had arrived in Maryland approximately fourteen years earlier as a French immigrant with no colonial
standing, no English family network, and no property. He had built an 800-acre estate, raised a family, traded in the
Chesapeake economy, and earned enough community respect to be appointed to one of the most consequential civic positions
available in his county. It is a story of immigrant achievement in the most fundamental sense: not of wealth or prominence,
but of recognized reliability, demonstrated competence, and earned trust. The Justice's appointment was not given — it was
merited. 10.6 Death and Legacy [VERIFIED] Antoine LeCompte was last documented alive on September 9, 1673, in
Dorchester County records. He died sometime after that date — the specific circumstances of his death are not recorded in
surviving documents. He was approximately fifty-three years old. On June 6, 1674, his widow Hester and all their children
were formally naturalized as British subjects — a legal act of considerable practical importance. Land ownership in Maryland
under English law required British subject status; naturalization protected the family's claim to "St. Antoine" and all other
property they had accumulated. It was also a declaration of commitment: this family, born in France, married in London,
settled on the Choptank River, would make Maryland and the English colonial world their permanent home. They would be
British subjects. Their children — born in Maryland, naturalized as British — would carry that legal identity into the next
generation of American colonial history. Hester LeCompte managed the estate and the family after Antoine's death with
evident competence. The naturalization proceeding, initiated within nine months of Antoine's death, suggests a widow who
knew exactly what she needed to do to secure her children's future and did it without delay. 10.7 Children of Antoine and

Record Among the genealogical documents of American Huguenot families, the 1819 LeCompte Manuscript occupies a place
of exceptional distinction. It is, in both its contents and its circumstances of creation, one of the more remarkable acts of
family memory preservation in the early American republic. The manuscript was dictated in 1819 in Dorchester County,
Maryland, by two brothers: Thomas LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte, fourth-generation descendants of Antoine and Hester
LeCompte. Both brothers were blind. Their testimony was recorded by their nephew, Benjamin Woodward LeCompte, who
transcribed their oral account into the written record that survives today. The extraordinary quality of the manuscript flows
directly from its extraordinary circumstances. These two men, having lost the ability to read or write, had nonetheless retained
within their memories a comprehensive accounting of the LeCompte family: names, birth dates, marriages, deaths, migrations,

disputes, and relationships extending across four generations and nearly a hundred and fifty years since Antoine's arrival in
Maryland. Their blindness had not diminished their memory — if anything, it had sharpened it, forcing them to carry within
their minds a record that seeing people could afford to leave to documents. They knew every name. They knew every birth.
They knew every removal to a new county, every marriage into a new family, every branch of the tree as it spread across
Maryland and into Virginia and beyond. The manuscript documents all known descendants of Antoine and Hester LeCompte
as of 1819 — a genealogical census of the family nearly 150 years after Antoine's death. It records the names, relationships,
and vital events of hundreds of LeCompte descendants scattered across the Chesapeake region. Its account of Moses
LeCompte's descendants — the line through which Shane descends — provides information that would be difficult or
impossible to reconstruct from surviving official records alone. The manuscript is held by the Maryland Historical Society in
Baltimore, Maryland, where it remains accessible to researchers. It is both a primary source document of the highest
genealogical value and a historical artifact that testifies to the depth of family identity among LeCompte descendants — the
conviction that knowing who you came from was important enough to justify the extraordinary effort of preserving that
knowledge even without the use of sight. Benjamin Woodward LeCompte's act of transcription, and the two blind brothers'
act of dictation, gave researchers a gift that has not diminished in two centuries of use. Chapter 12: The LeCompte Descent to

PART VI The Ohio Convergence: Two Lines Meet Chapter 14: Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte — The Joining of Lines
Sometime in the twentieth century, in the state of Ohio, two family lines came together that had traveled entirely separate
paths for more than two and a half centuries. The Goble line — born of West Sussex yeomanry, shaped by the Puritan Great
Migration to Massachusetts, hammered on the anvil of the Revolutionary War frontier, and carried through the new states of
Kentucky and Ohio by a generation of pioneers — converged with the LeCompte line — born of French Huguenot faith,
launched into exile by religious persecution, planted on the Choptank River of Maryland by a French soldier turned colonial
planter, and carried south and west across generations by the same forces of westward migration that moved every American
family in the nineteenth century. The person who brought these lines together was Rae LeCompte — Shane's paternal
grandmother, a tenth-generation descendant of Antoine and Hester LeCompte, born in the 1920s and documented in Ohio
through Census and Memorial Records. She married Kevin Goble — Shane's grandfather, a descendant of the West Sussex
Goble family through the Massachusetts-New Jersey-Ohio migration. Kevin Goble was born approximately between 1920 and
1935 and is documented in Ohio records through at least 1993. The convergence in Ohio was not accidental — Ohio had
drawn both family lines independently, and through different historical pathways. The Goble line arrived through the post-
Revolutionary War frontier migration: Caleb Goble was already in Clermont County, Ohio, by approximately 1798, and his
descendants spread through the southwestern and central Ohio counties over the subsequent generation. The LeCompte line
arrived through the broader pattern of mid-Atlantic family migration westward in the nineteenth century — Maryland families
seeking farmland in the expanding republic, following the same demographic gravity that pulled millions of Americans across
the Appalachians and into the Ohio Valley. In their marriage, Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte created a family that carried, in
its DNA, the genetic signatures of Bronze Age West Sussex and the Mesolithic ice-age survivors of Britain, the Norman
French founders of the Goble surname and the Huguenot refugees of Calais and Dieppe, the Puritan settlers of Charlestown
and the colonial planters of the Choptank River, the Revolutionary War spy of the Ohio frontier and the Justice of Dorchester
County who had carved a French-named estate out of the Maryland wilderness. All of it — all of those centuries, all of those
stories — flowed forward through Kevin and Rae into their descendants. Chapter 15: Kevin Goble and the Modern Family

Shane's father, representing the twelfth generation from Thomas Goble of Westergate and the eleventh generation from

VIII Voices from the Line: Narrative Portraits Chapter 17: Thomas Goble — The Man Who Crossed the Ocean Imagine him
on the dock at Southampton or Bristol — or perhaps at a smaller West Sussex port, Chichester Harbour or Littlehampton,
where a vessel bound for New England might take on passengers from the local parishes. He would have been forty-two or
forty-three years old in 1633, a yeoman of Westergate in the prime of his life but also the prime of his religious conviction. He
had married Alice Brookman fourteen years earlier. He had watched his children grow in the shadow of the parish church at
Aldingbourne. He knew every hedgerow and field boundary of the world he was leaving. And he was leaving it. The smell of
pine forests — vast, uninterrupted, nothing like the managed woodlands of West Sussex — would have been among the first
experiences of the New World as the ship approached the Massachusetts coast. The scale of the wilderness must have been
simultaneously exhilarating and terrifying to a man whose entire life had been lived within a landscape shaped by a thousand
years of human habitation. Charlestown, on the north shore of the Charles River, was a Puritan settlement of a few hundred
souls carved out of that wilderness — orderly in its congregational governance, rough in its physical reality, pungent with the
smells of new construction and hard living. Thomas's admission to the First Church of Charlestown on August 30, 1634, was
not the act of a man going through motions. In Puritan theology, church membership required a genuine and publicly narrated
experience of saving grace — a moment of spiritual autobiography before an assembled community that would judge the
authenticity of the account. Thomas had crossed an ocean on the strength of his convictions. His testimony before the
congregation at Charlestown was the fulfillment, the public declaration, of everything that crossing had meant. Six years later,
on the morning of October 1, 1640, he sat on the first jury ever convened in Boston. Whatever case was before them,
whatever the substance of the proceeding — the historical weight of the moment lay not in the verdict but in the act: a group
of English-born men, transplanted to the Massachusetts wilderness, sitting in formal judgment according to the principles of
English common law, building an institution that would outlast every one of them by centuries. Thomas Goble was in that
room. His name is in that record. His later years in Concord — the Harvard ledger references, the aging patriarch managing
his land and watching his children establish their own families — suggest a man who had built what he came to build and was
content to inhabit it. He could not have known that one of his youngest children would die in the fires of King Philip's War;
that his grandson would eventually migrate to New Jersey; that a direct descendant would serve as a spy in the Revolutionary
War; that the line would run, unbroken, through Ohio all the way to a young man in the twenty-first century who would hold a
smartphone showing him, through the magic of genomics, that his Ychromosome came from the Bronze Age peoples of
West Sussex — the very county his grandfather's grandfather had called home. Thomas Goble knew none of this. He knew
only that he had built something real and planted it in a new world. That was enough. It was, as it turned out, more than
enough. Chapter 18: Caleb Goble — The Spy on the Frontier He was sixteen years old when he enlisted. Sixteen — the age of
a boy in most human cultures, old enough to understand danger but not yet old enough to have fully calculated what it means
to walk into it deliberately. The year was 1776, the most electric year in American history: the year of the Declaration, the year
the question of independence became the question of survival. In Morristown, New Jersey — itself the site of the
Continental Army's winter encampments — the decision to fight was not abstract. It was personal, local, and immediate. He
helped build Fort McIntosh and Fort Laurens on the Ohio frontier — physical labor of the most consequential kind, the
construction of the westernmost fortifications of the Continental Army in territory that was still deeply contested, where
British-allied warriors could materialize from the forest in an hour's notice. The work of building a fort on the frontier was the
work of converting hope into timber and earth: the hope that an outpost placed here, in this river valley, in this wilderness,
would mean something. That it would hold. And then came the year as a spy. A full year. He moved through enemy-held

territory alone or in small groups, gathering intelligence on the forces arrayed against the Continental cause. He learned to read
the landscape the way a hunter reads it — for what is moving, for what is out of place, for the detail that does not belong. He
learned to be invisible. He learned that his life depended on the quality of his attention. For a full year, discovery meant death.
For a full year, he did not die. He came back with the intelligence. He did what was asked of him and more than most could
have imagined. After the war, he went west. Kentucky first, then Ohio, county by county, following the frontier as it moved,
planting fifteen children across the landscape of the new republic with the same deliberateness with which he had once
planted observation posts in enemy territory. He farmed. He aged. He watched his country grow into the promise of the
Revolution he had fought to make possible. At seventy-two, he filed his pension application, recording for posterity the exact
shape of his service — the militia companies, the fort construction, the frontier station, the year of espionage. It was the last
act of a soldier who had never stopped believing that what he had done mattered, that the government he had helped create
owed him an honest accounting. He died on March 22, 1838, in Shelby County, Ohio, without the pension he had earned. The
pension was approved seventeen years after his death. The government was slow. The spy on the frontier, who had never been
slow about anything that mattered, deserved better. He always deserved better. Chapter 19: Antoine LeCompte — The
Frenchman on the Choptank He crossed the Channel from Calais — the shortest crossing in the world, a crossing his city had
made a thousand times in its centuries of English and French entanglement — and arrived in England as a young Protestant
man looking for what France was trying very hard not to give him: the right to live according to his faith without being killed
for it. He served eleven years in the English army. He survived the English Civil War, the execution of a king, the Puritan
Commonwealth, and the Restoration. He married Hester Dottando — a woman from Dieppe, another Norman, another
Protestant, another person for whom the Channel was less a border than a road — in London in 1661. And then they crossed
the ocean. The land he built on the Choptank River he named "St. Antoine." This was not vanity — or not merely vanity. It
was declaration. A man who had left France because France did not want him, who had served an English king, who now lived
under English colonial governance in a colony named for a Catholic English queen, chose to name his estate in French, after
the French patron saint of his name. He would not be erased. He was Antoine, not Anthony. This was St. Antoine, not St.
Anthony's. The eight hundred acres of Maryland tobacco ground were his, and they bore his name in his language, and if the
English colonial courts wanted his business, they could come to him. When he was appointed Justice of Dorchester County in
1669, the refugee had become the magistrate. The man who had fled a country that denied him legal standing now presided
over the legal proceedings of an English colonial county. He heard cases. He administered oaths. He signed documents with
his name — LeCompte, which means "the count," which means he may have carried, somewhere in his family history, a
memory or a myth or a reality of nobility, or may simply have been given the name of a landlord or an employer or a
neighborhood. The etymology is uncertain. The man is not uncertain. He was real, and he was present, and for two years he
was the law on Taylor's Island. When he died — sometime after September 9, 1673, date unknown — he left behind six
children, 800 acres named for himself, and a widow who moved immediately and efficiently to secure what he had built. Hester
filed the naturalization papers within nine months of his death. She did not wait. She was, in her way, as formidable as her
husband: a woman from Dieppe who had crossed an ocean and built a life and was not about to let bureaucratic delay threaten
what she and Antoine had made together. Their children were naturalized. The land was secured. The family would continue.
The name would continue. Two hundred years later, a blind man in Maryland would dictate the names and birth dates of every
one of their descendants from memory. And two hundred years after that, a young man in Ohio would carry their DNA in
every cell of his body, and the thread would hold. Chapter 20: The 1819 Witnesses — Thomas and Daniel LeCompte Picture
the room in Dorchester County, Maryland, in the year 1819. It would have been a farmhouse room, probably — familiar-
smelling, the kind of space where a family has gathered for generations. Outside, the Eastern Shore landscape: the flat
marshland, the creeks and tributaries of the Choptank system, the long Maryland sky. Inside, two old men sitting in whatever
positions their bodies required for comfort, their eyes focused on nothing visible, attending to the interior landscape of their
memories. Thomas LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte were brothers, fourthgeneration descendants of Antoine and Hester.

Both blind. The blindness of brothers in the same family line suggests it may have been hereditary — possibly related to the
blindness that had afflicted their ancestor Moses LeCompte, Antoine's son, who had gone blind at age twenty-two and
nonetheless fathered eleven children. Whatever its cause in Thomas and Daniel, the blindness had done what blindness
sometimes does: it had turned their attention inward, toward the geography of memory, and they had cultivated that
geography with extraordinary care. Their nephew Benjamin Woodward LeCompte sat across from them with pen and paper,
and they began to talk. They told him the names of the children of Antoine and Hester. They told him the names of Moses's
children, and of Moses's children's children, and of the generation after that. They told him who had married whom, and
when, and where, and how many children had resulted, and which of those children had stayed in Dorchester County and
which had gone to Virginia or beyond. They told him about people who had been dead for a century — people whose names
no living person had spoken aloud in decades — with the casual precision of someone recalling last week's conversation. They
were making a gift, in that room. A gift to the family they could not see, the descendants who would come after them and
want to know where they had come from. They could not read what Benjamin wrote down; they would never see the
manuscript that preserved their testimony. But they knew what they were doing. They were building a record out of memory
the way their ancestor had built an estate out of wilderness — with determination, with craft, and with a conviction that what
they were making would matter to someone, someday, in a way they could not yet imagine. The manuscript they created —
held today at the Maryland Historical Society in Baltimore — has served researchers for more than two centuries. Every time a
LeCompte descendant opens that document and finds their ancestor's name in the flowing script of Benjamin Woodward
LeCompte's hand, they are receiving the gift that two blind brothers gave on an ordinary day in 1819. Without eyes, they gave
sight to their descendants across two hundred years of history. PART IX Research Frontiers and Recommendations Chapter
