Chapter 2: From Fox to Family — The GoupilGoble Connection The surname Goble did not arise spontaneously in the
English countryside. Every surname has an origin — a moment when a family, or a community's perception of a family,
crystallized into a word that would be passed forward across centuries. For the Goble family, that origin lies not in the Anglo-
Saxon linguistic tradition but in the Norman French spoken by the conquerors who remade England after 1066. The surname
Goble is, in all probability, a corruption of the Old French and Norman word goupil — meaning, simply, the fox. The
Norman Conquest of England, led by William the Conqueror in 1066 CE, brought not merely a new ruling dynasty but an
entirely new linguistic and cultural overlay. The conquerors spoke a dialect of Old French, and their surnames — where they
had them — derived from French words, places, and nicknames. The word goupil was common in medieval French
nomenclature as a personal nickname, applicable to an ancestor known for cunning, quickness, or possibly red-haired or fox-
like physical characteristics. In the fabliaux and beast-fable tradition of medieval French literature, Reynard the Fox — Renard
le Goupil — was the archetypal trickster figure of popular imagination. A man called Goupil in a Norman community would
have carried an immediately understood social meaning: clever, perhaps sly, certainly memorable. The linguistic evolution from
Goupil to Goble followed a predictable pattern of phonetic anglicization over several generations of integration with the
English-speaking population. The Sussex documentary record shows the surname appearing in variant forms as early as the
1400s — approximately 150 years before Thomas Goble's documented birth in 1590/91. These variants include Gopyll,
Gobel, Gobell, Gobyll, and related forms, concentrated in the coastal parishes of West Sussex, particularly in and around the
Arundel and Chichester areas — precisely the territory where the family would be definitively documented by the late
sixteenth century. The progression from these intermediate forms to the stabilized spelling Goble represents the completion
of a phonetic journey from the Norman French coast to the English countryside. The timing of this linguistic transition is
historically significant. The Norman settlers who arrived in England after 1066 were typically bilingual for two to three

generations, using French in formal and aristocratic contexts and English in everyday local life. By the thirteenth and
fourteenth centuries, the Norman elite had largely shifted to English as their primary language, and their surnames had begun
to anglicize accordingly. For a family of modest rather than aristocratic standing — the Goupil ancestors were almost certainly
yeoman farmers or craftsmen rather than knights — this anglicization would have occurred relatively early and completely. The
family's emergence in the Westergate and Aldingbourne parishes suggests the Goupil-to-Goble transition was essentially
complete before the Reformation of the sixteenth century. The Sussex documentary record establishes the family in the
coastal parishes of West Sussex — including the area around Westergate and Aldingbourne — where Thomas Goble's family
would be definitively documented by the late 1500s. The concentration of Goble/Goupil variants in these particular parishes,
across a span of more than a century before Thomas's birth, strongly suggests a family that had been settled in this specific
locality for several generations. These were not newcomers or migrants; they were established community members whose
name had simply been gradually reshaped by the linguistic forces of the surrounding English-speaking culture. The earliest
genealogically traceable members of the English Goble line — the parents of Thomas Goble, the first fully verified Goble
ancestor in the documentary record — are William Goble II, born approximately 1550 in Westergate, West Sussex
[PROBABLE], and his wife Alice Legard, born approximately 1552 [PROBABLE]. They represent the top of the
genealogically traceable English Goble family tree — the point at which the name had fully stabilized and the family could be
identified by future researchers as a distinct and documented lineage. The DNA evidence independently corroborates the
French dimension of the Goble family's heritage. Shane's ancestry composition includes a French component of
approximately 2.6%, which cannot be entirely explained by the documented LeCompte Huguenot line alone. French Huguenot
ancestry is typically somewhat underrepresented in genetic ancestry tests relative to documentary evidence, because Huguenot
refugees who settled in England often maintained endogamous marriage practices within their own community — which can
reduce the apparent genetic signal from that line. The presence of Norman French ancestors in the Goble family itself —
centuries before Antoine LeCompte arrived from Calais — provides a plausible and historically coherent additional source of
French genetic heritage in Shane's DNA. The fox that crossed the Channel with William the Conqueror may still be running,
molecularly, in the genes of a man living in Jefferson, Ohio, nearly a thousand years later. PART III Thomas Goble of
Colonial Massachusetts (1590/91–1657) Chapter 3: From Westergate to the New World — The Founding Ancestor 3.1 Birth
and English Origins [VERIFIED] Thomas Goble was born on January 2, 1590/91, in the parish of Aldingbourne, West
Sussex, England, in the village of Westergate. He was the son of William Goble II and Alice Legard of Westergate — the
family we have traced in the preceding chapter to the Norman French Goupil ancestry that gave the family its name. The dual-
year notation in his birth date — 1590/91 — reflects a historical calendrical complexity: England in the late sixteenth century
used the Julian (Old Style) calendar, in which the new year began not on January 1 but on March 25 (Lady Day). Under this
system, January 2, 1590 Old Style corresponds to January 2, 1591 New Style — the date we would use on a modern calendar.
Genealogists customarily write both years when a date falls in the January-to-March quarter under the Old Style, to prevent
ambiguity. The date as given here — January 2, 1590/91 — means unambiguously: the second day of January in the year we
now call 1591. West Sussex in the final decades of the sixteenth century was a county in profound transition. The English
Reformation, initiated by Henry VIII in the 1530s and consolidated under Elizabeth I, had permanently severed England from
Roman Catholicism and established the Church of England as the nation's official faith. In Sussex, as elsewhere, this religious
revolution produced both conformists and dissenters. The enclosure movement — the conversion of common agricultural
land into private holdings — was disrupting the traditional yeoman farming economy of the county. The coastal parishes of
Sussex, facing France across the narrow Channel, had long been connected to continental trade, ideas, and religious currents. It
was a world in ferment, and Thomas Goble grew up at its center. The parishes around Chichester — Westergate,
Aldingbourne, Barnham, Bognor, Pagham — formed a close-knit network of yeoman families, craftsmen, and local
merchants. The Goble family occupied the respectable middle tier of this society: landholders and tradespeople with deep
local roots, not gentry but not laboring poor. Thomas came of age during the reign of James I, as Puritan sentiment — the

conviction that the Church of England had not been sufficiently reformed and remained too close to Catholicism in its rituals
and hierarchy — was growing in intensity and social reach. The religious polarization of this period would ultimately drive
Thomas, and approximately twenty thousand of his contemporaries, across the Atlantic Ocean to build a new kind of society
in the Massachusetts wilderness. 3.2 Marriage to Alice Brookman [VERIFIED] On November 5, 1619, Thomas Goble
married Alice Brookman at the Parish Church of Aldingbourne, West Sussex. This marriage is a verified record drawn from
the Aldingbourne parish register — one of the most reliable categories of primary source documentation available to
genealogical research. Thomas was twenty-eight years old at the time of the marriage; the couple had likely known each other
through the close network of West Sussex parish families for many years. An important correction bears noting here. Earlier
genealogical literature — including some published works on the Goble family — erroneously identified Thomas's wife as
"Alice Mousall." This identification has been corrected through primary source research. Alice Brookman is confirmed as the
correct wife of Thomas Goble, and all subsequent family history built upon the Alice Mousall identification should be treated
with caution. The Aldingbourne parish register provides the authoritative record. Thomas and Alice Brookman Goble would
go on to have six children, several of whom were born in England before the family's emigration to Massachusetts. 3.3 The
Puritan Great Migration (1629–1640) and Emigration to Massachusetts [VERIFIED] Between 1629 and 1640, approximately
20,000 Puritan men, women, and children left England for New England in what historians call the Great Migration. The
drivers of this movement were multiple and interacting. Religious persecution under King Charles I and his Archbishop of
Canterbury, William Laud, made life increasingly difficult for Puritans, who faced fines, imprisonment, and the destruction of
their unlicensed congregations. Economic hardship during Charles I's "Personal Rule" — the eleven-year period from 1629 to
1640 when Charles governed without Parliament and imposed extra-parliamentary taxes — created widespread anxiety among
the yeoman and merchant classes. And the Puritan vision itself — the millennial conviction that they were called to build a
"City upon a Hill," a godly commonwealth that would demonstrate to the corrupt Old World what a truly reformed Christian
society could look like — provided the ideological engine that transformed individual desperation into collective purpose.
Thomas and Alice Goble emigrated approximately 1633–1634, sailing to Charlestown, Massachusetts — then a thriving
Puritan settlement on the northern bank of the Charles River, soon to be effectively absorbed into the growing town of
Boston. Their voyage across the North Atlantic would have taken somewhere between six and twelve weeks, depending on
wind and weather, aboard a vessel of two to three hundred tons carrying a hundred or more passengers in severely cramped
conditions below decks. The mortality rate on these voyages was not negligible. That Thomas and Alice arrived with their
family intact was itself a form of providence, in the Puritan understanding of the word. On August 30, 1634 [VERIFIED],
Thomas Goble was admitted as a member of the First Church of Charlestown — the established Puritan congregation that
served as both the spiritual and civic center of the settlement. Admission to the First Church was not a formality; it required a
public profession of faith before the assembled congregation, with the candidate expected to narrate their experience of
saving grace in terms that satisfied the gathered community. It was an act of spiritual autobiography and social commitment
simultaneously. For Thomas, a man who had crossed an ocean on the strength of his convictions, this public declaration would
have been the culmination of years of religious formation. Just four days later, on September 3, 1634 [VERIFIED], Thomas
Goble was granted Freeman status in Massachusetts Bay Colony. This designation — conferred by the General Court, the
colonial governing body — represented the full bestowal of civic rights: the right to vote in elections, to hold civic office, to
participate in the governance of the colony. In Puritan Massachusetts, Freeman status was restricted to members of approved
Congregationalist churches, which meant that Thomas's church admission four days earlier was the direct prerequisite for his
civic enfranchisement. Within a single week of these dual acts, Thomas Goble had been formally welcomed into both the
spiritual and political community of Massachusetts Bay Colony. He was no longer a refugee from an uncertain Old World; he
was a citizen of a new one. 3.4 Land Holdings and Civic Life [VERIFIED] By 1638, Thomas Goble had accumulated the
following landholdings in Charlestown and its environs, documented in colonial land records: ● A house lot in Charlestown
proper ● 4 acres of planting ground ● 15 acres of woodland ● 50 acres at a location known as "Waterfield" This represented a

substantial holding for a Puritan settler of the era. Many migrants arrived with little and struggled to secure land against the
competing claims of earlier settlers and the colonial government. Thomas's accumulation of nearly seventy acres within four
years of arrival places him firmly among the established yeoman landholders of the community — men of property and
standing, not the laboring poor who depended on others' land for their survival. His position gave him the economic
foundation to participate fully in community life, to raise his children in relative security, and to contribute to the social and
legal institutions that were being built, almost literally from the ground up, around him in the Massachusetts wilderness. 3.5
The First Jury in Boston, October 1, 1640 [VERIFIED] Of all the documented facts of Thomas Goble's life in
Massachusetts, none carries more historical weight than this: on October 1, 1640, Thomas Goble served on the first jury ever
convened in Boston, Massachusetts. His name is preserved in the colonial court records as one of the men who sat for this
inaugural proceeding. The establishment of formal jury proceedings in Massachusetts Bay Colony was a milestone in the
transatlantic transmission of English legal tradition. The right to trial by jury — rooted in Magna Carta (1215) and elaborated
through centuries of English common law — was among the most fundamental liberties that English colonists brought with
them to the New World, and among the most jealously guarded. For this tradition to be formally instituted required not just
law but people: citizens willing and able to sit in judgment of their peers according to established legal principles. Thomas
Goble was one of those people. He was present at the founding not merely of a colony but of an American legal institution.
It is impossible to reconstruct from this distance what Thomas thought as he sat for that first jury. But the historical
significance of the moment is not diminished by its obscurity. Every American who has ever served on a jury, invoked their
legal rights, or benefited from the tradition of due process in the courts is — in the longest sense of the word — a beneficiary
of the tradition that Thomas Goble and his fellow jurors helped establish on that October day in 1640. His descendant Shane,
living in Ashtabula County, Ohio, nearly four centuries later, is the inheritor of a lineage that helped lay the legal foundations
of the American republic. 3.6 Harvard College Tuition Records, 1653–1655 [VERIFIED] Harvard College, founded in 1636 in
Cambridge, Massachusetts — just two years after Thomas Goble's arrival in Charlestown — was the first institution of higher
learning established in the American colonies. Its founding purpose was the training of ministers for the Puritan congregations
of New England. Within two decades of its founding, it had also become a center of civic learning and a marker of social
achievement in the colony. Among the financial records of Harvard College for the years 1653–1655 appear the names
"goodman goobell" and "old gobbell" — almost certainly references to Thomas Goble, now in his early sixties and one of the
elder members of the Middlesex County community. The exact nature of his relationship with Harvard — whether he had a
son, grandson, or ward enrolled at the college; whether he performed services for the institution; or whether the entries reflect
some other form of association — has not been fully resolved by existing research. But his appearance in the Harvard ledger,
however ambiguous the context, establishes his continued civic prominence and community engagement during the early
1650s, more than fifteen years after his initial land grants and a decade after his jury service. Thomas Goble remained, in his
seventh decade of life, a man of standing and connection in his adopted community. 3.7 Children of Thomas and Alice Goble
[VERIFIED] Thomas and Alice Brookman Goble had six children, several born in England before the family's emigration
and the remainder born in Massachusetts: # Name Born Died Notes 1 John Goble 1629 1676 Born England; # Name Born
Died Notes died during or shortly after King Philip's War 2 Thomas Goble Jr. 1631/35 1690 Born England or early
Massachuset ts 3 Elizabeth Goble 1633/34 1689 4 Mary Goble 1636 1725 Lived to age 89 — remarkable for the era 5 Sarah
Goble 1638 1717 6 Daniel Goble ~1640/41 1676 Born Massachuset ts; direct ancestor of the Goble line to Ohio It is through
the youngest child, Daniel Goble, that the line descends to Shane Goble. Daniel's story — and the shadow it carries — is told
in the following chapter. 3.8 Death in Concord, December 30, 1657 [VERIFIED] Thomas Goble died on December 30, 1657,
in Concord, Middlesex County, Massachusetts, where the family had relocated from Charlestown at some point in the
preceding years. He was sixty-six years old — a good age for the seventeenth century, when average life expectancy at birth
was considerably lower, and when a man who reached middle age could nonetheless anticipate a reasonably full span of years
if disease and accident did not intervene. Alice Goble survived her husband. The life that ended that December day in

Concord had been shaped by extraordinary historical forces: the Reformation that drove his family toward Puritanism, the
Personal Rule of Charles I that made England inhospitable to dissenters, the transatlantic crossing that deposited him on the
shores of a continent unknown to his Sussex ancestors, and the founding decades of a colonial civilization that would
eventually become the United States of America. Thomas had cleared land, built a home, worshipped in a congregation he
helped establish, served on the first jury in Boston, accumulated seventy acres of English-speaking civilization carved from the
Massachusetts forest, and raised six children to adulthood in the New World. He could not have known — could not have
imagined — that four centuries later, one of his direct descendants would hold the molecular traces of his ancestry in every
cell of his body and would be able to trace that ancestry not just to West Sussex but to the Bronze Age peoples who first
brought the RZ198 haplogroup to the shores of southern England. He could not have known that the line he established
would survive King Philip's War, the founding of the republic, the frontier expansion into Kentucky and Ohio, a Civil War,
two world wars, and a century of industrial transformation, arriving finally at a young man named Shane living in a small city
on the shores of Lake Erie. But it did. The thread holds. Chapter 4: The King Philip's War Shadow — Daniel Goble (c.1640–
1676) Daniel Goble, the youngest son of Thomas and Alice Brookman Goble, was born approximately 1640–1641 in
Charlestown or Concord, Massachusetts — in the first generation of Gobles to be born on American soil. He is the critical
link in the chain connecting the founding ancestor to all subsequent Goble descendants in New Jersey and Ohio. And his
death, in 1676, places him at the center of one of the most catastrophic events in seventeenthcentury American history. King
Philip's War (1675–1676) was a conflict between the English colonists of New England and a confederation of Native
American tribes led by the Wampanoag sachem Metacom — called "King Philip" by the English in a sardonic appropriation of
European royal nomenclature. The war began in June 1675 and burned through New England for fourteen months with a
ferocity that neither side anticipated and neither could fully control. In proportion to the total population, it remains the
deadliest conflict in American history: approximately 10% of the English colonial population of New England was killed.
Dozens of towns were burned. Thousands of Native Americans were killed, enslaved, or driven from their ancestral lands.
The violence was intimate and ubiquitous — no settlement in Massachusetts, Connecticut, or Rhode Island was entirely
beyond its reach. Whether Daniel Goble died in combat during King Philip's War, from disease in one of the refuge camps
that colonial families fled to for protection, or from some other cause associated with the chaos of that year — the records do
not specify. What is known is that he died in 1676, the year of the war's climax and conclusion, and that his death at
approximately age thirty-five or thirtysix left his son, Daniel Goble Jr., to carry the family forward. Daniel Goble's story —
abbreviated by war and recorded in the barest outlines — nonetheless contains a kind of historical amplitude. He was born in
the New World that his father had helped build, came of age in the Puritan community his father had helped establish, and
died in the first great military crisis of that community's existence. He bridged two worlds: the founding generation of
Thomas Goble, and the migration generation of Daniel Jr. that would carry the Goble name south to New Jersey. The thread
of descent, though it nearly frayed in the fires of 1676, held. PART IV The Goble Migration: New Jersey and the
Revolutionary Frontier Chapter 5: Daniel Goble Jr. and the Move to New Jersey (1669–after 1724) [VERIFIED] Daniel Goble
Jr. was born on May 21, 1669, in Concord, Massachusetts — the town where his grandfather Thomas had died twelve years
earlier and where his father Daniel apparently lived before the King Philip's War crisis of 1676. Daniel Jr. was perhaps six or
seven years old when his father died, and his childhood was therefore shaped by the aftermath of the most devastating conflict
New England had known. He grew up in a world of burned towns, orphaned children, captive families, and the long recovery
of a colonial society that had been pushed to the edge of dissolution. He married Sarah Houghton, born July 30, 1672, in
Lancaster, Massachusetts [VERIFIED] — a town that had itself been a major site of destruction in King Philip's War,
attacked and largely burned in February 1676 when Mary Rowlandson was famously taken captive. Sarah Houghton's origins in
Lancaster give a particular texture to her biography: she was a daughter of one of the most traumatized communities in New
England's history. Daniel and Sarah subsequently migrated to New Jersey — part of a broader and historically significant
pattern of Massachusetts Puritan families moving south and west into New Jersey's fertile interior during the late seventeenth

and early eighteenth centuries. New Jersey offered inducements that the increasingly crowded and expensive land market of
Massachusetts could not: rich farmland available at lower prices, a more tolerant religious and political culture under the
Proprietors, and the opportunity to build new communities without the accumulated tensions and hierarchies of the older
settlements. Daniel Goble Jr. is documented in New Jersey records through at least 1724 — roughly fifty-five years after his
birth — suggesting he lived a full and productive life in his adopted colony before the record loses track of him. Chapter 6:
Kevin Goble — Patriarch of the New Jersey Branch (1700–1783) [VERIFIED] Kevin Goble was born on July 12, 1700, in
New Jersey, and died on March 29, 1783 — a lifespan of eighty-two years that encompassed the entire colonial period of
American history and carried him through the Revolution and into the early republic. He married Mary (born approximately
1701, died 1786) on December 26, 1724, in Morristown, New Jersey [VERIFIED]. Kevin and Mary Goble had at least
seventeen children — a number that situates them within the demographic reality of the frontier family, where high bir

th rates compensated for high child mortality and where a large family represented both an economic asset and a social
achievement. Seventeen children meant a household that expanded and contracted season by season, with older children
working alongside their parents as younger ones were born, and the Goble household gradually seeding the surrounding New
Jersey countryside with adult sons and daughters who established their own families and extended the family's geographic
footprint. Kevin Goble lived through the entirety of the colonial period and into the early republic. When he married Mary in
1724, George I sat on the English throne and American independence was a concept that would have seemed fantastical to
most colonists. When he died in 1783, the Revolution had been won, the Treaty of Paris had been signed, and the United
States of America was a functioning — if fragile — reality. Kevin witnessed the entire arc of the colonial-to-republican
transition without leaving New Jersey. He was a man of place, of deep roots in a specific soil, and his seventeen children
carried those roots forward into the wider American landscape. Chapter 7: Caleb Goble — Revolutionary War Spy and
Frontier Pioneer (March 1, 1760 – March 22, 1838) 7.1 Origins [VERIFIED] Caleb Goble was born on March 1, 1760, in
Morristown, New Jersey. He was a descendant of the Goble-Doud branch of the New Jersey Goble family, his father being
Daniel W. Goble (born approximately 1735, died after 1782), who married Rhoda Doud [PROBABLE]. Caleb grew up in
Morristown — a town that would itself become historically significant during the Revolution as the site of the Continental
Army's winter encampments in 1776–1777 and again in 1779–1780 — on the edge of the New Jersey frontier, at the precise
historical moment when the question of American independence was becoming impossible to avoid. He came of age in a
community where political opinion was galvanized by proximity to events: the Stamp Act, the Townshend Acts, the Boston
Massacre, the Tea Party, Lexington and Concord. By 1776, when the Declaration of Independence was adopted and the
Revolution became an open military conflict, Caleb Goble was sixteen years old — old enough to enlist, young enough to be
shaped entirely by the experience of the war that followed. 7.2 Revolutionary War Service [VERIFIED from pension
application, October 31, 1832] Caleb Goble enlisted in the Continental cause in 1776 at age sixteen. The full account of his
service is preserved in his pension application of October 31, 1832, filed when Caleb was seventy-two years old — a
document that provides an unusually detailed personal account of Revolutionary War service on the frontier. His service
unfolded in several phases: In 1776, Caleb served in Captain Benjamin Rice's Militia Company in New Jersey — one of the
countless local militia units that mobilized in the chaotic early months of the Revolution, before the Continental Army had
established the organizational structures that would eventually bring order to the American military effort. In 1777, he
transferred to Captain James Brinton's Company and participated in the construction of Fort McIntosh and Fort Laurens on
the Ohio frontier. These were critical fortifications in the defense of the western territories against British-allied Native
American forces — the westernmost outposts of the Continental Army's military reach, built at the edge of territory that was
still deeply contested. Fort Laurens, established on the Tuscarawas River in what is now eastern Ohio, was the only Continental
fort built in the territory that would become the state of Ohio. Caleb Goble helped build it. From 1778 to 1783, Caleb served
with the Rangers of the Frontier at Lindley's Fort, participating in the grinding, attritional work of frontier defense —
protecting isolated settlements from raids, gathering intelligence on enemy movements, and maintaining a military presence in

a landscape where the lines between soldier, settler, and target were often indistinguishable. And during this period, he
performed what may be the most remarkable chapter of his service: he served one full year as a spy for the Continental forces
on the Ohio frontier. The role of a frontier spy in the Revolutionary War was unlike anything in the conventional military
experience. There were no uniforms, no formations, no clear lines of battle. A spy operated alone or in small groups, deep in
territory controlled by British forces and their Native American allies, gathering intelligence on troop movements, supply lines,
and planned attacks. Discovery meant, in all probability, death — not the clean death of battle but the death of a captured
enemy combatant in enemy-held territory, where the laws of war provided no protection. To perform this work for a single
week required courage. To perform it for a full year required extraordinary endurance, wilderness skill, psychological fortitude,
and — not least — a measure of luck that not all his counterparts possessed. Caleb's brothers Ebenezer and Daniel also
served in the Continental Army, making the Goble family a multi-generational and multi-member contributor to American
independence. The family did not merely support the Revolution from a distance; they were in its trenches, on its frontiers,
and behind its enemy lines. 7.3 The Pension Injustice [VERIFIED] On October 31, 1832, at age seventy-two, Caleb Goble
filed his pension application with the federal government. The application documented his service with specificity and detail
— the militia companies he served in, the forts he helped build, the frontier stations where he stood watch, and the year he
spent gathering intelligence behind enemy lines. By any reasonable standard, his claim was ironclad. His pension was not
approved until 1855 — seventeen years after his death on March 22, 1838, in Shelby County, Ohio. He never received the
government recognition he had earned. The pension that his service had justified, the money that might have eased his final
years, arrived — bureaucratically, abstractly — after he was gone. He is buried at Medaris Cemetery, Shelby County, Ohio. This
injustice does not diminish what Caleb Goble accomplished or who he was. It is, however, an important part of his story and
of the broader history of how the new American republic treated its veterans — incompletely, bureaucratically, and often far
too late. The pension application itself, filed in 1832 and preserved in the federal archives, is the primary source document that
gives us the detailed account of Caleb's service. Without his willingness to file — even at age seventy-two, even with the
memory of decades of frontier hardship — that account would be lost. His words, preserved in the pension record, outlasted
the injustice done to him. 7.4 Family and Migration [VERIFIED] [PROBABLE] Caleb Goble married Sarah Leasure in 1786
— three years after the end of the Revolutionary War — and together they had fifteen children [VERIFIED]. The post-war
migration of Caleb's family traced the arc of the early American frontier with remarkable fidelity, charting the westward
movement of a generation that had fought for the land they were now claiming: ● ~1794 — Maysville, Kentucky: Caleb and
Sarah crossed the Ohio River into Kentucky, joining the wave of settlers who poured into the trans-Appalachian West
following the Revolution. ● ~1798 — Clermont County, Ohio: The family moved north across the Ohio River into the
Northwest Territory — the vast region that the Continental Congress had organized by the Ordinance of 1787, prohibiting
slavery and laying the groundwork for eventual statehood. ● ~1802 — Warren County, Ohio: Ohio achieved statehood in
1803; Caleb was already there, moving through the newly organized counties of southwestern Ohio. ● 1811 — Troy/Miami
County, Ohio: The family settled briefly in the Miami Valley, another productive agricultural region drawing settlers from the
eastern states. ● Shelby County, Ohio (died March 22, 1838): Caleb's final home, where he died and is buried at Medaris
Cemetery. This migration pattern — from New Jersey through Kentucky across southern and central Ohio — is not a random
wandering. It is a biographical map of the post-Revolutionary frontier, tracing the movement of a generation that fought for
independence and then lived it by moving into the continent that the Revolution had opened. Caleb Goble was, in the fullest
sense, a foundinggeneration American: a man who built forts on the Ohio frontier as a young soldier and then settled that
same frontier as an aging patriarch. He died in the state he had helped defend fifty years before. Chapter 8: The Ohio
Generations — The Intermediate Gap [RESEARCH TARGET] Following Caleb Goble's generation, the Goble line in Ohio

LeCompte Line: Huguenots from Calais to Maryland Chapter 9: Fire and Exile — The Huguenot Background The LeCompte
family's story does not begin with a marriage record or a land grant. It begins with catastrophe — with the specifically French
catastrophe of religious civil war that tore apart one of the most sophisticated civilizations in Europe and drove hundreds of
thousands of its citizens into permanent exile. The French Wars of Religion (1562–1598) were a series of eight distinct armed
conflicts between French Catholics and French Protestants — known, from the Greek word eugenots corrupted through
French usage, as Huguenots. These were not merely theological disputes; they were struggles for the soul, the governance, and
ultimately the survival of France itself, fought with the full ferocity of an age that had not yet developed the concepts of
religious tolerance or civilian immunity from war's violence. The opening atrocity — the Massacre of Vassy on March 1, 1562
— set the tone for all that followed. Catholic troops under the Duke of Guise attacked a congregation of Huguenot
worshippers in the town of Vassy in Champagne, killing more than sixty and wounding more than two hundred. The massacre
ignited the first of the eight wars. But it was the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of August 23–24, 1572 that burned itself
most deeply into Protestant memory across Europe. Beginning with the targeted assassination of Huguenot military leaders
gathered in Paris for a royal wedding, the violence spread within hours into a popular massacre: Parisian mobs, inflamed by
years of propaganda and weeks of political manipulation, fell upon the Protestant population of the city. The killing spread to
provincial cities. Estimates of the total dead range from 5,000 to 30,000 within a matter of days. For Protestant Europe —
including the Protestant communities of England from which the Goble family would emerge — the St. Bartholomew's Day
Massacre was a defining horror, the proof that Catholic power, given the opportunity, would destroy them without mercy. The
Edict of Nantes (1598), issued by King Henry IV — himself a converted Huguenot — provided a fragile peace, granting
Protestants limited religious freedoms and establishing Protestant garrison towns (places de sûreté) as physical guarantees of
the settlement. But this peace was always contingent, always dependent on the goodwill of a monarch who might be
succeeded by a less tolerant heir. When Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685 — the Edict of Fontainebleau — the
fragile peace shattered. Approximately 200,000 to 400,000 Huguenots fled France in the mass exodus known as the Refuge,
scattering to Protestant England, the Netherlands, Prussia, South Africa, and the American colonies. They brought with them
skills — in textiles, metalworking, clockmaking, glassblowing, commerce, medicine — that enriched every country that
received them. Antoine LeCompte had already left for Maryland by approximately 1655 — thirty years before the Revocation
— but his departure reflects the earlier, more gradual persecution that preceded the final cataclysm. For a young Protestant
man in Calais, the decision to leave was always available and never entirely surprising. Calais occupied a unique position: a city

on the English Channel that had been English from 1347 to 1558 — just sixty-two years before Antoine's birth. Despite its
return to French control, the city retained deep English connections in commerce, language, and culture. The Channel
crossing from Calais to Dover was the shortest in the world. For Antoine LeCompte, choosing England and its colonies was
not merely a political decision; it was, in many ways, a continuation of the cross-Channel life that Calais had always inhabited.
Chapter 10: Antoine LeCompte — The Patriarch of Maryland (c.1620–after September 9, 1673) 10.1 Origins and Early Life
[VERIFIED] [PROBABLE] Antoine LeCompte — also recorded in English colonial documents as "Anthony" — was born
approximately 1620 in Calais, Picardie, France [VERIFIED]. His Protestant faith marked him, from the beginning, as a
member of a community under existential pressure in Catholic France. His birth city connected him to England in ways that
most French Protestants could not claim. And his personal biography — before he ever set foot in Maryland — was already
remarkable: he had served approximately eleven years in the army of King Charles I of England, a detail preserved in the
family's oral tradition and recorded in the 1819 LeCompte Manuscript. This army service places Antoine in England — and in
the English military — during one of the most turbulent periods in English history: the years leading up to and including the
English Civil War (1642–1651) and the Cromwellian Interregnum that followed. Charles I's army included a significant number
of foreign Protestant soldiers, and a Huguenot-affiliated young man from Calais — already cross-culturally fluent, already
connected to England — would have been a plausible recruit. The precise record of Antoine's military service has not been
fully recovered, but his claim of eleven years places him as a soldier in a very specific historical context, and that context —
the English Civil War, the execution of Charles I in 1649, the Puritan Commonwealth — was exactly the kind of upheaval that
could redirect a man's life toward a new beginning in the colonies. 10.2 Marriage to Hester Dottando [VERIFIED] Antoine
LeCompte married Hester (Esther) Dottando on July 11, 1661, in London, England [VERIFIED]. Hester was born in Dieppe,
Normandy — another Norman French connection in the family's intersecting story. Dieppe was one of the major Huguenot
centers in Normandy, a port city with deep Protestant traditions and strong English commercial ties. That both Antoine and
Hester came from Norman coastal cities with English connections — Calais and Dieppe respectively — speaks to the network
of Franco-English Protestant commerce and culture within which both families moved. They were not strangers meeting by
accident; they were members of the same cross-Channel Protestant community, finding each other in the English capital
before making together the further crossing to the American colonies. 10.3 Arrival in Maryland and the Land Grant
[VERIFIED] Antoine LeCompte arrived in Maryland approximately 1655 — some six years before his London marriage to
Hester. It is possible he made an initial settlement voyage before returning to England to marry, or that his arrival date in
colonial records predates the marriage while both arrivals are documented separately. On January 17, 1659, he received a land
grant of 800 acres named "St. Antoine" on the Choptank River, Dorchester County, Maryland [VERIFIED]. The land grant
was issued under Maryland's headright system — the colonial policy of granting fifty acres of land per person transported to
the colony. An 800-acre grant indicated the transportation of Antoine himself plus a number of additional individuals. The
grant specifically names Thomas Raymond, Barbara Crouch, and Thomas Jones among those transported — indentured
servants or contracted laborers whose passage Antoine had financed in exchange for their labor and for the land their
transport entitled him to claim. The naming of the land "St. Antoine" was deliberate and revealing. Antoine is the French
saint's name form of Anthony — the specifically Catholic or traditional French rendering, as opposed to the anglicized
"Anthony" that colonial records would sometimes use for him. In naming his land after himself in French, Antoine LeCompte
was making a statement: this was a Frenchman's land. He had arrived in a new country, under English colonial governance,
speaking English well enough to navigate courts and contracts — but he would not surrender his French identity, his French
name, his connection to the culture and faith that had made him who he was. "St. Antoine" stood on the Choptank River as a
small monument to that refusal. 10.4 Taylor's Island Settlement [VERIFIED] Antoine and Hester LeCompte settled on
Taylor's Island in Dorchester County, Maryland — a peninsula in the upper Chesapeake Bay region, home to a small but
cohesive community of planters, merchants, and fishermen. Taylor's Island was connected to the Maryland mainland by the
creeks and tributaries of the Choptank River system, accessible by water to the trade routes of the Chesapeake and by land —

precariously, seasonally — to the county seat at Cambridge. In this community, Antoine established himself as a planter and
merchant. The 800-acre "St. Antoine" tract represented substantial agricultural capacity by the standards of Dorchester
County. With indentured servants and, eventually, the labor of his own growing family, he would have cultivated tobacco —
Maryland's primary cash crop — alongside subsistence agriculture in grain and livestock. He operated on a scale that
commanded local respect, and he integrated himself into the social and legal fabric of the county with a speed that speaks to
both personal capability and community acceptance. 10.5 Justice of Dorchester County (1669–1671) [VERIFIED] From 1669
to 1671, Antoine LeCompte served as a Justice of Dorchester County — a position of significant civic authority in colonial
Maryland. As a Justice, Antoine would have heard both civil and criminal cases, administered oaths, recorded deeds and
contracts, presided over local disputes, and served as a representative of the proprietary government of Maryland in his corner
of the Chesapeake world. It was, in the colonial context, roughly equivalent to a combination of judge, notary public, and local

room. A gift to the family they could not see, the descendants who would come after them and want to know where they had
come from. They could not read what Benjamin wrote down; they would never see the manuscript that preserved their
testimony. But they knew what they were doing. They were building a record out of memory the way their ancestor had built
an estate out of wilderness — with determination, with craft, and with a conviction that what they were making would matter
to someone, someday, in a way they could not yet imagine. The manuscript they created — held today at the Maryland
Historical Society in Baltimore — has served researchers for more than two centuries. Every time a LeCompte descendant
opens that document and finds their ancestor's name in the flowing script of Benjamin Woodward LeCompte's hand, they are
receiving the gift that two blind brothers gave on an ordinary day in 1819. Without eyes, they gave sight to their descendants

Connection — Shane's Most Ancient Named Relative In 1903, workmen excavating Gough's Cave in Cheddar Gorge,

cave floor. Initial examination suggested great age. Laboratory analysis later confirmed it: Cheddar Man, as the specimen came

modern standards — perhaps five feet five inches — but otherwise anatomically entirely modern. In 1997, Oxford University

spanning more than 9,000 years, the mitochondrial DNA had passed from mother to daughter to mother, unbroken, across

history of any kind. In 2018, the Natural History Museum in London undertook a far more ambitious project: full genome
sequencing of Cheddar Man using modern ancient DNA techniques that Sykes could not have employed in 1997. The results,

Neanderthal Ancestry 17.1 — Introduction: The Other Humans We Carry Inside Us For most of the 20th century,
Neanderthals were depicted in popular culture as brutish, dim-witted cave-dwellers — primitive near-misses on the path to
true humanity. Modern science has completely overturned this picture. Homo neanderthalensis — the Neanderthals — lived
in Europe and Western Asia from approximately 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. They were anatomically distinct from Homo
sapiens — stockier, with larger brow ridges, larger brains (actually somewhat larger on average than our own), and cold-
weather physiological adaptations developed over hundreds of thousands of years in Ice Age Europe. But they were not
primitive. Neanderthals made fire, used medicinal plants, buried their dead with flowers and pigment, created jewelry from
eagle talons and shells, produced musical instruments, and manufactured stone tools of remarkable sophistication (the
Mousterian industry). They were fully sapient by any meaningful standard. They were people. When anatomically modern
humans migrated out of Africa approximately 70,000 years ago, they encountered Neanderthals who were already established
across the Eurasian landmass. The two populations did not simply co-exist in parallel and then separate; they interbred —

briefly, in specific regions, most likely in the Levant (modern-day Israel, Lebanon, Syria, and Jordan), between approximately
60,000 and 50,000 years ago. The consequence of those encounters is preserved in Shane's genome today, and in the genomes
of every living person of non-African ancestry: between 1% and 4% of the modern human genome consists of DNA
inherited from Neanderthal individuals. These are not ancient, degraded fragments — they are fully functional DNA
sequences that have been maintained by natural selection across 50,000 years precisely because some of them confer real
biological advantages in specific environments. 23andMe identifies specific Neanderthal SNP variants — actual DNA
sequences that match the sequenced Neanderthal genomes — present in Shane's genome. Shane carries more Neanderthal
DNA than 74% of 23andMe customers — a higher-than-average Neanderthal genetic legacy. [Verification: Neanderthal
genome sequencing and modern human introgression — Prüfer et al., Nature 2014; Green et al., Science 2010. 23andMe
Neanderthal variant identification methodology uses confirmed Neanderthal SNPs from sequenced genomes, primary
reference: Vindija Cave, Croatia specimen. Source: 23andMe Neanderthal Ancestry feature; Prüfer et al., Nature 505, 43–49,
2014.] 17.2 — Shane's Four Documented Neanderthal Variant Clusters Neanderthal Variant Trait Influence Scientific and

damaging inflammatory response to gluten, the protein complex found in wheat, barley, and rye. Approximately 30% of
people of Northwestern European descent carry one or both of these variants — making them among the most common
disease-associated variants in the European genome — yet only approximately 1% of the general population develops clinical
celiac disease. Carrying these variants means the immune system possesses the biological mechanism to mount a gluten

gluten introduction in infancy, gut microbiome composition, intestinal infections, and other environmental triggers that are not
yet fully understood. The symptom profile of celiac disease is notoriously diverse and frequently misdiagnosed: persistent
digestive distress (bloating, cramping, alternating diarrhea and constipation), unexplained chronic fatigue, iron-deficiency
anemia that does not respond to supplementation, chronic headaches, neurological symptoms sometimes called "gluten
ataxia," skin conditions such as dermatitis herpetiformis, and generalized "brain fog." These symptoms are individually
nonspecific, and for this reason celiac disease is commonly misdiagnosed as irritable bowel syndrome, chronic fatigue
syndrome, anxiety, or depression — sometimes for years or even decades. If Shane or any family member experiences a cluster
of these symptoms, the appropriate first step is a gastroenterology consultation and a blood panel for tissue transglutaminase
IgA antibodies (tTG-IgA) and deamidated gliadin peptide antibodies (DGP) — the most sensitive and specific celiac screening

tests currently available. Critically: a gluten-free diet must not be started before testing, as it can clear the antibodies from the
blood and produce a false-negative result. The family significance of this finding is also noteworthy: first-degree relatives
(parents, siblings, children) of individuals who develop celiac disease have a 10–15% lifetime risk of developing the condition
themselves — substantially higher than the general population risk of approximately 1%. 18.3 — Carrier Status Results Carrier

conditions, a single copy produces no symptoms — the person is a healthy carrier. The clinical significance arises when two
carriers of the same condition have children together: each pregnancy carries a 25% probability of inheriting two copies of
the variant and developing the condition. Shane's carrier status results are important for family health planning, particularly if
considering children with a partner whose carrier status for the same conditions is unknown. Condition Shane's Result

19: Physical & Behavioral Trait Predictions 19.1 — Introduction: The Genetics of Everyday Life Beyond ancestry and health,
the genome encodes a remarkable range of physical characteristics, sensory experiences, dietary preferences, and behavioral
tendencies — the everyday texture of lived experience. The 23andMe Traits feature generates predictions for dozens of these
characteristics based on genome-wide association studies (GWAS) — largescale research projects, typically involving hundreds
of thousands of participants, that identify statistical associations between specific genetic variants and measurable traits. In
many cases, these studies have identified dozens or even hundreds of variants across the genome that each contribute a small
effect toward a given trait, and the combined effect of all these variants produces a probabilistic prediction. Traits are not
deterministic — they are tendencies. A genetic tendency toward morning wakefulness does not mean a person cannot be a
night owl; it means the genome has positioned them to find it somewhat easier. Genes establish the landscape; environment,
habit, and choice determine where within that landscape a person lives. What makes trait genetics particularly engaging for
family history is that many of these findings are immediately recognizable: "Oh — that's why everyone on that side of the
family has that." Traits that family members have attributed to habit, coincidence, or personality often have a legible genetic
component that reaches back through the same ancestral populations documented in the pages above. The lactose tolerance
that allowed English dairy farmers to thrive, the pale skin adapted to lowlatitude sun, the spatial navigation tendency honed by
a hundred thousand years of hunter-gatherer life — these are not merely abstract science. They are the living inheritance of
the exact same people whose migrations and marriages are chronicled throughout this report. 19.2 — Shane Goble's Complete

H E G O B L E F A M I L Y I N A M E R I C A The New Jersey Gobles Establishing the American Line, 1700–1760 “They
came to a country that had not yet imagined what it would become, and they became part of what it was.” 1.1 — From
Concord, Massachusetts to the Jersey Frontier The story of the New Jersey Gobles begins not in New Jersey at all, but in the
shadow of a catastrophe. When Thomas Goble, the family patriarch who had sailed from West Sussex, England, died in
Concord, Massachusetts, on December 30, 1657, he left behind a family that was still finding its footing on the New England
frontier. His son Daniel Goble, born approximately 1640 or 1641 in Charlestown, Massachusetts, carried the family name
forward into the most turbulent decades of colonial New England history. Daniel died in 1676 — a year that stands as one of
the most violent and devastating in all of colonial American experience. [VERIFIED] The year 1676 was the year of King
Philip's War. Between June 1675 and August 1676, the Wampanoag sachem Metacomet — known to the English colonists as
“King Philip” — united a broad coalition of Algonquian-speaking peoples in a desperate, ultimately failed attempt to drive the
English from New England. The war was proportionally the deadliest in American history: nearly 600 English colonists were
killed outright, and thousands more died from exposure, starvation, and disease as towns were destroyed and farms
abandoned. Approximately 3,000 Native Americans perished in the same conflict. Twelve of Plymouth Colony's ninety towns
were completely destroyed. Concord itself — the very town where Thomas Goble had built his life and where his son Daniel
had grown to manhood — was attacked on March 13, 1676, in a raid that left buildings in flames and inhabitants fleeing for
their lives. Whether Daniel Goble's death in 1676 was directly connected to King Philip's War, we cannot say with
documentary certainty. The timing is, at the very minimum, haunting. He was a young man — perhaps thirty-five or thirty-six
years old — with a young son named Daniel Goble Jr., born in 1669, who was only seven years old when his father died. The
widow and the boy survived. They survived the war, survived the years of reconstruction, survived the slow, painful
reassembly of a New England that had been shattered by the most violent conflict it had ever experienced. And then — as so
many New England families did in the decades after King Philip's War — they moved. The post-war migration from New
England southward into New Jersey and Pennsylvania was one of the great demographic movements of early colonial
America. The war had revealed the limits of the first Puritan settlement — its vulnerability to the peoples whose land it
occupied, its fragility in the face of organized resistance. The generation that survived King Philip's War was a chastened and
transformed generation. Many sought land beyond the scarred Massachusetts frontier, following routes south along the
Hudson River corridor and west across the Delaware River into the territory that had become the English province of New
Jersey in 1664. Among these migrants, sometime after 1690, was Daniel Goble Jr. — the grandson of Thomas Goble of West
Sussex, the son of Daniel Goble of Concord, the first of the family's New Jersey chapter. ✦ Historical Context: Colonial New
Jersey (1664–1720) ✦ New Jersey became an English colony in 1664 when the Duke of York granted the territory to Sir
George Carteret and John Berkeley, dividing it into East Jersey and West Jersey. The colony attracted a remarkably diverse
population from its earliest years. Puritan refugees from the Connecticut and New Haven colonies established towns along the
Raritan Valley; Quakers dominated West Jersey and established Philadelphia across the Delaware; Dutch settlers from the
former New Netherland held onto communities in Bergen County and along the Hudson; Scottish Presbyterians, arriving after
1683, brought their austere Calvinist theology to the highlands of what would become Morris County. This Presbyterian
community — theologically aligned with, though politically distinct from, the New England Puritans — was the natural
destination for a family like the Gobles, who had been rooted in the Puritan tradition since Thomas Goble's arrival in
Massachusetts in the 1640s. Morris County, where the Goble family established itself over the first half of the eighteenth
century, was a landscape of particular character: hardwood forests covering rolling hills, cold streams running from the
Watchung Mountains into the Raritan River drainage, and iron-bearing rock that would make the county one of colonial
America's most important ironworking centers. The iron furnaces and forges along the Rockaway and Whippany Rivers —
operations like the Hibernia Furnace and the Mount Hope Iron Works — gave Morris County both economic vitality and
strategic military significance that would become critical during the Revolution. Morristown, the county seat, was founded in
1710 and grew rapidly into a thriving market town of taverns, Presbyterian churches, artisan shops, and farms. It was a place

where a family from New England's Puritan tradition could find community, find land, and find work. By the time Kevin
Goble was born in 1700 and Daniel Goble Jr. was establishing his household in New Jersey, the province was entering its most
prosperous preRevolutionary decades. The transition from proprietary to royal government (East and West Jersey reunited as a
single royal colony in 1702) brought political stability. Population grew steadily, farms expanded, and the iron industry
connected New Jersey to the broader Atlantic commercial economy. The Goble family arrived at precisely the right moment in
New Jersey's development. Historical Image Early Map of New Jersey and Parts of Pennsylvania, 1703. From the New York

(born July 12, 1700, New Jersey) Daniel Goble Jr. was born into a world of provincial certainty and frontier peril. His birth
date — May 21, 1669 — places him in a Concord that was still very much a frontier Puritan community: a town of church
meetings, militia musters, and the constant pressure of the wilderness beyond the cleared fields. His father Daniel was a young
man of about thirty. His grandfather Thomas had been dead for twelve years. The Goble family of Concord was a family of
the second generation of New England settlement — not the original founders, not the great Puritan divines, but the ordinary
farming and artisan families who made the colony function from day to day. [VERIFIED] When his father died in 1676 —
Daniel Jr. was seven years old — the boy entered the care of his mother and, presumably, the broader Concord community
that was itself struggling to recover from the devastation of King Philip's War. He grew up in a town that had been attacked,
that had lost neighbors to violence and fire, that was rebuilding its structures and its confidence simultaneously. This is not an
abstract historical backdrop; it is the specific emotional and social environment in which Daniel Goble Jr. became a man. The
trauma of King Philip's War was not a distant event for a seven-year-old boy in Concord in 1676. It was the defining fact of
his childhood. The marriage of Daniel Goble Jr. to Sarah Houghton adds another layer of profound historical meaning to this
genealogical record. Sarah was born on July 30, 1672, in Lancaster, Worcester County, Massachusetts — a detail that carries
enormous weight. Lancaster, Massachusetts, was one of the towns most catastrophically destroyed during King Philip's War.
On February 10, 1676 — the same year that Daniel Goble's father died in Concord — a large force of Narragansett and
Nipmuc warriors attacked Lancaster, killing twelve residents, burning nearly every building in the town, and taking forty or
more inhabitants captive, including the minister's wife, Mary Rowlandson, whose famous narrative of her captivity became one

necessary to understand Morristown — the town that defined them. Morristown, New Jersey, sits at the center of Morris
County in what was, in the colonial period, a landscape of extraordinary natural richness: hardwood forests of oak, hickory,
and chestnut covering rolling hills that concealed vast deposits of magnetite iron ore; clear cold streams running down from
the First and Second Watchung Mountain ridges toward the Raritan River system; black loamy soil in the valley floors that
rewarded careful farming with generous crops. The town itself, incorporated in 1739 but settled meaningfully from around
1710, was the commercial and legal center of Morris County. Its court sessions, its market days, its taverns and inns, its
Presbyterian church (organized in 1733), and its network of roads connecting to New York, Newark, and Philadelphia made it
a genuine community with all the structures that a farming family needed: places to sell produce, places to transact legal
business, places to worship, places to meet potential spouses, places to hear the political news of the colony and the empire.
Kevin Goble and his extended family were part of this community for three generations — from approximately 1700 to the
1790s when the Ohio migration began. The iron industry was the economic engine that distinguished Morris County from
other New Jersey farming communities. The Hibernia Furnace, established in the 1760s on the Rockaway River, was one of
the largest iron-producing operations in colonial America. The Mount Hope Iron Works, the Boonton Iron Works, and
numerous smaller forges and bloomeries employed hundreds of workers and supplied iron products — pots, tools, wagon
parts, and crucially, weapons and cannon shot — to the colonial market. During the French and Indian War (1754– 1763),
Morris County's iron furnaces supplied military materiel to the British Army and colonial militia. During the Revolution, they
supplied the Continental Army. The ironmasters and their workers were not peripheral figures in Morris County society; they

were its backbone, and the Goble family — as farmers, as militia members, as community participants — lived within and
depended upon this iron-powered economy. The density of the Goble name in Morris County records from 1700 to 1800 is
remarkable. Kevin Goble's seventeen or more children, each reaching adulthood and marrying into other Morris County
families, created a web of Goble connections that touched nearly every aspect of the county's social life. The Morris County
Abstract of Wills is dense with Goble entries. Court records show Goble family members as plaintiffs, defendants, witnesses,
and jurors. Land records document Goble purchases, sales, and inheritances across the county's townships. The Presbyterian
church registers of Morristown contain Goble baptisms, marriages, and burials. In the second half of the eighteenth century,
to be a resident of Morris County was to know the Goble family. ✦ Historical Context: The French and Indian War and
Morris County ✦ The French and Indian War (1754–1763) — the American theater of the global Seven Years' War, fought
between Britain and France for dominance of the North American continent — brought conflict to within striking distance of
the Goble family's Morris County home. French-allied Native American war parties, operating from Canada and from the
Ohio Country, periodically penetrated as far south as New York and northern New Jersey in the early years of the war. The
frontier raids of 1755 and 1756, following the catastrophic British defeat at the Battle of the Monongahela (where General
Braddock was killed), sent shock waves of fear through colonial communities from Virginia to New England. Morris County
responded to this threat in ways that directly shaped the Goble community. The county's militia was organized and drilled. The
iron furnaces redoubled their production, supplying military materiel. Tax records show increased assessments for military
funding. Young men from Morris County families — including, almost certainly, men of the Goble family — served in the
colonial militia forces that guarded New Jersey's northern frontier. Jonas Goble, born around 1707, was approximately forty-
seven years old at the war's outbreak in 1754; his son Henry was perhaps six years old. By the war's end in 1763, Henry Goble
was fifteen — old enough to understand what frontier conflict meant and young enough to have his view of the world shaped
by the anxious, martial atmosphere of a colony on a war footing. The war also had a profound long-term consequence for the
Goble family's future trajectory. The British victory in 1763 opened the trans-Appalachian west to colonial settlement — or so
colonists assumed, until the Proclamation of 1763 drew a line at the Appalachians and forbade settlement beyond it. This
imperial interference with westward expansion was one of the specific grievances that fed the colonial resentment culminating
in revolution. The Goble family, established in Morris County, had every reason to want western land and every reason to
resent a British government that seemed determined to prevent them from getting it. — 18 — Chapter Two ✦ ✦ T H E A M

his brothers in the Revolution's most desperate years. Then he walked to Ohio and built a new life from scratch.” Historical

Pennsylvania, and Ohio frontier corridor from 1776 through 1782. 2.1 — Birth and Boyhood in Revolutionary New Jersey G e
n e r a t i o n 6 ( D i r e c t L i n e ) Caleb Goble [VERIFIED] Born: March 1, 1760 — Morristown, Morris County, New

Buried: Medaris Cemetery, Shelby County, Ohio Military Service: 1776–1782 (age 16 to 22) — Continental Militia, Frontier
Rangers, Spy Service Caleb Goble was born on the first day of March, 1760, in Morristown, Morris County, New Jersey. He
was the son of Daniel W. Goble and Rhoda (Doud) Goble, the grandson of Kevin Goble the New Jersey patriarch, and the
great-great-grandson of Thomas Goble who had crossed the Atlantic from West Sussex more than a century before Caleb's
birth. He entered a world already charged with the electricity of imperial crisis: in the year of Caleb Goble's birth, the French
and Indian War was in its sixth year, New Jersey was supplying men and material for the British war effort, and the colonial
assemblies were beginning to test their authority against the demands of the Crown in ways that would, within fifteen years,
produce open revolution. [VERIFIED] The Morristown of Caleb Goble's childhood was a community being rapidly
politicized by the same forces that were transforming every colonial American town in the 1760s and early 1770s. When Caleb

was five years old, the Stamp Act (1765) ignited colonial fury over parliamentary taxation without representation. When he was
seven, the Townshend Acts (1767) extended that fury. When he was ten, news reached Morristown of the Boston Massacre
(March 5, 1770), in which British soldiers had fired on a crowd of civilians, killing five. When he was thirteen, word came of
the Boston Tea Party (December 16, 1773). By the time Caleb Goble was fifteen years old, the battles of Lexington and
Concord (April 19, 1775) had transformed political argument into armed conflict. Caleb was fifteen when the war that would
define his life began. He was sixteen when he first took up a musket for the patriot cause. The physical landscape of Caleb's
boyhood — the hills and forests and iron-worked valleys of Morris County — were themselves being transformed during
these years into a theater of war. New Jersey, positioned between British-controlled New York to the north and the
Continental Army's operational areas to the south and west, was the most militarily contested territory in the entire
Revolutionary War. The British used New York as their primary base; the Continental Army used New Jersey as its corridor
between New England and the southern colonies. The roads that Caleb Goble had walked as a child — to church, to market,
to visit his grandfather Kevin's farm — became military highways. The farms that had produced wheat and corn were stripped
by foraging parties from both armies. The forests that had been hunting grounds became cover for militia ambushes and
Loyalist raids. ✦ Historical Context: Morristown and the Revolution ✦ Morristown, New Jersey, occupied one of the most
strategically critical positions in the entire Revolutionary War. Its location in the Watchung Mountain highlands, protected by
ridges that were nearly impassable for conventional armies, made it a natural defensive position. Its iron furnaces produced
weapons and war materiel. Its farms and stores could supply an army. And its road network connected it to all the critical
theaters of the New Jersey campaign. George Washington recognized Morristown's value immediately. Following his stunning
victories at Trenton (December 26, 1776) and Princeton (January 3, 1777), Washington moved his battered army to
Morristown for the winter of January through May 1777 — a winter of rebuilding, recruiting, and training that transformed
the Continental Army from the ragged, demoralized force that had been chased across New Jersey in the fall of 1776 into a
fighting force capable of sustained operations. Washington quartered at the Arnold Tavern in Morristown; his officers spread
through the town's homes and businesses; his soldiers camped in the surrounding countryside. The Goble family of
Morristown — farmers, community members, Patriots — lived through this military occupation of their town. Washington
returned to Morristown for the winter of December 1779 through June 1780 — the famous “Hard Winter” that tested the
Continental Army more severely than Valley Forge. Twenty-six blizzards struck New Jersey in the winter of 1779–1780.
Snowdrifts reached six feet. The Raritan River froze solid enough to bear wagons. Soldiers at Jockey Hollow, the encampment
three miles from Morristown, ate their boots, bark, and each other's horses. Mutiny was narrowly averted twice. The Morris
County community — including the Goble family — fed and sheltered soldiers, donated food and firewood, and endured the
additional hardship of housing an army in the midst of a record winter. Caleb Goble was nineteen or twenty years old during
the Hard Winter, already a veteran of three or four years of military service. Washington's Ford Mansion in Morristown —
where the General headquartered in 1779–1780 — is preserved today as a National Historic Site. It stands as a physical
monument to the community that sustained the Continental Army through its darkest winter. Historical Image Washington's
Headquarters: The Ford Mansion, Morristown, New Jersey, circa 1901. This building served as General Washington's
headquarters during the Hard Winter of 1779–1780, when twenty-six blizzards struck New Jersey and the Continental Army
nearly perished from cold and starvation. Caleb Goble, at nineteen to twenty years old, was a veteran soldier serving on the
frontier during these same desperate months. The Goble family of Morristown lived in direct proximity to this encampment.
2.2 — Military Service: The Complete Record Caleb Goble served the patriot cause for approximately six years, from 1776 to
1782, spanning his ages sixteen through twenty-two. His documented service record is one of the most comprehensive and
distinguished in the extended Goble family genealogical record. 1776 — First Service (Age 16): Captain Benjamin Rice's
Company In 1776, the most consequential year in American political history, Caleb Goble was sixteen years old. He enlisted in
Captain Benjamin Rice's Militia Company — one of the Morris County militia units organized to defend the New Jersey
corridor against British operations from New York. His enlistment at sixteen years old was not unusual in the Revolutionary

context; the Continental Army and state militias accepted boys as young as fourteen in some cases, and Morris County in 1776
needed every able-bodied man and boy it could find. [VERIFIED] The year 1776 placed extraordinary demands on the Morris
County militia. In August and September, the British and Hessian forces defeated Washington's army at the Battle of Long
Island and drove the Continentals from Manhattan. In November, Fort Washington and Fort Lee fell, and Washington's
retreating army crossed New Jersey in what appeared to many observers to be a fatal rout. British and Hessian troops spread
through New Jersey, occupying towns, foraging farms, and terrorizing civilian populations with a thoroughness that destroyed
whatever Loyalist sentiment remained. Morristown, protected by its mountain position, was not occupied — but the farms and
roads surrounding it were under constant pressure from British raiding parties. It was in this desperate context that Caleb
Goble first served. Morris County militia companies like Captain Rice's did not fight pitched battles; they harassed British
foraging parties, protected supply lines, gathered intelligence, and provided the local knowledge that Continental commanders
depended upon for their operations. For a sixteen-year-old from Morristown, this service meant nights in the field, exposure
to all weather, the ever-present risk of capture or death, and the formative experience of operating in a war zone in the
landscape of his own childhood. His first year of service ended with Washington's stunning victory at Trenton on December
26, 1776 — a victory made possible in part by the intelligence-gathering and logistical support provided by exactly the kind of
militia units that Caleb Goble was serving in. [VERIFIED] 1777 — Second Service: Captain James Brinton's Company Caleb's
second enlistment, in Captain James Brinton's Company in 1777, came in the year of Valley Forge. While Washington's main
army suffered through its legendary winter at Valley Forge in Pennsylvania, the New Jersey militia — including Brinton's
company — maintained active operations against the British garrison in New York and against the Loyalist and British raiding
forces that continued to harass New Jersey's civilian population. The New Jersey militia of 1777 were no longer raw recruits;
they were veterans who had spent a year learning the brutal calculus of partisan warfare. Caleb Goble was seventeen in 1777,
already one year seasoned. [VERIFIED] Jackson's Fort — Captain Charles Crawford's Company At some point in his military
service — probably 1777 or 1778 — Caleb Goble served in Captain Charles Crawford's Company at Jackson's Fort. Frontier
forts were the fixed nodes in a network of frontier defense that extended across the Pennsylvania and New Jersey backcountry,
providing supply depots, rally points, and refuges for the scattered settler populations of the frontier zone. Service in a frontier
fort garrison was simultaneously safer than open-field fighting — the walls provided physical protection — and more
continuously dangerous, as frontier forts were targets for concerted attacks and were often isolated from rapid reinforcement.
[VERIFIED] 1778–1782 — Rangers of the Frontier and the Spy Year The most remarkable and, in many respects, the most
consequential phase of Caleb Goble's military service was his years with the Rangers of the Frontier — an elite posting that
required exceptional woodcraft, physical endurance, navigational skill, and the kind of precise local knowledge that only years
of living in a specific landscape could provide. Frontier Rangers operated on the edges of settled territory, ranging far beyond
the fixed military positions into territory that was genuinely contested between colonial, British, and Native American forces.
They gathered intelligence, protected isolated settler families, tracked enemy movements, and conducted the kind of
independent, small-unit operations that formed the essential infrastructure of frontier defense. [VERIFIED] Within this
Ranger service, one detail stands apart from all others in Caleb Goble's military record: he served for one year as a spy. The
significance of this cannot be overstated. Revolutionary War espionage was not the romanticized profession of later popular
culture. It was a specific military function that placed its practitioners at the absolute highest level of personal risk that the war
could impose. Spies were not protected by the laws of war. They wore no uniform that would identify them as combatants
entitled to prisoner-of-war status. They operated in enemy-controlled territory under false identities, gathering information on
troop dispositions, supply movements, fortification strengths, and command intentions. If captured, they were tried as civilians
and hanged. [VERIFIED] Nathan Hale had been hanged in New York in September 1776 — the same year Caleb Goble first
enlisted — with the words attributed to him: “I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country.” The execution of
spies was not an aberration; it was the standard. British military law and the informal rules of war that governed both sides in
the Revolutionary conflict were unambiguous: a spy caught behind enemy lines without a uniform faced the rope. Caleb Goble

accepted this risk for a full year — a full year of operating in territory where discovery meant death without the dignity of a
soldier's execution — and returned. He came back. Whatever he did, wherever he went, whomever he deceived and reported
upon, he did it and survived it and returned to his family and his fellow Rangers. “ In the shadows between armies, there
moved men who wore no colors and carried no flags, who slept in barns and spoke in borrowed accents and sent their
knowledge back to commanders who never acknowledged them. These men were the nervous system of the Revolution —
invisible, essential, and entirely expendable. Caleb Goble was one of them. ” — Narrative reconstruction based on
documented historical record; compiler's characterization of Caleb Goble's spy service, Volume II, Chapter 2 1782 — With

settlements through the war's final months. The families of Washington County were not safe simply because the main armies
had stopped fighting at Yorktown; the frontier war continued until the treaty made further operations indefensible.

backs in a landscape that had been contested for six years. They were the Morris County Gobles, these three young men, and
they were there at the end, together. [VERIFIED] Caleb Goble's Complete Military Service — Summary Table Table 2.1 —

now it is January, and the world has reduced itself to the essential facts: wood, fire, cold, ice on the creek, the smell of
woodsmoke from the blockhouse chimney, the distant possibility of spring. I am twenty-two years old. I have been a soldier
since I was sixteen. Ebenezer is asleep by the fire. Daniel coughed all night again and I lay awake listening to him, which is a
thing I have been doing since we were boys and he would cough through the winter in the house on the hill in Morristown,
