are proceeding — but the frontier does not seem to know this. There were raids on the settlements at Buffalo Creek not three
weeks ago. The Delawares, or men dressed as them. We rode out and found cold ashes and a family gone. The frontier ends
wars on its own schedule. I think sometimes about the year I spent as a spy. I have not spoken of it much, not even to
Ebenezer, who would understand better than most. A year is a long time to be someone else. To learn the rhythm of a
different name, a different story — I was a merchant from Philadelphia, then a farmer from Bucks County, then simply a
traveler with no particular reason for being wherever I was. You learn to talk slowly and listen fast. You learn that British

officers, like all men, will speak freely over a good meal and a second cup of wine. You learn that the most valuable
intelligence is often the most ordinary: how many wagons are at which crossroads, which road is being repaired, where the
pickets are posted at two in the morning. You carry this knowledge in your head because putting it to paper means death if
you are searched. You deliver it to men whose names you sometimes do not know. And then you disappear again into the
countryside, and you are someone else, and the noose that has been hanging invisible above your head for the past six months
goes with you, still there, still waiting. I regret nothing about that year. I did not like the lying — I am a Presbyterian, my
grandfather Kevin's grandson, and the habit of plain dealing is bred into me — but I understood that the lying was in service
of something true. There is a country trying to be born here. It does not yet fully exist. It is an idea that men are arguing about
in Philadelphia and London and Paris, and men are dying for in the forests of Pennsylvania and the frozen fields of New
Jersey. I have watched men die for it. I watched James Barton die of a musket ball in the side at a nameless creek in the fall of
1779, and he was twenty-three years old, and he had never seen a city or read a newspaper, and he died for this idea that men
who had read Locke and Montesquieu were having elegant arguments about in heated rooms. It seems like a fair bargain. The
idea is worthy. I believe the idea is worthy. The fire pops. Ebenezer shifts and mumbles something. Daniel has stopped
coughing. Outside, through the gap in the blockhouse wall, I can see stars over the dark line of the forest. There is a whole
country out there, west of here, that no one I know has ever walked in. New territory, the Congressmen call it — the
Northwest, past the Ohio River, past the Muskingum, a continent of black soil and hardwood forest and rivers that flow to the

— The Scene: Dorchester County, Maryland, 1819 In 1819 — the year that Spain ceded Florida to the United States under the
AdamsOnís Treaty, when James Monroe was in his second year as president, when the Missouri Compromise was being
debated in Congress and the question of slavery in the western territories was beginning to fracture the republic's political
consensus — two elderly blind men sat in a room in Dorchester County, Maryland, and dictated history. Thomas LeCompte
and Daniel LeCompte were the great-great-grandsons of Antoine and Hester LeCompte, the French Huguenot knight and his
wife who had arrived in Maryland in 1655. They were the sons of Moses LeCompte II, the grandsons of William LeCompte,
the great-grandsons of Moses LeCompte the blind patriarch who had fathered eleven children on the Choptank River shore.
They were, in other words, five generations removed from the original arrival of the family in America, and they were blind —
had been blind, it appears, for most or all of their adult lives, in a perhaps hereditary echo of their ancestor Moses who had
lost his sight centuries before. And they had never, being blind, been able to read the records that preserved their family's
history. What they had instead was memory. The memory was comprehensive. It was specific. It named names, gave dates,
described relationships, traced lines of descent through multiple branches, and reached back — with the confident detail of
men who had spent decades rehearsing and maintaining this knowledge internally — to a soldier of Calais who had fought
eleven years for the King of Great Britain and been knighted for his valor. This was not vague family tradition of the “we
came from somewhere in Europe” variety. This was genealogical data, precise and structured, carried in the minds of two old
blind men who understood that when they died, this memory would die with them unless it was put on paper. Benjamin
Woodward LeCompte sat with pen and paper as the two brothers dictated. The document he produced — running to multiple
pages, covering five or six generations of family history, naming scores of individuals, recording births, marriages, deaths, and
relationships across the LeCompte extended family — is one of the most remarkable genealogical documents produced in
early American history. It is the 1819 LeCompte Manuscript, and it is held today at the Maryland Historical Society in
Baltimore. “ [Antoine LeCompte] joined the British army and fought eleven years for the King of Great Britain and when the
wars were over his name was so great, and for his valor, had him knighted and the title of ‘ Monsieur ’ given to him, and his
coat of arms. ” — Thomas LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte, as dictated to Benjamin Woodward LeCompteDorchester
County, Maryland, 1819 | 1819 LeCompte Manuscript, Maryland Historical Society, Baltimore 4.2 — The Content and
Significance of the Manuscript The quotation above — dictated by Thomas and Daniel LeCompte in 1819 from memory
spanning five generations — is the primary source for Antoine LeCompte's military service and the claim of knighthood that
has been a central element of LeCompte family tradition since the family's colonial period. It is a remarkable document in
multiple respects, and it requires the same careful critical assessment that all genealogical sources deserve. The claim of
knighthood presents a specific interpretive challenge. A 2004 search by William Hunt, Windsor Herald at the College of Arms
in London, found no record of an English knighthood granted to Antoine LeCompte. This negative result does not
conclusively disprove the claim; the College of Arms records are extensive but not universally complete for the 17th century,
and a French Protestant soldier serving the English Crown in the period of the Huguenot alliance might have received a
French honor that was described by his descendants in English-language terms as a “knighthood.” The title “Monsieur” that
the Manuscript specifically mentions is itself a term of social honor in the French system — equivalent to the English “Sir” in
practical social use, though not in formal heraldic meaning. It is possible that what the family tradition preserved as a
“knighthood” was a French honorific, or a military commendation that carried social prestige without formal elevation to
English knighthood. The tradition of valor and military service is historically plausible given Antoine's documented Huguenot
military context. Beyond the knighthood question, the Manuscript's value as a genealogical source is extraordinary. It provides

the primary documentation for five or six generations of LeCompte family history that would otherwise rest on scattered
court records, land documents, and church registers — sources that are fragmentary and difficult to assemble into a
continuous family narrative. The Manuscript names children, traces marriages, identifies locations, and preserves family stories
that exist in no other documentary form. It is, in the truest sense of the word, irreplaceable. The Manuscript is held at the
Maryland Historical Society in Baltimore. The Society's library and manuscript collections are open to researchers by
appointment, and staff genealogists can assist in locating and interpreting the document. Transcriptions or photographs of the
Manuscript may also be available through the Dorchester County Public Library in Cambridge, Maryland, and through the
Maryland State Archives in Annapolis, which maintains extensive finding aids for Dorchester County genealogical sources.
Researchers wishing to verify specific details of the LeCompte family narrative against the Manuscript should contact the
Maryland Historical Society directly. The fact that a partial transcription or summary of the Manuscript has been incorporated
into published LeCompte genealogies — including works available through the Genealogical Publishing Company in
Baltimore and through the Maryland Historical Magazine — means that some of its content is accessible without a visit to
Baltimore. However, for the purposes of primary source genealogical research, a direct examination of the original document
is always preferable to transcriptions, which introduce the possibility of additional errors and omissions. 4.3 — Memory as a
Genealogical Medium The 1819 LeCompte Manuscript raises a question that extends beyond the LeCompte family to the
fundamental nature of genealogical knowledge: what is memory, as a medium for preserving the past, and what are its
capacities and limits when compared with documentary sources? The manuscript demonstrates, with extraordinary force, that
genealogical memory is not confined to paper. Thomas and Daniel LeCompte had never read a word. They had never
consulted a court record or a church register or a land deed. They had never held in their hands the naturalization document
of June 6, 1674, that formally recorded their ancestor Moses's transition to British subject status. They had never seen Antoine
LeCompte's land grant for “LeCompte's Desire” on Taylor's Island. And yet they preserved, in comprehensive and specific
detail, a family genealogy that covered five or six generations and reached back 164 years to a Huguenot soldier from Calais.
This is a demonstration of the human memory's capacity for structured preservation of information — a capacity that is far
greater than modern technological culture, which externalizes memory into devices and databases, tends to appreciate or
cultivate. Thomas and Daniel LeCompte, unable to externalize their family's history into documents, had internalized it
instead, with results that have proven historically invaluable. At the same time, oral genealogical tradition has limitations that
the researcher must recognize. Memory is reconstructive rather than reproductive: we do not store and retrieve the past like a
recording device; we store frameworks and narratives and fill in the gaps with what seems consistent and plausible. After five
generations, a family narrative that began as specific historical detail can become smoothed and improved — dates rounded to
convenient numbers, honorifics elevated from modest commendations to formal titles, geographical distances compressed,
relationships simplified for narrative coherence. The 1819 Manuscript should be read as a precious and substantially reliable
record of the LeCompte family's oral tradition — not as an infallible documentary source. Where it can be confirmed against
documentary evidence, it should be. Where it cannot, it should be preserved with appropriate qualifications. The two blind
brothers who dictated it did something extraordinary for their family and their family's descendants. Shane Goble, reading
their words in Jefferson, Ohio, two centuries later, is the direct beneficiary of their extraordinary gift. — 42 — Chapter Five ✦

Y I N H A B I T E D Historical Context, 1700–1850 The Events and Forces That Shaped the Goble and LeCompte Families
6.1 — The Colonial-to-Revolutionary Transformation (1700–1776) Kevin Goble, born July 12, 1700, in New Jersey, entered a
world that was recognizably a colonial order: British governance, mercantilist economy, established churches, and the
assumption that the relationship between colony and metropole would continue indefinitely. He died on March 29, 1783, in
Morristown — in the year that the Treaty of Paris formally ended the Revolutionary War and Britain acknowledged the
independence of the United States. The arc of his eighty-three years perfectly maps the arc of colonial America's
transformation into something entirely new. He was born a British subject and died a citizen of a republic. His son Caleb
fought for that transformation. Kevin himself may have seen it as the fulfillment of everything that colonial life had been
building toward: the extension of English liberties into their logical conclusion, the assertion of the rights of Englishmen
against a government that had forgotten its obligations to them. The colonial-to-Revolutionary transformation did not happen
overnight. It was the product of seven decades of accumulated grievance, institutional development, economic change, and
ideological ferment that made the generation of 1776 capable of imagining and executing a political revolution that had no
genuine precedent in the world they knew. The key events of the period, seen through the lens of the Goble family's Morris
County experience, form a narrative of escalating crisis: ● The Albany Plan of Union (1754): Benjamin Franklin's proposal for
a unified colonial government, presented at the Albany Congress, was rejected by both the colonial assemblies and the British
Crown. It was the first significant attempt to imagine the colonies as something other than separate dependencies of the
British Empire. Kevin Goble was fifty-four years old when Franklin proposed it; his son Daniel W. was approximately
nineteen; his future grandson Caleb had not yet been born. The Plan's failure was, in retrospect, the opening act of the long
drama that would end at Yorktown. ● The French and Indian War (1754–1763): Fought on the very frontiers that the Morris
County Goble family inhabited, this war transformed the colonial relationship with the British Crown in ways that made
eventual independence almost inevitable. The war proved that British regular army officers and the colonial militia forces did
not understand each other, respect each other, or operate effectively together. It imposed a massive financial burden on the
British government, leading directly to the parliamentary taxation schemes that would trigger the Revolution. And it opened
the trans-Appalachian west to colonial imagination — and then slammed that door with the Proclamation of 1763, an imperial
fiat that told American colonists they could not settle the lands their soldiers had just fought to win. ● The Stamp Act (1765):
Parliament's first direct tax on colonial Americans — a tax on paper goods, legal documents, and newspapers — triggered the

first coordinated colonial resistance. The Stamp Act Congress of 1765, the first intercolonial body to organize political
resistance to British policy, included representatives from New Jersey. Morristown's lawyers, merchants, and newspaper
publishers were among the New Jersey citizens most directly affected by the tax. Daniel W. Goble, Caleb's father, was
approximately thirty years old; Caleb himself was five. ● The Boston Massacre (March 5, 1770): The killing of five Boston
civilians by British soldiers transformed abstract political argument into visceral outrage. The news traveled within days
through every colonial newspaper network to Morris County and every other colonial community. Caleb Goble was ten years
old when the Massacre occurred. The generation that would fight the Revolution grew up with this event as a formative
political memory. ● The Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776): For the Goble family of Morristown, New Jersey, the
Declaration of Independence was not an abstraction — it was a statement that transformed their already ongoing military
service from rebellion into founding. Caleb Goble was sixteen years old, already enlisted in Captain Rice's Militia Company.
His family had been in America for 136 years by the time Jefferson's document was signed. They were not newcomers
asserting rights they barely understood; they were a family of fourth-generation Americans defending a way of life they had
built across three generations in New Jersey. The Declaration gave that defense a name and a purpose. ✦ Historical Context:
The French and Indian War and Morris County ✦ The French and Indian War (1754–1763) — the American theater of the
Seven Years' War — was fought partly on the Goble family's doorstep. French-allied Native American war parties, operating
from Canada and from the Ohio Country, conducted raids into northern New Jersey and New York in the war's early years.
The Morris County iron works became suppliers of military materiel. The county's militia companies were organized and
called up repeatedly during the war's seven-year duration. The war's most significant consequence for the Goble family was not
military but political: the British victory opened the trans-Appalachian west to colonial settlement — or appeared to, until the
Proclamation of 1763 closed it again. The resentment of New Jersey farm families who saw the western lands they had been
promised during wartime then denied to them in peacetime was a specific, material grievance that fed the broader colonial
anger against parliamentary authority in the decade before the Revolution. Morris County farmers like the Gobles understood,
in the most practical terms, that the British government was preventing them from getting the one thing a farm family most
needed: more land. Historical Image North America at the time of the French and Indian War, 1755. This map shows the
contested territory of the mid-Atlantic and Great Lakes region where British, French, and Native American forces fought for
control of the continent. Morris County, New Jersey — the Goble family home — sits within the British colonial zone on the
Atlantic seaboard, but the frontier of active conflict ran through Pennsylvania and New York, less than a hundred miles from
Morristown. The war's outcome opened the Ohio Valley — where Caleb Goble would eventually settle — to American
settlement. 6.2 — The Revolutionary War Era (1776–1783) No family in Shane Goble's genealogical record was more directly
and personally affected by the Revolutionary War than the Morris County Goble family. They did not experience the
Revolution as distant events reported in newspapers. They experienced it as a military occupation of their town, a series of
desperate battles fought on roads they knew by name, a hard winter that nearly killed the army camped three miles from their
farm, and the personal military service of a young man named Caleb who would spend six years — from age sixteen to
twenty-two — fighting for a country that did not yet fully exist. The key military events of the Revolution in the New Jersey
theater, seen from the Goble family's perspective in Morristown: ● The Battle of Trenton (December 26, 1776): Washington
crossed the Delaware River at McConkey's Ferry, approximately thirty miles south of Morristown, in the early hours of
December 26, 1776, and attacked the Hessian garrison at Trenton with complete surprise. The victory — the first significant
American military success since the disastrous summer campaigns — transformed the political and military situation
overnight. Caleb Goble was sixteen years old, already serving in Captain Rice's company. News of Washington's victory
arrived in Morristown within hours of the battle; the town that had watched the Continental Army retreat through New Jersey
in November now saw it turn and strike back. ● Washington's First Morristown Headquarters (January–May 1777): Following
Trenton and Princeton, Washington moved his army to Morristown for the winter of 1777. The Continental Army camped in
and around the town; Washington himself quartered at Arnold's Tavern on the town green. For the Goble family of

Morristown, this meant billeting soldiers, providing food and firewood, and living within the constant activity of a military
headquarters town. It also meant seeing, directly and personally, the men and the commanders who were making American
independence. ● The “Hard Winter” (December 1779–June 1780): Washington's second Morristown encampment was the
most severe military crisis of the entire Revolution that did not involve battlefield combat. Twenty-six blizzards struck New
Jersey in the winter of 1779–1780 — the worst winter in colonial American memory. Snowdrifts reached six feet. The
Continental Army at Jockey Hollow, three miles from Morristown, was on the verge of starvation. Soldiers ate their horses and
their boots and the bark of trees. Mutiny was averted twice, barely, by Washington's personal authority and the timely arrival of
some supplies. The civilian community of Morristown — including the Goble family — gave what they had to keep the army
alive. Caleb Goble was nineteen or twenty during this encampment, likely deployed on frontier duty with the Rangers rather
than at Jockey Hollow himself, but his family in Morristown lived through its full severity. ● The Battle of Yorktown (October
19, 1781): The surrender of Lord Cornwallis to Washington at Yorktown, Virginia, effectively ended the active military phase
of the Revolutionary War. Caleb Goble would have learned of the surrender while serving with the Frontier Rangers — still
operational because the frontier war did not end with Yorktown. When he finally mustered out with Captain Miller's company
in Washington County in 1782, he was a twenty-two-year-old veteran of six years of war who had outlasted most of the
conflict's central characters. A specific note on Caleb Goble's spy service in this context: when Caleb operated as a spy during
his year of intelligence work (within the 1778–1782 Ranger service period), he operated in a landscape that was simultaneously
his family's home territory and an actively contested military zone. The roads of Morris County and Washington County —
roads he had walked since childhood — were the highways of armies. The farms he passed were farms he may have known
from peacetime visits. The taverns where he gathered intelligence were taverns where his father and grandfather had drunk
cider and argued politics before the war. His local knowledge — his ability to move through this landscape as a native rather
than a stranger, to recognize people and be recognized, to know which road went where and which farm family was Loyalist
and which was Patriot — was precisely the intelligence asset that made him valuable as a spy. He was not a professional
intelligence operative parachuted into unfamiliar territory. He was a local man with a local man's comprehensive knowledge of
his own place, deployed by the patriot command to exploit that knowledge for the Republic's benefit. 6.3 — The New
Republic and Western Expansion (1783–1850) The sixty-seven years between the Treaty of Paris (1783) and the midpoint of
the nineteenth century (1850) were the formative years of the American republic — and the years in which the Goble family
completed its transformation from New Jersey colonial patriarchs to Ohio pioneer farmers. Every major event of this period
— the Northwest Ordinance, Ohio statehood, the War of 1812, the Erie Canal, the rise of abolitionism — directly touched
the world in which the Goble and LeCompte families lived. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 was the enabling legislation for
the Goble family's Ohio migration. Without it, the orderly survey and sale of Ohio lands — the legal mechanism by which
Caleb Goble and his contemporaries obtained land titles — would not have existed. The Ordinance's prohibition of slavery in
the Northwest Territory also defined the political character of Ohio for the next century: as a free state, Ohio attracted anti-
slavery settlers, supported anti-slavery politics, and became one of the most active nodes in the Underground Railroad
network that would help freedom seekers reach Canada across Lake Erie. Ohio Statehood on March 1, 1803 — the same day,
by a remarkable coincidence, as Caleb Goble's forty-third birthday — formalized the transition from territory to state that had
been underway since Caleb's arrival around 1798. The first Ohio constitution, adopted in 1802, established the legal and
governmental framework within which the Goble family would spend the rest of its Ohio decades. It was, by the standards of
the era, a broadly democratic document: broad suffrage for white male citizens, a strong legislature, restrictions on executive
power that reflected the Revolutionary generation's distrust of concentrated authority. The War of 1812 brought conflict back
to the Ohio frontier that Caleb Goble had been part of settling. British forces from Canada, allied with Native American
confederacies under the leadership of Tecumseh, threatened the Ohio Valley settlements in 1812 and 1813. The surrender of
Detroit to the British in August 1812 sent shock waves of fear through Ohio communities. The Battle of Lake Erie
(September 10, 1813), in which Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry's fleet defeated the British naval force on Lake Erie with the

immortal signal “We have met the enemy and they are ours,” was fought in the very waters that border the northeastern Ohio
county where Shane Goble's family is rooted. Ashtabula County, on the Lake Erie shore, was both threatened by British naval
activity and galvanized by Perry's victory. The War of 1812 demonstrated, in the most vivid possible terms, why the Ashtabula
County settlement that Shane's ancestors were joining was not simply a prosperous agricultural community but a frontier
community in the truest sense — a community on the edge of an international border, subject to the consequences of great-
power conflict, dependent on its own resources and courage. The Erie Canal (1825) transformed northeastern Ohio's
economic geography. Completed between Albany and Buffalo, the Canal connected the Great Lakes to the Atlantic seaboard,
making Lake Erie ports — including the Ashtabula harbor — into commercial gateways through which Ohio grain, lumber,
and manufactured goods flowed east and immigrant settlers and manufactured goods flowed west. Ashtabula County's
position on the Lake Erie shore, which had been a strategic vulnerability during the War of 1812, became an economic asset
of the first order after 1825. The Goble family's eventual settlement in Ashtabula County cannot be separated from the
economic transformation that the Erie Canal produced. ✦ Historical Context: The Underground Railroad in Ashtabula
County ✦ Ashtabula County, Ohio — home to Jefferson, Ohio, where Shane Goble's family is rooted — was one of the most
important and active nodes in the Underground Railroad network that operated from the 1830s through the Civil War. The
county's Lake Erie harbor provided a direct escape route to Canada — a boat crossing of less than sixty miles from the
Ashtabula port to the safety of the Canadian shore, beyond the reach of the Fugitive Slave Act and the slave catchers who
enforced it. The Western Reserve, the northeastern Ohio region of which Ashtabula County is a part, was settled primarily by
New England families who brought with them the strong Calvinist anti-slavery tradition that had deep roots in Puritan New
England theology. These were communities that did not need to be persuaded that slavery was wrong; they already knew it,
and they acted on that knowledge. Jefferson, Ohio, was the hometown of Representative Joshua Reed Giddings (1795– 1864),
one of the most fervent and courageous anti-slavery voices in the United States Congress. Giddings was elected to Congress
in 1838 — the same year that Caleb Goble died in Shelby County — and served continuously until 1859. In 1842, he was
formally censured by the House of Representatives for defending the right of enslaved people who had seized a slave ship (the
Creole case) to seek freedom. He immediately resigned, returned to Jefferson, and was re-elected by his Ashtabula County
constituents with a massive majority — one of the most extraordinary expressions of popular anti-slavery sentiment in pre-
Civil War America. The citizens of Jefferson, Ohio, did not censure Joshua Giddings for defending freedom seekers. They sent
him back to Congress to do it again. The Goble family's settlement in Ashtabula County placed them in one of the most
politically charged anti-slavery communities in the pre-Civil War United States. Whether members of the family participated
directly in Underground Railroad activity is not yet documented, but the community they joined was one where such
participation was the norm rather than the exception. Jefferson, Ohio, had more Underground Railroad stations per capita
than almost any other community in the state. Historical Image Map showing routes of the Underground Railroad, 1830–

Chapter Seven ✦ ✦ T H E E X T E N D E D L E C O M P T E L E G A C Y Notable Descendants in the Extended
LeCompte Line Congressional Service, Maryland Legacy, and the Family Bible's Journey 7.1 — Congressman Joseph
LeCompte: 19th-Century Political Achievement Among the most remarkable figures in the extended LeCompte family line is
Joseph LeCompte, who served as a United States Representative and embodied the family's journey from Huguenot refugee to
American political leader. His congressional service represents the highest level of formal political achievement reached by any
member of the extended LeCompte family in the nineteenth century — a fact that takes on additional meaning when viewed
against the family's origins as stateless religious refugees in 17th-century France. Joseph LeCompte's congressional career
placed him in the center of American political life during one of its most turbulent decades. The United States Congress of

the early 19th century was a body wrestling with the fundamental questions of the new republic: the balance of power
between the states and the federal government; the expansion of slavery into western territories; the development of national
economic policy; and the definition of American citizenship and rights in a nation that had declared all men equal while
practicing slavery. For a LeCompte to reach that body — the representative institution of the nation that his Huguenot
ancestors had crossed an ocean to find freedom in — was a trajectory that began with Antoine and Hester LeCompte's
desperate departure from France and ended, five generations later, in the halls of the United States Congress. The significance
of Congressman LeCompte's career for Shane Goble's family history lies not only in the individual achievement but in what it
demonstrates about the LeCompte family's arc in American life. Antoine and Hester arrived as refugees, stateless and
dispossessed. Moses, their son, was naturalized as a British subject in 1674. His descendants married into English colonial
families, adapted to the colonial social order, and gradually moved from the margins of the established community to its
center. By the time Joseph LeCompte reached Congress, the family had completed a transformation that required five
generations: from French Protestant refugee to American congressman, from the banks of the Choptank River to the
chambers of federal power. This is the American story at its most fundamental and most hopeful. 7.2 — The Extended
LeCompte Dynasty: A Maryland Legacy The full scope of the LeCompte family's impact on Maryland and American life is
visible only when the individual biographical chapters of this genealogical record are placed alongside each other and seen as a
single, continuous story. Antoine and Hester arrived in Maryland in 1655 — French Huguenots, military veterans, religious
refugees, with nothing but their name, their faith, their courage, and a specific claim to land on the Choptank River shore. By
1720, when Moses LeCompte died blind in Dorchester County, he had fathered eleven children. Those eleven children
married, had children of their own, and the multiplication began in earnest. By the middle of the 19th century, the LeCompte
name was documented across Maryland, Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, and beyond. The family tree that began with a single
immigrant couple had, through the arithmetic of generations and the fertility that frontier conditions both required and
rewarded, grown into a network of American families that touched every region of the developing nation. Families named
LeCompte appeared in antebellum census records from the Eastern Shore of Maryland to the frontier counties of Indiana.
The Huguenot name — the name that Antoine had carried from France, that Moses had carried through blindness, that
Thomas and Daniel had preserved in their memories for five generations — was by 1850 a recognizably American name,
appearing in the public records of a republic that its bearers had helped to build. The LeCompte Family Bible, passed from
eldest son to eldest son for three generations after Hugh LeCompte's custodianship, now displayed in Richmond, Virginia, is
the most tangible symbol of this extraordinary continuity. The Bible has outlasted everyone who has touched it. It has
survived the Revolution, the War of 1812, the Civil War, the long quiet decades of the American 19th century, and both World
Wars of the 20th. It is a physical object made of paper and leather and glue — materials not designed for permanence — that
has nonetheless persisted for more than two centuries, carrying in its handwritten front pages the births, marriages, and deaths
of people who are now dust but whose names survive in this document and in the descendants who trace their lines back to
the Choptank River shore. When Shane Goble reads the story of the LeCompte family, he is reading the story of that Bible's
journey — a journey that began in a Philadelphia print shop and is still, through this genealogical record, continuing. ✦ ✦ ✦

This volume is the first installment of a comprehensive four-volume genealogical masterwork assembled for Shane Goble of

Jefferson, Ashtabula County, Ohio. The complete series constitutes the most thorough and systematically documented account
of the Goble and LeCompte family lines ever compiled — tracing Shane's ancestry from the genetic dawn of Homo sapiens
through to the present day, across three continents, five centuries of documented records, and 275,000 years of human
prehistory. The Complete Four-Volume Series Volume I: Ancient Origins & Colonial Foundations (Pre-History through 1700)
Haplogroup origins, genetic prehistory, Neanderthal legacy, Thomas Goble in Massachusetts, Antoine LeCompte in Maryland,

Meaning The surname Goble carries two documented etymological traditions, both of which explain its geographic
concentration in southern England and its presence among craftsmen and merchants of the medieval period. The primary
etymology traces the name to Old French gobel — meaning "drinking vessel" or "cup." In medieval England, this was a
metonymic occupational surname: a name given to craftsmen who made goblets — skilled artisans in wood, pewter, silver, or
clay whose identity became so associated with their product that the product itself became their name. This is the same
naming convention that gave English surnames like "Smith," "Cooper" (barrel-maker), "Fletcher" (arrow-maker), and "Mason"
their origins. The secondary etymology traces the name to Old High German Godebert — a compound personal name
meaning "God-bright" — carried by Germanic settlers who arrived in England during the Anglo-Saxon period (450–1066 CE)
and whose patronymic descendants eventually anglicized the name through several generations of phonetic evolution. A third
strand connects to the Norman French variant Goupil — Old Norman for "fox" — a name documented in West Sussex
records as early as the 1400s, suggesting the Goble family may have arrived in England as part of the Norman Conquest of
1066 and slowly anglicized the name over generations, from Goupil to Gobel to Goble. This Norman connection would make
the family's presence in West Sussex not merely geographic coincidence but historical consequence: Normans settled heavily in
Sussex following the Conquest, and Westergate sits within that zone of Norman influence. [PROBABLE] Worth noting: the
Harvard College Treasurer's Records of 1653–1655 spell Thomas as "goodman goobell" and "old gobbell" — demonstrating

kings and had no patience for religious nonconformity. His Archbishop of Canterbury, William Laud (appointed 1633),
launched a systematic campaign to enforce religious uniformity in the Church of England. Puritans who refused to use
prescribed prayer books, who held unauthorized religious meetings, or who questioned episcopal church governance faced
fines, public humiliation, imprisonment, and in some cases mutilation. John Burton had his ears cut off. William Prynne had
his ears cropped, his cheeks branded. The message was unambiguous. For a man of conscience like Thomas Goble, England
in 1633 offered a stark choice: conform, suffer, or leave. He left. 3.2 The Atlantic Crossing — The Great Puritan Migration

(~1633–1634) Thomas Goble emigrated approximately 1633–1634, most likely aboard one of the ships regularly serving the
Massachusetts Bay Colony trade routes during those years. Three vessels made well-documented crossings in that period: the
Abigail, the Hopewell, and the Lion. The specific ship has not been identified in surviving passenger lists. [ESTIMATED]
With him: his wife Alice and their son John, then approximately 3 or 4 years old. Their daughter Elizabeth — born 1633/1634

the world somewhere between two continents, which is, in its way, a metaphor for everything the Goble family was becoming.
The Atlantic crossing in 1634 was a voyage of approximately six to twelve weeks, depending on winds and weather. Passengers
lived below decks in cramped, dark conditions, with limited food and water, surrounded by strangers and the constant risk of
storm. Disease — particularly dysentery, typhoid, and scurvy — claimed lives on every crossing. That Thomas, Alice, John,
and the newborn Elizabeth all survived speaks to their constitution and perhaps to fortune. ■ Historical Context — The Great
Puritan Migration (1629–1640) Approximately 20,000 English Puritans crossed the Atlantic to Massachusetts Bay Colony
between 1629 and 1640 — one of the largest voluntary migrations in early modern history. They were not, by and large, the
destitute or the desperate. They were merchants, craftsmen, ministers, lawyers, physicians, and yeoman farmers — skilled,
literate, property-holding people who had too much to give up and chose to give it up anyway, because the alternative was the
violation of conscience. They brought with them the English common law tradition, the deeply held belief in local governance
by consent, and the Calvinist conviction that they were building, in John Winthrop's phrase, "a city upon a hill" — a model of
godly community for a watching world. Thomas Goble was one of them. He was not an adventurer or a fortune-seeker. He
was a believer, crossing an ocean for the right to worship as he understood God required. 3.3 Life in Colonial Charlestown

lineage to Magna Carta (1215) and the centuries of common law tradition the Puritan settlers carried across the Atlantic in

their minds and in their chests of books. But in 1634, Massachusetts Bay Colony was still building its legal infrastructure from
scratch. Courts existed, but formal jury mechanisms were still being established. The first formally convened Boston jury
(October 1640) represents a milestone in the colony's legal maturation — the moment it moved from improvised justice to
institutionalized jurisprudence. That Thomas Goble was among the twelve men selected speaks to his standing in the
community: only freemen of established good character and community trust were chosen. This is not a footnote in family
history. It is an act of legal founding — one man among twelve who built, brick by procedural brick, the legal culture that
would eventually become American constitutional democracy. Harvard College Connections (1653–1655) In the Harvard
College Treasurer's Records for 1653 and 1655, entries appear for tuition payments recorded as "goodman goobell" (1653) and

Harvard College. [VERIFIED: Harvard College Treasurer's Records, 1653– 1655, Harvard University Archives] Harvard
College was founded in 1636 — just two years after Thomas arrived in Massachusetts. To have a son at Harvard by the 1650s,
a generation after his arrival, was an extraordinary testament to the family's ambition, resources, and standing. The Puritan
migrants had come to build a godly civilization, and for Thomas Goble, that civilization included one of his children in the
colony's premier institution of higher learning. The phonetic spellings — "goobell," "gobbell" — are charming evidence of
the fluid orthography of the era. Spelling in 17th-century New England was largely phonetic; scribes wrote what they heard.
The man who had built seventy acres of Massachusetts estate out of nothing was recorded in the ledgers of the colony's
greatest institution by the sound of his name, written by someone who had perhaps only ever heard it spoken. ✦ ✦ ✦ 3.4
Relocation and Death At some point in the 1640s or early 1650s, Thomas and Alice relocated from Charlestown to Concord,
Middlesex County, Massachusetts — following the characteristic pattern of established settlers moving inland as the
Massachusetts frontier expanded and land in the coastal settlements became more expensive and crowded. Thomas Goble
died on December 30, 1657, in Middlesex County, Massachusetts, at approximately age 66 or 67. His will was probated in
Middlesex County. [VERIFIED: Middlesex County, Massachusetts, Probate Records, December 30, 1657] The estate inventory
is a tender catalogue of a life fully lived: one featherbed, two feather pillows, wool blankets, iron pots, earthenware,
woodworking tools, farm implements, livestock, and a small amount of currency. It is the inventory of a working farmer and
craftsman of modest but real means — a man who had built, maintained, and now bequeathed a life. His will included this
provision, as recorded in the probate document: "I give and bequeath to Alice my wife fair profit on all my stock so long as
she liveth a widow." He was thinking of her, at the end, the way you think of someone you have crossed an ocean with. ✦ ✦

Creative Reconstruction The air smells different here. I have been on this shore four weeks now, perhaps five, and still I
cannot name the difference — only that it is not the Channel salt I grew up breathing at Westergate, not the wet chalk and
meadow grass of Sussex. This air is heavier, greener, full of tree-smell from the forests that begin where the settlement ends.
They go on, those forests. I do not yet know how far. This morning, September 3, I stood before the General Court and they
read my name aloud and gave me the franchise of a free man in this Colony. A voter. A juror. A man with a lawful voice in the
making of this place. I said nothing — there was nothing to say; it is not the custom to make speeches in such circumstances
— but I felt it move through me, the weight of it. In England I was a man who had to watch what he said in church, who had
to hold his tongue about the Prayer Book, who had to keep his conscience quiet as a church mouse lest Laud's men find a
reason to make an example. And here, four days after Alice and I were admitted to the church — here they give me a vote.
Alice is well. The baby — Elizabeth, we have named her, though some say she came into the world before we quite reached
shore, and others say after — the baby is well. John has taken to this place with the easy confidence of a child who does not
yet understand what has been left behind. He runs between the houses. He knows every dog in the settlement by name. I think
of my father's fields at Westergate. I think of the church at Aldingbourne, the Norman flint, the smell of old stone in summer.
I think of Alice Brookman on our wedding day fifteen years ago, and what she could not have known she was agreeing to. But
I am free here. Whatever this forest holds, whatever this winter brings — and they tell me the winters are merciless, and I
believe them — I am free here in the way I was not free there. That is worth an ocean. I believe that. I have to believe it. I have

H A P T E R F O U R The LeCompte Surname: Norman Nobility, Huguenot Faith, and French Heritage 4.1 Etymology and
Meaning The surname LeCompte derives from Old French le comte — literally "the count" or "the earl." In the lexicon of
medieval French society, this designation carried one of two meanings: it signified either actual descent from a member of the
comtes — the French nobility of comital rank, one step below a duke in the feudal hierarchy — or service in the household of
such a count, where a le comte or le comte's man might carry the lord's name as an occupational identifier. The earliest
documentary record of the name is striking. "Johannes le Comte" appears in the Cartulaire de l'abbaye de Jumièges — a 13th-
century manuscript from the Benedictine abbey of Jumièges, Normandy, France. The abbey of Jumièges was one of the great
ecclesiastical institutions of Normandy, founded in the 7th century and rebuilt after Viking raids by the Normans themselves.
That the LeCompte name appears in its records places the family within the documented social and geographic world of
Norman medieval France. [VERIFIED: published in J.J. Vernier, ed., Chartes de l'abbaye de Jumièges, Rouen, 1916] The name
was particularly prevalent in Normandy and Picardy — the two northern French provinces most closely associated with the
Norman heritage, and the region from which Antoine LeCompte would emerge in the early 17th century. The LeCompte
family is registered in the U.S. National Huguenot Society's register of qualified Huguenot ancestors — a formal genealogical
recognition of the family's documented Huguenot heritage and their emigration to America as religious refugees. [VERIFIED:
Huguenot Society of America, hsofamerica.org] [IMAGE PLACEHOLDER: Heraldic coat of arms associated with the

LeCompte family. Secondary image: Historical map of Normandy and Picardy showing the geographic heartland of the
LeCompte name, including the location of the Abbey of Jumièges on the Seine.] ✦ ✦ ✦ 4.2 The Huguenot Heritage —
Faith, Persecution, and Refuge To understand Antoine LeCompte, you must understand what it meant to be a Huguenot in
17th-century France. The word "Huguenot" — whose etymology is disputed, possibly deriving from the Swiss German
Eidgenosse (confederate) or from the name "Hugues" — designated French Protestants who followed the Reformed
(Calvinist) tradition. In a deeply Catholic France, they were a perpetual minority, alternately tolerated, persecuted, massacred,
and expelled across more than a century of religious warfare. The major events of that century are inseparable from the story
of the LeCompte family: ● The French Wars of Religion (1562–1598): Eight separate civil wars convulsed France across
thirty-six years. Estimated total dead: three million people — from battle, massacre, disease, and famine directly caused by
religious conflict. The wars defined the France that the LeCompte family lived in. ● The Massacre of Vassy (March 1, 1562):
On a Sunday morning, the Duke of Guise and his men attacked a congregation of approximately 500 Huguenots worshipping
in a barn in Vassy, Champagne. Sixty Huguenots were killed and over 200 wounded. The event triggered the First War of
Religion and established the pattern of anti-Huguenot violence that would recur for a century. ● The St. Bartholomew's Day
Massacre (August 23–24, 1572): In Paris and across France, Huguenot nobles and their households were systematically
slaughtered by Catholic mobs and royal troops. Estimates of total deaths range from 10,000 to 30,000. It was one of the most
catastrophic episodes of religious violence in Western European history. The news of it caused Protestant Europe to recoil in
horror. ● The Edict of Nantes (1598): King Henry IV — himself a former Huguenot who converted to Catholicism to secure
the throne — granted Huguenots a fragile legal tolerance: the right to worship in specified locations, to maintain certain
fortified cities, and to hold certain public offices. It was a peace of exhaustion rather than conviction. ● The Fall of La
Rochelle (October 28, 1628): Cardinal Richelieu besieged the great Huguenot fortress-city of La Rochelle for fourteen months.
When it fell, the Huguenots lost their last fortified strongholds and with them their political autonomy. Religious toleration
continued on paper, but the community's capacity for self-defense was destroyed. Antoine LeCompte was approximately eight
years old. ● The Edict of Fontainebleau (October 18, 1685): Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes entirely. Huguenot
churches were demolished, schools closed, pastors expelled, and Huguenot children ordered baptized Catholic. The result: the
Réfugié — an exodus of 200,000 to 400,000 Huguenots from France, scattering across England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia,
South Africa, and America. Antoine had already left by this point, but the world that drove him out culminated in this
catastrophe. ■ Historical Context — The Huguenot Exodus and Its Legacy The Huguenots who fled France were not, by and
large, the poor or the marginalized. They were skilled artisans, merchants, physicians, lawyers, military officers, scientists, and
intellectuals — the productive middle and upper-middle classes of French society. Their departure impoverished France and
dramatically enriched every nation that received them. In South Carolina, Huguenot refugees established rice plantations and
helped build one of the most prosperous colonial economies in North America. In New York, they brought textile and
merchant trade. In Prussia, Frederick the Great welcomed them precisely for their skills and industry. In Maryland — where
Antoine LeCompte arrived around 1655, before the great exodus but as part of its early wave — they joined a colony
specifically designed on a principle of religious tolerance. The Huguenot diaspora was, in modern terms, a refugee crisis of the
first order — one whose long-term consequence was the enrichment of the world beyond France and the permanent
weakening of France itself. Antoine LeCompte was one of its earliest American representatives. ✦ ✦ ✦ 4.3 LeCompte Name

of Calais, Picardie (Picardy), France. [PROBABLE: based on family records and genealogical documentation] The choice of
Calais as his birthplace was not accidental in the larger historical sense — it was consequential. Calais sits at the narrowest
point of the English Channel, where France and England are separated by only twenty-one miles of water. It is a city that had
been under English control from 1347 to 1558 — a period of 211 years, ending just sixty-two years before Antoine's birth.
Within the living memory of many Calais residents in 1620, the city had been English. It remained a place of extraordinary

cultural mixing: French, Flemish, English, and Spanish communities intersected in its markets, its docks, its churches, and its
streets. For a Huguenot family of Norman or near-Norman origin, Calais represented both danger — as a French city where
Protestantism was increasingly persecuted — and opportunity: a gateway city with direct commercial and cultural connections
to England, across the water that Antoine would eventually cross for good. Antoine's family background suggests connections
to either French Protestant nobility or the Anglo-French merchant and military world that flourished in Calais's borderland
culture. The 1819 LeCompte Manuscript's account of his military valor and subsequent knighthood — even if the specifics
are difficult to verify through English heralds — is consistent with a man of means and martial training from a distinguished
family. 5.2 Military Service in King Charles I's English Army Antoine LeCompte served approximately eleven years in King
Charles I's English Army, entering service during the turbulent 1640s. [VERIFIED: LeCompte Family Manuscript, 1819] This
was one of the most chaotic decades in British history. The English Civil War (1642–1651) pitted Royalists (supporting King
Charles I) against Parliamentarians (supporting Parliament). As a Protestant Huguenot from a noble or near-noble French
family, Antoine's alignment with the Royalist cause was comprehensible: Charles I, despite his conflicts with English Puritans,
represented legitimate monarchical authority, the kind of rule that offered some protection to Continental Protestant families
with military traditions. On January 30, 1649, Charles I was executed by order of Parliament — an event that shocked all of
monarchical Europe. For Antoine, it meant the end of his service. A royalist soldier in Cromwell's Commonwealth England
had no future. He chose, as Thomas Goble had chosen fifteen years earlier and for different reasons, to leave England behind.
The 1819 Manuscript records the family tradition: "joined the British army and fought eleven years for the King of Great
Britain and when the wars were over his name was so great, and for his valor, had him knighted and the title of 'Monsieur'
given to him, and his coat of arms." In 2004, William Hunt, Windsor Herald at the College of Arms in London, conducted a
search of English heraldic records and found no record of an English knighthood for Antoine LeCompte. The scholarly
consensus is that the arms were almost certainly French noble arms carried from the continent — a family inheritance rather
than an English award — and that the tradition of military valor is historically plausible even if the specific honor may have
been embellished or misremembered across five generations of oral transmission before the 1819 Manuscript was dictated.
[PROBABLE] 5.3 Maryland — Arrival and Early Settlement (~1655– 1659) Antoine arrived in Maryland approximately 1655
— among the earliest European settlers of that colony. Maryland was only twenty-one years old as an English colony when he
arrived. Its defining legal characteristic was the Maryland Toleration Act of 1649, which granted religious freedom to all
Trinitarian Christians — Catholic and Protestant alike. For a Huguenot Protestant who had just spent eleven years serving a
Catholic-sympathizing English king and found himself stateless in its aftermath, Maryland's promise of religious tolerance
made it the natural destination. [VERIFIED] His earliest documented Maryland records: ● February 7, 1655: Antoine assigned
his right to two hundred acres to Ishmael Wright — an early land transaction evidencing his presence in the colony and his
active participation in the headright land system from his first year. [VERIFIED] ● 1657: Calvert County charged Antoine

three hundred pounds of tobacco for killing three wolves. The colonial wolf bounty was a practical mechanism for frontier
settlement: colonists were incentivized to eliminate predators threatening their livestock. That Antoine collected a substantial
bounty suggests he was ranging widely through the Maryland wilderness, comfortable in the frontier environment, and actively
engaged in the work of colonial agriculture. [VERIFIED] 5.4 The "St. Antoine" Land Grant — January 17, 1659 On January
17, 1659, Antoine LeCompte secured one of the defining achievements of his American life: an 800-acre land parcel through
the headright system. [VERIFIED: Maryland State Archives, Land Office Records, MSA S 11] The headright system awarded
land to colonists who paid the transportation costs of other individuals immigrating to Maryland. Antoine paid the passage of
three individuals: Thomas Raymond, Barbara Crouch, and Thomas Jones. In return, he received rights to 800 acres. The parcel
was formally surveyed on August 13, 1659, and the grant was named "St. Antoine" — also recorded in various documents as
"Antonine" and "St. Anthonia." Located in Dorchester County, Maryland, on the Choptank River, flowing into the
Chesapeake Bay. Eight hundred acres. Named for himself. It was an act of self-naming, of permanence, of declaration.
Antoine LeCompte had arrived in America with nothing but his military training, his French noble heritage, and his Protestant
faith. He was leaving an 800-acre mark on the map of Maryland with his name on it. In 1659, that was an extraordinary
statement. 5.5 Marriage to Hester Dottando — London, July 11, 1661 Following his land grant, Antoine returned to Europe,
where he met and married Hester (Esther) Dottando. Hester was born in Dieppe, Normandy, France — another Norman,
another French Protestant. They were married in London on July 11, 1661, recorded in London parish registers. [VERIFIED:

Calais, a Huguenot woman from Dieppe, meeting in London, which had become a haven for French Protestant refugees —
and then sailing together to build a life on the banks of the Choptank River in Maryland. Two French Protestants, two
Normans, two refugees, beginning again in a new world. Then they sailed for America. ✦ ✦ ✦ 5.6 Life on Taylor's Island —
Planter, Merchant, and Justice The LeCompte household was established in Dorchester County, Maryland, on Taylor's Island,
on the shores of the Choptank River — a tidal river of the Chesapeake Bay watershed, its banks low and marshy, its waters full
of crab and oyster, its forests dense with white oak and loblolly pine. Antoine worked simultaneously as a planter (cultivating
tobacco and corn, the twin economies of the Maryland Chesapeake) and as a merchant, trading up and down the Choptank
River and out into the broader Chesapeake Bay economy. The plantation was fortified — this was still a frontier. History of
Dorchester County (Elias Jones, 1902) records that when hostile Native American bands approached the LeCompte
settlement, Antoine "would disperse them by firing his large guns, and it is said, killed some of them." He had kept his
cannons from his years of military service, and he used them. The man had not left his military training behind at the Channel.
He was not merely a planter and soldier, however. From 1669 to 1671, Antoine served as Justice of Dorchester County — a
formal civic role requiring the adjudication of local disputes, the administration of oaths, and the enforcement of colonial law.
It is the exact equivalent, in civic terms, of Thomas Goble's jury service in Boston three decades earlier: both men, in their
respective colonies, chose public service as an expression of their investment in the societies they were building. [IMAGE

Antoine because I needed something in this country to be named after me, to prove I had actually arrived. She walked off the
ship and looked at the flat marshes and the low sky and the enormous American trees and she said nothing for a long
moment, and then she said: "We will need more beds." I laughed. I could have wept. I laughed. Last week there were men at
the tree line again — the same men who came in the autumn, watching. I do not know their nation or their intentions. I fired
the gun. Not at them. Above them, into the canopy. The sound rolls across the marsh for what seems like minutes. They were
gone by the time it stopped echoing. I am not a man who fires at people he does not know. But I will not be taken unaware on
my own land. I know what it is to be driven from a place. I will not be driven from this one. The land is called St. Antoine and
someday, God willing, it will be called by other names — the names my children carry, the names my children's children will
give to their own parcels carved from this country's incomprehensible space. I think of the Huguenot families I knew in
London, in Calais, scattered now across every Protestant corner of the world. I think of France, which I will not see again. I
think of the army, of the King whose cause we lost, of the years in England that led nowhere except here. Here is not
nowhere. I have eight hundred acres and a wife from Dieppe and the river breathing in the dark. Here will have to be enough.

the towns and then be pushed back in turn. He died in 1676, at the approximate age of 35 or 36. [VERIFIED] The date of his
death — 1676 — is haunting in its context. King Philip's War (June 1675 – August 1676) was one of the most catastrophic
conflicts in American colonial history: a war between the English settlements of Massachusetts and the Wampanoag
confederation and their allies, which killed approximately 600 English soldiers and militia, destroyed twelve English towns, and
killed or displaced thousands of Native Americans. It nearly destroyed the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Whether Daniel's death
was connected to this conflict is not documented in surviving records — but the timing is inescapable. He died in the year the
war ended. [ESTIMATED connection to King Philip's War; death date is VERIFIED] Daniel's lasting legacy was his son:
Daniel Goble Jr., born approximately 1669, who would carry the family name southward and eventually westward — through
New Jersey, through Pennsylvania, toward Ohio. ■ Historical Context — King Philip's War (1675–1676) King Philip's War was
named for Metacom, the Wampanoag leader the English called "King Philip." It began in June 1675 after the execution of
three Wampanoag men for the murder of a Christian Native American. By the war's end in August 1676, an estimated 5,000
Native Americans had died in battle or from disease and starvation, and thousands more were sold into slavery. For the
English colonists of Massachusetts, it was a trauma of the first order. Fifty-two colonial towns were attacked; twelve
destroyed. The colony's prosperity was set back by a generation. For a young colonial man of fighting age in 1675–1676, the
war was impossible to avoid. Daniel Goble lived and died in its shadow. ✦ ✦ ✦ 6.2 Moses LeCompte (Maryland – 1720)
Moses LeCompte, son of Antoine and Hester, was born in Maryland and was naturalized as a British subject on June 6, 1674,

Manuscript: A Rare Genealogical Treasure 7.1 The Document and Its Origins In the year 1819, in Dorchester County,
Maryland, one of the most remarkable acts of genealogical preservation in American family history took place. Two elderly
men — Thomas LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte, fourth-generation descendants of Antoine and Hester LeCompte — sat
down with Benjamin Woodward LeCompte and began to speak. What they spoke was the entire genealogy of the LeCompte
family. Names. Dates. Relationships. Family branches. Marriages. Deaths. The trajectories of children and grandchildren and
great-grandchildren across two centuries of American colonial and early national life. They knew all of it. And they dictated it,
from pure memory, to Benjamin Woodward LeCompte, who wrote it down. The result is what genealogists and historians now
call the 1819 LeCompte Manuscript — a comprehensive oral history of all known descendants of Antoine and Hester
LeCompte, covering at least four generations and documenting dozens of family members across Maryland and beyond.
[VERIFIED: LeCompte Family Manuscript, 1819, Maryland Historical Society, Baltimore] The manuscript is held by the
Maryland Historical Society in Baltimore. Transcription copies may be consulted at the Dorchester County Public Library
(Cambridge, Maryland) and the Maryland State Archives, Annapolis. 7.2 The Blind Brothers and Their Memorial Here is the
detail that transforms this document from a remarkable genealogical record into something genuinely extraordinary: Thomas
LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte were both blind. They could not read a single word of the document they were creating.
They could not see the paper on which their words were being recorded. They could not verify what Benjamin Woodward
LeCompte was writing, could not check a date against a document, could not read a Bible record or a county courthouse file.
They had only one resource: memory. And in that memory, they carried — between them, across their combined decades of
living — the entire genealogy of the LeCompte family of Dorchester County, Maryland, going back to a Frenchman from
Calais who had arrived on the Choptank River approximately 165 years before they were born. The 1819 Manuscript includes
this direct quotation regarding Antoine LeCompte, preserved exactly as the brothers dictated it: "joined the British army and
fought eleven years for the King of Great Britain and when the wars were over his name was so great, and for his valor, had
him knighted and the title of 'Monsieur' given to him, and his coat of arms." — Thomas LeCompte and Daniel LeCompte, as
dictated to Benjamin Woodward LeCompte, 1819 Consider the scene in full. Two elderly men, blind, seated perhaps near a
window through which they cannot see the Maryland light — the same low tidal-marsh light that their ancestor Antoine had
stood in, at the Choptank River's edge, firing his cannon at the tree line 157 years before. Their voices low and steady. Their
hands perhaps in their laps, or resting on the arms of chairs, still. They unspool a genealogy that begins in Calais, in the age of
Richelieu and Cardinal Mazarin and the English Channel at its narrowest, and arrives here, in this room, in the mouths of two
men who cannot see the paper on which their words are being written. It is an act of extraordinary fidelity to family and to
memory. It is an act of love for people they have never met — the future descendants who will need this record, who will
arrive in some century not yet imaginable and want to know where they came from. They were right. We arrived. And we
needed it. ■ Historical Context — Oral Genealogy and the Preservation of Family Memory Before the era of mass printing,
systematic civil registration, and widespread literacy, family history was preserved almost entirely through oral transmission —
through the deliberate act of telling and retelling, across generations, the names and stories of those who came before. This
was the primary genealogical technology of virtually all human societies for most of human history. The 1819 LeCompte
Manuscript is a rare surviving example of the transition between oral genealogy and written documentation: two men from the
oral tradition, recognizing that the chain of living memory was about to break, taking steps to preserve it in a form that could
outlast them. In its way, it is as precious a document as a 13th-century Norman charter — because it preserves what no charter
could: the human texture of the family, the stories passed down by firelight and at kitchen tables, the tradition of a soldier's
valor that traveled four generations by word of mouth before it was finally written down. ✦ ✦ ✦ Page 45 C H A P T E R E I

Hostages — R1b Paternal Haplogroup Connection Shane's paternal haplogroup R-Z198 belongs to the broader R1b-L21
family that is the most common Y-chromosome haplogroup in the British Isles and Ireland. Within this family, the most
historically famous Y-chromosome belongs to Niall of the Nine Hostages — the legendary High King of Ireland, who ruled
approximately 379–405 CE. Niall's Y-chromosome haplogroup signature belongs to the same deep Bronze Age R1b ancestral
family as Shane's R-Z198. A landmark 2006 study by Moore, McEvoy, Cape, Simms, and Bradley, published in the American
Journal of Human Genetics, identified a distinctive Y-chromosome signature present in approximately 3 million men
worldwide — in Ireland alone, approximately 1 in 12 men (over 21% of all Irish males) carries this signature, making it one of
the most successful Y-chromosome lineages in human history. [VERIFIED: Moore et al., American Journal of Human
Genetics 78(2), 334–338, 2006] Shane and Niall of the Nine Hostages share a common paternal ancestor — not a direct
descent, but a divergence from the same Bronze Age R1b trunk, in the mists of prehistoric Northwestern Europe,
approximately 2,000 to 3,000 years ago. They are, in the language of population genetics, ancient Y-chromosome cousins —
their lines branching from the same Bronze Age warrior population that spread R1b across the British Isles. ✦ ✦ ✦ 9.2
Cheddar Man — U5b Maternal Haplogroup Connection As documented in Chapter 1, Shane's maternal haplogroup U5b2c
places his direct maternal line within the same ancient haplogroup family as Cheddar Man — a Mesolithic human skeleton
discovered in Gough's Cave, Cheddar Gorge, Somerset, England, dated to approximately 7,150 BCE. In 1997, Oxford
University scientists extracted mitochondrial DNA from Cheddar Man's molar and confirmed haplogroup U5b. They then
identified a living Cheddar resident — Adrian Targett, a secondary school history teacher — as Cheddar Man's direct
maternal-line descendant: an unbroken chain of mother-to-daughter transmission across approximately 300 generations and
9,000 years. In 2018, the Natural History Museum, London, completed a full ancient genome sequencing of Cheddar Man
(Brace et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2019). The results confirmed haplogroup U5b and produced a striking facial
reconstruction: medium-to-dark brown skin, dark curly hair, and blue or green eyes. He was a Mesolithic hunter-gatherer of
the ancient type that populated post-glacial Britain — nothing like the fair-skinned ancient Briton of popular imagination, and
everything like the actual genetic history of the island. [VERIFIED: Brace et al., 2019] Shane Goble's maternal line connects,
across 9,150 years of unbroken transmission, to the same ancient family as this man — one of the earliest modern human
inhabitants of the British Isles. It is among the most striking genealogical connections revealed by his genetic results. [IMAGE
