By the middle of the nineteenth century, two ancient streams of American family history were converging upon the broad
interior plains and lake-carved valleys of Ohio — converging not by design, not by any conscious plan, but by the irresistible
pressure of time, geography, and the great westward momentum that has always been the defining force of American life. One
stream ran cold and clear from the stony coast of Massachusetts, carrying with it the austere faith of English Puritans who had
crossed a gray ocean to build a city upon a hill. The other ran warm and amber from the tidal shores of the Chesapeake, heavy
with the memory of French Huguenots who had crossed an even older Europe to escape the fury of kings. They were

different waters. But they were flowing toward the same Ohio ground. The Goble line — tracing its American origin to
Thomas Goble of colonial Charlestown, Massachusetts, who received his freedom as a full citizen of the Massachusetts Bay
Colony in 1634 — had moved, as English Puritan families habitually did, in a slow and relentless westward procession across
the American landscape. From Charlestown to Middlesex County; from Massachusetts to New Jersey, where the family planted
deep roots in the colonial period; from New Jersey through the mountain gaps and river crossings of the frontier into Ohio's
fertile river valleys during the early years of the new republic. They were, by the mid-nineteenth century, thoroughly Ohioan
— married into Irish and German and Dutch families, farming the black soil of Butler and Champaign Counties, pushing
further north toward the lake, entirely at home in a state that had not existed when their grandfather's grandfather was born.
They carried, in their blood, the ancient R-Z198 haplogroup — the genetic signature of Bell Beaker warriors who had swept
into Britain four thousand years before Thomas Goble's birth — but they would not know this for another two centuries.
They knew only Ohio. They knew the particular smell of turned earth in spring, the sound of the Miami River in flood, the
names of their neighbors, the dates of their marriages in the county courthouse record books. The LeCompte line —
descending from Antoine LeCompte, the Huguenot soldier from Calais who planted his flag and his name on the Choptank
River of Maryland in 1659 — had followed a different path, though one equally driven by the conviction that the frontier held
promise that the settled East had exhausted. For two full centuries, the LeComptes had been a Maryland family — planting
tobacco, serving as county justices, filling the tidewater landscape with their name, their Bibles, their children, and their graves.
But the tremors of the Civil War, the disruption of the border-state society that had been their world, and the pull of Ohio's
growing industrial economy set the family in motion. By the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, a branch of the
LeCompte line had crossed from the Eastern Shore of Maryland into Ohio — carrying with them the French Huguenot
Protestant tradition that had survived two centuries of Atlantic crossings, frontier hardship, and the violence of American
history. In this volume — the third of four — we trace that convergence in its final, decisive phase. We follow the Ohio Goble
families who populated Butler, Champaign, Athens, and eventually Ashtabula Counties across the early-tomid nineteenth
century. We examine the crucible of the Civil War, which tested every Ohio family without exception and shaped the
communities into which Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte would eventually be born. We trace the LeCompte line through its
final Maryland generations and its migration into Ohio, paying careful attention to the remarkable figures — the Francis
Asbury LeCompte who bore the name of Methodism's American founder, the Francis Layton Foxwell LeCompte whose
triple-barreled name encoded a whole social world, the long-lived Benjamin Berry LeCompte Sr. who may have bridged the
Reconstruction era and the late twentieth century in a single remarkable life. And we arrive, finally, at the moment that gives
this volume its central meaning: the marriage of Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte — Shane's paternal grandparents — in mid-
twentieth-century Ohio, the meeting point of two ancient American lines whose roots reach back, independently, to the same
decade of the 1620s, when one English Puritan was preparing to cross the Atlantic and one French Huguenot was preparing
to survive. There is something worth pausing over in that coincidence of origins. Thomas Goble and Antoine LeCompte were
contemporaries. They were born within a generation of each other — one in West Sussex, England, around 1590; one in
Calais, France, around 1620. Both were Protestant men from persecuted minorities, driven by conviction and by danger to seek
a new world. Both crossed oceans. Both planted families in American soil in the 1650s. Both became patriarchs of lines that
would survive and expand across three and a half centuries of American history — lines that would eventually, by a
convergence no one planned or predicted, join in an Ohio marriage and produce a man named Shane Goble, born in 1993,
living in Jefferson, Ashtabula County, Ohio, who has commissioned this record to understand from where, and from whom,
he comes. That is the deepest purpose of genealogical research: not merely to compile names and dates, though names and
dates are the essential foundation, but to recover the full human weight of the lives that made your life possible — the
crossings and the hardships, the marriages and the children, the wars survived and the frontier cleared, the faith maintained
across generations of testing, and the love that is carried forward, silently, in the very fact of your existence. This volume is
offered to Shane Goble as a record of that weight, and as an act of gratitude toward the people who bore it. — — ✦ ✦ ✦ C

H A P T E R O N E Ohio: The Promised Land 1803 – 1860 1.1 The Northwest Territory and Ohio Statehood The story of
Ohio begins, constitutionally and legally, with one of the most consequential legislative acts in American history. The
Northwest Ordinance of 1787 — passed by the Confederation Congress while the Constitutional Convention was still
meeting in Philadelphia — established the legal framework for the organization and eventual statehood of the territory lying
north and west of the Ohio River. It did three things of permanent importance: it prohibited slavery throughout the territory,
guaranteeing that the states carved from it would enter the Union as free states; it guaranteed religious freedom and the right
to trial by jury for all settlers; and it established the mechanism by which territories could progress, in an orderly and
democratic fashion, toward full statehood. It was, in its way, as important as the Constitution itself — and it shaped the Ohio
that the Goble and LeCompte families would eventually make their home. Ohio became the seventeenth state of the Union on
March 1, 1803 — an event that, in retrospect, seems almost inevitable, but that required thirty years of extraordinary effort,
conflict, and human endurance to achieve. The territory had been, within living memory, a wilderness known primarily to
Native nations — the Shawnee, the Delaware, the Miami, the Wyandot — who had inhabited these lands for centuries and
who resisted displacement with fierce determination. The conflicts of the 1790s, culminating in General Anthony Wayne's
victory at the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794) and the subsequent Treaty of Greenville (1795), opened the Ohio country to
large-scale EuroAmerican settlement. Within a decade, the population surge was remarkable: by 1810, Ohio counted more
than 230,000 residents; by 1820, that number had more than doubled to 581,000; by 1830, it had nearly doubled again to
937,000; and by 1850, Ohio's population exceeded 1.9 million people — making it one of the most populous and
economically significant states in the entire nation. The men and women who poured into Ohio during these decades came
from every direction and from every background. They came from New England — the Connecticut families of the Western
Reserve who brought their town- meeting culture, their white-steepled churches, and their passionate Calvinist conviction to
the northeastern corner of the new state. They came from the middle states — New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Delaware
— bringing with them the diverse Protestant traditions and the commercial energies of the coastal cities. They came from
Virginia and Kentucky, crossing the Ohio River at Wheeling, at Marietta, at Cincinnati, carrying the Southern agricultural
traditions and, in too many cases, the institution of slavery that the Northwest Ordinance had banned but could not entirely
prevent from casting its shadow across the river. And they came from Europe — Germans fleeing the failed revolutions of
1830 and 1848, Irish fleeing the famine of the 1840s, Welsh miners and English craftsmen — transforming Ohio from an
Anglo-American frontier into one of the most ethnically diverse societies on the continent. Historical Context Sidebar Ohio as
the Great Convergence Point: Settlement Routes and the Making of a State Ohio in the early nineteenth century was the
destination for families arriving from every compass point, and its geography made it uniquely suited to receive them. From
New England came the Western Reserve settlers who populated the state's northeastern corner — including Ashtabula
County, where Shane Goble lives today — bringing with them the civic culture, educational values, and fierce anti-slavery
conviction of the Puritan tradition. From New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Maryland came middle-state families like the Gobles
and LeComptes, following the National Road westward or the river valleys northward. From Virginia and Kentucky came
Southern families crossing the Ohio River, often with complex loyalties and, in the antebellum years, deeply contested views
on the question of slavery. Ohio's geography was its destiny. The Ohio River to the south served as both a border and a
highway. Lake Erie to the north provided access to the entire Great Lakes system and, via the Erie Canal (completed 1825), to
the markets of New York City and the Atlantic seaboard. The National Road — the first federally funded highway in
American history, pushed through Ohio in the 1820s and 1830s — connected the state to the East Coast and transformed it
from frontier to commercial heartland within a single generation. By 1850, Ohio had the railroad infrastructure to complete its
transformation: iron rails linked Cleveland to Columbus to Cincinnati, and the state that had been wilderness sixty years earlier
was now the beating heart of the American interior economy. Historical map of Ohio, 1817 (by Lucas Fielding). By this date,
the state was barely fourteen years old, yet already the framework of county organization that would structure Goble and
LeCompte family settlement was taking shape. The northeastern corner — the Connecticut Western Reserve, future home of

Ashtabula County and Jefferson — is visible along the Lake Erie shore. Into this remarkable confluence of humanity, the
Goble families of New Jersey began to arrive in the first decade of the nineteenth century. They came, as the records confirm,
into Butler County in the state's southwestern corner — a logical destination for families moving west along the National Road
corridor from New Jersey and Pennsylvania. From Butler County, the family spread: northwest into Champaign County,
southeast into Athens County, and eventually, over the following half-century, north toward the lake and the Western Reserve
counties that form the northeastern corner of the state. By the time of the Civil War, the Goble name was present across
nearly every quadrant of Ohio — a testament to the family's extraordinary westward momentum and to the degree to which
Ohio had become, for this ancient New England and New Jersey line, a permanent home. 1.2 The Western Reserve —
Ashtabula County and Jefferson, Ohio Of all the regions of Ohio, none has a more distinctive identity — or a more directly
relevant history for the Goble family — than the Connecticut Western Reserve. The Western Reserve was a strip of land in
northeastern Ohio, approximately 120 miles long and 50 miles wide, that the state of Connecticut retained after ceding its
other western land claims to the federal government in 1786. Connecticut sold most of the Reserve to the Connecticut Land
Company in 1795, which surveyed and subdivided the land according to the New England township system — a six-mile-
square grid that imposed a distinctly New England spatial logic on the Ohio landscape. The towns that grew up across the
Western Reserve reflected this origin: they had town greens, white-steepled Congregationalist churches, common schools
established at the earliest opportunity, and a civic culture rooted in the townmeeting tradition of colonial New England.
Ashtabula County was among the first to be organized within the Western Reserve. Created in 1807 from Geauga County,
Ashtabula County occupies the extreme northeastern corner of Ohio — bounded by Lake Erie to the north, Pennsylvania to
the east, and the surrounding Ohio counties to the south and west. Its landscape is shaped by the deep ravines and ridges
carved by glacial action during the last Ice Age: the Grand River and its tributaries cut through the county's interior, creating a
topography of unusual beauty and agricultural variety. Jefferson, the county seat, was platted in 1804 and formally
incorporated as a village in 1818 — just fifteen years after Ohio statehood. It was named for President Thomas Jefferson,
whose principles of democratic self-governance resonated deeply with the New England settlers who founded it. Historical
Context Sidebar Jefferson, Ohio, and Joshua Giddings: The Moral Capital of the Western Reserve Jefferson, Ohio's most
famous antebellum resident was Congressman Joshua Reed Giddings (1795–1864), and his presence transformed the town
from a county seat into one of the moral capitals of the abolitionist movement. Giddings represented the Ashtabula
Congressional district from 1838 to 1859 — twentyone years — and was among the most radical and uncompromising
opponents of slavery in the entire Congress. In 1842, following the Creole case — in which enslaved people aboard a ship
bound for New Orleans revolted, took command, and sailed to the Bahamas, where they claimed freedom — Giddings rose in
Congress to defend their right to resist enslavement. He was censured by the House of Representatives for this position. He
resigned his seat, returned to Jefferson, and presented himself to his constituents for judgment. They reelected him in a special
election, overwhelmingly, within weeks. Ashtabula County had made its position clear. The Underground Railroad was not a
metaphor in Ashtabula County — it was a physical reality, a network of safe houses, hidden cellars, and trusted guides that
moved freedom-seeking people northward from the Ohio River to the Lake Erie shore, where boats could carry them to
Canada and permanent freedom. Ashtabula County is documented as having one of the densest concentrations of
Underground Railroad stations in all of Ohio. The lake — visible from the county's northern shore on a clear day — was the
final crossing: cold, wide, and free. The Goble family who eventually settled in this county settled in one of the most morally
charged and historically significant landscapes in antebellum American history. I m a g e P l a c e h o l d e r Map of
northeastern Ohio showing Ashtabula County, Jefferson (county seat), Lake Erie to the north, and documented Underground
Railroad routes running north from the Ohio River; accompanied by a historical street-level image of Jefferson, Ohio's main
street and courthouse square, circa 1860–1880, showing the New England-influenced architecture of the Western Reserve's
county seat town. The significance of the Western Reserve as the eventual home of the Goble line cannot be overstated. By
the time Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte settled in this region in the mid-twentieth century — and by the time Shane Goble

was raised in Jefferson — the county had accumulated more than two centuries of moral, civic, and political tradition. It was a
place that had argued, at enormous cost, for the freedom and dignity of all human beings. It was a place built by New England
families who believed that civic life was a sacred obligation, that education was a prerequisite for self-governance, and that the
community's collective character was expressed in the quality of its schools, churches, courthouses, and public debates. The
Goble family, carrying the ancient Puritan tradition of Thomas Goble's Massachusetts, found themselves in a corner of Ohio
that had been shaped by precisely that tradition — a long way from Charlestown, Massachusetts, but spiritually and culturally
continuous with it. 1.3 The Ohio Goble Community — Documented Families (1804–1860) The documentary record of

thoroughly and irreversibly Ohioan. They had come as frontier settlers; by the time of Andrew Jackson Goble's marriage in
1859, they were settled citizens of established counties in an established state with a halfcentury of civic history behind it. The
diversity of Goble spouses recorded in this table is itself a genealogical document of the first importance. The surnames of
those who married into the Goble family — Ayres, Mansfield, Case, Reed, Dillon, Morris, Wing, Fuller, Secoy, Fitzgerald —
represent a cross-section of the ethnic and cultural communities that were flooding Ohio during the same period. Reed and
Morris are Anglo-Welsh surnames, common in the Pennsylvania and New Jersey communities from which many Ohio settlers
had come. Fitzgerald is unmistakably Irish — a surname that arrived in Ohio in great numbers during and after the Great
Famine of the 1840s, when a million Irish men and women poured into the American industrial cities and frontier counties.
Secoy and Ayres carry the suggestion of Dutch and German origins, communities that had deep roots in the Ohio River
Valley from the early settlement period. The Goble family was not a family that kept to itself: it married outward, married
broadly, and integrated itself into every layer of the Ohio immigrant and settler community. The name "Andrew Jackson
Goble" — recorded in Athens County in 1859, fourteen years after the seventh president's death in 1845 — is a window into
the naming conventions of mid-nineteenth-century American families. Jackson remained, even in death, a towering figure in
the American political imagination: the champion of the common man, the hero of New Orleans, the embodiment of frontier
democracy and personal force. A family that named a son for Andrew Jackson in 1859 was making a political and cultural

statement about its values and its identity — and it was doing so in a year that was among the most politically charged in
American history, with John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry only months away and the election of Abraham Lincoln
approaching like a storm on the horizon. Andrew Jackson Goble was born, so to speak, into the last year of the old America
— and would have reached military age just in time for the war that ended it. 1.4 Benoni and Abner Goble — Indiana
Pioneers The westward momentum of the Goble family did not stop at the Ohio state line. Two documented Goble figures
— Benoni Goble and Abner Goble — pushed further west into Indiana, representing the family's continuation of the great
American westward movement that had carried them, across successive generations, from Massachusetts to New Jersey to
Ohio and now beyond. Their migration from Ohio to Indiana followed the same logic that had driven every previous Goble
migration: land was available, opportunity beckoned, and the frontier, as always, promised more than the settled country
behind it. Benoni is a name of striking Biblical provenance — the name given by the dying Rachel to her youngest son in the
book of Genesis, meaning "son of my sorrow," quickly renamed Benjamin by his father Jacob. The name was used throughout
the colonial and early republic period by Puritan and post-Puritan families as a marker of religious identity and scriptural
literacy. Its appearance in the Goble family — a family whose origin lies with Thomas Goble of Puritan Massachusetts — is
entirely consistent with the family's naming traditions. Abner, similarly, is a Hebrew Old Testament name (meaning "father of
light"), carried by David's general in the books of Samuel. Both names identify their bearers as members of a family that had
not yet abandoned the Biblical naming conventions of the Puritan tradition, even as the family had moved hundreds of miles
from its New England origin. The Indiana Gobles are a research frontier in their own right. Indiana's statehood in 1816 — just
thirteen years after Ohio's — opened a new wave of westward migration from the established Ohio counties. Families who
had settled in Butler, Champaign, or Athens County in the first decade of the century had children and grandchildren by the
1820s and 1830s who were ready to move again, following the same westward impulse that had defined their parents' and
grandparents' lives. Benoni and Abner Goble's Indiana migration is a microcosm of that great American momentum — the
ceaseless pushing forward, the refusal to be stopped by any river or mountain range or state boundary, the conviction that the
next territory over always held something better than what had been left behind. C H A P T E R T W O The Civil War and the
Goble Family 1861 – 1865 Ohio sent more than 319,000 men to fight for the Union — the most of any northern state relative
to its population. The Goble families of Ohio were embedded in communities where the war touched every household. Ohio
Union soldiers at camp, circa 1862–1864. Ohio contributed more soldiers per capita than any other northern state, and the
Goble families settled across the state's counties — Butler, Champaign, Athens, Allen, and eventually Ashtabula — would have
been deeply embedded in the communities that sent these men to war. 2.1 Ashtabula County Goes to War When the first
shots were fired at Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861, Ashtabula County did not wait to be told what it thought. This was the
county of Joshua Reed Giddings — the county that had censured a congressman for defending human freedom and then
immediately re-elected him to prove the point. This was a county crisscrossed by Underground Railroad routes, a county
where the cause of the enslaved had been preached from pulpits and debated in town squares for three decades. When
Abraham Lincoln called for volunteers following Fort Sumter, Ashtabula County responded with a speed and enthusiasm that
reflected two generations of moral preparation for exactly this moment. The regiments that drew from the Western Reserve
counties were among the most motivated and ideologically committed in the entire Union Army. These were men who had
grown up hearing Giddings thunder against slavery; who had, in some cases, helped freedom-seekers reach the Lake Erie
shore; who understood, in a way that not every Ohio county could claim, precisely what was at stake in the conflict. The 29th
Ohio Volunteer Infantry, the 104th Ohio Volunteer Infantry, and other regiments recruited heavily from Ashtabula and the
surrounding Western Reserve counties. They fought at Antietam, at Chickamauga, in Sherman's March through Georgia —
wherever the Union Army was tested most severely. Historical Context Sidebar Ohio and the Civil War: The Soldier State
Ohio's contribution to the Union cause was staggering in its scale and consequence. The state sent more than 319,000 men to
serve — a figure representing virtually every able-bodied man of military age in the state. More soldiers were contributed per
capita by Ohio than by any other northern state, a fact that speaks to the depth of the Union sentiment that had been

cultivated in the state's Western Reserve communities and reinforced across the rest of the state by the decades of abolitionist
activism centered in Jefferson. Three future presidents of the United States served from Ohio: Ulysses S. Grant, who had
resigned from the Army in 1854 but returned to train Ohio regiments at the outbreak of war and rose to command all Union
armies; Rutherford B. Hayes, who was wounded four times and commanded a brigade at the Battle of Cedar Creek; and James
Garfield, who fought at Shiloh and Middle Creek and left his command to take a seat in Congress. The Battle of Antietam on
September 17, 1862 — the bloodiest single day in American military history, with nearly 23,000 casualties — saw Ohio
regiments in the center of the fighting, at the Cornfield and the Sunken Road that became known forever after as Bloody
Lane. Ashtabula County's young men were in that fight, as they were in nearly every significant engagement of the Western
Theater. I m a g e P l a c e h o l d e r Ohio Civil War regimental flag, showing the state seal and battle honors; portrait of Ohio
Union soldiers in camp formation, circa 1862–1864; detailed map of Ohio showing county contributions to the Union Army
by regiment, with the Western Reserve counties of northeastern Ohio — including Ashtabula County — highlighted. 2.2 The
Goble Families in the Civil War Era No specific Goble-surname Civil War service record has yet been confirmed in Shane's
direct ancestral line — a gap that represents one of the highest research priorities identified in this volume. But the absence of
a confirmed record is emphatically not the same thing as an absence of service. The documented Goble families across Butler,
Champaign, Athens, Allen, and Ashtabula Counties were, by 1861, deeply embedded in Ohio communities that sent men to
war in extraordinary numbers. The intermediate Ohio Goble generations — the men who would occupy approximately the
seventh and eighth generations from Thomas Goble — would have been born roughly between 1830 and 1845, placing them
squarely in the cohort of men most likely to have served. Consider the arithmetic: Isaac Goble Jr., who married in Butler
County in 1804, would have had sons born approximately 1805–1825. Those sons would have had sons born approximately
1830–1850. Those grandsons — two generations from the earliest documented Ohio Goble — would have been twenty to
thirty years old in 1861: precisely the military prime. If the Goble family's Ohio fertility pattern followed the American norm
of the period (and the evidence from the LeCompte side, where Moses LeCompte fathered eleven children while blind,
suggests these were not small families), the number of Goble men of military age across Ohio's documented Goble counties
in 1861 could easily have been in the dozens. Research Note — Civil War Records for Ohio Goble Families Ohio's Civil War
records are among the most comprehensively preserved and accessible in the entire Union. The Ohio Roster of Soldiers in the
War of the Rebellion — a multi-volume work published by the state between 1886 and 1895 — lists every documented Ohio
soldier by county, regiment, rank, and service record. This roster is available online through the Ohio Memory digital archive
(www.ohiomemory.org) and in hard copy at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus. A systematic search of this roster for
all Goble-surname soldiers across every Ohio county where the family is documented — Butler, Champaign, Athens, Allen,
Ashtabula, and surrounding counties — is a high-priority research action that should be completed before Volume IV is
prepared. The roster will identify every documented Goble-surname soldier from Ohio, potentially including Shane's direct
ancestor in the Civil War generation. 2.3 The Home Front — Ohio Families During the War For every Ohio man who went to
war, there was a family at home that bore the weight of his absence — and often, the finality of his loss. The draft, instituted
in 1862 and expanded by the Enrollment Act of 1863, transformed the war from a matter of voluntary service into a legal
obligation that touched every household without exception. The draft lottery — men's names drawn from a box in the county
courthouse — was one of the most traumatic social rituals in American history, a moment when ordinary families confronted
the full coercive power of the nation in its moment of crisis. Communities responded with a mixture of patriotism, fear,
resignation, and, in some cases, violent resistance — the New York draft riots of July 1863 being the most extreme expression
of the rage that the lottery could provoke. Ohio families who did not send men to the front experienced the war through the
casualty lists published weekly in local newspapers — lists that grew longer with every major engagement, that arrived in the
morning edition and were read aloud in general stores and church vestibules and farmhouse kitchens across the state. The
Battle of Antietam alone cost Ohio nearly four thousand men killed, wounded, or missing. The Battle of Chickamauga in
September 1863 cost Ohio regiments heavily. By the summer of 1864, with Grant hammering at Lee in Virginia and Sherman

pushing toward Atlanta, Ohio's casualty lists had become a chronicle of grief that touched nearly every extended family in the
state. The agricultural demands of the war also transformed the Ohio home front profoundly. With the men away, the women
and children who remained on Ohio's farms bore the full burden of keeping the land productive — and Ohio's farms were
essential to feeding the Union Army. Women drove plows, operated machinery, managed livestock, negotiated with grain
brokers, and made every economic decision that had previously been the province of their absent husbands. This was not
merely a wartime adaptation; it was a permanent expansion of women's economic authority and self-reliance, one that would
have lasting consequences for Ohio family life in the decades that followed. The Goble and LeCompte women of the Civil
War generation — unnamed in most of the records, but present in the evidence of the farms that survived and the families
that persisted — deserve to be counted among the architects of the family's Ohio continuity. 2.4 The LeCompte Line and the
Border State Experience For the LeCompte family, the Civil War was not an Ohio experience but a Maryland one — and
Maryland's experience of the war was among the most anguished and complicated of any state in the nation. Maryland did not
secede, but only because President Lincoln moved with extraordinary speed and extralegal force to prevent it: in September
1861, he had Maryland's secessionist legislators arrested preemptively and held without charge at Fort McHenry — the same
fort whose defense had inspired Francis Scott Key's anthem forty-seven years earlier. Maryland remained in the Union by
presidential fiat rather than by popular conviction, and the division of sentiment within the state ran through communities,
churches, and families with a sharpness that left wounds lasting long after the war's end. Dorchester County on Maryland's
Eastern Shore — the LeCompte family's ancestral home for two centuries — was a slave-holding county. The 1860 census
shows that Dorchester County had nearly 4,000 enslaved people, representing a significant fraction of its total population of
approximately 15,000. The LeCompte family's Huguenot Protestant tradition — a tradition of religious dissent, of conscience
over convention, of the individual's obligation to resist unjust authority — existed in profound tension with the social and
economic reality of Eastern Shore Maryland. The LeComptes who had made their lives in this landscape for two hundred
years occupied a morally complex position: descendants of refugees who had themselves fled persecution, now embedded in a
society built on the most absolute form of human oppression. The LeComptes who had already migrated to Ohio by the
1860s would have stood unambiguously with the Union cause — they were Ohioans now, in a free state, in communities
shaped by abolitionist conviction. But for the family members who remained in Maryland, the war was far more complicated.
It set neighbor against neighbor, family member against family member, and forced every person in the border states to make
an explicit choice between the constitutional order represented by the Union and the social world represented by the
Confederacy. The LeCompte family's eventual migration to Ohio — fully complete by the early twentieth century, if not
before — can be understood in part as a consequence of that rupture: families that could leave the border-state tensions
behind often did, and Ohio, with its free-state heritage and its expanding economy, beckoned with the same force it had
beckoned to the Gobles decades before. C H A P T E R T H R E E The Maryland LeCompte Dynasty Final Maryland
Generations and Ohio Migration, 1820–1920 3.1 The LeCompte Family Bible — A Physical Heritage An 18th-century family
Bible of the type used by the LeCompte family — published in Philadelphia by Kimber & Sharpless (1784–1800) — in which
births, marriages, and deaths were recorded by hand across three generations. The physical Bible survives today, displayed in
Richmond, Virginia [PROBABLE]. To hold it would be to touch the handwriting of people born within two generations of
Antoine LeCompte himself. Before there were courthouses with standardized record books, before there were state bureaus of
vital statistics, before the federal census provided a systematic snapshot of every American household, there was the family
Bible. In Protestant American households

of the seventeenth, eighteenth, and early nineteenth centuries, the family Bible was simultaneously a religious text, a vital
records register, and a genealogical archive — the place where births were noted, marriages recorded, and deaths marked, in
the handwriting of whoever happened to be present when the event occurred. These Bibles were among the most carefully
preserved possessions in American family life, passed from parent to child, carried across frontiers and ocean crossings,
protected from fire and flood and the general entropy of time. The LeCompte Family Bible — published in Philadelphia by

the Quaker printers Kimber and Sharpless during the period 1784 to 1800 — served this function for the LeCompte family
across at least three generations. [PROBABLE] It was the family's practice to pass the Bible to the eldest son of each
generation, and in its front pages — the traditional location for family records — births, marriages, and deaths were recorded
in multiple hands across the decades of its use. This Bible is now understood to be displayed in Richmond, Virginia, where it
represents a physical bridge between the Maryland colonial world of Antoine LeCompte and the present day. The significance
of this document cannot be overstated. The 1819 LeCompte Manuscript — the oral history dictated by the two blind brothers
Thomas and Daniel LeCompte to Benjamin Woodward LeCompte and preserved at the Maryland Historical Society — gives
us the family's history as narrative. The Family Bible gives us the family's history as raw vital data: names, dates, relationships,
recorded at the moment of occurrence by people who were there. Together, these two documents form the evidentiary
foundation for the LeCompte genealogical record in a way that official government records, which did not exist in Maryland
until the Civil War era, cannot provide. For Shane Goble's family, the Bible is an ancestor's handwriting — a literal trace of a
hand that has been still for two hundred years, suddenly present on the page. Research Note — Accessing the LeCompte
Family Bible If the Family Bible is currently held in a private collection in Richmond, Virginia, access may be arranged through
a formal written request to the holding institution or family. Alternatively, the Maryland Historical Society in Baltimore may
hold a transcription or photographic reproduction of the Bible's family record pages, as part of its extensive LeCompte
genealogical collection. A transcription of all names, dates, and relationships recorded in the Bible should be obtained and
compared systematically against the 1819 Manuscript and against county and church records from Dorchester County,
Maryland, to identify any discrepancies or additional data points. 3.2 Francis Asbury LeCompte — The Methodist Connection
(~1770–1800) Among the children of Hugh LeCompte — himself a son of the Maryland LeCompte dynasty whose roots
extended directly to Antoine and Hester LeCompte of the Choptank River — one name stands apart for the extraordinary
historical weight it carries: Francis Asbury LeCompte. [PROBABLE] The given name Francis Asbury is not an accident and
not a mere aesthetic choice. It is a declaration of religious identity as precise and intentional as any document the family ever
produced. Francis Asbury (1745–1816) was the founder and architect of American Methodism — the English-born bishop
who arrived in America in 1771 at John Wesley's direction and who, over the next forty-five years, traveled an estimated
275,000 miles on horseback to establish Methodist congregations in every region of the country. He crossed the Appalachian
Mountains more than sixty times. He ordained more than four thousand ministers. He established Methodism not as an elite
urban institution but as a movement of the frontier and the countryside — democratic in its governance, emotional in its
worship, and deeply committed (through John Wesley's own passionate conviction) to the abolition of slavery. When a
LeCompte family named their son for Francis Asbury — in the period roughly 1770 to 1800 — they were announcing that the
family had found a new spiritual community. The ancient French Huguenot Reformed tradition of Antoine LeCompte had
evolved, across five or six generations of American life, into the rising Methodist movement that was transforming American
religious culture from the ground up. Historical Context Sidebar Methodism and American Frontier Religion: The Great
Democratization of Faith John Wesley's Methodism arrived in America via Francis Asbury in 1771, but it did not achieve
dominance immediately. The American Revolution temporarily disrupted the movement — many Methodist leaders were
English-born and faced suspicion as potential Loyalists, and Asbury himself spent much of the war in hiding. But by 1790,
Methodism had found its footing in American life, and by 1820 it was the largest Protestant denomination in the United States
— a position it would hold for most of the nineteenth century. The genius of frontier Methodism was its adaptability. The
circuit rider — a Methodist minister who traveled a regular circuit of rural communities, often covering hundreds of miles by
horseback in all weathers — made it possible to sustain religious community in places where no settled minister could survive
economically. The camp meeting — the outdoor revival, lasting several days, where hundreds or thousands of frontier families
gathered to sing, pray, preach, and experience the emotional conversion that was central to Methodist theology — was one of
the most powerful social institutions on the American frontier, and it was distinctively Methodist. For isolated farm families in
Maryland, Ohio, Kentucky, and Indiana, the camp meeting was often the largest social gathering of the year. John Wesley had

called slavery "the sum of all villanies" — and American Methodism, in its early years, carried that abolitionist conviction. By
the midnineteenth century, the denomination had split over slavery, with Southern Methodist churches accommodating the
institution; but the Northern Methodist tradition maintained its opposition. A LeCompte family aligned with Methodism in
the late eighteenth century was a family aligned with one of the most democratically spirited and morally serious religious
movements in American history — entirely consistent with their Huguenot ancestors' tradition of costly religious conviction.
The naming of a child "Francis Asbury" represents a moment of spiritual transition in the LeCompte family's long religious
history. Antoine LeCompte had come to America as a Huguenot — a member of the French Reformed Protestant tradition
that traced itself to John Calvin and that had paid for its convictions with three generations of persecution, massacre, and exile
before the Edict of Fontainebleau (1685) drove the final wave of Huguenots from France. That tradition — austere, learned,
convinced of the absolute sovereignty of God and the utter inadequacy of all human institutions — had sustained the family
through its first century in America. But the frontier was doing to American religion what it was doing to American politics:
democratizing it, emotionalizing it, making it accessible to people who had never attended a university or read Calvin in Latin.
The LeComptes who named their son Francis Asbury were, in a real sense, following their ancestors' deepest instinct:
choosing the faith that spoke most directly to the life they were actually living, rather than the faith their grandparents had
imported from Europe. 3.3 Francis Layton Foxwell LeCompte — The Transitional Generation (~1800–1870) The son of
Francis Asbury LeCompte carries one of the most genealogically rich names in the entire LeCompte record: Francis Layton
Foxwell LeCompte. [ESTIMATED] Three given names, each of them a potential clue to the family's social world at the
moment of the child's birth. In the naming conventions of the nineteenth century — particularly among families with strong
community ties and a tradition of genealogical memory — each element of a multi-part name almost always carried a specific
meaning: a family connection, a beloved neighbor, a respected community figure, a maternal surname preserved in the absence
of a biological male line. "Francis" is inherited from his father, Francis Asbury LeCompte — a continuity of the religious
naming tradition, and a marker of filial respect. "Foxwell" is a more distinctive and genealogically interesting element. The
Foxwell surname is documented in the records of Maryland's Eastern Shore counties — particularly in Dorchester County, the
LeCompte family's ancestral territory — from the colonial period forward. A Foxwell in a LeCompte child's given name
strongly suggests either a direct family connection (a Foxwell ancestor through a female line, or a marriage between Foxwell
and LeCompte families not yet documented) or a close community bond with a Foxwell family that rose to the level of
godparenthood or naming honor. Either interpretation points directly back to the Dorchester County community and its
dense network of intermarried colonial families. "Layton" similarly appears in Maryland Eastern Shore records as both a given
name and surname, suggesting another community or family connection of the same type. Francis Layton Foxwell LeCompte
represents the transitional generation in the most literal sense of that phrase. Born approximately 1800 and living through
approximately 1870 [ESTIMATED], his life spanned the most transformative period in American history since the Revolution:
the antebellum era of westward expansion and intensifying sectional conflict; the Civil War itself; and the Reconstruction
period that followed, during which the South — including Maryland's Eastern Shore — was fundamentally reorganized. For a
LeCompte born in Dorchester County, Maryland, this was a lifetime of upheaval. The social world that his grandfather and
greatgrandfather had inhabited — the tidewater planter society of the Eastern Shore, with its tobacco culture, its seasonal
rhythms, its hierarchies of race and class — was dismantled in the space of four years of war. The question of where to go
next, and what kind of life to build in the ruins of the old one, was the defining question of his later years. The migration
from Maryland to Ohio that the LeCompte family eventually accomplished was, in the context of post-Civil War America, a
common solution to an uncommon set of problems. The Eastern Shore's economy, built on tobacco culture and enslaved
labor, could not survive emancipation intact. Families that had the social capital, the financial resources, and the initiative to
relocate often did so — moving to the growing industrial cities of the North and Midwest, where the economy was expanding
and the past could be, at least partially, left behind. Francis Layton Foxwell LeCompte's generation was the hinge on which that
relocation turned. 3.4 Benjamin Berry LeCompte Sr. — The Long-Lived Patriarch (~1830–1870, died 1989) Among all the

figures in the LeCompte genealogical record, Benjamin Berry LeCompte Sr. presents the most puzzling and potentially the
most remarkable biographical profile. [PROBABLE] Son of Francis Layton Foxwell LeCompte, he is documented with a
death year of 1989 — a date that, combined with the estimated birth range of 1830 to 1870, creates a biographical arithmetic
that demands careful attention. If Benjamin Berry LeCompte Sr. was born at the later end of the estimated range —
approximately 1870 — and died in 1989, he would have lived approximately 119 years. This is an extraordinary longevity, but
not an unprecedented one: the documented record of supercentenarians (people who have lived to 110 or more) is maintained
by the Gerontology Research Group and includes several American cases from this period. The conditions that produce
extreme longevity — genetic predisposition, moderate diet, physical activity, low stress, and social engagement — are not
incompatible with the life of a rural Ohio family in the early-to-mid twentieth century. If born closer to 1830 and died in 1989,
the arithmetic becomes impossible, and the death year likely reflects a transcription or indexing error that requires verification
through primary source documents. Set aside the arithmetic for a moment and consider the human possibility. If Benjamin
Berry LeCompte Sr. was born around 1870 — in the immediate aftermath of the Civil War, in the upheaval of Reconstruction
— he was a child of the New South's birth and the Old South's death simultaneously. He may have heard, from his father
Francis Layton Foxwell LeCompte, personal memories of antebellum Maryland that reached back to the 1820s and 1830s —
stories of the Eastern Shore before the war, of the world that existed before everything changed. He would have grown to
adulthood in an Ohio that was being transformed by industrialization, immigration, and the rise of the labor movement. He
would have lived through the Progressive Era, two world wars, the Great Depression, the post-war boom, the Civil Rights Act,
the moon landing, the fall of the Berlin Wall. If he died in 1989 — the year the Cold War effectively ended — he was a living
bridge between the Reconstruction era and the modern world, a man whose memory stretched across the entire span of
American modernity. That he exists in the genealogical record at all — that his name was preserved and indexed — is an act of
survival that mirrors, in miniature, the larger survival of the LeCompte family across four centuries of American history.

Geauga courts 4.2 The Name "Rae" The name Rae carries its own quiet story. A diminutive of Rachel — the Biblical
matriarch of the Book of Genesis, wife of Jacob, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, whose name in Hebrew (rahel) meant
"ewe," an image of gentleness and nurturing warmth — or alternatively a feminine form of Ray, derived from the Germanic
Raginhar ("counsel-power"), the name Rae occupied a particular place in the naming fashions of the 1920s and 1930s. It was a
Jazz Age name — short, bright, modern, stripped of the Victorian elaboration that had produced names like Prudence and
Temperance and Mehitabel in earlier generations. A girl named Rae in 1925 or 1930 was a girl whose parents were looking
forward rather than backward, toward the radio and the automobile and the talking picture rather than toward the formal
portraits of grandmothers in black dresses. And yet the name carried its ancient root with it. Rachel in the Bible is one of the
most fully realized and sympathetic figures in the Hebrew scriptures — a woman who waited, who grieved, who loved fiercely,
who died in childbirth at the moment of her greatest happiness, and whom the prophet Jeremiah invoked centuries later as the
voice of all mothers weeping for their lost children. A girl named for Rachel, however indirectly, inherited a long tradition of
female emotional depth and resilience. In the compressed elegance of Rae — three letters, one syllable, simple as a stone —
there is a whole world of association quietly present. The full name Rae LeCompte has a particular resonance. LeCompte —
"the count," from the Old French word for the highest administrative official below a duke — is a surname that carries the
ghost of French aristocratic government within it. Rae LeCompte: the bright American diminutive joined to the French title. It
is a name that embodies the family's history without announcing it — the product of a Huguenot soldier's American dynasty,
worn lightly by a twentieth-century Ohio woman who had other things on her mind than the Choptank River of 1659. 4.3
Imagined Voice — Rae LeCompte, Ohio, circa 1945 Imagined Voice — Creative Reconstruction I am twenty-something years
old and I live in Ohio and it is nearly the end of the war, or maybe it is just the beginning of the peace, and I am not sure yet
which it is. My mother calls me Rae the way you call someone a name that has always been theirs, without thinking about it at
all. But I think about it sometimes. Rae. Three letters. My grandmother — or maybe it was her mother, I am not sure the story
is entirely accurate by the time it reaches me — said the family name was French. LeCompte. That it meant something like
"the count" in French. That we came from Maryland before we came to Ohio. That before Maryland there was France, and
that there was a story about a soldier, about a ship, about a piece of land beside a river that our ancestor named after himself. I
don't know all of it. I know Ohio. I know the particular light of a Western Reserve October, when the maples go red and gold
all at once and the sky turns a blue that has no equivalent anywhere else on earth. I know the smell of Lake Erie in August —
that particular mineral coldness underneath the warmth, the smell of ancient water and deep time. I know the sound of the
county courthouse clock at noon, the way it carries across the whole town square and tells you exactly where you are and what
time it is, and that there is no ambiguity about either of those things. I am here. It is now. That is enough. There is a man I
have met, or am about to meet. His name is Goble. Kevin Goble. It sounds solid to me. It sounds like something that will
hold. I don't know anything yet about the man who brought his name to Massachusetts from England three hundred years
before he was born, or about the jury in Boston, or about the spy who moved through enemy lines in the Revolution. I just
know his name is Goble and that when I say it — Kevin Goble — it feels like a name I have been waiting to say. Like a door I
didn't know was there, and now I've found the handle. The war is almost over. The light is extraordinary. I am a LeCompte,
which means I am the daughter of someone who is the son of someone who is the son of someone who crossed oceans and
named rivers and built families in the wilderness of the new world. I don't know all of that yet. I just know the October light. I

just know his name. Note: The 1940 and 1950 Federal Census records, Ohio residence, and marriage to Kevin Goble are

most thoroughly documented ancestors in the colonial Goble record, Kevin Goble — the fourth-generation descendant of
Thomas Goble of Massachusetts, born July 12, 1700, in Morristown, New Jersey, and died March 29, 1783 — stands as one of
the most important patriarchal figures in the family's New Jersey history. Born in the final year of the seventeenth century, this
Kevin Goble lived through the entirety of the colonial period, the Revolution, and the establishment of the republic — dying
in 1783 in the same year that the Treaty of Paris formally ended the war that his generation had endured. His life spanned
nearly the whole of British colonial America and extended into the first years of the new nation. If Shane's grandfather Kevin
Goble — born in Ohio approximately 1920 to 1935 — was named in honor of this colonial ancestor, the naming represents a
remarkable act of genealogical memory: a twentieth-century Ohio family preserving a connection to a seventeenth-century
New Jersey ancestor by giving his name to a new generation. This pattern of ancestral namerepetition is well-documented in
American genealogy and was particularly common in families with strong oral genealogical traditions — families that knew, or
at least half-remembered, the names of ancestors several generations back. The recurrence of "Kevin" across the Goble family
record, from the New Jersey colonial generation of 1700 to the Ohio mid-century generation of the 1920s or 1930s, is a
thread worth following in the research. 5.3 Imagined Voice — Kevin Goble, Ohio, circa 1950 Imagined Voice — Creative
Reconstruction The war is over. I know this because the men are coming back — not all of them, never all of them, but
enough that you can feel the town breathing again, feel the particular relief of ordinary life reasserting itself over the
emergency that has defined everything for four years. I have a job. I have a place to live. I have a future that extends further
forward than the next week, the next month, the next mission. That is not a small thing. That is everything. My name is Kevin
Goble. I have been Kevin Goble my entire life, which in 1950 is something between twenty and thirty years, and I have never
thought much about the name beyond the fact of it. I know my father was a Goble and his father before him. I know we are
Ohio people — that this state, this county, this particular corner of the world along the lake is where we are from, where we
belong, where I expect to be buried. Beyond that, the history thins out. I don't know about the man who brought the name
across the ocean from England. I don't know about the jury in Boston, or about the spy who moved through enemy territory
in the Revolution. I don't know that there is a DNA signature in my blood that reaches back four thousand years to warriors
who crossed from Europe into Britain with bronze tools and herding cattle. I just know I am Kevin Goble, of Ohio, and that I
am about to begin my life in earnest. There is a woman named Rae LeCompte. Her name sounds like it comes from
somewhere else — somewhere older than Ohio, older than America. LeCompte. French, maybe. She says her family was from
Maryland, before Ohio. She says there are stories about France, about a soldier. I find I am not uninterested in stories about
soldiers. I am thinking about her name — Rae LeCompte — and how it sounds when it is followed by mine. Rae LeCompte

a genealogical perspective, the marriage of Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte is the single most significant event in Shane
Goble's family history that falls within the period covered by this volume — and one of the most significant events in the

entire four-volume record. Not because marriages are unusual, or because this particular couple was famous, or because their
union was accompanied by any outward drama or historical event of note. But because it represents the moment at which two
extraordinary and independent streams of American history, flowing through ten generations each from opposite shores of
the Atlantic, finally joined. In Kevin Goble came the line of Thomas Goble of colonial Charlestown — Freeman of the
Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1634, juror on the first Boston jury in 1640, father of six children in the new world, whose

T E R N I N E The World They Inhabited Historical Context, 1850–1950 9.1 The Industrial Transformation of Ohio (1850–
1900) The decades following the Civil War transformed Ohio so completely and so quickly that the state of 1900 was barely
recognizable as the same entity as the state of 1860. The agricultural frontier of the antebellum period — the Ohio of log
farmhouses, county seat courthouses, and river-valley commerce — gave way to one of the most concentrated industrial
landscapes in the world. The process was driven by geography, by raw materials, and by the relentless ingenuity and appetite of
American capital in its most expansive phase. Oil was discovered in northwestern Ohio in 1885, transforming Lima and the
surrounding counties into a petroleum producing center of national significance. Standard Oil — John D. Rockefeller's
Cleveland-based trust, which had already established its dominance over the Pennsylvania oil fields — moved quickly to
control the Ohio fields as well, making Cleveland one of the financial capitals of the American oil industry. Steel came to the
Mahoning Valley, where Youngstown's furnaces were burning twenty-four hours a day by the 1880s, consuming the iron ore
that Great Lakes freighters brought from the mines of Minnesota's Iron Range and the coal that came up from the
Appalachian fields of southeastern Ohio and West Virginia. Akron became the center of the American rubber industry — a
position it would hold for most of the twentieth century. Toledo's glass industry supplied windows, bottles, and industrial glass
to the entire nation. Cleveland's factories produced machine tools, electrical equipment, and automotive components that
made it one of the most diversified industrial cities in the country. Ashtabula County, on Lake Erie's southern shore, became
an important node in this industrial system — not as a manufacturing center itself, but as a point of commercial and logistical
significance. The Ashtabula harbor handled enormous quantities of coal and iron ore moving between the Great Lakes ports,
and the county's rail connections made it part of the transportation grid that tied the industrial cities of the interior to the
markets of the East. For the Goble families who were establishing themselves in northeastern Ohio during this period, the
industrial transformation meant new economic possibilities: factory employment, commercial opportunity, and the expansion
of the professional and service economy that always follows industrial growth. 9.2 Immigration Waves and Ohio's Changing
Demographics (1850–1920) The same decades that saw Ohio's industrial transformation also saw the most dramatic
demographic transformation in the state's history since the pioneer period. Between 1850 and 1920, successive waves of

immigration brought millions of new Americans into Ohio's cities and factory towns, transforming communities that had
been predominantly Anglo-American into the diverse, multi-ethnic societies that Ohio's cities became by the early twentieth
century. The Irish arrived first and in the greatest numbers — driven by the catastrophic potato famine of 1845 to 1852, which
killed approximately one million people and forced another million and a half to emigrate. Irish immigrants settled across
Ohio's canal and railroad construction projects, then built communities in the cities and smaller industrial towns. The Germans
came in two waves: the "old immigration" of the 1830s and 1840s, which brought skilled craftsmen, farmers, and intellectuals;
and the "48ers" — the German refugees who fled the failed revolutions of 1848 and brought with them a tradition of radical
democratic politics, labor organization, and cultural seriousness. The Welsh brought their mining skills to the coal fields of
southeastern Ohio. The Italians, Poles, Slovaks, Czechs, Hungarians, and other Southern and Eastern European groups arrived
in the 1880s, 1890s, and 1900s, drawn by the steel mills and rubber factories that needed unskilled labor in enormous
quantities. For the Goble and LeCompte families — Anglo-American families of English and French Huguenot origin,
established in Ohio since the early nineteenth century — this immigration wave was an experience of watching their
communities transform around them. They were, by this period, the established families, the settled Americans, the people
whose names appeared in the county directories and the church membership rolls and the school board records. The arriving
immigrants were the newcomers, the strangers, the people learning English and finding their footing in an unfamiliar country.
The dynamic was complex: the established families provided employment, civic leadership, and the social models that the
immigrants were expected to assimilate to; the immigrants brought labor, cultural energy, and eventually political power that
transformed the character of Ohio's communities in ways the established families had not anticipated and did not always
welcome. 9.3 World War I and Ohio Families (1917– 1918) When the United States entered the Great War in April 1917, Ohio
mobilized with a speed and thoroughness that reflected both patriotic conviction and the state's industrial capacity for military
production. Approximately 200,000 Ohio men served in the armed forces during the war — a smaller number than the Civil
War, but deployed in a conflict of incomparably greater industrial violence and geographic scale. The trench warfare of the
Western Front, the artillery barrages that could be heard hundreds of miles away, the poison gas attacks that incapacitated
entire battalions — these were forms of violence for which nothing in American military history had prepared the young men
of Ohio who found themselves in Flanders and the Argonne Forest in 1917 and 1918. Raymond LeCompte — the estimated
father of Rae and a man born approximately 1890 to 1915 — would have been of military age during this conflict. If born at
the early end of this range, he would have been twentyseven years old when the U.S. entered the war, a prime conscription age.
The Selective Service Act of 1917 required all men between the ages of 21 and 30 to register; a third registration in 1918
extended the obligation to men between 18 and 45. Raymond LeCompte's draft registration card — if it survives, and many
do — would place him in a specific Ohio location in 1917 or 1918, with a physical description, occupation, and employer. This
single document could be one of the most important primary source records yet obtained for the LeCompte line in its Ohio
phase. Ohio's home front during World War I was equally transformed by the conflict. The state's industrial capacity was
redirected toward war production: steel became shells and armor plate, rubber became gas masks and vehicle tires, chemical
plants produced explosives and poison gas. The wartime economy created full employment and rising wages for Ohio's
industrial workers — a prosperity that was, for many families, the first they had ever known. The influenza pandemic of 1918,
which arrived in Ohio in the autumn of that year, killed tens of thousands across the state — more deaths than the war itself
— and left a demographic mark on every Ohio community that was not fully understood for a generation. 9.4 The Great
Depression and Ohio (1929– 1939) The Great Depression arrived in Ohio with particular severity, because Ohio's economy
had become so thoroughly dependent on the industrial sector that the collapse of industrial production translated almost
immediately into mass unemployment and economic devastation. By 1932, the worst year of the Depression, unemployment
in Ohio's industrial cities — Cleveland, Youngstown, Akron, Toledo — had reached 30 to 40 percent. Steel mills that had
operated continuously for decades stood idle. Rubber factories ran at a fraction of capacity. The agricultural sector, already
weakened by the price declines of the 1920s, suffered further from the collapse of consumer purchasing power. Farm

foreclosures multiplied. Banks failed — including many of the small county seat banks that had been the financial backbone
of rural Ohio communities. Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte — both born in the 1920s or early 1930s, based on the best
available evidence — came of age during the Depression. Their formative years were shaped by scarcity, by the knowledge that
security was fragile and that prosperity could vanish overnight, by the daily reality of making do with less and finding ingenuity
where abundance was unavailable. The character traits that are commonly attributed to the "Greatest Generation" — frugality,
work ethic, stoicism in the face of hardship, commitment to family stability above individual gratification — were forged in the
crucible of the Depression. Kevin Goble and Rae LeCompte belonged to that generation, and the Depression was the shared
experience that, more than any other single event, shaped the people they became before they met each other. Franklin
Roosevelt's New Deal brought relief to Ohio's hardest-hit communities — through the Civilian Conservation Corps, which
put young men to work in the state's parks and forests; through the Works Progress Administration, which built schools,
courthouses, and highways across the state; through the agricultural programs that stabilized farm prices; and through the
Social Security Act of 1935, which established the foundational safety net that Americans had never previously enjoyed.
Ashtabula County — like most of northeastern Ohio — was a Democratic stronghold during the New Deal years, its voters
understanding with visceral immediacy what federal intervention in the economy meant for their daily lives. 9.5 World War II
and the Ohio Home Front (1941–1945) Kevin Goble, born approximately 1920 to 1935, was of military age during World War
II — and Ohio men of his generation served in extraordinary numbers. The Second World War was, in scale and consequence,
the most total mobilization of American society in the nation's history: not only the twelve million men and women who
served in the armed forces, but the one hundred million civilians who rationed food and gasoline, bought war bonds, worked
double shifts in defense factories, grew victory gardens, and gave up the normalcy of peacetime life for the duration of a
conflict that lasted three years and eight months from Pearl Harbor to V-J Day. Ohio's industrial capacity made it one of the
most critical states in the war production effort. Youngstown steel went into the ships and tanks and artillery pieces that
equipped the Allied armies. Akron rubber went into the tires of every military vehicle and the synthetic rubber substitutes for
which the country's chemists worked night and day after the Japanese seizure of Southeast Asian rubber plantations.
Cleveland's factories — Warner and Swasey, Thompson Products, Lincoln Electric — produced precision instruments, aircraft
components, and electrical equipment that equipped the air forces and navies of the Allied powers. The Ohio industrial
heartland was, in a very real sense, the workshop of victory. For Kevin Goble, if he served — and this is a research question
of the first importance — World War II military service would be one of the defining experiences of his life. WWII draft
registration cards are available through Ancestry.com for all men born between 1886 and 1926; a registration card for Kevin
Goble would confirm his physical description, address, and occupation at the time of registration (approximately 1940 to
1942) in a primary source document. If he served in the Army or Air Force, his personnel file may have been lost in the 1973
NPRC fire; but Navy and Marine records largely survived, and many Army records were subsequently reconstructed from
alternative sources. A National Archives records request (Standard Form 180) should be submitted as part of the research
