English Origins — Sussex and the First Goble Chapter 1: Roots in Sussex — The World Thomas Goble Left Behind Thomas
Goble was born somewhere around the year 1590 or 1591, most likely in the village of Westergate, which lies within the
ancient parish of Aldingbourne in West Sussex, England. The chalk downs rise to the north, and the coastal plain stretches
south toward the English Channel. The parish of Aldingbourne — its name deriving from the Saxon "Ealda's bourne," a
stream belonging to an early Saxon settler — was ancient even by Thomas Goble's time. The parish church of St. Mary the
Virgin, a Grade I listed building, had stood since the twelfth century, its chancel built in the thirteenth, its stone walls worn
smooth by generations of Sussex hands. It was the kind of church that small-village England built to last: solid,
unornamented, present in the landscape the way a hill is present, as though it had simply grown there. The Parish Church of
St. Mary the Virgin, Aldingbourne, West Sussex, England — the ancient stone church where Thomas Goble and Alice
Brookman were married on November 5, 1619, in the opening year of the reign of James I. The church has stood since the
twelfth century and remains in active use today. The West Sussex of Thomas Goble's youth was an agricultural landscape —
wheat fields, dairy farms, the cathedral city of Chichester nearby, the road between Chichester and Arundel cutting through
the northern end of Aldingbourne parish. The soil was good, the land relatively flat between the South Downs and the coast.
Westergate, the village where the Gobles likely lived, was the chief center of population in the parish — a community of
smallholders, yeoman farmers, craftsmen, and agricultural laborers who had worked this ground for generations. The Bishop
of Chichester maintained an ancient palace and demesne farm of some 500 acres in Aldingbourne, and the great episcopal
presence over this landscape had shaped its character for centuries. Thomas Goble belonged to the middling sort — what the
seventeenth century called "yeomanry." Not gentry, not nobility, but not poor. A man who worked his own land, or rented
land he worked as if it were his own, who could read and write (his will, signed in his own hand, confirms this), who was
known in his community as a man of standing. The inventory of his estate at death would confirm him as, by the standards of
his time and place, a wealthy man. He was the kind of man England produced in its best agricultural parishes: capable, literate,
Godly, and ready for something more. The England Thomas Goble Knew: James I, Charles I, and the Puritan Crisis In the
year of Thomas Goble's birth, England was ruled by Elizabeth I, who would die in 1603, leaving the throne to James VI of
Scotland, who became James I of England and began the Stuart dynasty. The England of Thomas Goble's youth and young
adulthood was an England in religious ferment. The Church of England, established by Henry VIII and reformed under
Elizabeth, was under sustained pressure from two sides: Catholic recusants who refused to accept Protestant rule, and Puritans
who believed the Reformation had not gone nearly far enough. The Puritans — the name was a term of mockery that became
a badge of honor — wanted to purify the Church of England of what they saw as the corrupt remnants of Roman
Catholicism: elaborate ceremony, hierarchical bishops, liturgical performance. They wanted plain worship, plain speech, the
unmediated encounter between an individual conscience and the Word of God as written in Scripture. They were, in the most
literal sense, earnest, driven, and deeply uncomfortable in a Church that compromised their beliefs at every turn. Under James
I, the Puritans had initially hoped for sympathy — James had been raised in Calvinist Scotland, after all. But the King proved
hostile to their aspirations, and the famous Hampton Court Conference of 1604, which did produce the King James Bible, did
almost nothing to advance the Puritan program. Under Charles I, who inherited the throne in 1625, the situation grew
dramatically worse. Charles embraced High Anglican ceremony, elevated the anti-Puritan Archbishop William Laud, and in
1629 dissolved Parliament entirely — beginning eleven years of personal rule that would eventually lead to civil war. For a
Puritan family in West Sussex in the late 1620s and early 1630s, this political and religious environment was not merely
uncomfortable — it was threatening. Puritan ministers were ejected from their pulpits. Churchgoing was policed. The future
seemed to close down around them. Into this climate came the news of what John Winthrop and the Massachusetts Bay

Company were building on the other shore of the Atlantic: a "City upon a Hill," a Puritan commonwealth where Godly people
could live as they believed God intended, without compromise and without persecution. Alice Brookman and the Marriage at
Aldingbourne On November 5, 1619 — Guy Fawkes Day in the English calendar, the anniversary of the foiled Catholic plot
to blow up Parliament, a date charged with Protestant memory — Thomas Goble and Alice Brookman stood before the
congregation of St. Mary the Virgin in Aldingbourne and were joined in marriage. Alice's surname, Brookman, was confirmed
by newly discovered marriage records that supersede older genealogical theories that identified her as Alice Mousall. Alice
Brookman was almost certainly a West Sussex woman of yeoman stock, the daughter of a farming family of the same parish
or a neighboring one. In the close-knit world of seventeenth-century village England, marriages were local affairs — a young
man married a young woman he had known since childhood, whose family his family had known for generations, whose name
was already woven into the fabric of parish life. What their courtship looked like, we cannot know with certainty, but we can
imagine it within the world it inhabited: meetings at the church, at the market, at the great seasonal feasts that punctuated the
agricultural year. A November wedding was common in the farming calendar — the harvest was in, the hardest labor of the
year was done, and there was a brief window of celebration before the long English winter settled in. They were married, and
they began their family in Sussex. Their son John was born around 1629, making him approximately ten years younger than
the marriage — suggesting either a late start or the loss of earlier children to the high infant mortality rates of the era. H istor
ica l Context : The Pur itan Cr is is and the Dec is ion to Leave England The years between 1629 and 1640 saw the most
concentrated emigration in English colonial history. Charles I's dissolution of Parliament in 1629, Archbishop Laud's
aggressive enforcement of High Anglican conformity, and the economic dislocations of a country in political crisis combined
to make England, for Puritan families, a place from which departure seemed not merely attractive but necessary. Between 1630
and 1640, approximately 20,000 English men, women, and children crossed the Atlantic to New England — a mass movement
unprecedented in scale and remarkable in its character. These were not, for the most part, the desperately poor. The Puritan
Great Migration was dominated by middling-sort families: literate, skilled, rooted in their communities, and possessed of
enough resources to pay for passage. They left not because they had nothing to lose, but because they believed they were
losing something more important than material comfort — the right to worship as their conscience demanded. Thomas and
Alice Goble were part of this tide. They left a life they had built — their land, their community, their parish church with its
stone walls and its twelvecentury history — for an ocean crossing they knew would be arduous and a new world they had
never seen. That decision, made in a West Sussex farmhouse in the early 1630s, is the founding act of the American Goble
family. For the full account of the Puritan theological tradition and its influence on Goble family values across generations,
see Volume IV: Faith and Conscience — Religion in the Goble Ancestral Line. Chapter 2: The Great Migration — Crossing to
Massachusetts (1634) On August 30, 1634, the record of the First Church of Charlestown, Massachusetts, records the
following: "Thomas Goble and Alice his wife" were admitted to the church. This single line in a colonial church record is the
most important date in the entire Goble American genealogy. It is the first confirmed evidence of the family's presence in the
New World, and it anchors the entire subsequent American story of the Goble name. The date of their departure from
England and the name of the ship they sailed on are not recorded with certainty. One careful genealogical study of Thomas
Goble, compiled by Evelyn Goble Steen, suggests the family probably sailed on one of the ships that regularly carried
passengers to Massachusetts Bay in 1633 and 1634 — possibly the Abigail, the Hopewell, or the Lyon, all of which made
Atlantic crossings during this period. They brought with them their son John, who was approximately three or four years old.
The passage itself, whether on one of these named ships or another, would have been among the most harrowing experiences
of Thomas Goble's life. The Atlantic Crossing: Eight Weeks Between Worlds A crossing from England to Massachusetts Bay
in 1634 took, on average, eight to twelve weeks. The ships were small by modern standards — typically under 300 tons,
carrying anywhere from a hundred to several hundred passengers in addition to the crew and cargo. Passengers were crowded
into the lower decks in what were called "tweendecks" spaces: low-ceilinged, poorly ventilated, dark, and perpetually damp.
Hammocks or crude wooden berths were the sleeping arrangements. Meals were cooked communally when the weather

allowed, and when the weather did not allow — when storms drove the ship and the sea ran high — passengers could go days
without a cooked meal, subsisting on ship's biscuit and salt meat. Disease was the constant companion of the Atlantic
crossing. Typhus, dysentery, and scurvy were endemic on passenger ships of this era. Children were especially vulnerable.
Young mothers gave birth at sea. The elderly died en route. The historical record of the Great Migration ships is littered with
the small, private tragedies of families who embarked whole and arrived diminished. The Gobles arrived intact — we know
this because both Thomas and Alice were present at that August church admission — but the crossing would have tested them
in ways we can only partly imagine. What they would have seen as their ship finally entered Massachusetts Bay and made for
the anchorage at Charlestown: a harbor of extraordinary beauty, the wooded hills of the Massachusetts shore, the settlement
of Charlestown crowded onto a small peninsula between two rivers, the steepled meetinghouse already visible from the water.
After two or three months at sea, with England receding into memory and America resolving from rumor into reality, the sight
of land would have carried an almost religious force. For a Puritan family convinced they were enacting God's plan for a holy
commonwealth in the wilderness, arrival in Massachusetts Bay was arrival in the Promised Land. Charlestown and the First
Years: 1634–1638 Thomas Goble received his Freeman status — citizenship in the Massachusetts Bay Colony — on
September 3, 1634, just four days after his church admission, at a session of the General Court. He was the sixth in a sequence
of six Charlestown men to be admitted that day. Freeman status was essential: it conferred the right to vote in colonial
elections, to hold office, to participate in the governance of the colony. It was not given casually — it required church
membership and the attestation of one's good standing — and Thomas Goble received it within a week of his arrival. This
rapidity suggests he was not an unknown quantity; he may have had letters of recommendation from ministers in England, or
his standing in the Puritan community may have preceded him across the Atlantic. On January 10, 1634/5 (under the Old Style
calendar in which the new year began in March, a notation that creates the double-year references found in colonial records),
Thomas Goble was granted four acres of planting ground in Charlestown. By 1638, he had dramatically expanded his
landholdings. The Charlestown Book of Possessions records "Thomas Goble" as holding five distinct parcels: a half-acre at
the west end of the common with a dwelling house, four acres of arable land in the Line Field, commons for milch cows,
fifteen acres of woodland in Mystic Field, and fifty acres in the Water Field. This is a remarkable accumulation for a man who
had arrived in the colony only four years earlier. It confirms the impression of Thomas Goble as a man of energy, capability,
and practical intelligence. Their family continued to grow in the New World. Elizabeth Goble was born in 1634, possibly en
route or shortly after arrival — the ocean crossing itself may have been Alice's term. Thomas Jr. followed around 1635, Mary
on February 27, 1636, and Sarah in May of 1638. These were the children born in Charlestown, in the early years of a young
colony that was already transforming the Massachusetts landscape with furious rapidity. In October 1640, Thomas Goble
served on what may have been the first jury ever to convene in Boston — a remarkable civic distinction for a man only six
years arrived from England. He took an active role in the public life of the colony, and the colony recognized him for it. The
Ships of 1634 : What We Know The year 1634 was one of the peak years of the Great Migration. Ships arriving in
Massachusetts Bay that year included the Griffin (which carried the Puritan leader John Cotton and the famous Anne
Hutchinson), the Francis, the Mary and John, and several others. R. C. Anderson's authoritative Great Migration series, which
is the primary scholarly source for Thomas Goble's immigration, notes his arrival in 1634 but does not specify a ship — the
date of emigration and ship of passage are recorded as unknown. Thomas and Alice Goble arrived in Charlestown and were
admitted to the church on August 30, 1634: this we know with certainty from church records. Everything else about the
crossing itself must be reconstructed from the general history of the period. The best genealogical scholarship on the Goble
family, compiled by Evelyn Goble Steen, suggests the ship was probably the Abigail, the Hopewell, or the Lion, all of which
made the crossing in this period. The Lion, in particular, made multiple Atlantic voyages in the early 1630s and is associated
with several Puritan families who appear in Charlestown records alongside Thomas Goble. “Thomas Goble and Alice his wife
were admitted to the church in Charlestown.” — First Church of Charlestown, Massachusetts, August 30, 1634 ✦ ✦ ✦ P A R
T T H R E E The Concord Years — Building a Colonial Estate Chapter 3: Thomas Goble in Concord — Farmer, Taxpayer,

Patriarch At some point in the 1640s or early 1650s, Thomas Goble removed from Charlestown to Concord, the frontier town
that had been incorporated in 1635 and settled in the years following by some of the most determined of the Puritan
colonists. By the time of his death in 1657, his will identified him explicitly as "Thomas Goble of Concord." The house at
Charlestown, which his will specifically mentions — "my house at Charlestowne with all belongings thereto" — he left to Alice
for the term of her life, with instructions that it pass equally to the children at her death. But it was in Concord that the mature
years of Thomas Goble's American life were spent, and it is in Concord that his story reached its fullest expression. Concord
in the 1640s and 1650s was a frontier settlement in the most literal sense. It lay approximately eighteen miles northwest of
Boston, at what was then the edge of the English colonial world. Beyond Concord, the forest thickened, the trails became less
reliable, and the indigenous world pressed close against the English settlements. The town had been laid out around a
common, with a meetinghouse at its center — the meetinghouse being simultaneously the house of worship, the town hall,
and the social center of Puritan community life. Farms radiated outward from the center into land that was being steadily
cleared, fenced, and plowed. Concord, Massachusetts — the Colonial Inn, built 1716, stands as one of the surviving structures
from the era of the Goble family's settlement in Concord. The town where Thomas Goble farmed, paid taxes, paid Harvard
College tuition in grain, and wrote his will in November 1657 retains architectural elements continuous with his time. The
Goble farmhouse stood in this same landscape. The Farm at Concord: Land, Labor, and the Agricultural World Thomas
Goble's Concord farm was a working agricultural enterprise of the kind that sustained the colony's physical existence. The
land required constant labor: clearing stumps and stones, plowing, planting, cultivating, harvesting, preserving. The agricultural
year in seventeenth-century New England ran from the first plowing in April to the last harvest in October, with every month
in between filled with specific, demanding work. Thomas Goble grew wheat and Indian corn — documented in the Harvard
College tuition payments — and almost certainly maintained cattle, swine, and poultry as well. His estate inventory at death,
which included "one musket, two old swords and bandoliers," confirms that he was a farmer who also bore arms, as all male
colonists of military age were expected to do. The farmhouse itself — built sometime in the mid-1600s as the family
established itself in Concord — would have been constructed in the New England post-and-beam tradition: heavy timber
framing, mortise-and-tenon joints, a massive central chimney serving multiple fireplaces on each floor. The walls would have
been filled with wattle-and-daub or, as the colony matured, clapboard siding. The rooms were low-ceilinged, dark by modern
standards, and centered on the hearth, which served simultaneously as cooking surface, heat source, and the gathering point of
family life. Interior of a seventeenth-century New England colonial home, from The History of Our Country (published
1899). This illustration represents the kind of domestic interior Thomas and Alice Goble would have inhabited at their
Concord farmhouse: exposed timber beams, a great central hearth, rough-hewn furnishings, and the particular quality of light
that filtered through small leaded-glass windows into the dim, warm interior of the Puritan home. It was in a room very much
like this that Alice Brookman Goble raised their six children on the Massachusetts frontier. Alice Brookman Goble presided
over this interior world. In the Puritan household, the wife's domain was the home itself: the cooking, the preservation of
food, the making and mending of clothing, the care of children and animals, the management of a household economy that
required her to be simultaneously cook, nurse, seamstress, dairymaid, and keeper of accounts. Thomas Goble's will speaks of
Alice with clear affection and practical concern, bequeathing to her "the profit of all my stock so long as she keepeth a widow"
— a provision that gave her economic independence so long as she did not remarry. He trusted her to manage the estate. She
had earned that trust over decades of shared labor. Thomas Goble and Harvard College: A Farmer Funds America's First
University Among all the documented details of Thomas Goble's colonial life, one stands out for its remarkable historical
resonance. On December 13, 1653, a colonial court record identifies "goodman goobell" — Thomas Goble — as paying 1
pound, 16 shillings "in Indian" (corn) for tuition and fees to Harvard College. This payment was followed by a second on
January 15, 1654, of 1 pound "in wheatt and Indian," and a third on December 8, 1655, by "old gobbell" (again identified as
Thomas Goble by the Records of Court of Assistants) of 1 pound, 14 shillings, 6 pence — partly in wheat and partly in
Indian corn. Harvard College had been founded in 1636 by a vote of the Massachusetts Bay Colony General Court, which

appropriated £400 — almost half the colony's entire tax levy for that year — to establish an institution that would ensure the
colony did not, in the memorable phrase of the 1643 pamphlet New England's First Fruits, "leave an illiterate Ministry to the
Churches." The college was still a tiny and financially fragile institution in the 1650s, drawing its income from whatever the
surrounding community could provide. In a subsistence economy built on agricultural commodities rather than cash, "country
pay" — payment in corn, wheat, cattle, or other goods — was entirely normal. Harvard's early financial records document
exactly this: payments accepted in corn, in wheat, in cattle, in virtually any commodity that could be converted to use. The
index of the Records of Court of Assistants of the Colony of Massachusetts Bay identifies both "goodman goobell" and "old
gobbell" as Thomas Goble. This means that our Thomas Goble — the farmer from Aldingbourne, West Sussex, the man who
crossed the Atlantic with his wife and son in 1634, who built his farm and raised his family in Charlestown and Concord —
was among the early financial supporters of Harvard University, America's oldest institution of higher learning. He paid not in
coin, which he may not have had, but in the grain he grew on his Concord farm. The wheat and Indian corn of Thomas
Goble's fields fed the students of Harvard College, and Thomas Goble's name — however misspelled in the colonial record
— is part of the financial history of one of the world's great universities. “goodman goobell paid 1 pound, 16 shillings in
Indian for tuition and fees to Harvard College.” — Records of the Court of Assistants, Colony of Massachusetts Bay,
December 13, 1653 What does this mean for the Goble family? It means that before the Revolution, before Ohio, before any
of the chapters of the American Goble story that follow this one, a Goble stood at the material foundation of American
intellectual life and contributed what he had — his grain, his harvest, the produce of his labor — to ensure that learning
would survive on the American frontier. There is a quiet nobility in that. The Will of Thomas Goble, November 30, 1657 On
November 30, 1657 — a Monday in late autumn, with the Massachusetts winter already pressing down — Thomas Goble took
up his pen and wrote his will. He was approximately 66 years old. He knew, as all men of his age and condition knew, that time
was running short. The will he wrote is the most intimate documentary record we have of Thomas Goble as a person: his
concerns, his relationships, his sense of justice and obligation, his love for his family. The Wi l l of Thomas Goble , 1657 —
What M iddlesex County Probate Records Te l l Us Thomas Goble's will was dated November 30, 1657, proved December 29,
1657 (indicating he died sometime in December of that year), and inventoried December 11, 1657. The inventory preceded
the probate — suggesting he died very shortly after writing the will, perhaps within days. The will was drawn up formally:
"Thomas Goble of Concord..." He addressed his wife Alice first, leaving her "the profit of all my stock so long as she keepeth
a widow" and "my house at Charlestowne with all belongings thereto for term of life." This provision — the house in
Charlestown, the income from the estate's livestock — gave Alice material security as long as she remained unmarried. If she
remarried, the estate would be divided among the children. Thomas Goble, even in his final illness, was thinking practically
about his wife's welfare. He named "my three sons" — Thomas (the eldest, "being now in England"), Daniel, and a third
unnamed son who was not yet married — and "my three daughters," including Sarah, who was also not yet married. The eldest
son John appears to have remained in England (or died without issue before the will was executed), which explains his absence
from the named beneficiaries. His will specified that daughters were to receive one-third of what each son received — "one-
fourth part of my estate then in stock" — a provision that conformed to the Puritan understanding of equitable distribution
that nonetheless maintained the primogeniture-influenced hierarchy of the era. A later document, dated March 26, 1675 —
nearly twenty years after Thomas's death — records that Thomas Goble, Daniel Goble, Daniel Deane, and John Shepard of
Concord (along with John White of Sudbury) sold land earlier held by "our father Thomas Goble deceased." This document
confirms that the children of Thomas Goble divided and eventually sold their inheritance from the Concord farm, as the next
generation began to disperse across the wider colonial landscape. Primary Source: Middlesex County Probate Records; R. C.
Anderson, The Great Migration, Series 2, Vol. 3, p. 81; Evelyn Goble Steen genealogical compilation. Thomas Goble died in
December 1657, in Concord, Massachusetts, surrounded by the family he had built over nearly forty years of American life.
He died in the farmhouse he had built, in the town he had helped establish, on land he had cleared and cultivated and paid his
debts from. Alice Brookman Goble survived him, holding the estate in trust for the children as her husband had specified. She

had crossed the Atlantic as a young wife with a small child in tow. She had endured decades on the Massachusetts frontier,
borne and raised six children, managed a household and farm economy that would exhaust a modern person to contemplate.
She was still there when Thomas died. She was still there after him. 1 WikiTree, "Thomas Goble (abt. 1604–bef. 1657)"; R. C.
Anderson, The Great Migration, Series 2, Vol. 3, p. 81. 2 Evelyn Goble Steen, "Thomas (1) Goble" genealogical compilation,
FamilySearch Memories. 3 Records of the Court of Assistants of the Colony of Massachusetts Bay, Vol. 2; Charlestown Book
of Possessions (ChBOP), 1638. 4 Margery Somers Foster, "Out of Smalle Beginings...": An Economic History of Harvard
College in the Puritan Period, 1636–1712 (Belknap Press, 1962). ✦ ✦ ✦ P A R T F O U R King Philip's War and the Next
Generation Chapter 4: John Goble, Thomas Goble Jr., and the Sons on the Frontier The children of Thomas Goble and Alice
Brookman grew up on the colonial frontier in the truest sense of that term. Concord was not a comfortable English town
transplanted to America — it was an outpost of English civilization in an indigenous landscape that was watching, with
increasing alarm and anger, the expansion of English settlement across the land. The Goble children played and worked and
grew to adulthood in a world that was, beneath its Puritan surface of prayer and industry and scriptural order, a world on the
edge of violence. That violence came in 1675. King Philip's War — 1675–1676: The War That Shook New England to Its
Foundations King Philip's War — known in the Wampanoag tradition as Metacom's Resistance — was the most destructive
conflict, measured per capita in casualties relative to total population, in American history. More than three centuries later, it
retains that grim distinction. When it was over, approximately 600 English colonists had been killed in combat, thousands
more had died of disease and related causes, and twelve colonial towns had been completely destroyed. The proportion of the
total colonial population killed or displaced was larger than any subsequent American war, including the Civil War. The leader
of the indigenous resistance was Metacom — known to the English as King Philip — the sachem of the Pokanoket
Wampanoag, who had watched for years as English settlement encroached on Wampanoag lands, as English courts claimed
jurisdiction over Wampanoag people, and as the political sovereignty of the Wampanoag nation was systematically dismantled.
The crisis came to a head in the spring of 1675, when Plymouth Colony authorities hanged three Wampanoag men on
evidence that the colonial courts themselves acknowledged was questionable. The executions were read by Metacom and his
people as a final provocation, and on June 20, 1675, attacks began on English settlements in the Plymouth Colony. The war
spread rapidly. Through the summer and autumn of 1675, the Wampanoag and their allies — the Nipmuck, the Narragansett,
the Podunk — struck English settlements across a wide arc from Plymouth Colony through the Connecticut River valley and
into the Middlesex County towns northwest of Boston. Concord, where the Goble children had grown up, was directly in the
zone of conflict. The Great Swamp Massacre — December 19 , 1675 On December 19, 1675, one of the most brutal
engagements of King Philip's War took place in Rhode Island. A combined force of approximately 1,000 New England
militia, under Governor Josiah Winslow of Plymouth, attacked the main Narragansett winter encampment — a fortified
village built on an island in a great swamp in what is now South Kingstown, Rhode Island. The Narragansett, who had not yet
formally entered the war, were nonetheless suspected of harboring Wampanoag warriors and refugees. The attack was
devastating. Colonial soldiers broke through the Narragansett palisade, killed hundreds of Narragansett men, women, and
children, and set fire to the village. Estimates of Narragansett dead range from 300 to 600 people, though some historians
believe the true number was higher. The destruction of the winter village also meant the destruction of the Narragansett food
stores, condemning the survivors to starvation in the worst winter months. The Great Swamp Massacre did not end the war —
it intensified it. The surviving Narragansett joined Metacom's alliance in fury, and the winter of 1675–1676 saw the most
intense and widespread attacks on English settlements of the entire conflict. Concord was directly threatened. The Goble
family, farming their land in Concord through these months, lived through one of the most dangerous winters in colonial New
England history. The Capture of Thomas Goble Jr. and the Death of His Wife: February 1676 The winter of 1675–1676
brought the war directly to Concord. In February 1676, during a series of raids by indigenous war parties operating in the
Middlesex County region, Thomas Goble Jr. — the son of Thomas and Alice, born approximately 1631 in England and raised
in Charlestown and Concord — was captured by indigenous raiders. His wife, whose name has not been confirmed in the

primary records available to us, was killed in the attack. This event is documented in colonial records, though the primary
sources are fragmentary, as is so much of the documentation of individual colonial experiences during King Philip's War. The
Goble family capture is part of the larger pattern of raids in the Concord-Sudbury-Lancaster corridor during February 1676
— a month that was, by any accounting, the worst single month of the war for English settlements in Middlesex County. On
February 10, 1676, the town of Lancaster was attacked and Mary Rowlandson, the minister's wife, was taken captive in an
account that became one of the most famous narratives of colonial New England. Other towns were raided in the days and
weeks surrounding Lancaster's devastation. For Thomas Goble Jr., the February 1676 raid was a catastrophe. His wife was
dead. He himself had been taken — the experience of captivity among the indigenous peoples was, for most captives, a
passage through a world so alien to their own that it reshaped them permanently. Some captives were adopted into indigenous
families, some were ransomed back to the English settlements, some were killed. Thomas Goble Jr.'s fate after the capture —
whether he was ransomed, escaped, or was otherwise released — is not confirmed in the records currently available to this
research. What we know is this: his brother Daniel survived the war, and in March 1675 (actually 1675 by new style — this
predates the worst of the war, and the land sale document likely dates from March 1676), the surviving Goble siblings
collectively sold their inheritance from their father's estate. The family had endured. Thomas Goble's children, born on the
Massachusetts frontier, had faced the worst that frontier could offer, and they had not been destroyed by it. “The war is named
for Metacom, the Pokanoket chief and sachem of the Wampanoag, who watched as English settlement consumed the world
his father had inhabited. He chose to fight. The English colonists of Concord, including the sons of Thomas Goble, lived
through the consequences of that choice.” For a full account of King Philip's War and its meaning for the indigenous
peoples of New England, as well as the full documentary record of Thomas Goble Jr.'s captivity, see the Research Notes in
Appendix B of this volume, and the forthcoming supplementary historical narrative in Volume VI: The World They Inherited
— Indigenous History and the Goble Frontier. Chapter 5: Peter Goble and the Family After the War King Philip's War ended
in August 1676 with the killing of Metacom himself, his severed head displayed on a pike in Plymouth for twenty-five years as
a monument to colonial victory. The war was over, but its consequences for New England were profound and lasting. Twelve
towns had been destroyed. The colonial economy was severely disrupted. The indigenous peoples of southern New England
had been decimated — through death, enslavement, and dispersal — and the political landscape of the region was
permanently altered in favor of English expansion. For the Goble family, the war's end marked the beginning of a period of
reconstruction and expansion. The surviving sons of Thomas Goble — Thomas Jr., Daniel, and the children born in America
— rebuilt their lives in the postwar landscape of Middlesex County. Among the documented children, Peter Goble emerges as
a key figure in the continuation of the line. The Goble Line After Concord: Middlesex County and the Dispersal The late
seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries saw the Goble descendants spread outward from their Concord base. The pattern
was typical of New England families of this generation: as the founding generation died, as the original land grants were
divided among heirs, and as the frontier moved steadily outward, the sons of the founding generation scattered. Some stayed
in Middlesex County. Others moved to the newer settlements to the north and west. Still others, following a pattern that would
accelerate dramatically in the eighteenth century, began moving south and west — into Connecticut, into New York, into New
Jersey. It is through this southward and westward dispersal that the Goble line eventually found its way to New Jersey by the
mid-eighteenth century, and it is in New Jersey that the next great chapter of the Goble story — the Revolution — unfolded.
The Chi ldren of Thomas Goble Sr . — What the Record Confirms Thomas Goble's will and the various colonial records
associated with his name allow us to reconstruct his family with reasonable confidence, though not with complete certainty.
The children confirmed or strongly suggested by the documentary record include: • John Goble (b. c. 1629, England) — the
eldest son, who was "in England" at the time of his father's death in 1657. Anderson concludes he may have never come for
his portion, or died without issue; he does not appear in the 1675 land sale. • Thomas Goble Jr. (b. c. 1631, England) —
captured in the February 1676 raids near Concord; his wife was killed. Continued the line. • Elizabeth Goble (b. c. 1634) —
born en route to Massachusetts or shortly after arrival; later married into the Carter family. • Mary Goble (b. February 27,

1636, Charlestown) • Sarah Goble (b. May 1638, Charlestown) — "not yet married" at the time of the will; later married into
the Shepard family. • Daniel Goble — appears in the 1675/1676 land sale with Thomas Jr.; one of the sons who remained in
the Concord area. Note: Some genealogical sources list Peter Goble as an additional son; others conflate him with one of the
sons named in the will. The research on this remains open. What is confirmed is that the line continued through the sons of
Thomas Goble Sr. into the next century and ultimately into the New Jersey branch from which the Revolutionary War
generation descends. Primary Sources: Middlesex County Probate Records; Charlestown Church Records; R. C. Anderson,
The Great Migration, Series 2, Vol. 3; WikiTree profile for Thomas Goble (abt. 1604–bef. 1657). ✦ ✦ ✦ P A R T F I V E
The Revolutionary Era — Caleb Goble, Soldier and Spy Chapter 6: Caleb Goble — The Patriot of Morristown By the time
the generation of 1776 came of age, the Goble family had been in America for more than 140 years. They were, by any
measure, more American than English. Their English origins — the chalk downs of West Sussex, the parish church of
Aldingbourne, the world of James I and Charles I and Archbishop Laud — had receded into the distant past. They were New
England-formed in their religion and their values, and now they were New Jersey-settled in their daily lives. They were
colonists whose grandparents had been colonists, and they were watching, through the 1760s and into the 1770s, as the
relationship between those colonists and the British Crown deteriorated with accelerating speed toward open war. Caleb Goble
stepped forward from this background to serve the Revolution — not merely as a soldier in the line of battle, but as an
intelligence operative in the most dangerous of the war's operational theaters: the New Jersey borderlands, where the lines
between Patriot and Loyalist ran through families and farms and church congregations, and where the work of gathering and
transmitting intelligence was as essential to the Continental cause as any battle fought on any named field. Morristown, New
Jersey — The Hard Winter of 1779–1780 When historians remember the suffering of the Continental Army, they remember
Valley Forge — the winter of 1777–1778, the frozen encampment in Pennsylvania, the barefoot soldiers and the desperate
appeals to Congress. Valley Forge was real, and its suffering was real. But the winter of 1779–1780 at Morristown, New Jersey,
was worse. Measured by temperature, by snowfall, by the duration of suffering, and by the proportional casualties sustained,
the Morristown winter was the hardest the Continental Army ever endured. General Washington moved his army into the
Jockey Hollow area outside Morristown beginning December 1, 1779. What greeted them — and what continued to assault
them through February and March of 1780 — was the worst winter of the entire eighteenth century. Twenty-six snowstorms
struck New Jersey over the course of that winter, including six blizzards. Every saltwater inlet from North Carolina to Canada
froze over. New York Harbor froze solid enough for British soldiers to march on the ice from Manhattan to Staten Island.
When Washington's soldiers arrived at Jockey Hollow in November 1779, they found a foot of snow already on the ground.
Snowfalls during the winter dropped more than four feet at a time, with drifts over six feet burying the roads and fences that
marked the landscape. "We experienced one of the most tremendous snowstorms ever remembered; no man could endure its
violence many minutes without danger to his life. ... When the storm subsided, the snow was from four to six feet deep,
obscuring the very traces of the roads by covering fences that lined them." — Surgeon's account, Continental Army,
Morristown encampment, winter 1779– 1780 Washington's troops — an estimated 10,000 to 12,000 men — built a "log house
city" of more than a thousand wooden structures in the Jockey Hollow forest, cutting down thousands of acres of timber to
construct shelters that, despite their construction, proved inadequate against the cold. Desertions and deaths reduced the
effective force to approximately 8,000, of whom Washington estimated that one-third were unfit for duty. The provisioning
system collapsed entirely: roads were impassable, supply wagons could not move, and the army was, at various points during
the winter, literally starving. "We were absolutely literally starved — I do solemnly declare that I did not put a single morsel of
victuals into my mouth for four days and as many nights, except for a little black birch bark which I gnawed off a stick of
wood." — Private Joseph Plumb Martin, Connecticut Line, Morristown, 1780 In January 1780, two regiments of the New
Jersey Line mutinied — driven to desperation by a combination of hunger, cold, and the knowledge that the civilian
population around Morristown was, comparatively, well supplied while the soldiers starved. Washington suppressed the mutiny,
but he understood its cause. He wrote to Congress in the aftermath that "the oldest people now living in this Country do not

remember so hard a winter as the one we are now emerging from." Caleb Goble: Intelligence Operative in the New Jersey
Borderlands It was into this context — the frozen siege of Morristown, the intelligence war being fought daily in the New
Jersey countryside between Continental forces and the Tory population — that Caleb Goble's service falls. The New Jersey of
1779–1780 was one of the most politically divided places in all of revolutionary America. The state had a substantial Loyalist
population — particularly among the older-established families of the coastal regions and the farming communities of the
interior. Tory militias operated in the countryside, passing information to the British garrison in New York City, harassing
Patriot families, and providing cover for British raiding parties. Intelligence work in this environment was essential and
extraordinarily dangerous. Washington was deeply aware of the intelligence dimension of the New Jersey theater — his own
network of spies and informants (the famous Culper Ring was operating simultaneously in New York) was one of the most
sophisticated intelligence operations of the war. In the local New Jersey context, men like Caleb Goble — men who knew the
roads and farms and personalities of the local area, who could move through the countryside without arousing suspicion, who
had relationships with neighbors on both sides of the political divide — were invaluable. The specific details of Caleb Goble's
service — the precise units he served with, the pension records that document his service, the county histories that mention
him by name — are the proper subject of continued primary-source research. Revolutionary War pension records are held at
the National Archives in Record Group 15 (Pension and Bounty Land Warrant Application Files, microfilm series M804), and
New Jersey state archives maintain compiled service records for militia units of the period. These records should be among
the first priorities for the next phase of this genealogical project. Ca leb Goble — Research Status and Pr imary Sources to
Pursue Caleb Goble's Revolutionary War service is part of the Goble family oral and genealogical tradition. To fully document
and verify his service, the following primary sources should be consulted: • National Archives, Record Group 15:
Revolutionary War Pension and Bounty Land Warrant Application Files (M804). Search for "Caleb Goble" or variants. Pension
files contain service depositions, family information, and sometimes detailed accounts of military activities. • Compiled Service
Records of Soldiers, Revolutionary War (M881, RG 93): These carded records abstract muster rolls and pay lists for soldiers in
the Continental Army and state militia. • New Jersey State Archives: Revolutionary War Record Search, including compiled
service cards and manuscript sources for New Jersey militia units, particularly those operating in the Morristown area. • New
Jersey County Histories: Morris County histories published in the nineteenth century frequently contain rosters and
biographical notices for Revolutionary War participants from the county. The intelligence operative tradition associated with
Caleb Goble is part of the family's historical understanding of his service. This tradition deserves primarysource verification
and is assigned Research Priority 2 in Appendix D. “George Washington wrote to Congress that 'the oldest people now living
in this Country do not remember so hard a winter as the one we are now emerging from.' Caleb Goble endured that winter,
and the family he came home to built Ohio.” Chapter 7: From Jersey to the Frontier — The Ohio Migration The American
Revolution ended with the Treaty of Paris in September 1783. For a soldier like Caleb Goble, returning from service to the
New Jersey he had left, the postwar world was both familiar and transformed. The political landscape had been remade — the
Loyalists had fled or been suppressed, the British garrisons had departed, and the new United States was beginning the
uncertain experiment of self-governance. But for ordinary farming families in New Jersey, the more immediately pressing
reality was economic: the war had disrupted agriculture, depreciated currency, and left debts. And there was land. There was
always the question of land. The Northwest Ordinance and the Opening of Ohio In July 1787, the Continental Congress
passed the Northwest Ordinance — one of the most consequential pieces of legislation in American history. The Ordinance
organized the territory northwest of the Ohio River (what would become Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin)
into an orderly system for territorial governance and eventual statehood. Critically, it established that the Northwest Territory
would be free of slavery — a provision that would shape the political character of Ohio for generations — and it laid out a
framework for the survey and sale of public land that made the territory accessible to ordinary farming families. The migration
to Ohio that followed the Ordinance was one of the great demographic movements in American history. From New England,
from New Jersey, from Pennsylvania and Virginia and Kentucky, families loaded their wagons and walked or rode west to the

Ohio River, crossed over, and staked their claims in the new territory. The routes were multiple: the Great Wagon Road from
Pennsylvania down the Shenandoah Valley, across the Cumberland Gap and into Kentucky, then north over the Ohio River.
Or the more northerly route through Pennsylvania over the Alleghenies and down to the Ohio at Pittsburgh, then by flatboat
down the river to the settlements around Marietta or Cincinnati or the river towns of the southern Ohio shore. The Goble line
followed this general tide. The specific decade of their Ohio arrival — whether in the early territorial years of the 1790s and
1800s, or in the flood tide of migration that peaked in the 1810s and 1820s — is a question that continued primary-source
research in Ohio land records and county histories can answer. What is certain is the destination: Madison County and
Franklin County in the heart of central Ohio, the same counties where the living Goble family makes its home today. Madison
County, Ohio — The Settled Land Madison County was established by the Ohio General Assembly in 1820, carved from the
frontier territory of central Ohio. Its county seat is London, Ohio. West Jefferson, the town where Kevin and Penny Goble
live today at 163 South Chester Street, lies in the eastern part of Madison County, just inside the Madison-Franklin County
line. In the early nineteenth century, this was rich agricultural land — the same broad central Ohio plain that the glaciers of the
last Ice Age had smoothed and enriched over millennia, leaving behind some of the most fertile soil in North America. The
Gobles who came to Madison County and the surrounding Franklin County area came as farmers, as the family had always
been farmers. From the chalk downs of West Sussex to the cleared land of Concord to the New Jersey farmsteads to the Ohio
frontier, the Goble identity has been rooted in the land. They knew how to read soil and weather, how to build a house and
clear a field, how to survive a winter and plan for the next planting season. These were the skills that Thomas Goble had
brought across the Atlantic in 1634, and they were the skills that his descendants carried west across the continent over the
following two centuries. For the full documentation of the Ohio land records, county histories, and migration routes
specific to the Goble line's arrival in Madison and Franklin Counties, see Appendix B: Source Notes, and Research Priority 3 in
Appendix D. ✦ ✦ ✦ P A R T S I X The LeCompte Connection — A Note on Corrected Ancestry Chapter 8: Lena Rae
LeCompte Goble — The French Acadian Heritage Robert Kevin Goble descends not only from the English Puritan world of
Thomas Goble of Sussex and Concord. Through his mother, Lena Rae LeCompte Goble (1937–2014), Kevin descends from
a second great stream of American heritage — one that is as French and Catholic as the Goble line is English and Puritan, one
that flows from the farmlands of Picardie through the city of Québec, through the bayou parishes of Louisiana, through the
heartbreak of the Grand Dérangement, and finally up the Ohio River to Scioto County and West Jefferson. This is the
LeCompte line — and before we can tell it properly, we must clear up a significant genealogical confusion that has complicated
this research. IMPORTANT CORRECTION : The Mary land LeCompte Line Is a Separate Fami ly In the course of
researching the Goble family's LeCompte ancestry, a distinction of fundamental importance has emerged: the Goble family's
LeCompte heritage does NOT descend from the famous Maryland "Blind Patriarch" Moses LeCompte line. The Maryland
LeCompte family traces from Antoine LeCompte of Calais (c. 1620) and his son Moses LeCompte of Maryland — a
prominent Huguenotorigin family who settled on the Eastern Shore of Maryland in the seventeenth century and whose
descendants include many notable Maryland and Virginia families. This is a large and well-documented genealogical tree with
thousands of confirmed descendants. The Goble family's LeCompte line is a distinct, separate French family that shares the
surname but is not related to the Maryland Moses LeCompte line. Both are French surnames ("le compte" — the
accountant/count), and both emigrated from France to the New World, but they are different families who settled in different
colonies (Louisiana vs. Maryland) at different times and through entirely different migration routes. This distinction matters
because significant amounts of online genealogical material conflate the two families. Any research that traces the Goble
LeCompte line back through Maryland should be treated with skepticism unless it can independently verify the connection
through primary sources. The Goble family's confirmed LeCompte ancestry traces through a French Catholic Acadian line —
from Picardie and Brittany through Québec, through colonial Louisiana, and up the Ohio River to Ohio. See Appendix C for a
full note on the Maryland Moses LeCompte line and the reasons for the distinction. The True LeCompte Line — Generation

generation, with source citations for each confirmed individual. This is the lineage as it has been verified through primary

the Ohio River Among the LeCompte ancestors of the modern Goble family, Oscar "Frenchie" Raymond LeCompte occupies
a place of particular poignancy. He was born in 1915, the son of Joseph Edward LeCompte and Carman E. Moore. His
mother died in 1921, when Raymond was six years old. Joseph Edward LeCompte lived on to the extraordinary age of 95,
dying in 1989 — thirty years after his own son Raymond. To outlive your child by three decades is one of the most painful
experiences a parent can know, and Joseph Edward LeCompte carried that loss for most of his long life. Raymond LeCompte
grew up without his mother, in Ohio, carrying the French Acadian heritage of his Louisiana-born grandfather Sylvestre in his
blood and, evidently, in the nickname that followed him through life: "Frenchie." The nickname was not casual or accidental
— it reflected something that everyone around Raymond could see. He looked French. He was French, or felt French, in some
way that registered to the people of the Ohio River country where he lived and worked. The Acadian identity — that fierce,

particular sense of cultural continuity that had survived deportation and dispersal and a century of forced assimilation — had
not entirely vanished, even in the Ohio of the mid-twentieth century. Raymond LeCompte worked in New Boston, Ohio — a
river town in Scioto County, on the north bank of the Ohio River just west of Portsmouth. New Boston was, in the mid-
twentieth century, a working-class industrial community whose economy centered on steel production. The Detroit Steel
Corporation had a major plant in the area. Raymond LeCompte died in 1959 at the age of 43 — a young death, the kind of
death that comes from the physical demands of industrial labor, from the stresses of a working-class life in the Ohio River
towns. He left behind his daughter Lena Rae, who would marry into the Goble family and give birth to Kevin. The Grand
Dérangement — The Expuls ion of the Acadians , 1755– 1764 The Acadian heritage that runs through the LeCompte line to
Kevin Goble and his sons is inseparable from one of the most traumatic events in North American history: the Grand
Dérangement — the Expulsion of the Acadians. The Acadians were the French-speaking Catholic settlers of what is now
Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island — communities established in the early seventeenth century that had
farmed the tidal lands of the Maritime provinces for five generations by the time the British finally seized control of the
region. The Acadians had attempted a precarious neutrality in the long wars between Britain and France, refusing to take
unconditional oaths of loyalty to either crown. Britain finally lost patience. Beginning on August 10, 1755, and continuing
through 1764, the British undertook the systematic forced removal of approximately 11,500 Acadians from their homelands.
Families were separated, farms and homes were burned, people were loaded onto ships and dispersed to British colonies from
Massachusetts to Georgia, to France, to England, and eventually to Louisiana. Of an estimated 14,100 Acadians,
approximately 5,000 died of disease, starvation, or shipwreck during the Expulsion and its aftermath. It is recognized by
historians and by the Canadian government as one of the great atrocities of the colonial era. Many of the dispersed Acadians
eventually made their way to Louisiana, which was then under French and later Spanish control and where a French-speaking
Catholic community already existed. It is in this Louisiana context that the LeCompte family's American history is rooted —
and it is the Louisiana Acadian community, later known as the Cajuns, that forms the specific cultural and ethnic identity of
the Goble family's French ancestral heritage. The Le Bon Papa and its sister ships of 1785 were, in a direct sense, the final
chapter of the Grand Dérangement — the last major organized movement of Acadian exiles from France to their new
Louisiana home. The Le Bon Papa — The Ship That Carried the Acadian Network On May 10, 1785, a French frigate called
the Le Bon Papa — "the Good Grandfather" — departed from the port of Paimboeuf, near Nantes, on the Atlantic coast of
France. Under the command of Captain Pelletier, the ship carried 156 passengers — 34 to 36 family groupings — on an
eighty-one-day Atlantic crossing to New Orleans, Louisiana. They arrived on July 29, 1785. During the crossing, the weather
was favorable and the ship was free of disease — a mercy, given the terrible losses that Atlantic crossings could exact. One
death was reported: a young daughter of Eustache Govin, who did not survive to see Louisiana. The Le Bon Papa was the
first of seven ships that carried Acadian exiles from France to Spanish Louisiana in 1785. The seven ships together
transported approximately 1,584 people — families who had spent years, in many cases decades, in exile in France after the
Grand Dérangement, waiting for the chance to return to a French-speaking Catholic world. Louisiana, under Spanish rule but
overwhelmingly French in culture, was the closest thing available. Among the ancestral network connected to the Goble
family's LeCompte line through the Acadian community, the following individuals are confirmed or strongly suggested by
documentary evidence: ● Simon Babin (1735–1780) and Anastasie Theriot (1741–1775) — directly confirmed in Raymond
LeCompte's ancestral network. The Babin and Theriot surnames are among the oldest and most prominent of the Acadian
founding families. ● Pierre I. Heuze (1723–1783) and Cecile Bourg (1736–1797) — documented on the Le Bon Papa
passenger manifest. The Bourg family is another of the core Acadian surnames. ● The Joanes family — Françoise Joanes, who
married Jean B. Lecompte in Generation 3, connects the LeCompte line to the Joanes family of colonial Louisiana: Philibert
Joanes (1681–1756) and Claudine Joanes (1670–1731). ● The Breaux family — Madeleine C. Breaux, who married Sylvestre R.
LeCompte in Generation 7, carries one of the most ancient and distinguished Acadian surnames into the LeCompte/Goble
family tree. ● The Melançon family — connected through the extended Acadian network of the Louisiana parishes. "The Le

Bon Papa departed Paimboeuf on May 10, 1785, with 156 Acadians aboard — 34 families, three of whom came from Belle-
Île-en-Mer. After 81 days at sea, they arrived at New Orleans on July 29. Thirty-seven of the 38 family groupings settled along
the Mississippi River near St. Gabriel, Louisiana." — Passenger records, Le Bon Papa , 1785; Gérard-Marc Braud, From
Nantes to Louisiana (La Rainette, 2001) The connection between the Le Bon Papa passenger network and the LeCompte
family of the Goble line is established through the shared Acadian community of Louisiana — the interconnected web of
families (Babin, Theriot, Heuze, Bourg, Joanes, Breaux, Melançon, LeCompte) who formed the Cajun world of south
Louisiana and whose descendants eventually made their way northward to Ohio through the migrations of the late nineteenth
and early twentieth centuries. For the full account of the Acadian heritage — the Grand Dérangement, the Louisiana
settlement, the Cajun cultural formation, and the complete LeCompte genealogy from Simon Vincent Lecompte through Lena
Rae LeCompte Goble — see Volume II: The LeCompte Line — From Picardie to the Bayou and Up the Ohio River. ✦ ✦ ✦
P A R T S E V E N The Living Family — West Jefferson and the Goble Legacy Chapter 9: The Goble Family Today West
Jefferson, Ohio, sits in the broad flat country of Madison County, about twenty-five miles west of Columbus on Route 40 —
the old National Road, the first federally funded highway in American history, which ran from Cumberland, Maryland, to
Vandalia, Illinois, and which carried hundreds of thousands of settlers west through Ohio in the early nineteenth century. The
town is small and settled, with the particular quality of the small Ohio towns that grew up along the National Road corridor: a
main street, a courthouse square in the county seat of London nearby, churches of multiple Protestant denominations, and the
surrounding farmland that has been the economic base of Madison County since the first Ohio settlers arrived in the 1800s.
The Goble family home at 163 South Chester Street is on a residential street in West Jefferson — the kind of address that
grounds a family in a specific, particular place, that gives them roots in the Ohio soil as concrete and real as the roots Thomas
Goble put down in Concord in the 1640s. This is the address that Kevin and Penny have kept, the house that Zac left when he
went west and that Shane returned to when he came home. It is the family's anchor in the present, just as the Concord farm
was the family's anchor in the seventeenth century. Kevin Goble — The Cancer Sun Dynasty One of the most remarkable
patterns to emerge from this ancestral research is what might be called the Cancer sun dynasty of the Goble line. Kevin Goble
was born July 20, 1962 — a Cancer sun, the sign of home, memory, ancestry, and the keeper of family bonds. His ancestor
Thomas Goble Sr. is estimated to have been born around the winter of 1590–1591, in or near Westergate in Aldingbourne
Parish — placing his birth potentially within the Cancer range of the solar year. His mother Lena Rae LeCompte Goble was
born in 1937 — and the LeCompte ancestral connection through the Cancer sun pattern is one of the fascinating resonances
that the astrological dimension of this project has uncovered. The Cancer archetype — the sign ruled by the Moon, associated
with home, family, memory, ancestry, and the nourishing of those we love — runs through the Goble line like a thread of
recognition. Thomas Goble, the colonial farmer who paid Harvard College in the grain of his fields, was a Cancer archetype: a
man who built a home in a new world and filled it with children and fed it with his labor. Kevin Goble, the patriarch of 163
South Chester Street, is his descendant in the most direct sense. For the full astrological analysis of the Cancer sun dynasty
in the Goble ancestral line, including natal chart comparisons across generations, see Volume V, Chapter 2: The Cancer Sun
Dynasty — From Thomas Goble to Robert Kevin Goble. Penny Sue Riffe-Goble — The Mountain Matriarch The Scorpio
sun of Penny Sue Riffe-Goble is the other pole of the family's astrological portrait — the deep, penetrating, surviving intensity
of the Appalachian mountain heritage meeting and complementing the nurturing, home-centered depth of the Cancer-sun
Goble patriarch. Penny's Riffe heritage — the full account of which is reserved for Volume III — brings to the Goble family
the fighting spirit of the Kentucky and West Virginia borderlands, the tradition of self-reliance and fierce loyalty that
characterized the Scots-Irish and German-descended families of the Appalachian ridge. Together, Kevin and Penny Goble
embody the two great American frontier traditions that meet in their family: the Puritan New England tradition of the Goble
paternal line (discipline, learning, civic responsibility, the covenant community) and the Appalachian mountain tradition of the
Riffe maternal line (independence, survival, fierce family loyalty, the community of the hollow and the ridge). Shane and Zac
are the inheritors of both. For the complete account of Penny Sue Riffe-Goble's Riffe and Potter heritage — the

Appalachian origins, the Kentucky mountain communities, the migration to Ohio — see Volume III: The Riffe-Potter
Heritage — Mountain Borderlanders and the Making of Penny Sue Goble. Zachary and Shane — The Next Generation
Zachary Goble, the eldest son, has carried the Goble name to its westernmost expression yet: from Madison County, Ohio, to
Los Angeles to San Diego. He has done what every generation of Gobles has done — gone to the frontier, wherever the
frontier happens to be in their historical moment. In Thomas Goble's century, the frontier was Concord. In Caleb Goble's
century, the frontier was the Ohio Territory. In Zachary Goble's century, the frontier is the Pacific Coast. Shane Alexander
Goble, the youngest son, has done something different and equally essential: he has stayed, or come back. He was born
outside Ohio — the only Goble of his immediate family born outside the state — and he returned. He is keeping the record.
He is the family's memory in the most literal sense, the person who sat down and began pulling the threads of this four-
hundred-year story out of the archives and genealogical databases and family histories where they had been waiting, and
weaving them into a narrative that the whole family could read. This is the oldest human task: remembering who we are. Every
civilization that has endured has had its memory-keepers — the people who understood that the future depends on knowing
the past, that identity is not simply who you are today but who you are in the full context of everyone who made you possible.
Shane Alexander Goble has taken on that task for the Goble family. The series of which this volume is the first is the result.

Note on the Moses LeCompte of Maryland — Why He Is Not Our Ancestor The "Blind Patriarch" Moses LeCompte of
Maryland is one of the most prominently documented LeCompte families in American genealogical literature. His ancestor,
Antoine LeCompte of Calais (c. 1620), emigrated from northern France to the English colonies in the seventeenth century,
and Moses LeCompte established himself on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, where his descendants became prominent in
Maryland colonial society. His line has thousands of confirmed descendants and is extensively documented in published
genealogies, county histories, and online databases. The Goble family's LeCompte ancestry is not this family. The confusion

arises naturally from several converging factors: both families bear the same French surname ("LeCompte," "Lecompte," or
"Leconte" — spelling variants are common in both lines); both are of French origin; and both eventually have American
descendants in the general South-to-Ohio migration corridor. Online genealogical databases, which aggregate usersubmitted
family trees without always verifying the connecting links, frequently merge the two families — attaching the well-documented
Maryland Moses LeCompte line to individuals who are, in fact, members of the entirely separate Louisiana Acadian LeCompte
family. The distinguishing markers are clear: ● Geography: The Maryland LeCompte family settled in Maryland and the
Chesapeake Tidewater region. The Goble family's LeCompte line is documented in Québec, Canada, and then in Louisiana —
specifically in the Acadian communities of south Louisiana. ● Religion: The Maryland LeCompte family was Huguenot
(French Protestant) in origin. The Goble family's LeCompte line is French Catholic — confirmed by the Québec Catholic
parish records (NotreDame de Québec, Drouin Collection) and the Acadian Catholic community identity. ● Migration pattern:
The Maryland LeCompte family's Ohio descendants came through the Maryland-Virginia-Ohio migration corridor. The Goble
family's LeCompte line came through the Louisiana-Mississippi-Ohio migration corridor — up the Ohio River from the south.
● Primary sources: The Goble family's LeCompte line is confirmed by the Drouin Collection (Québec Catholic parish

Van der Keere. Simon Vincent Lecompte was born in Ramecourt, Aisne, in the northeastern reaches of this province, in 1649,
a generation after this map was drawn. The province that shaped him is visible here: a land of rolling plains, river valleys, and
ancient villages, bounded to the north by Flanders and to the east by Champagne. (Image: Buyenlarge/Getty Images) Your
oldest known ancestor in the LeCompte line drew his first breath on a cool October morning in 1649, in a village so small that
it leaves almost no trace in the grand narratives of French history. Ramecourt, in the Aisne department of Picardie, northern
France — a hamlet of farmers and craftsmen tucked into the ancient agricultural plain that has been worked since Roman
times. Simon Vincent Lecompte's world was one of small stone churches, rutted farm lanes, and the slow rhythm of planting
and harvest that had governed life in this corner of France for a thousand years before his birth. But that world, which seemed
so timeless, had been anything but stable. The France of Simon Vincent Lecompte's childhood had been torn apart within
living memory by the Wars of Religion — the savage conflict between French Catholics and French Protestants (Huguenots)
that had consumed the sixteenth century and bled into the seventeenth. Picardie itself was not a stranger to this violence. The
province sat directly in the path of Spanish armies invading from the south Netherlands, and it bore the scars of conflict in its
burned villages and restless frontiers. Simon was born eleven years after the Peace of Westphalia (1648) was supposed to have
settled Europe's religious wars — but the peace was fragile, the wounds were fresh, and the Edict of Nantes (which had
granted Huguenots limited religious freedom since 1598) would be revoked by Louis XIV in 1685, just two years after the
greatest tragedy of Simon's life. In this world of religious uncertainty, the Lecompte family of Ramecourt was Catholic. This is

an important distinction. The surname Lecompte — literally "the count" in French, most likely an occupational or status
surname for someone who counted, kept accounts, or served in an administrative role for a noble household — appeared in
both Catholic and Huguenot communities across France. Your family's line is the Catholic branch: baptized, married, and
buried in the Roman Catholic parish, embedded in the rhythms of the Catholic liturgical year, faithful to the Church that
would follow them to New France, to Louisiana, and into Ohio over the next three centuries. The Double Marriage of New
Year's Eve, 1671 The documentary record of Simon Vincent Lecompte's life begins in earnest on the last day of 1671, when
the parish records of Guignes, Seine-et-Marne, record something extraordinary: on 31 December 1671, Simon Vincent
Lecompte is recorded as marrying both Marie Catherine Mercier (born 1643, then 28 years old) and Jeanne Seredot (born
1645, then 26 years old). Both marriages are recorded on the same date, at the same Catholic parish. "Two marriages, one date,
one Catholic parish, one New Year's Eve in the village of Guignes — this is among the most unusual entries in the confirmed
family record." How do we interpret this? The Catholic Church, of course, does not permit polygamy. Several explanations are
possible, and the honest answer is that without the original parish register in hand, we cannot be certain which is correct. The
most likely explanation is that this represents a double-wedding ceremony — Simon marrying one woman, and a close male
relative or neighbor marrying the other woman, at a combined ceremony recorded by a clerk who listed both brides under
Simon's name through error or abbreviated record-keeping. This was not uncommon in 17th-century French parish records,
particularly in smaller villages where a single ceremony might serve multiple couples. A second possibility — less likely but
worth noting — is that one of the two marriages is recorded in error, a misfiled or duplicated entry reflecting only one actual
wife. The fact that both women lived in the same place, died on the same day, and were connected to the same household
suggests they may indeed have cohabited in Simon's life — possibly as sisters who both became his wives sequentially (one
woman dying shortly after marriage, the other taking her place), with the records collapsing two events into a single date entry.
What the records make clear is that Simon Vincent Lecompte was connected to both Marie Catherine Mercier and Jeanne
Seredot, and that he was the father of children by at least one of them. The son Jean Baptiste, born 25 October 1674 in
Guignes, is confirmed as Simon's son — and Marie Catherine Mercier is identified as his mother in the genealogical sources.
Whether Jeanne Seredot bore children who did not survive, or whether she served as a second mother to Jean Baptiste, we do
not yet know. September 11, 1683: The Day Both Women Died The most shocking entry in Simon Vincent Lecompte's
documented record arrives twelve years after the wedding. On 11 September 1683, both Marie Catherine Mercier and Jeanne
Seredot died — on the same day, in Guignes, Seine-et-Marne. Think for a moment what this means. Simon Vincent Lecompte,
33 years old, lost both of the women in his household on a single September day. And his son Jean Baptiste Lecompte — your
direct ancestor — was eight years old when both of his mothers vanished from the world on the same Tuesday in early
autumn. What Killed Them? The Epidemics of 17th-Century France The death of two women in the same household on the
same day in September 1683 almost certainly reflects an epidemic event sweeping through Guignes. The most probable
candidates: • Bubonic Plague: Though the worst plague outbreaks in France were in the previous century, localized outbreaks
occurred throughout the 1600s, particularly in northern France. Plague was still present in France as late as the 1720 Marseille
outbreak. • Typhus: Spread by lice and fleas, typhus swept through cramped communities with brutal speed, particularly in the
late summer and early autumn months when populations were gathered for harvest. • Dysentery / Enteric Fever:
Contaminated water supplies in agricultural villages made summer and early autumn the peak season for intestinal disease
mortality. • Smallpox: Major smallpox epidemic waves passed through France repeatedly in the 17th century, capable of killing
multiple household members in rapid succession. In any of these scenarios, the village of Guignes in September 1683 was
almost certainly in the grip of community-wide illness, and Simon and Jean Baptiste survived what the two women could not.
The silence that must have descended on that household in Guignes on the evening of 11 September 1683 is beyond our
power to fully imagine. Simon Vincent was not yet 35 years old. Jean Baptiste was 8. The harvest was coming in. The village
church would have rung the death knell — once for each year of the deceased's life, the slow counting toll that everyone in a
small village could hear from their fields and cottages. And on that September day, the bell tolled twice, a long time. An

Extraordinary Life: 81 Years Simon Vincent Lecompte outlived both his wives by nearly half a century. He lived until 12 April
1731 — dying at the extraordinary age of 81, at a time when average life expectancy in France rarely exceeded 35 to 40 years.
Most men of his era were dead before their sons were grown. Simon watched his son Jean Baptiste emigrate to Canada, marry
twice, and raise a family across the Atlantic Ocean — and he was still alive in Guignes, or somewhere in France, for the first
decades of his grandchildren's lives in New France. What kept him alive? We cannot know. Genetics, certainly. Perhaps
temperament — the kind of steady, grounded disposition that endures hardship rather than breaking under it. Perhaps the
same quality that his descendants would demonstrate again and again across twelve generations: an extraordinary will to
survive. The Brittany Mystery: Why Was He Buried in Quévert? Here is one of the most intriguing puzzles in Simon's
documented record. The death record states clearly: Simon Vincent Lecompte died on 12 April 1731 in Guignes, Seine-et-
Marne, Île-de-France — southeast of Paris, in the country where he had lived for most of his adult life. But his burial record,
from the Upper Brittany, France Deaths & Burials collection, places him in Quévert, Côtes-d'Armor, Brittany — on the same
date. Quévert is not near Guignes. It is a Breton village in the very northwest of France, hundreds of miles from Île-de-
France, near the ancient town of Dinan in the Côtes-d'Armor department. For a man to die in one province and be buried
hundreds of miles away in another province on the same day is, physically, impossible in 1731. The most logical explanations
are: 1. Family in Brittany: Simon had family connections in Brittany — perhaps through a third relationship after his wives died
in 1683, or through extended family who had migrated to Brittany over the decades. He may have actually died in Brittany,
with the Guignes death record reflecting an administrative error or a delayed filing of an older record from his period of
residence there. 2. Return to Ancestral Homeland: It was common in 17th–18th century France for elderly individuals to
return to their family's ancestral region to die among relatives. If Simon had Breton family connections, he may have
undertaken the journey to Brittany in his final years, dying there at 81 while his last recorded residence remained associated
with Guignes. 3. Two Men Named Simon Vincent Lecompte: A more prosaic explanation — there may have been a second
person of the same name in the records, and the Quévert burial refers to a different individual. However, the same death date
argues against coincidence. The Brittany burial, whatever its explanation, is a clue that Simon Vincent Lecompte's life was
larger, and more widely connected across France, than the sparse records fully reveal. For future researchers in this family: the
parish records of Quévert, Côtes-d'Armor, and the surrounding Breton villages may hold the answer. "He was born in
Picardie, lived in Île-de-France, and was buried in Brittany. In between, he survived plague, outlived two wives by half a
century, and watched his son sail for the New World. Simon Vincent Lecompte was the first of a long line of survivors." The
name he passed to his son — Lecompte — would cross the Atlantic, descend the Mississippi, plant itself on the Louisiana
bayous, ride a flatbed north to Ohio, and arrive, three centuries later, in the blood of Lena Rae LeCompte Goble, who stood
in a West Jefferson schoolroom and taught Ohio's children year after year after year. All of it began in Ramecourt, in 1649,
with a farmer's son who lived to be 81 and was buried in a province far from where he was born. ✦ ✦ ✦ P a r t T w o New
