of 1683, in the village of Guignes southeast of Paris, when the plague or fever or whatever dark thing swept through that
September took both women from his household in a single day. Jean Baptiste Lecompte grew up in the shadow of that loss,
raised by his father Simon — who was himself barely 34 years old, newly bereaved, and managing a household and farm with
a child and no wife. What was Jean Baptiste's world like in the years between 1683 and his departure for New France? He grew
up in Guignes, in the Seine-et-Marne department south of Paris, during the reign of Louis XIV — the Sun King at the height
of his power. The 1680s and 1690s were decades of constant French warfare: the Nine Years' War (1688–1697) drained France
of men and money, and the countryside was periodically stripped by military levies and taxation. For a young man with no
aristocratic connections and limited prospects in Île-de-France, the call of New France was compelling. The Call of New
France New France — la Nouvelle-France — was the vast French colonial territory in North America: Québec, Acadia
(present-day Nova Scotia and New Brunswick), and the great river territories stretching south through the Great Lakes to the
Gulf of Mexico. Since the founding of Québec by Samuel de Champlain in 1608, the French Crown had struggled to populate
its colony. The famous filles du roi program (the King's Daughters, young women sent to New France as brides for male
colonists) had run from 1663 to 1673 — it was winding down as Jean Baptiste was being born in Guignes in 1674. But young
Catholic Frenchmen were still actively recruited to emigrate, offered land grants, passage assistance, and the promise of
opportunity in a new world. Between approximately 1691 and 1698 — when Jean Baptiste was between 17 and 24 years old —
he made the crossing. The North Atlantic voyage in the late 17th century was a formidable undertaking. Ships left from ports
like La Rochelle, Rochefort, or Bordeaux, sailed southwest to catch the trade winds, and then arced northwest across the
Atlantic before threading through the Gulf of St. Lawrence and up the river to Québec. The crossing took between six and
twelve weeks depending on weather, and the conditions aboard the merchant and emigrant vessels of the era were brutal:
cramped quarters, salt fish and ship's biscuit for food, no privacy, and ever-present danger from the storms of the North
Atlantic. Men fell ill. Some died before they ever saw the Canadian shore. Jean Baptiste Lecompte survived the crossing.
Sometime between 1691 and 1698, he arrived in Québec City — the fortified capital of New France, perched on its
spectacular cliff above the Saint Lawrence River, anchored by Champlain's old settlement in the lower town and the growing
upper town with its government buildings, convents, and the great church of Notre-Dame de Québec. Marie-Madeleine Judith
Willey: The English Name in French Quebec On 29 September 1698, Jean Baptiste Lecompte married Marie-Madeleine Judith
Willey at Québec City. She was born in 1676 — approximately his own age — and she bore a surname that rings strikingly out
of place in the French Catholic city of Québec: Willey. This is an unmistakably English surname. The Mystery of Marie-
Madeleine Judith Willey An English surname in French Catholic Québec in 1698 demands explanation. Three possibilities are
most historically plausible: 1. English Captive: The late 17th century saw repeated conflicts between French and English
colonies in North America. French and Abenaki raiding parties frequently attacked English settlements in New England —
Deerfield (1704), Haverhill, and dozens of smaller communities — taking captives who were brought to New France, often
converted to Catholicism, and frequently integrated into French Canadian families through marriage. A "Willey" taken in a
1680s or 1690s raid on an English New England settlement, baptized Catholic in Quebec, would bear an English surname but
be completely integrated into French Canadian life. 2. English Trader's Daughter: English merchants occasionally worked in
the mixed-culture fur trade zones around Québec and the Great Lakes. A Protestant English trader who had married a French
woman, or whose daughter had converted and joined the Catholic community, could produce a Marie-Madeleine Willey. 3.
Surname Corruption: A French Canadian surname may have been anglicized or phonetically transcribed as "Willey" by a clerk
unfamiliar with the original. However, no obvious French source name for "Willey" comes readily to mind. For future
researchers: The captive theory deserves particular investigation. The New England captives taken to New France are
welldocumented, and several databases exist for tracking their identities. Searching the captive records for a "Willey" family in
the 1680s–1690s New England raids could resolve this mystery. Whatever Marie-Madeleine Judith Willey's origins, she was
Jean Baptiste's wife, and she bore him four children in the first years of their marriage: Jeanne Therese (born 2 September
1699), Marie Jeanne Therese (born 20 September 1699 — note the very close birthdate to her sister, perhaps indicating a twin

or a recording error), Etienne (born 23 November 1700), and Louis (born 19 May 1702). Louis died in 1707 at age five — the
first of many losses this family would endure. Marie-Madeleine herself died in 1703, just five years into the marriage. She was
27 years old. Jean Baptiste was 29. He had four children under the age of five, and no wife, in a city thousands of miles from
his French homeland. The echo of his own childhood — the motherless boy of 1683 — must have been heartbreaking.
Marguerite Hedouin dite Laforge: The Dit Name Almost immediately after Marie-Madeleine's death, Jean Baptiste married
again: on 1 May 1703 at Notre-Dame de Québec, he wed Marguerite Hedouin dite Laforge. Born in 1684, Marguerite was 19
years old to Jean Baptiste's 29. She would outlive him, dying in 1753 at age 69. The designation dite Laforge is richly
informative. In New France, the dit name (for men) or dite (for women) was a secondary surname, usually indicating a trade, a
physical characteristic, or a family origin. Laforge means "the forge" — the smithy. Marguerite's father or grandfather was
almost certainly a blacksmith, or was strongly associated with iron-working. It was a skilled trade, an honorable profession, and
the forge was the essential technological heart of any frontier settlement. The Hedouin family, with their forge surname, were
working-class Catholic Québécois — exactly the community into which Jean Baptiste Lecompte had woven himself. Jean
Baptiste Lecompte died on 29 November 1745 in Québec City — at the age of 71, an extraordinary lifespan matching his
father Simon's exceptional longevity. He had spent nearly half a century in New France, watched his children grow up in the
shadow of Notre-Dame de Québec, and presumably witnessed the birth of his grandchildren in the colony that his son Jean
B. would eventually leave for Louisiana. He was buried in the city he had called home for nearly fifty years — the motherless
boy from Guignes had built a life of substance and duration in the New World. The Drouin Collection — Québec 's Greatest
Genealogical Treasure The Drouin Collection (formally: Quebec, Canada, Vital and Church Records [Drouin Collection]
1621–1968) is the single most important genealogical resource for French Canadian ancestry. Compiled by Joseph-Aimé
Drouin beginning in the late 19th century, it represents a systematic microfilming and indexing of Catholic parish registers
throughout Québec — baptisms, marriages, and burials — covering three and a half centuries of French Canadian life. Every
baptism at Notre-Dame de Québec, every marriage registered in the colony's hundreds of parishes, every burial entry — all
are represented in this collection. It is because of the Drouin Collection that we can confirm Jean Baptiste Lecompte's 1698
marriage to MarieMadeleine Judith Willey with certainty, document his children's baptisms, and trace the second marriage to
Marguerite Hedouin dite Laforge in 1703. The companion Tanguay Collection (compiled by Abbé Cyprien Tanguay in his
monumental Dictionnaire généalogique des familles canadiennes, 1608–1890) cross-references the Drouin records with family
linkages, making it possible to trace multi-generational French Canadian lines with confidence rarely achievable in European
genealogy of the same era. Access: Both collections are available through Ancestry.com and the FamilySearch genealogy
database. ✦ ✦ ✦ C h a p t e r T h r e e The Louisiana Migration Jean B. Lecompte (1703–1746) and the Joanes Connection

ACAD A 1718 map of Louisiana and the course of the Mississippi River — the vast French colonial territory that connected
Québec to the Gulf Coast through the great interior waterway. Jean B. Lecompte made this journey sometime in the early 18th
century, traveling the same river corridor shown here, from New France south to Louisiana. (Photo: MPI/Getty Images) How
does a man born in Québec City, the son of a French immigrant and an English-named woman in the Catholic heart of New
France, end up in Louisiana? The question is simpler than it might appear — because in the French colonial world, Québec
and Louisiana were not separate countries. They were the two anchors of a single imperial system, connected by the world's
greatest river. The French colonial network in North America functioned like a vast river highway. Fur traders — the legendary
voyageurs and coureurs des bois — paddled their canoes from Québec south through the Great Lakes, portaged to the Illinois
River, and descended to the Mississippi, which carried them all the way to the Gulf of Mexico. Soldiers were posted between

the great forts of the system: Fort Frontenac on Lake Ontario, Fort Niagara, Fort de Chartres in Illinois, Fort Rosalie at
Natchez, Fort Condé at Mobile, and the capital of French Louisiana at New Orleans. Missionaries traveled the same routes.
Settlers followed the soldiers and missionaries. The French colonial world was, in modern terms, a single interconnected
civilization stretching from the mouth of the St. Lawrence to the mouth of the Mississippi. Jean B. Lecompte — son of Jean
Baptiste and Marie-Madeleine, born approximately 1703 in Québec City — made this journey sometime before his son
Nicolas was born around 1740. He may have been a fur trader who went south and stayed. He may have been a soldier posted
to Louisiana. He may have followed a network of family or community connections southward. Whatever the precise
circumstances, he arrived in Louisiana's French Acadian community and married there. The Joanes Family: A Name That
Does Not Belong Jean B. Lecompte's wife was Françoise Johannes (Joanes), born 1713, daughter of Philibert Joanes (1681–
1756) and Claudine Joanes (1670–1731). And like his own father's marriage to Marie-Madeleine Judith Willey, this marriage
carried an intriguing anomaly: the surname Joanes/Johannes is not French. Johannes is the German (and Dutch/Flemish)
form of John — the Latin Joannes, the French Jean. A family named Johannes or Joanes in Louisiana's French Acadian
community is most likely of German, Dutch, or Flemish origin — immigrants who had come to Louisiana through the
German Coast, the stretch of the Mississippi River north of New Orleans settled by Germanspeaking immigrants from the
1720s onward under French colonial recruitment. By the 1730s and 1740s, the French and German immigrant communities of
Louisiana had begun to intermarry, and German surnames were being rapidly Frenchified — Heinrich became Henri, Müller
became Miller or Meunier, and Johannes, in the French-speaking Catholic community, would naturally contract to Joanes or
even Jean. Philibert Joanes (1681–1756) and Claudine Joanes (1670–1731) had arrived in Louisiana and built a life there well
before their daughter Françoise was born in 1713. Whether they came directly from Germany, from Alsace (the borderland
region that was both French and German), or from the Flemish regions of what is now Belgium, they had been absorbed into
the French Catholic community of Louisiana by the time their daughter married Jean B. Lecompte. The Melançon
Connection: Acadian Blood Enters the Line The family network around Jean B. Lecompte and Françoise Joanes includes a
name of great significance: Marguerite Melançon (1701–1761). The Melançon surname is one of the founding families of
Acadia — the original French settlement on the Atlantic coast of what is now Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince
Edward Island. The Melançon family is documented in Acadian censuses from the very beginning of the 17th century, tracing
to the original Port-Royal settlement of 1604–1605. Her presence in the family network around the Lecompte-Joanes
household is strong evidence that by the 1730s–1740s, this family had been fully integrated into the Louisiana Acadian
community — the community of deportees, exiles, and survivors who had been building their lives in the great triangle
between Québec, Louisiana, and the Atlantic coast for over a century. The Acadian Family Network in Your Family Tree The
following families appear in the extended family network around Jean B. Lecompte and Nicolas M. Leconte — all confirmed

community that maintained its identity through two centuries of catastrophe. Jean B. Lecompte died in 1746 — at
approximately 43 years of age — when his son Nicolas was barely 6 years old. The terrible pattern repeated: as Jean Baptiste
had lost his mothers at age 8 in Guignes in 1683, as Lecompte men through history seemed fated to face early loss, young
Nicolas M. Leconte grew up without his father. Françoise Joanes, who would live until 1778, raised her son in the Louisiana
Acadian community that would soon be shattered by one of the greatest forced migrations in North American history. ✦ ✦

✦ P a r t T h r e e Le Grand Dérangement The Great Upheaval — 1755 and Its Aftermath C h a p t e r F o u r The Great
Upheaval 1755 and the Acadian Deportation — The World Your Ancestors Lost To understand the world your Louisiana
ancestors inhabited — and the catastrophe that defined it — you must first understand what Acadia was, and what happened
to it. What Was Acadia? Acadia (l'Acadie) was the name of the original French settlement on the Atlantic coast of North
America — the territory that encompasses modern Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, as well as
portions of what is now the state of Maine. The French first settled at Port-Royal on the Nova Scotia coast in 1604 — sixteen
years before the English Pilgrims landed at Plymouth Rock. By the mid-17th century, a distinct and deeply rooted French-
speaking Catholic culture had taken hold on the Atlantic coast: the Acadians. The Acadians were farmers, fishermen, and
hunters who had been living in Acadia for five or six generations by the time the catastrophe came. They had developed
sophisticated aboiteau systems — tidal dike networks that reclaimed the salt marshes of the Bay of Fundy for agriculture —
and had built thriving communities of several thousand people. Their surnames were the founding names of a culture:
LeBlanc, Landry, Melanson, Babin, Theriot, Boudrot, Hébert, Breau, Thibodeau, Guérin, Broussard — all of these names
appear in the earliest Acadian censuses, and most of them appear, centuries later, in the family network of your LeCompte
ancestors. The Acadians occupied an unenviable political position from the early 18th century onward. The Treaty of Utrecht
in 1713 transferred Acadia (renamed "Nova Scotia" by the British) from France to Britain — but it left the Acadians in place, a
French-speaking Catholic population living under British Protestant governance. For four decades, the Acadians maintained a
precarious neutrality, refusing to swear unconditional oaths of loyalty to the British Crown (which would have required them,
among other things, to take up arms against France and against their own relatives in Québec and Louisiana). They called
themselves "les Neutres" — the Neutrals — and tried to live peaceably between two empires. The Decision to Destroy a
People By the 1750s, with the Seven Years' War (known in North America as the French and Indian War) beginning to gather
momentum, the British authorities in Nova Scotia decided that the Acadian "Neutrals" represented an unacceptable security
risk. On 28 July 1755, British Governor Charles Lawrence issued a secret order — without any declaration from London,
without any due process, without any warning to the Acadian population — to deport the entire Acadian people from their
homeland. A contemporary illustration depicting the expulsion of the Acadians from Halifax in 1755 — Le Grand
Dérangement, The Great Upheaval. The British rounded up Acadian families at their churches, separated husbands from wives
and children from parents, loaded them onto overcrowded ships, and scattered them across the Atlantic world. (Illustration:
Getty Images) The mechanics of the deportation were systematically cruel. Acadian men were summoned to their local
churches for announcements of supposed importance. Once gathered, they were told they were prisoners of the Crown and
that their lands, livestock, and property were forfeit. They were held under guard while soldiers went to their farms to round
up their families. Husbands were separated from wives, parents from children, deliberately — the British authorities
understood that keeping families together would maintain community cohesion and resistance. The goal was to scatter the
Acadian people so thoroughly across the British colonial world that they could never reconstitute their community. Ships were
loaded beyond capacity, often with standing room only. Families were put on different vessels. Some men watched the ships
carrying their wives and children sail away, not knowing where they were going. Acadians were dispersed to British colonies
from Massachusetts to Georgia, to England, to the Caribbean, and eventually, through a long and harrowing diaspora, some
made their way to France, and from France — thirty years later — back to Louisiana. The Babin Family: Grand Pré to
Southampton Prison The family network of your LeCompte ancestors included the Babin family — and the Babin story is
among the most heartbreaking documented in this lineage. Simon Babin (1735–1780), who appears in your family tree as a
connected family, was deported from Grand Pré, Nova Scotia — the most famous of the Acadian deportation sites — in
1755. He and his family were sent first to Boston, Massachusetts. The treatment of Acadians sent to Massachusetts was, by
many historical accounts, among the worst of the entire deportation. The Puritan Protestant communities of New England
had no sympathy for French Catholic deportees and actively worked to disperse and exploit them. Many arrived without
adequate clothing or shoes. The Massachusetts authorities separated families further, indenturing Acadian children as servants.

The Bostonians — acting under British imperial authority — had effectively stolen everything the Acadians owned: their
farms, their livestock, their tools, their savings, the centuries of labor that had gone into those remarkable aboiteau marshland
farms. From Boston, Simon Babin and his family were transported to England — and then interned in a prison camp in
Southampton. They were there for years, living on minimal rations, confined in appalling conditions, while the British
government debated what to do with the Acadian population it had so casually destroyed. "Marie Babin was born on
September 30, 1760 — in a Southampton, England prison camp — because the British Crown had taken everything her family
had ever built and left them with nothing but each other." Marie Babin — who would eventually sail on Le Bon Papa to
Louisiana and become part of the family network connected to your LeCompte ancestors — was born in that Southampton
prison camp on 30 September 1760. Her mother was Anastasie Theriot Babin, her father was Simon Babin. Both Anastasie
and her mother Marguerite Theriot died in the Southampton prison camp. When the Acadians were finally released from
imprisonment in England in 1763, after the Treaty of Paris ended the Seven Years' War, Marie Babin left with her father Simon
and her grandfather Jean Babin — without her mother, without her grandmother, without a home to return to. The Guérin
Family: Six Children, Four Dead Crossing the Atlantic Of all the individual stories of Le Grand Dérangement that orbit this
family's history, the story of the Guérin family may be the most devastating. The Guérin family — connected to your family's
Acadian community network — suffered losses that defy the imagination. Dominique Guérin, born approximately 1721 at
Cobeguit, Nova Scotia, was the son of Jérôme Guérin and Isabelle Aucoin. He had married Anne LeBlanc (daughter of
Jacques à François LeBlanc and Catherine Landry) around 1746 and built a life on Île Royale (Cape Breton Island) with their
growing family. By 1752, they had three daughters. By the time the deportation came, they had six children. Dominique, Anne,
and their six children — Anne-Josèphe (approximately 12 years old), Nastay (Anastasie, approximately 10), Marguerite
(approximately 8), Joseph (approximately 6), François le jeune (approximately 3), and infant Marie (born October 1758) —
were loaded onto one of the deportation ships crossing the Atlantic to France. It was late 1758 or early 1759, the middle of
the Seven Years' War, and the North Atlantic was winter-cold and stormwracked. Four of the six Guérin children did not
survive the crossing. Anastasie, approximately 10 years old, died at sea. Little François, approximately 3, died at sea. Only
Marguerite, 8, and Joseph, 6, made it to the harbor at St.-Malo. Then, in the hospital at St.-Malo where the survivors were
taken for care, two more children died: Anne-Josèphe, the eldest daughter, died. And infant Marie died. Of six children who
had boarded that ship with Dominique and Anne Guérin, only two — Marguerite and Joseph — were left standing in France.
The Five Ships — And the Duke William The transport fleet that crossed from Louisbourg, Cape Breton Island, in late
November 1758 — carrying Acadian deportees including the Guérin family — was known informally as the Five Ships. It
carried hundreds of Acadian prisoners across the winter North Atlantic to France. Among the fleet: • The Duke William: This
transport ship sank in a storm off the southwest coast of England in mid-December 1758 — a total loss. Everyone aboard,
Acadians and crew alike, perished. Historians estimate between 300 and 400 people died in this single sinking, making it one of
the greatest losses of life in the entire Acadian deportation. • The Duc Guillaume: This vessel survived a mid-ocean
emergency and limped into St.-Malo, France, severely damaged, with its surviving passengers in desperate condition. The
families who had the misfortune of boarding the Duke William did not survive to tell their story. Those who arrived at St.-
Malo faced a foreign country, a language that was their own but a culture that did not recognize them, and a government that
had no real plan for what to do with thousands of homeless, destitute, traumatized exiles. Your ancestor Nicolas M. Leconte
(born c. 1740) would have been approximately fifteen years old in 1755 when the Great Deportation began sweeping through
the Acadian communities. Old enough to understand. Old enough to remember everything. Old enough to be terrified.
Whether Nicolas himself was directly caught up in the deportation, or whether his Louisiana community was insulated from
the worst of the initial expulsion (Louisiana Acadians were somewhat more protected by distance from the British military's
reach), the events of 1755 shook the entire Acadian world — and Nicholas would have heard, through the tight-knit network
of Acadian families, the stories of what was happening to their people in Nova Scotia. ✦ ✦ ✦ C h a p t e r F i v e Exile and
Return Dominique Guérin and the Survivors — The Road to Louisiana The walled port city of Saint-Malo, Brittany, France

— the harbor where Acadian deportation ships arrived from North America in the late 1750s. Dominique Guérin and the
surviving children arrived here after crossing the winter North Atlantic, carrying the grief of four children who had died on
the voyage. Engraved by R. Wallis, c. 1700–1800. (Photo: Archive Photos/Getty Images) The story of Dominique Guérin's
survival — and the twenty-five-year odyssey that eventually brought him and what remained of his family to Louisiana — is
one of the most thoroughly documented individual family narratives from Le Grand Dérangement, and it is part of the
network of families directly connected to your LeCompte ancestors through the Le Bon Papa voyage of 1785. Arrival in
France: The Survivors Dominique Guérin and his wife Anne LeBlanc arrived in St.-Malo, France, with their two surviving
children: Marguerite (approximately 8 years old) and Joseph (approximately 6). The four others were gone. The loss was total
and immediate — there was no time to grieve, no safe place to grieve, in a hospital ward in a foreign city. They were Acadians
in France — theoretically French by culture and language, but strangers in a country that had not been home to their family
for a century and a half. The French government did not quite know what to do with them. From St.-Malo, Dominique moved
his family to the Breton coastal communities. He settled in Ploubalay and then Trigavou, villages near Dinan in the Côtes-
d'Armor department — very close, remarkably, to Quévert, where your ancestor Simon Vincent Lecompte had been buried in
1731. The Acadian exile community in Brittany was real, documented, and connected. In Brittany, Dominique and Anne had
four more daughters: Isabelle (October 1760), Françoise (May 1763), another Anastasie — named for the daughter lost at sea
— (February 1766, who died at 18 months old), and Brigide (August 1769). Anne LeBlanc Guérin died in Nantes, at the parish
of St.-Jacques, in May 1782. She was 56 years old. She had survived the deportation, the winter crossing, the loss of four
children, twenty years of French exile, and a failed agricultural colonization experiment. She had built a new family in Brittany,
watched her surviving children marry, and helped hold the community together through two decades of hardship. And then
she died — in Nantes, on the Loire River, far from everything she had ever called home. The Poitou Disaster In 1773, the
French government made an offer to the Acadian exiles: land grants in the Poitou region of central France, to establish
farming communities. It seemed like an opportunity. Dominique Guérin joined the Poitou colonization experiment, moving
his family inland to the farming country of western France, leaving the Atlantic coast behind. The experiment was a failure.
The land grants were inadequate, the support was insufficient, and the Acadian community — accustomed to the specific
agriculture and fishing life of the Atlantic coast — struggled to adapt to the central French farmland. By March 1776, the
Poitou Acadians were retreating to Nantes on the Loire, living on 3 centimes per day in government assistance. Three centimes
a day. After twenty years in France. After everything they had survived. Louisiana at Last — 1785 The opportunity for final
return came in 1785. The Spanish Crown, which had governed Louisiana since 1762, offered to pay for the transportation of
Acadian exiles from France to Louisiana — providing ships, provisions, and land grants in the new territory. For aging
Dominique Guérin — now in his early 60s, his wife dead, his children scattered — this was the last and final chance to go
home. Not to Acadia, which was forever lost. But to Louisiana, where the Acadian community had been rebuilding for
decades, where the language and the faith and the culture survived. Dominique joined the Louisiana emigration of 1785 with
his daughters Isabelle and Brigide — the two unmarried daughters who remained with him. Both daughters married into
Louisiana Acadian families upon arrival: Isabelle into the Landry family, Brigide into the Thibodeau family — both founding
Acadian surnames, the same names that appear in the Acadian census records of 1671, the same names that recur throughout
the family network of your LeCompte ancestors. Dominique Guérin's story — from Cobeguit, Nova Scotia, to the
deportation ships, to the hospital in St.-Malo, to the Breton villages, to the failed Poitou colonization, to Nantes on three cents
a day, to Louisiana at last in his 60s — is the story of Le Grand Dérangement in its fullest human dimension. He did not give
up. He could not give up. The Acadian people, as a whole, did not give up. That is why the culture survived. "After thirty years
of exile — of prison camps, of winter crossings, of dead children, of failed colonies, of government charity at three cents a
day — the Acadians finally came home to Louisiana. They had built it once, from wilderness. They would build it again." ✦ ✦

May 1785, on the quays of Nantes, on the south bank of the Loire River. One hundred and fifty-six men, women, and
children — some who had been born in this exile, some who were old enough to remember what they had lost — were
loading their meager belongings onto a 280-ton merchant vessel called Le Bon Papa: The Good Father. It was an evocative
name. These were people who had been waiting for a good father — a benevolent authority — to restore what had been taken
from them for thirty years. The Spanish Crown, in a characteristic act of pragmatic Catholic solidarity, had agreed to fund the
Acadian return to Louisiana. Louisiana was Spanish territory since 1762 — but it remained a French-speaking Catholic
community, and the Spanish governors recognized that settling productive, hardworking, Catholic French-speaking farmers on
the Louisiana lands would strengthen the colony against both American expansion to the north and British competition to the
east. The Spanish king was not being purely charitable. But for the Acadians, the motive hardly mattered. They were going
home. Family Number 29: The Stievens-Babin Household Among the 156 souls who boarded Le Bon Papa on that May
morning was a family whose story connects directly to the Acadian network of your LeCompte ancestors: the Stievens family,

approximately 7 years based on birth record of 30 Sep 1760; she was approximately 24–25 at departure. Louis William

ships, which would have made him invaluable on the Le Bon Papa crossing. Marie Babin was the daughter of Simon Babin and

mother had not. She had grown up in the French exile community, specifically in the village of Hermitage on a hilltop in
Nantes, where her father Simon Babin had settled in the parish of Chantenay nearby. Marie and Louis married in France in
1775 — she was approximately 15, he was approximately 26. In the exile community, such marriages were common: you
married within your community, you married early, and you built the family that would carry on. They had three children by
the time Le Bon Papa sailed: Louis (age 3), Marie (age 2), and the unnamed unbaptized infant. And Marie's brother François
Babin, a sailor like his brother-in-law Louis, sailed with them — two sailors and an Acadian girl and three small children,
crossing the Atlantic to a Louisiana they had never seen but that their blood remembered. Family Connection: The Heuze
Household on Le Bon Papa The Heuze family that appears in your family tree — Pierre I. Heuze (1723– 1783) and Cecile
Bourg (1736–1797) — is confirmed on the Le Bon Papa manifest. Pierre himself had died in 1783, just two years before the

from the confirmed family tree. The manifest lists Ignace HEUZE as the deceased husband — this may reflect a name

the Atlantic with five of her children on a 280-ton ship, to start over in Louisiana. She had been born in 1736. She had
survived the deportation era, the exile, the loss of her husband. And she was getting on a ship with her children and going to
build something new in Louisiana. She would die there in 1797, at age 61 — having made it. Having done it. Eighty Days at
Sea The crossing took eighty days. On a 280-ton ship carrying 156 people plus crew, in the summer heat of the Atlantic
crossing, eighty days was a long time. There was not enough space. There was not enough food. The water went stale. Children
cried. Old men and women struggled with the heat. One child died at sea — a death recorded in the manifest, a small tragedy
folded into the larger hope of the voyage. Louis and François, as confirmed sailors, likely worked the ship during the crossing
— helping manage the rigging, the sails, the pumps. This may have been part of the arrangement for their passage. A sailor's
family was worth keeping on a ship when the sailor himself was working. It gave Louis a purpose and perhaps a sense of
control in a situation where most passengers had none. On 29 July 1785, after eighty days, the mouth of the Mississippi came
into view. The delta — flat, green, stretching to the horizon, smelling of salt marsh and river mud and the wet heat of the
Louisiana summer. New Orleans. The city that had been French, then Spanish, and that remained unmistakably, defiantly,
French in its culture, its faith, its food, and its language. They had made it. Settlement at St. Gabriel / Manchac After
approximately a month of recuperation in New Orleans, the Le Bon Papa families joined the expedition north along the
Mississippi to the settlement area designated for them: St. Gabriel and the Manchac district, in the area that is now Iberville
Parish, Louisiana — just south of Baton Rouge, along the great river. Thirty-seven of the thirty-eight surviving family
groupings chose this settlement. One family chose Bayou Lafourche — the long, meandering bayou that flows south from the
Mississippi through the heart of what would become Cajun country. The St. Gabriel/Manchac settlement was not empty land.
Acadian communities had already been building there for years. The Le Bon Papa arrivals were joining an existing French
Catholic world, reinforcing it with new blood and new families. The Stievens-Babin family, the Heuze family, the Guérins, the
Landrys, the LeBlancs — they found their people already there. They found French spoken in the streets, Catholic mass in the
churches, aboiteau-inspired farming on the river bottomlands. They found home. "After thirty years of prison camps, winter
crossings, failed colonization attempts, and government charity at three centimes a day — the Acadians arrived in Louisiana
and found their language still spoken, their faith still practiced, their culture still breathing. They had not been destroyed. They
had been scattered. And they came back together." Other Founding Families on Le Bon Papa Among the families who sailed
on Le Bon Papa alongside the StievensBabin and Heuze households, the following surnames represent the core Acadian
founding families — most appearing in Acadian census records from as early as 1671: • Landry — One of the most prolific
founding Acadian surnames, from the original Port-Royal settlement • LeBlanc — Another foundational Acadian family; name
means "the white one" • Doiron — A founding Acadian family from the Port-Royal area • Aucoin — Founding Acadian
surname; Isabelle Aucoin was the mother of Dominique Guérin's father Jérôme • Boudrot — An ancient Acadian name
dating to the first generation of Port-Royal settlers • Dugas — Founding Acadian family; name well-documented in
17thcentury Acadian censuses • LeJeune — "The young one" — a French colonial surname found throughout the Acadian
diaspora • Hébert — One of the oldest Acadian surnames, among the first families at Port-Royal in 1604 • Broussard — A
prominent Acadian family; the Broussard family produced the resistance leader Joseph "Beausoleil" Broussard who fought the
British deportation The Broussard family connection is particularly significant: Jean Charles Broussard, son on the manifest,
would later marry Anne Sophie Nanette Stievens — daughter of Louis and Marie Babin Stievens — weaving the family
network tighter still. ✦ ✦ ✦ P a r t F i v e Bayou Country Le Pays du Bayou — The Land of the Bayou C h a p t e r S e v e n

in a bayou, Schriever, Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana — June 1940. This was the world of the LeCompte/Leconte family on
Bayou Little Caillou a century earlier: a waterway community built on fishing, trapping, and subsistence farming in the cypress
swamp country of south Louisiana. (Photo: Marion Post Wolcott for the Farm Security Administration / GHI/Universal

Images Group via Getty Images) Old-growth bald cypress trees draped in Spanish moss in the Louisiana bayou country — the
landscape that defined the world of the LeCompte family for generations before the northward migration to Ohio. This is the
environment that shaped Sylvestre and Madeleine, and through them, every generation after. (Photo: Jon G. Fuller/VW
Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) The land records of Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, tell a story in the most
mundane possible language — the dry prose of legal conveyances, boundary descriptions, and notarized transactions. But read
carefully, those records reveal an entire community: the LeCompte/Leconte/Compte family living and working and trading
land on Bayou Little Caillou in the 1830s and 1840s, embedded in a neighborhood of Acadian-descended families whose
surnames have echoed through this book since the first pages. Bayou Little Caillou: The World of the Leconte Family Bayou
Little Caillou — Petit Caillou in French — is a meandering waterway in Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, flowing south from the
town of Houma (then known as Thibodauxville) toward the Gulf of Mexico. "About 24 miles below Thibodauxville" — as
Delfin Leconte's land record describes the location — places these land parcels deep in the bayou country, in a world of
cypress swamp, live oak, Spanish moss, and tidal marsh that was unlike anything in Picardie or Québec or even the Mississippi
River bottomlands. Life on Bayou Little Caillou in the 1830s and 1840s was built on the water. The bayou was the road —
pirogue canoes (dugout or plank-built flatbottomed boats perfectly adapted to shallow water) were the primary transportation.
Families fished the bayou for catfish, bass, and gar; trapped fur-bearing animals (muskrat, nutria, beaver, otter) whose pelts
were traded in Houma or New Orleans; and farmed the narrow strips of higher ground along the bayou banks. Cypress
logging was becoming a significant industry — the old-growth cypress forests of the Louisiana swamps produced enormous,
rot-resistant timber that commanded high prices throughout the Gulf Coast building industry. The land-measurement system
in use in these records is revealing. Lands are described in arpents — a French colonial measurement of approximately 192
feet (about 58.5 meters) — not in the American acres and rods system. Louisiana had been American since 1803 and a state
since 1812, but in 1835, these communities were still measuring land in the old French colonial system. The French language,
French law (the Napoleonic Code governing Louisiana's legal system to this day), and French measurement — all survived the
American acquisition. These were Acadians who had simply kept their world intact. The Leconte Land Transactions

variant spelling of LeCompte). These are almost certainly related individuals — probably siblings or first cousins — living in
the same waterway community on Bayou Little Caillou. The most electrifying detail in these records is the Babin connection.
When Modeste Leconte (then wife of Chresustin Martin) engaged in a land exchange on January 8, 1835, the land she was
dealing with had been "acquired from widow Francois BABIN." And when Francois Compte sold his land on Bayou Little
Caillou in July 1842, the boundary was the land of "Francois BABIN Jr." The Babin family — the same Babin family from
Grand Pré, from the Southampton prison camp, from Le Bon Papa — were immediate neighbors of the LeCompte family on
Bayou Little Caillou. This is not coincidence. In the tight-knit Acadian community of Terrebonne Parish, the same families
who had traveled together on deportation ships, who had survived exile together, who had sailed back on Le Bon Papa
together, settled together and lived next to each other, generation after generation. The Pelegrin Network Laurent Pelegrin
appears as a witness and principal party in at least eight recorded transactions on Bayou Little Caillou between 1835 and 1847.

He and his wife Eulalie Lasingne were major landowners in the community — with property at Section 47, Township 18,
Range 18 — and the Pelegrin family boundary markers appear repeatedly surrounding the Leconte land parcels. Adolphe
Pelegrin, Fortune Pelegrin, and Joseph Pelegrin also appear in the records, indicating a large, established Pelegrin family firmly
rooted in the same bayou community. The Pelegrin family name is not a classic Acadian founding surname, but it was present
in Louisiana's French Catholic community from at least the early 19th century. The proximity of the Pelegrin and Leconte
lands — they surround each other as boundary markers — almost certainly indicates a family connection through marriage: a
Leconte daughter who married a Pelegrin, or a Pelegrin son who married into the Leconte family, in the generation before
these 1835 records begin. The names bouncing through these Terrebonne Parish records — Landry, Savoie, Guidry,
Robichaux, Broussard, Bergeron, Chaville, Duplanti — are all Acadian founding surnames, the same names documented in the
original Port-Royal settlement, the same names on the Le Bon Papa manifest, the same names in the Acadian census of 1671.
In 1835, on Bayou Little Caillou in Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana, an Acadian community was still an Acadian community —
230 years after the first settlement of Port-Royal, 80 years after the deportation, 50 years after the return on Le Bon Papa.
They had kept their world. ✦ ✦ ✦ P a r t S i x The Great Northward Migration From the Bayous of Louisiana to the Banks

War era and the Civil War era, whose names appear in no record yet recovered for this family line. The Terrebonne Parish

Breaux Blood: Three Centuries of Acadian Founding Stock What we know with certainty is this: Sylvestre R. LeCompte, born
1868 in Louisiana, married Madeleine C. Breaux, born 1873 in Louisiana. And the Breaux surname is among the original
founding families of Acadia. The Breaux (also Bray, Brau, Breau in variant spellings) family appears in Acadian census records
from 1671 — the earliest comprehensive census of the Acadian settlements at Port-Royal, Nova Scotia. They were there at the
beginning, in 1604. They survived the deportation. They returned. The Breaux family is documented in Louisiana Acadian
communities from at least the late 18th century. When Madeleine Breaux married Sylvestre LeCompte, she was bringing to the
union a lineage of Acadian blood as old and as pure as any in Louisiana. Your grandmother Lena Rae LeCompte carried
Madeleine Breaux's blood. Which means she carried blood that had been at Port-Royal in 1604, that had built the aboiteau
dikes of the Bay of Fundy, that had been deported in 1755, that had survived prison camps and winter crossings and thirty
years of exile, that had come home on Le Bon Papa in 1785, that had fished the bayous of Terrebonne Parish, and that had
finally, in the early 20th century, crossed the Ohio River and planted itself in the American heartland. That blood ran in the

educator who stood in Ohio classrooms for 42 years. It runs in Robert Kevin Goble. It runs in Zachary and Shane. Louisiana
to Ohio: The Great Northward Journey Sylvestre and Madeleine made the journey from Louisiana to Ohio sometime in the
late 19th or very early 20th century. The precise date and route are not yet documented, but the context is clear: the post-
Reconstruction era (1877 onward) saw significant migration of Southern families — both Black and white — northward to
industrial employment. Ohio was a magnet for this migration, particularly the southern Ohio cities along the Ohio River:
Portsmouth, Ironton, Gallipolis, Huntington (just across the river in West Virginia), and the smaller communities clustered
between them. New Boston, in Scioto County, sat on the north bank of the Ohio River just west of Portsmouth — the county
seat and largest city in the area. New Boston was defined by the river: by its commerce, by its flooding, by its industrial
economy built on river transport, ore processing, and the steel and iron industries that were transforming southern Ohio in the
decades around 1900. Portsmouth was home to shoe factories (the Selby Shoe Company was a major employer) and steel mills
(including the facility that would eventually become Detroit Steel Corporation — the same company Sylvestre's grandson
Oscar "Frenchie" Raymond would work for decades later). Imagine the journey: from the cypress swamps and French-
language Catholic community of Louisiana bayou country, to the industrial river towns of southern Ohio. The Ohio River was
familiar — a river was a river, the defining geography of both worlds. But everything else was different. The language (English,
not French Acadian), the religion (still Catholic, but now a minority faith in Protestant Ohio), the weather (Ohio winters were
nothing like Louisiana winters), the landscape (Ohio hills and river bluffs, not flat bayou wetlands). Sylvestre and Madeleine
made this crossing and built a life in New Boston that would root the family in Ohio for the next century. 1941: They Left
Together Sylvestre R. LeCompte died in 1941. Madeleine C. Breaux LeCompte died in 1941. The same year. After a lifetime of
having arrived together in Ohio, built a home together, raised a family together — they left together. Whether one died shortly
after the other from grief, or whether they succumbed to the same illness, or whether their deaths were separated by more
months than the annual record captures — we do not yet know. But the symmetry is haunting. These were two people from
Louisiana who had come to Ohio together and shared everything that followed. In 1941, as the United States was entering
World War II and the world was convulsing with a violence that would have been familiar to their Acadian ancestors, Sylvestre
and Madeleine LeCompte departed the world they had built, within the same calendar year. ✦ ✦ ✦ C h a p t e r N i n e

continued, somehow, forward. Joseph Raising Raymond Joseph Edward LeCompte raised his youngest son Oscar Raymond in

the 1920s in New Boston, Ohio, as a single father. The 1920s in New Boston would have been shaped by the same forces
shaping all of southern Ohio's river communities: the residual trauma of World War I, the brief prosperity of the Roaring

nickname acknowledges everything: the French surname carried three centuries from Picardie through Québec to Louisiana
and finally to Ohio, the exotic syllables of "LeCompte" in a world of Smiths and Millers and Joneses, and perhaps a quality in
the man himself — something in his manner or his bearing — that marked him as different, as carrying something older and
stranger than the Ohio River valley had produced on its own. The name was not an insult. In small-town America, a good
nickname is a term of affection, a mark of distinction, a way the community holds a person in its identity. Raymond was
"Frenchie" because he was known, because he was liked, because the LeCompte name meant something even in Ohio — even
four generations removed from the Louisiana bayous, even six generations removed from the Québec church where Jean
Baptiste married MarieMadeleine Judith Willey in 1698. A 1920s Childhood: Motherless in New Boston Raymond's mother
Carman E. Moore died in 1921 when he was approximately six years old. His childhood unfolded in the New Boston of the
1920s and 1930s — Depression-era Ohio, the Ohio River as both backdrop and boundary, his father Joseph raising him in a
household that had known loss from its earliest days. New Boston in the 1920s was a working-class river town: men worked in
the steel mills, the shoe factories across the river, the river trade itself. The Ohio River that ran along the southern edge of the

community was simultaneously the town's economic artery and its periodic scourge. The river flooded. It flooded badly. The
communities along the Ohio lived in a complicated relationship with the water — dependent on it, shaped by it, occasionally
devastated by it. The worst came in January and February of 1937 — the year before Raymond's daughter Lena Rae was born.
The Ohio River Flood of 1937 was the greatest flood in the river's recorded history. The Ohio crested at record levels all the
way from Pittsburgh to Cairo, Illinois, inundating communities from Louisville to Cincinnati to Portsmouth. New Boston
flooded. Harrisonville Street, where the family lived according to the 1940 census, was in the flat river-bottom terrain that went
under when the Ohio rose. The community spent weeks pumping out, repairing, rebuilding. And on 2 July 1937 — just a few
months after the floodwaters receded — Lena Rae LeCompte was born. Detroit Steel and the Lodge Oscar Raymond F.
LeCompte worked for Detroit Steel Corporation — the steel company that, in various corporate incarnations, was one of the
dominant employers of the Scioto County area's industrial workforce. Steel was the backbone of mid-century Ohio's
economy. The mills ran around the clock. Men worked shifts — days, afternoons, midnights — in the heat and noise of a
steel-producing facility, doing the work that built America's postwar world. But Raymond was more than a steelworker. He was
a Master Mason — a member of Western Sun Lodge No. 91 in New Boston, having achieved the third degree of
Freemasonry, the highest rank in the symbolic degrees of the Masonic craft. What It Meant to Be a Master Mason — Western
Sun Lodge No . 91 Freemasonry in mid-20th century America was not a secret society so much as a brotherhood of civic-
minded men committed to mutual aid, moral improvement, and community service. In a small Ohio River town like New
Boston, the Masonic Lodge was one of the most important social institutions: a place where men from different economic
backgrounds met as equals, worked through the fraternity's ritual degrees together, and committed to supporting one another
in times of need. To become a Master Mason (the Third Degree) required: • Years of study of Masonic ritual, history, and
philosophy • Demonstrated moral standing in the community — you had to be vouched for, and you could be blackballed by
any current member • Successful passage through the Entered Apprentice (First Degree) and Fellow Craft (Second Degree)
ceremonies • The Master Mason ritual itself, which dramatizes themes of death and resurrection drawn from the legend of
Hiram Abiff, the architect of Solomon's Temple For Raymond to have achieved the Master Mason degree tells us something
important: he was a man his community respected. He was known for his integrity. He took his commitments seriously. He
was not simply an industrial worker who came home and watched television — he was an active participant in his community's
civic and fraternal life. The French Catholic Lecompte lineage and the Protestant-rooted Masonic fraternity made for an
interesting combination — but by the mid-20th century, American Freemasonry had long since transcended its Protestant
origins, and Catholic men were members of many lodges. Raymond's membership suggests he was a bridge figure: carrying

Not Your Ancestors This chapter exists because the surname LeCompte is uncommon enough to seem distinctive, but
common enough in 17th–18th century France to have produced multiple unrelated families. The Maryland Moses LeCompte
line has appeared in various genealogical databases associated with the LeCompte name, and because of how family tree
software can automatically connect same-surname individuals across time and geography, it has occasionally been suggested as
a connection to this family. It is not. The Maryland LeCompte Line: Who They Actually Were The Moses LeCompte line of
Dorchester County, Maryland descends from Antoine LeCompte, born approximately 1620 in Calais, France — on the
northern coast of France, on the English Channel. Antoine LeCompte was a French Huguenot Protestant — a Calvinist
Reformed Christian, not a Catholic. He emigrated to the English colonies of North America, specifically to Maryland's
Eastern Shore on the Chesapeake Bay, and established himself there in the mid-17th century. The Maryland LeCompte family
became fully English-speaking, fully Protestant, and fully integrated into the English colonial world of the Chesapeake. They
produced a remarkable dynasty: a succession of prominent men, including several who bore the nickname the "Blind
Patriarchs" due to a hereditary tendency toward vision loss. The family became significant landowners in Dorchester County,
with a plantation called Taylor's Island. In the 20th century, the artist Rowan LeCompte — a member of this Maryland family
— designed the magnificent Space Window at Washington National Cathedral, one of the most visually striking stained-glass
works in America, containing a fragment of actual lunar rock from the Apollo 11 mission. This is a fascinating, historically
significant American family. They deserve their own heritage volume. But they are not your family. Why the Confusion Arises

that would have appeared independently in multiple French communities, both Catholic and Huguenot, across the 17th
century. Two families with the same surname, originating in different parts of France, practicing different faiths, and
immigrating to entirely different parts of the New World, have no necessary genealogical connection — and in this case, no
connection has been established. The Maryland LeCompte family represents a parallel line — a French surname in America
that happened to develop along completely different cultural, religious, and geographic lines from your family. Rowan
